(3) The complexity and granularity of the firm’s stress testing must take into account the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s credit portfolio. The firm must carry out stress testing at a sufficiently granular level to be adequately sensitive to the risk characteristics of different types of exposures. (4) The scenarios used for stress testing must include severe but plausible adverse conditions. (5) The firm must consider the results of stress testing in its overall limit-setting and monitoring process. QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.2.33 Controls over credit risk
doc_path: BANK Subdivision 4.2.B.4 Ensuring adequate controls over credit risk
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must establish a system of independent, regular reviews of the firm’s credit risk management processes and practices. The results of a review must be communicated directly to the firm’s governing body and senior management.
(2) The firm must ensure that the credit origination, credit assessment and approval function is properly managed and that credit exposures are within levels consistent with the firm’s limits. The firm must establish and enforce internal controls and other practices to ensure that overrides, waivers or exceptions to policies, processes and limits are reported in a timely manner to the appropriate level of management for action.
(3) The firm must have an appropriate system for early remedial action on problem exposures, managing problem exposures and similar workout situations. The firm’s collections systems must bring together a borrower’s arrears profile and must be able to be scaled to manage high volumes in a time of stress.
(4) The firm must have an effective workout programme for problem exposures, and the workout function must be separate from the function that originated the exposures. The firm must have an effective strategy and appropriate organisational resources and personnel to manage problem exposures.
(5) The firm must have prudent policies and processes that assist the firm to recover as much of an exposure as is reasonably possible within the requirements established by applicable law and also having regard to community expectations as to how borrowers are to be treated. The firm must consider the risk to its reputation in such circumstances.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.2.34 Classification of exposures and provisions
doc_path: BANK Subdivision 4.2.B.4 Ensuring adequate controls over credit risk
BANK 4.2.34 Classification of exposures and provisions
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must have prudent policies and processes to classify its credit risk exposures for prudential reporting purposes and to establish appropriate and robust provisioning levels. The system must take into account exposures both on and off the firm’s balance sheet.
(2) The firm must classify its credit risk exposures as performing or non-performing, and must have adequate documentation to support its classification of exposures and its provisioning levels. The firm must also classify its exposures when payments are past-due for a minimum number of days (for example, 30, 60 and 90 days).
(3) The firm must regularly review its exposures at individual or portfolio level to ensure that exposures are appropriately classified, appropriate provisioning levels are set and appropriate write-offs are applied.
(4) The firm must have sound policies and processes to ensure that provisions and write-offs are timely and reflect realistic expectations as to repayment and recovery, taking into account market and macroeconomic conditions.
(5) The firm’s governing body must obtain timely and appropriate information on the condition of the firm’s credit portfolio, including the classification of exposures as performing and non-performing and the level of provisions. The information must include:
(a) the results of the latest credit risk review process;
(b) comparative trends in the overall quality of exposures; and
(c) measurements of:
(i) deterioration or expected deterioration in asset quality; and
(ii) expected credit losses.
(6) The firm must ensure that valuation, classification and provisioning for material non-performing exposures are done on an individual exposure basis.
(7) The firm must regularly assess any trends and concentrations in risk and risk build-up in relation to credit exposures, and must take into account any observed concentration in the risk mitigation strategies adopted and the potential effect on the efficacy of the mitigant in reducing loss. The firm must consider the adequacy of provisions in the light of that assessment.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.2.35 Regulatory Authority may set supervisory limits
doc_path: BANK Subdivision 4.2.B.4 Ensuring adequate controls over credit risk
BANK 4.2.35 Regulatory Authority may set supervisory limits
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If the Regulatory Authority considers that a banking business firm is taking excessive credit risk relative to its financial or operational capacity to manage or absorb that risk, the Authority:
(a) may set limits on particular exposures or categories of exposures that the firm may hold (including limits on growth or limits on the share of the firm's portfolio); or
(b) may direct the firm to cease a particular type of lending or credit activity.
(2) If the Authority considers that there is an excessive level of, or excessive growth in, higher-risk lending or credit activity, the Authority may set limits, by notice published on an approved website, on particular types of lending, the share of lending, or the growth rate of lending, for all banking business firms or a specified class of banking business firms.
(3) In considering whether there is an excessive level of, or excessive growth in, higher-risk lending or credit activity, the Authority will take into account any easing of credit standards and practices and the proportion of banking business firms’ higher-risk lending, including whether the lending is high-leverage, high-LTV-ratio or interest-only.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.2.36 Directions about adequacy of credit risk management and provisions
doc_path: BANK Subdivision 4.2.B.4 Ensuring adequate controls over credit risk
BANK 4.2.36 Directions about adequacy of credit risk management and provisions
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
If the Regulatory Authority considers that a banking business firm’s policies, processes and practices across its credit risk activities do not meet the requirements of this Division, or that the firm’s credit risk management is otherwise deficient, the Authority may direct the firm:

(a) to amend its credit risk management policies, processes, and practices;
(b) to adopt appropriate credit risk management policies, processes and practices;
(c) to increase its levels of provisions or write-offs; or
(d) to increase its regulatory capital.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.2.37 Direction about independent review etc
doc_path: BANK Subdivision 4.2.B.4 Ensuring adequate controls over credit risk
BANK 4.2.37 Direction about independent review etc
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) The Regulatory Authority may direct a banking business firm to appoint an independent person to review the firm’s credit risk management (including the firm’s provisioning practices) or a particular aspect of it, and report to the Authority. The Authority may direct the firm to carry out such a review without first consulting the firm.
(2) The Authority may set the terms of the review and may direct the firm to meet the cost of it.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK Division 4.2.C Guidance
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
Collateral can include guarantees, insurance arrangements and, importantly, security held over various forms of assets. This Division applies to all forms of collateral, including all types of assets taken as security.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.2.38 Identification and documentation of collateral
doc_path: BANK 4.2.38 Identification and documentation of collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must ensure that an asset that is to be taken as security is accurately identified and documented.
(2) The firm must ensure that the relevant legal requirements are met to maintain and enforce the firm’s security position. The firm must confirm that:
(a) the borrower has, or will have when the exposure is extended, clear title to the asset;
(b) the characteristics of the collateral are as they have been represented; and
(c) if appropriate, an asset serving as collateral is appropriately insured at the time of origination and the insurance is maintained under the contractual terms of the exposure.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.2.39 Valuation of collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must obtain a valuation of the security for an exposure:
(a) before the loan is drawn down; and
(b) if appropriate, on a continuing basis.
(2) If the fair value of a security is based on observable market prices, the firm’s policies and processes must have regard to:
(a) when observable market prices would be used;
(b) the basis for selecting the market prices to be used;
(c) the effect of market liquidity on the pricing of assets and the timing of their disposal; and
(d) the costs of accessing and disposing of assets held as collateral.
(3) In determining the fair value of a security, a banking business firm may use a valuation by a suitably qualified internal appraiser or by an external valuer, or an alternative valuation method. The firm’s policies and processes covering the fair value of a security must address the circumstances in which such valuations would be sought.
(4) If the firm uses valuations from internal appraisers, it must have policies and processes that address:
(a) when valuations should be provided by internal appraisers to remove the potential for real or perceived conflicts of interests that might affect the valuations; and
(b) the qualifications and experience required of internal appraisers.
(5) If the firm relies on external expertise for security valuations, it must establish robust selection and review mechanisms. Factors that must be considered in the selection process include:
(a) the professional qualifications to be required;
(b) relevant experience, including local knowledge;
(c) breadth of expertise to cover both standard and specialised security assessments; and
(d) appropriate professional insurance cover.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.2.40 Valuation of collateral — use of alternative methods
doc_path: BANK 4.2.40 Valuation of collateral — use of alternative methods
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If a banking business firm relies on the use of alternative valuation methods (such as desktop assessments, kerbside assessments and automated valuation methods) to produce a security valuation, it must have appropriate policies and processes that address:
(a) when valuations would be provided by the alternative method;
(b) monitoring, validation and reporting of valuation data; and
(c) asset values including adequate haircuts for conservatism when using automated valuation methods.
(2) A banking business firm that is considering the use of alternative valuation methods must thoroughly analyse any such proposal and must develop a risk management capability that includes:
(a) a hierarchy of acceptable methods of determining value that is appropriate to the level of risk;
(b) analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of the approaches or models being considered, including an understanding of the methods used, the sources of data employed and how a service provider might be able to assist in re-engineering the firm’s processes;
(c) details of any back-testing of a statistically random sample of alternative methods or auditing arrangements undertaken by a service provider;
(d) clarity of the output to be provided and how it would be integrated with the firm’s processes; and
(e) continuing monitoring of the tools used, processes that capture evidence of action taken when values are considered to be unreliable and periodic back-testing undertaken by the firm to independently validate the reliability of outcomes.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.2.41 Valuation of collateral — instructions to valuers etc
doc_path: BANK 4.2.41 Valuation of collateral — instructions to valuers etc
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm’s policies and procedures must include procedures for giving instructions for the conduct of valuations.
(2) Each valuation request must be the subject of specific instructions to the appraiser or valuer. These instructions must cover (as relevant in each case) appropriate issues such as:
(a) the purpose of the valuation;
(b) the valuation basis required;
(c) whether the valuation is for insurance purposes;
(d) the valuation method;
(e) whether a market summary or commentary is required; and
(f) the form of report that is to be provided.
(3) If a party other than the firm instructs the valuer:
(a) the valuation must be appropriately endorsed for the firm’s use; and
(b) the valuation must be confirmed by:
(i) an internal appraiser; or
(ii) an external valuer with the appropriate expertise.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.2.43 Valuation of collateral — professional standards
doc_path: BANK 4.2.43 Valuation of collateral — professional standards

If a banking business firm uses valuations to determine the fair value of collateral, the firm must require valuers and appraisers, in preparing their reports, to adopt the standards and practices of a relevant professional body. Reports must be based on the standard format advocated by a relevant professional body.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.2.44 Valuation of collateral — reliability of processes
doc_path: BANK 4.2.44 Valuation of collateral — reliability of processes
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
A banking business firm must have policies and processes directed at ensuring that the valuation processes and valuations received for collateral are reliable. There must be independent and regular internal reviews of valuations and the results of automated valuation methods by appropriate management or audit personnel and formal reviews by an independent valuer.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.2.45 Valuation of collateral — regular reassessment
doc_path: BANK 4.2.45 Valuation of collateral — regular reassessment

A banking business firm’s policies and processes must provide for regular assessment of collateral values so as to ensure that the fair value of collateral that supports provisioning and reserves, and any collateral coverage measures applied to exposures, is kept current and reliably reflects the values that the firm might realise.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.2.46 Valuation of real estate as security
doc_path: BANK 4.2.46 Valuation of real estate as security
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) For the purposes of determining the fair value of security involving real estate, a banking business firm must assume that:
(a) the relevant property is accessible in the near future;
(b) the period for marketing the property will be up to 12 months (but the firm may adopt a period of up to 24 months for a specialised or unusual property if a professional valuer advises that it would be appropriate to do so); and
(c) market conditions and asset values will not change during the marketing period.
(2) The marketing period must be treated as retrospective and must be assumed to have ended at the date of valuation, rather than taking into account any improvement in market conditions.
(3) The valuation of real estate must be based on fair values. In determining fair values, the firm must use conservative estimates in imputing future income streams, such as lease payments that are not already contracted for.
(4) The firm must ensure that the key assumptions used in the valuation approach are appropriate and that there is sufficient evidence to support them. The firm must review the assumptions and must be satisfied that they are reasonable before the valuation is done.
(5) In determining fair values, a valuation that is based on highest and best use rather than existing use must be adequately supported and documented. If applicable, the valuation report must set out how highest and best use was determined.
(6) In circumstances in which it is difficult to determine the fair value of a property that has not yet achieved a stable income, or that is experiencing fluctuations in income, a forecast of expected cash flows must be used to estimate the value of the property.
(7) The discount rates used in calculating the value of security must reflect the opportunity cost of holding the property, determined by way of comparison with prevailing returns on competing investments, and assuming a long-term holding. Capitalisation rates must reflect expectations about the long-term rate of return that investors require under normal, orderly and sustainable market conditions.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.2.47 Valuation of security in other forms
doc_path: BANK 4.2.47 Valuation of security in other forms
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) For collateral in the form of a security interest over assets other than real estate, a banking business firm must ensure that all relevant security is properly scrutinised.
(2) If a third party supplies information about a security interest held by the firm (for example, outstanding debtors), asset values must be objectively assessed to ensure that security coverage is adequate. The assessment may include testing the information supplied.
(3) In determining the fair value of security not in the form of real estate, the firm must also take into account market liquidity, legal costs, impediments to realisation and prior charges.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.3.1 Meaning of ECRA
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
In these rules:

ECRA (or external credit rating agency) means any of the following:

(a) Standard and Poor’s;
(b) Moody’s Investors Service;
(c) Fitch Ratings;
(d) a rating agency that is affiliated with an agency mentioned in paragraph (a), (b) or (c);
(e) Capital Intelligence Ratings Limited;
(f) any other agency approved by the Regulatory Authority.

(b) the Code of Conduct Fundamentals for Credit Rating Agencies published by the International Organization of Securities Commissions in March 2015.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.3.3 Meaning of rating etc for Chapter 4
doc_path: BANK 4.3.3 Meaning of rating etc for Chapter 4
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) In this Chapter:
rating means a rating issued by an ECRA.
Guidance
For this Chapter, an instrument or counterparty is rated only if an ECRA has issued a rating of it. If no ECRA has issued a rating of an instrument or a counterparty, the instrument or counterparty is unrated.
(2) A rating is a solicited rating if the rating was requested and paid for by the issuer of the rated instrument, the rated counterparty or another entity in the same corporate group as the issuer or counterparty. Any other rating is an unsolicited rating.
Note Unsolicited ratings are not to be used without the Regulatory Authority’s consent — see rule 4.3.5.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.3.4 Using ratings
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must use ratings consistently and in accordance with these rules and its credit risk management policy.
(2) The firm must ensure that a rating of an instrument takes into account the total amount of the relevant exposure (that is, the principal and any interest due).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.3.5 Only solicited ratings to be used
doc_path: BANK 4.3.5 Only solicited ratings to be used
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Subject to subrule (2), a banking business firm must use only a solicited rating in determining risk weights for the firm’s exposures.
(2) A banking business firm may use an unsolicited rating with the written approval of the Regulatory Authority or in accordance with a direction by the Authority. The Authority may give a written direction setting out conditions that must be satisfied before the firm may use an unsolicited rating.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

(2) A banking business firm may use an unsolicited rating with the written approval of the Regulatory Authority or in accordance with a direction by the Authority. The Authority may give a written direction setting out conditions that must be satisfied before the firm may use an unsolicited rating. Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.3.6 Multiple ratings for same exposure etc
doc_path: BANK 4.3.6 Multiple ratings for same exposure etc
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If there is only 1 rating for a particular exposure, that rating must be used to assign a risk weight to the exposure.
(2) If there are 2 ratings and the ratings map to different risk weights, the higher risk-weight must be applied.
(3) If there are 3 or more ratings for an exposure, and those ratings map to different risk weights, only the ratings that map to the 2 lowest risk weights may be taken into account, and:
(a) the higher of those 2 risk weights must be applied; or
(b) if both ratings map to the same risk weight, that risk weight must be applied.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.3.7 Choosing between issuer ratings and issue ratings
doc_path: BANK 4.3.7 Choosing between issuer ratings and issue ratings
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If an issue to which a banking business firm is exposed has an issue-specific rating, the firm must use that rating to assign a risk weight to the exposure.
(2) For an exposure to an issue that does not have an issue-specific rating, the firm must assign a risk weight to it as set out in subrules (3) to (5).
(3) If an issuer has a specific rating for an issue, but the firm’s exposure to the issuer is not to that issue, the firm may assign to its exposure a risk weight lower than that for an unrated exposure only if the firm’s claim on the issuer ranks equally with, or is senior to, the rated issue. Otherwise the firm must treat the exposure as unrated.
(4) If the firm’s exposure is to an unrated issue by the issuer and:
(a) either the issuer, or another issue by it, has a low-quality rating (that is, a rating that would map into a risk weight equal to or higher than that for an unrated exposure); and
(b) the issue to which the firm is exposed ranks equally with, or is junior to, either a senior unsecured claim on the issuer or the issue with a low-quality rating;
the firm must assign the same risk weight to the unrated exposure as it would to the issue with the low-quality rating.
Guidance
If the issuer has an issuer rating, that rating typically applies to senior unsecured claims on that issuer. Consequently, only senior claims on that issuer benefit from a high-quality issuer rating. Other unassessed exposures of a highly rated issuer are treated as unrated.
(5) If an issuer has a specific high-quality rating (that is, a rating that would map to a lower risk weight) that applies only to a limited class of its liabilities (such as a deposit assessment or a counterparty risk assessment), the firm may use that rating only for exposures to the issuer that fall within that class.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.3.8 Ratings within financial group
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
A banking business firm must not use a rating for 1 entity in a financial group to assign a risk weight to an unrated entity in the group.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.3.8 Guidance
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.3.9 Using foreign currency and domestic currency ratings of similar exposures to same counterparty
doc_path: BANK 4.3.9 Using foreign currency and domestic currency ratings of similar exposures to same counterparty
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If a banking business firm proposes to assign a risk weight to an unrated exposure based on the rating of a rated (but otherwise similar) exposure to the same counterparty, it may do so if either of the following paragraphs is true:
(a) the rating is a domestic-currency rating and the rated exposure is denominated in the counterparty’s domestic currency;
(b) the rating is a foreign-currency rating and the rated exposure is denominated in a foreign currency.
(2) Subrule (3) applies to an exposure that arises through a banking business firm’s participation in a loan that has been extended, or has been guaranteed against convertibility and transfer risk, by an MDB, if an exposure to the MDB is to be assigned a risk weight of 0% under rule 4.4.16.
(3) For an exposure to which this subrule applies, the borrower’s domestic currency rating may be used to assign a risk weight to the exposure instead of its foreign currency rating. In the case of a guarantee against convertibility and transfer risk, the local currency rating may be used only for the part that has been guaranteed, and the remainder that does not benefit from the guarantee must be assigned a risk-weight based on the borrower’s foreign currency rating.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.3.10 Using short-term ratings
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm may use a short-term rating to assign a risk weight only to a short-term bank exposure or short-term corporate exposure.
(2) For risk weighting purposes, a banking business firm must treat a short-term rating as being issue-specific. The firm may use a short-term rating to assign a risk weight only to an exposure arising from the rated facility, and must not apply it to any other short-term exposure.
(3) A banking business firm must not use a short-term rating to assign a risk weight to an unrated long-term exposure.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.1 What Part 4.4 does — calculation of risk-weighted assets for credit risk
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK 4.4.1 What Part 4.4 does — calculation of risk-weighted assets for credit risk
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This Part sets out how a banking business firm must calculate its risk-weighted assets for credit risk.
Guidance
1 A banking business firm’s credit risk capital requirement is the sum of:
• its risk-weighted assets for credit risk, as calculated in accordance with this Part (but subject to any capital relief that is available under Part 4.5)
• its risk-weighted assets for securitisation exposures in the banking book (see Divisions 4.6.E, 4.6.F and 4.6.G).
2 For how to calculate the firm’s credit risk capital requirement, see rule 4.1.4. The following components of the credit risk capital requirement are calculated in accordance with this Part:
• RWA for exposures in the banking book (except those mentioned in the next point)
• RWA for the risk posed by unsettled transactions and failed trades, in both the banking book and the trading book.
3 The firm’s RWA for counterparty credit risk for exposures in both the banking book and the trading book also forms part of its credit risk capital requirement. This is dealt with in Part 4.6A.
4 The sum of a banking business firm’s risk-weighted assets for credit risk, used for calculating its credit risk capital requirement, is not the same as its total risk-weighted assets (see rule 3.2.1), which is used for calculating the firm’s capital adequacy ratios under Chapter 3.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2015-3 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.3 Risk weights to be assigned
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK 4.4.3 Risk weights to be assigned
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must assign risk weights to on-balance-sheet exposures and off-balance-sheet items. This Part sets out how to do so.
Guidance
Risk weights are broadly aligned with the likelihood of the counterparty’s default. If an exposure or item is rated (see rule 4.3.3), the risk weight to be assigned is determined in accordance with the rating; otherwise, the risk weight is determined directly by this Part (but in both cases subject to the outcome of due diligence by the firm (see rules 4.2.25, 4.2.26 and 4.2.27).
(2) The firm must assign the risk weight set out in, or determined in accordance with, this Part to a claim or asset, subject to:
(a) the outcome of the credit assessment required by rules 4.2.25, 4.2.26 and 4.2.27; and
(b) its assessment of the exposure, as required by rule 4.4.4.
(3) Under this Part, risk weights must be assigned to exposures of a particular kind at specified levels (for example, in the case of rated bank exposures (other than certain short-term exposures), the risk weights that can be assigned are 20%, 30%, 50%, 100% and 150%, according to the rating of the counterparty (see rule 4.4.18)). If this Part specifies a set of such levels in relation to a kind of exposure, only risk weights in the set may be assigned to such an exposure.
Guidance
Subrule (3) would prevent a banking business firm from assigning an intermediate risk weight (say 60%) to a rated bank exposure.
(4) For the purpose of assigning risk-weights, interest is treated as suspended on a non-performing exposure.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-2 (as from 1st January 2015).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.content_text: (1) A banking business firm must assign risk weights to on-balance-sheet exposures and off-balance-sheet items. This Part sets out how to do so. Guidance Risk weights are broadly aligned with the likelihood of the counterparty’s default. If an exposure or item is rated (see rule 4.3.3 ), the risk weight to be assigned is determined in accordance with the rating; otherwise, the risk weight is determined directly by this Part (but in both cases subject to the outcome of due diligence by the firm (see rules 4.2.25 , 4.2.26 and 4.2.27 ). (2) The firm must assign the risk weight set out in, or determined in accordance with, this Part to a claim or asset, subject to: (a) the outcome of the credit assessment required by rules 4.2.25 , 4.2.26 and 4.2.27 ; and (b) its assessment of the exposure, as required by rule 4.4.4 . (3) Under this Part, risk weights must be assigned to exposures of a particular kind at specified levels (for example, in the case of rated bank exposures (other than certain short-term exposures), the risk weights that can be assigned are 20%, 30%, 50%, 100% and 150%, according to the rating of the counterparty (see rule 4.4.18 )). If this Part specifies a set of such levels in relation to a kind of exposure, only risk weights in the set may be assigned to such an exposure. Guidance Subrule (3) would prevent a banking business firm from assigning an intermediate risk weight (say 60%) to a rated bank exposure. (4) For the purpose of assigning risk-weights, interest is treated as suspended on a non-performing exposure. Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-2 (as from 1st January 2015). Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.4 Requirement to decide whether risk weight appropriate
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK 4.4.4 Requirement to decide whether risk weight appropriate
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must assess every exposure (whether rated or unrated) to decide whether the risk weight to be assigned to it under this Part is appropriate. The firm’s decision must be based on the exposure’s inherent risk.
(2) If there are reasonable grounds to believe that the inherent risk of an exposure is significantly higher than that implied by the risk weight to be assigned to it under this Part, the firm must consider the higher risk (and assign a higher risk weight) for the purpose of calculating its credit risk capital requirement.
(3) In particular, the firm must use the results of due diligence carried out on the counterparty to decide whether a risk weight that is solely based on a rating would be appropriate and prudent. If the results show that the exposure poses greater risk than is implied by the rating, the firm must assign a higher risk weight to the exposure than the risk weight that would be assigned on the basis of the rating.
Note For the risk weights that can be assigned, see rule 4.4.3 (3).
(4) However, due diligence analysis must never result in the application of a lower risk weight than that determined by the rating.
(5) For an exposure to an entity that is part of a corporate group, the firm must, as far as possible, carry out due diligence at the level of the entity to which there is an exposure. However, in evaluating the entity’s repayment capacity, the firm must take into account the support of the group and the possibility that the support would be adversely affected by problems in the group.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2015-3 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.6 Regulatory Authority can direct firms as to risk weights and impose requirements
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK 4.4.6 Regulatory Authority can direct firms as to risk weights and impose requirements
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Despite anything in these rules, the Regulatory Authority may direct a banking business firm as to the risk weight to be assigned to a particular exposure if the Authority considers that the firm has assigned an inappropriate risk weight to the exposure. The direction must be in writing.
(2) The Authority may also impose specific capital requirements or limits on significant exposures, including any exposure that, in the Authority’s opinion, has not been adequately transferred or mitigated.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.7 Risk weight multiplier for exposures with currency mismatch
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK 4.4.7 Risk weight multiplier for exposures with currency mismatch
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to an exposure if:

(a) the exposure and the counterparty’s income are denominated in different currencies; and
(b) the counterparty does not have a sufficient natural or financial hedge against the resulting foreign exchange risk.
Guidance
A counterparty has a natural hedge if the borrower normally receives foreign currency income (such as remittances, rental incomes, or salaries) in the currency of the relevant loan. A financial hedge generally includes a contract with a financial institution.
(2) This rule applies to all exposures referred to in subrule (1) regardless of whether the exposure is to an individual, a corporate body or a sovereign.
(3) The exposure must be assigned a risk weight 1.5 times the risk weight that would otherwise be assigned under this Part, subject to a maximum risk weight of 150%.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.9 Types of exposures by counterparty
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.1 General concepts and definitions
BANK 4.4.9 Types of exposures by counterparty
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) For this Division, an exposure on a banking business firm’s balance sheet may be classified as of one of the following types:

(a) a sovereign exposure (see subrule (2));
(b) a PSE exposure (see subrule (3));
(c) an MDB exposure (see subrule (4));
(d) a bank exposure (see subrule (5));
(e) a corporate exposure (see subrule (6)).

(2) A sovereign exposure is a claim on a counterparty that is:

(a) a national government (or the government of a body politic that is part of a nation, such as a State or Province);
(b) a national central bank; or
(c) a body whose obligations are implicitly or explicitly guaranteed by a national government or the government of a part of a nation.
(3) A PSE exposure is a claim on a counterparty that is a PSE.
(4) An MDB exposure is a claim on a counterparty that is an MDB.

(5) A bank exposure is a claim on a financial institution that is licensed to take deposits and is subject to standards and a level of supervision compliant with the Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision published by the BCBS in April 2024.

Note 1 The Principles are available at: https://www.bis.org/bcbs/publ/d573.pdf.
Note 2 Some exposures to securities firms may be treated as bank exposures — see rule 4.4.17 (3).
(6) A corporate exposure is a claim that is not a sovereign exposure, a PSE exposure, an MDB exposure, a bank exposure nor a retail exposure.
(7) For this Division, a retail exposure is an exposure that would qualify for inclusion in the regulatory retail portfolio under the criteria in CRE20.65 in the Basel III framework.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.14 Risk weights — PSE exposures
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm may assign a risk weight of 0% to an exposure to a non-commercial PSE in Qatar that is denominated in Qatari riyals.
Guidance — deciding whether a PSE is commercial
1 The following examples outline how PSEs might be categorised when focusing on one specific feature, namely revenue-raising powers. However, there may be other ways of determining the different treatments applicable to different types of PSEs; for instance, by focusing on the extent of guarantees provided by the central government.
2 A claim on a regional government or local authority could qualify for the same treatment as a claim on its sovereign or central government if the government or authority has revenue-raising powers and institutional arrangements the effect of which is to reduce its risk of default.
3 A claim on an administrative body that is responsible to a central government, regional government or local authority, or on another non-commercial undertaking owned by a government or local authority, may not warrant the same treatment as a claim on the sovereign if the body does not have revenue-raising powers or other arrangements as described. If strict lending rules apply to such a body or a declaration of bankruptcy is not possible because of its special public status, it may be appropriate to treat the body as a PSE.
4 A commercial undertaking owned by a central government, regional government or local authority may be treated as a normal commercial enterprise. In particular, if such an undertaking functions as a corporate in competitive markets even though the central government, a regional authority or a local authority is the major shareholder, the undertaking should be treated as a corporate and exposures to it should be assigned risk weights accordingly.
(2) The firm must assign a risk weight to any other PSE exposure in accordance with table 4.4.14.
Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.

Table 4.4.14 Risk weights for PSE exposures

Rating of relevant sovereign Risk weight (%)
AAA to AA- 20
A+ to A- 50
BBB+ to BBB- 50
BB+ to B- 100
Below B- 150
Unrated 50
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

(1) A banking business firm may assign a risk weight of 0% to an exposure to any of the following MDBs:
(a) the African Development Bank (AfDB);
(b) the Asian Development Bank (ADB);
(c) the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank;
(d) the Caribbean Development Bank (CDB);
(e) the Council of Europe Development Bank (CEDB);
(f) the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD);
(g) the European Investment Bank (EIB);
(h) the European Investment Fund (EIF);
(i) the Inter-American Development Bank (IADB);
(j) the International Finance Facility for Immunization;
(k) the Islamic Development Bank (IDB);
(l) the Nordic Investment Bank (NIB);
(m) the World Bank Group (comprising the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA) and the International Development Association (IDA)).
(2) The firm must assign a risk weight to an exposure to any other MDB in accordance with table 4.4.16, but may assign a risk weight of 0% if the Regulatory Authority so approves.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.16 Guidance
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
The Authority will evaluate eligibility for 0% risk weight case by case. The eligibility criteria for MDBs to be risk weighted at 0% are as follows:

• very high quality long-term issuer ratings — the majority of the MDB’s external assessments must be AAA
• its shareholder structure is made up of a significant proportion of sovereigns with long-term issuer credit ratings of AA- or better, or the majority of its fund-raising is in the form of paid-in equity/capital and there is little or no leverage
• strong shareholder support demonstrated by the amount of paid-in capital contributed by the shareholders; the amount of further capital the MDB has the right to call, if required, to repay its liabilities; and continued capital contributions and new pledges from sovereign shareholders
• adequate level of capital and liquidity (a case-by-case approach is necessary in order to assess whether the MDB’s capital and liquidity are adequate)
• strict statutory lending requirements and conservative financial policies, including a structured approval process, internal creditworthiness and risk concentration limits (per country, sector, and individual exposure and credit category), approval of large exposures by the board or a committee of the board, fixed repayment schedules, effective monitoring of use of proceeds, status review process, and rigorous assessment of risk and provisioning.

Table 4.4.16 Risk weights for MDB exposures

Rating Risk weight (%)
AAA to AA- 20
A+ to A- 30
BBB+ to BBB- 50
BB+ to B- 100
Below B- 150
Unrated 50

Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.18 Risk weights — rated bank exposures
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement

BANK 4.4.18 Risk weights — rated bank exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to rated bank exposures (other than bank exposures to a specific short-term-rated facility such as a particular issue of commercial paper).
(2) A rated bank exposure must be assigned a risk weight in accordance with table 4.4.18.
(3) In table 4.4.18:
(a) Column A applies only to the following rated bank exposures:
(i) exposures that relate to trade finance activities between banks and have an original maturity of 6 months or less;
(ii) other exposures with an original maturity of 3 months or less; and
(b) Column B applies to all other rated bank exposures.
Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.
(4) For this rule, the rating must be one that makes no implicit assumption of government support for the counterparty.
(5) Despite subrule (4), a banking business firm may, with the written approval of the Regulatory Authority, use for this rule a rating of a counterparty that assumes implicit government support of the counterparty. This subrule ceases to apply at the end of 31 December 2027.

Rating of counterparty
 		 Risk weight (%)
Column A: short-term exposures Column B: other bank exposures
AAA to AA- 20 20
A+ to A- 20 30
BBB+ to BBB- 20 50
BB+ to B- 50 100
Below B- 150 150
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.19 Risk weights — rated bank exposures — specific short-term-rated facilities
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK 4.4.19 Risk weights — rated bank exposures — specific short-term-rated facilities
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Table 4.4.19 sets out risk weights that a banking business firm may assign to a bank exposure to a specific short-term-rated facility, such as a particular issue of commercial paper.

Table 4.4.19 Risk weights for bank exposures — specific short-term ratings

Rating Risk weight (%)
A-1/P-1 20
A-2/P-2 50
A-3/P-3 100
Others 150
Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.
(2) If a short-term-rated facility is assigned a 50% risk weight, the firm must not assign a risk weight lower than 100% to an unrated short-term exposure to the same issuer.
(3) If an issuer has a short-term-rated facility with an external rating that maps to a risk weight of 150%, the firm must assign a risk weight of 150% to any unrated exposure to the same issuer, whether long-term or short-term, unless the firm uses a CRM technique for such exposures.
(4) If there is a specific short-term rating of such an exposure, and the rating maps to a risk weight that is the same as, or lower than, the rating based on the general treatment, the short-term rating may be used for that exposure (and only for that exposure).
(5) If there is a specific short-term rating of such an exposure, and the rating maps to a risk weight that is higher than the rating based on the general treatment, the general treatment may not be applied to the exposure, and the exposure must receive the risk weight implied by the short-term rating.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.21 Grade A unrated bank exposures — criteria
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK 4.4.21 Grade A unrated bank exposures — criteria
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) An unrated bank exposure is to be classified as grade A if the bank:
(a) meets whichever is the more onerous of:
(i) the minimum regulatory requirements and capital buffers imposed by the counterparty’s national supervisor, as most recently published by the supervisor; and
(ii) the minimum regulatory requirements and capital buffers imposed by the Basel framework, as most recently published by the BCBS; and
(b) has adequate capacity to meet its financial obligations (including repayments of principal and interest) in a timely manner, throughout the projected life of the exposure, regardless of economic cycles and business conditions.
(2) For paragraph (1) (a), a requirement that is specific to the bank, and has been imposed by its supervisor as part of the bank’s supervisory review process, is not to be taken into account.
(3) If the requirements and buffers referred to in paragraph (1) (a) (i) have not been published either by the bank’s supervisor or the bank itself, the exposure must be classified as grade B or grade C.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.22 Grade B unrated bank exposures — criteria
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement

BANK 4.4.22 Grade B unrated bank exposures — criteria
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) An unrated bank exposure is to be classified as grade B if the bank:
(a) meets whichever is the more onerous of:
(i) the published minimum regulatory requirements (but not the capital buffers) imposed by the counterparty’s national supervisor; and
(ii) the minimum regulatory requirements (but not the capital buffers) imposed by the Basel framework, as most recently published by the BCBS; but
(b) is subject to substantial credit risk (for example, its repayment capacity depends on stable or favourable economic or business conditions).
(2) For paragraph (1) (a), a requirement that is specific to the bank, and has been imposed by its supervisor as part of the bank’s supervisory review process, is not to be taken into account.
(3) If the requirements referred to in paragraph (1) (a) (i) have not been published either by the bank’s supervisor or by the bank itself, the exposure must be classified as grade C.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.25 Scope of Subdivision 4.4.B.6 — general corporate exposures
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK 4.4.25 Scope of Subdivision 4.4.B.6 — general corporate exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This Subdivision is about how a banking business firm must assign risk weights to general corporate exposures that are on its balance sheet. A general corporate exposure is a corporate exposure that is not any of the following:
(a) a specialised lending exposure (see Subdivision 4.4.B.7);
(b) an exposure to subordinated debt, equity or other capital instruments (see Subdivision 4.4.B.8);
(c) an equity investment in an investment fund (see Subdivision 4.4.B.9);
(d) an exposure secured on real estate (see Subdivision 4.4.B.10);
(e) an exposure to covered bonds (see Subdivision 4.4.B.11).
(2) This Subdivision does not apply to a defaulted exposure, nor to an exposure resulting from an unsettled or failed transaction.
Note For the treatment of exposures resulting from unsettled or failed transactions and defaulted exposures, see Subdivisions 4.4.B.12 and 4.4.B.13 respectively.
(3) An exposure to a securities firm that is not treated as a bank exposure (see rule 4.4.17 (3)) must be treated as a general corporate exposure.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

(3) An exposure to a securities firm that is not treated as a bank exposure (see rule 4.4.17 (3)) must be treated as a general corporate exposure. Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.27 Using short-term ratings — general corporate exposures
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK 4.4.27 Using short-term ratings — general corporate exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm may use a short-term rating to assign a risk weight to:
(a) a general corporate exposure that arises from trade finance activities and has an original maturity of 6 months or less; or
(b) any other general corporate exposure with an original maturity of 3 months or less.
(2) Table 4.4.27 sets out the risk weights that the firm may assign to an exposure to a specific short-term facility, such as a particular issue of commercial paper.

Table 4.4.27 Risk weights for specific short-term ratings

Rating Risk weight (%)
A-1/P-1 20
A-2/P-2 50
A-3/P-3 100
Others 150
Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.
(3) If a short-term rated facility is assigned a 50% risk weight, the firm must not assign a risk weight lower than 100% to an unrated short-term exposure to the same issuer.
(4) If an issuer has a short-term facility with an external rating that warrants a risk weight of 150%, the firm must assign a risk weight of 150% to any unrated exposure to the same issuer, whether long-term or short-term, unless the firm uses a CRM technique for such exposures.
(5) If there is a specific short-term rating of such an exposure, and the rating maps to a risk weight that is the same as, or lower than, the rating based on the general treatment, the short-term rating may be used for that exposure (and only for that exposure).
(6) If there is a specific short-term rating of such an exposure, and the rating maps to a risk weight that is higher than the rating based on the general treatment, that treatment must not be applied to the exposure, and the exposure must receive the risk weight implied by the short-term rating.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement

BANK 4.4.28 Scope of Subdivision 4.4.B.7 — specialised lending exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This Subdivision is about how a banking business firm must assign risk weights to specialised lending exposures that are on its balance sheet. A specialised lending exposure is an exposure to project finance, object finance or commodities finance that:
(a) is not related to real estate; and
(b) has (in legal form or economic substance) 1 or more of the following characteristics:
(i) the relevant loan is to an entity that was created specifically to finance or operate physical assets;
(ii) that entity has few or no other material assets or activities, and therefore little or no independent capacity to repay the loan (apart from the income that it receives from those assets) so that the primary source of its repayment capacity is the income generated by those assets rather than its own independent capacity;
(iii) the terms of the loan give the lender a substantial degree of control over the assets and the income that they generate.
(2) This Subdivision does not apply to a defaulted exposure, nor to an exposure resulting from an unsettled or failed transaction.
Note For the treatment of exposures resulting from unsettled or failed transactions and defaulted exposures, see Subdivisions 4.4.B.12 and 4.4.B.13 respectively.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.29 Other definitions for Subdivision 4.4.B.7
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
In this Subdivision:

commodities finance means short-term lending to finance reserves, inventories, or receivables of exchange-traded commodities (for example, crude oil, metals or crops), where the loan will be repaid from the proceeds of the sale of the commodity and the borrower has no independent capacity to repay the loan.

object finance means lending to finance the acquisition of equipment (for example, ships, aircraft, satellites, railcars or fleets) in which the repayment of the loan is dependent on the cash flows generated by the specific assets that have been financed and pledged or assigned to the lender.

project finance means lending in which the lender looks primarily to the revenues generated by a single project both as the source of repayment and as security for the loan.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Subject to rule 4.4.31, a specialised lending exposure for which an issue-specific rating is available must be assigned a risk weight in accordance with table 4.4.30. Issuer ratings must not be used.
Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.

Table 4.4.30 Risk weights for specialised lending — issue-specific rating

Rating of counterparty Risk weight (%)
AAA to AA- 20
A+ to A- 50
BBB+ to BBB- 75
BB+ to B- 100
Below B- 150
(2) A specialised lending exposure for which no issue-specific rating is available must be assigned a risk weight as follows:
(a) an exposure to project finance while the project is in its pre-operational phase — 130%;
(b) subject to rule 4.4.31, an exposure to project finance while the project is in its operational phase — 100%;
(c) an exposure to object finance or commodities finance — 100%.
(3) For subrule (2) and rule 4.4.31, a project is in its operational phase if the entity that was specifically created to finance the project has:
(a) a positive net cash flow that is sufficient to cover any remaining contractual obligation; and
(b) declining long-term debt.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.31 Risk weights — high-quality specialised lending exposures to project finance
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK 4.4.31 Risk weights — high-quality specialised lending exposures to project finance
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm may assign a risk weight of 80% to a project finance exposure if the exposure is of high quality and the project is in its operational phase.
Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.
(2) For subrule (1), a project finance exposure is of high quality if the exposure meets all of the following conditions:
(a) the project finance entity (that is, the entity to which the firm is exposed) is able to meet its financial obligations in a timely manner, and its ability to do so is assessed to be robust against adverse changes in the economic cycle and business conditions;
(b) the entity is restricted from acting to the detriment of its creditors (for example, because it cannot issue additional debt without their consent);
(c) the entity has sufficient reserve funds or other financial arrangements to cover contingency funding and the project’s working capital requirements;
(d) the entity’s revenues are availability-based or subject to a rate-of-return regulation or take-or-pay contract;
Guidance
Availability-based revenues means that once construction is completed, the project finance entity is entitled to payments from its contractual counterparties (for example, a government), as long as contract conditions are fulfilled. Availability payments are sized to cover operating and maintenance costs, debt service costs and equity returns as the project finance entity operates the project. Availability payments are not subject to swings in demand, such as traffic levels, and are adjusted typically only for lack of performance or lack of availability of the asset to the public.
(e) the entity’s revenue depends on 1 main counterparty that is:
(i) a sovereign;
(ii) a PSE; or
(iii) a corporate entity that has a risk weight of 80% or lower;
(f) the project’s revenues are sufficient to cover the costs of operation, maintenance and debt-service, and equity returns, as the entity operates the project;
(g) the contractual provisions that govern the exposure give the firm a high degree of protection if the entity defaults;
(h) the main counterparty (or another entity that satisfies paragraph (e)) will protect creditors from the losses that would result from the termination of the project;
(i) all of the assets and contracts necessary to operate the project have been pledged to the creditors to the extent permitted by law;
(j) it will be possible for the project’s creditors to take control of the entity if it defaults.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

(1) This Subdivision is about how a banking business firm must assign risk weights to exposures to subordinated debt, equity and other capital instruments that are on its balance sheet.
(2) This Subdivision does not apply to instruments that, under Division 3.2.D, are to be deducted from the firm’s CET 1 capital.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.33 Definitions for Subdivision 4.4.B.8 — equity exposure and equity instrument
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.8 Exposures to subordinated debt, equity and other capital instruments
BANK 4.4.33 Definitions for Subdivision 4.4.B.8 — equity exposure and equity instrument
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Whether an instrument creates an equity exposure is to be determined on the basis of its economic substance.
(2) Equity exposures include both direct and indirect ownership interests (whether voting or non-voting) in the assets and income of a commercial enterprise or of a financial institution that is not consolidated or deducted. An instrument is an equity exposure if it meets all of the following requirements:
(a) it is irredeemable (that is, the return of invested funds can be achieved only by the sale of the investment or sale of the rights to the investment or by the liquidation of the issuer);
(b) it does not embody an obligation on the part of the issuer;
(c) it conveys a residual claim on the assets or income of the issuer.
Guidance
Indirect equity interests include holdings of derivative instruments tied to equity interests, and holdings in corporations, partnerships, limited liability companies or other types of enterprises that issue ownership interests and are engaged principally in the business of investing in equity instruments.
(3) An instrument of any of the following kinds is also treated as an equity instrument:
(a) an instrument with the same structure as one permitted as tier 1 capital under rules 3.2.8 to 3.2.11;
(b) an instrument that embodies an obligation on the part of the issuer but satisfies any of the following conditions:
(i) the issuer can defer settling the obligation indefinitely;
(i) the issuer can defer settling the obligation indefinitely;
(ii) the issuer is required or permitted to settle the obligation by the issue of a fixed number of the issuer’s equity shares;
(iii) if the issuer is required or permitted to settle the obligation by the issue of a variable number of the issuer’s equity shares — other things being equal, a change in the value of the obligation is attributable to, is comparable to, and is in the same direction as, a change in the value of a fixed number of the issuer’s equity shares;
(iv) subject to subrule (4), the holder can require the issuer to settle the obligation in equity shares.
Example for subparagraph (iv)
A contingent convertible bond (also called a “CoCo”).
(4) Subrule (3) (b) (iv) does not apply if, on application by the firm, the Regulatory Authority is satisfied that:
(a) in the case of a traded instrument — the instrument trades more like the issuer’s debt than its equity, or
(b) in the case of an instrument that is not traded — the instrument should be treated as a debt position.
(5) In the cases mentioned in paragraphs (4) (a) and (b), the firm may decompose the risks for regulatory purposes, with the Authority’s approval.
(6) A holding in a vehicle that is structured to convey the economic substance of equity ownership is to be treated as creating an equity exposure, including the following:
(a) a debt obligation or other security;
(b) a partnership;
(c) a derivative;
(d) a liability the return from which is linked to that of equity.
Guidance
The Regulatory Authority may decide not to require that liabilities the return from which is linked to that of equities be included if they are directly hedged by an equity holding, such that the net position does not involve material risk.
(7) However, an equity investment that is structured to convey the economic substance of a debt holding or a securitisation exposure is not to be considered as creating an equity exposure.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

BANK 4.4.34 Regulatory Authority’s power to direct treatment
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
The Regulatory Authority may, either on application by a banking business firm or on its own initiative, give a direction as to whether a particular instrument is to be treated as debt or equity.

Note The Regulatory Authority also has the power to direct that a particular instrument is to be held in a banking business firm’s trading book — see rule 3.1A.17.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.35 Risk weights — subordinated debt, equity investments and other capital instruments
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.8 Exposures to subordinated debt, equity and other capital instruments
BANK 4.4.35 Risk weights — subordinated debt, equity investments and other capital instruments
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) An exposure to subordinated debt, or a capital instrument that is not an equity investment, must be assigned a risk weight of 150%.
Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.
(2) An exposure to an equity investment must be assigned a risk weight as follows:
(a) for an equity investment to which rule 4.4.36 applies — as directed under that rule;
(b) for a speculative unlisted equity investment — 400%;
(c) for any other equity investment — 250%.
(3) For paragraph (2) (b), an exposure is to a speculative unlisted equity investment if the investment is in an unlisted company and is:
(a) held for short-term resale; or
(b) considered venture capital or an investment of a similar kind that is subject to price volatility and is acquired in the expectation of significant future capital gains.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.36 Equity instruments issued under certain national programmes
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This rule applies in relation to equity instruments issued under a law of Qatar that:

(a) provides significant subsidies for investment; and
(b) involves government oversight and restrictions that limit the risk that such an investment presents to a banking business firm.
Examples of restrictions
Limitations on:
• the size and types of businesses
• allowable amounts of ownership interests
• location.
(2) The Regulatory Authority may, either on its own initiative or on application by a banking business firm, direct that a part of the firm’s holding of a particular such instrument may be assigned a risk weight of 100% (despite rule 4.4.35).

(3) The firm may treat in that way only so much of the firm’s holding of the instrument as is no more than 10% of the firm’s total regulatory capital.

Note For the meaning of total regulatory capital, see rule 3.1.1 (2).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.37 Certain investments in commercial entities
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.8 Exposures to subordinated debt, equity and other capital instruments
BANK 4.4.37 Certain investments in commercial entities
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to an investment by a banking business firm in a commercial entity (that is, an entity that is not a banking, financial or insurance entity) if:
(a) the investment is a direct or indirect equity exposure or equity investment: and
(b) it represents more than 10% of the common shares, or other instruments that qualify as capital, of the entity.
Guidance
The operation of this rule in relation to such investments by a banking business firm depends on 2 materiality thresholds:
• for a single investment — whether or not it represents 15% or more of the firm’s total regulatory capital
• for the total of all such investments by the firm — whether or not the total of all such investments represents 60% or more of the firm’s total regulatory capital.
(2) Such an investment that represents less than 15% of the firm’s total regulatory capital must be assigned a risk weight in accordance with rule 4.4.35.
(3) If such an investment represents 15% or more of the firm’s total regulatory capital, the amount of the excess must be assigned a risk weight of 1,250%.
(4) If the total of such investments by the firm represents 60% or more of the firm’s total regulatory capital, the amount of the excess must be assigned a risk weight of 1,250%.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) The Regulatory Authority may declare, by notice published on an approved website, that a banking business firm need not take into account, for the purposes of calculating its risk-weighted assets under this Subdivision, a part of its investment in a fund to which subrule (2) applies. QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.42 Calculation of RWA for investment in fund — approaches
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.9 Equity investments in funds
BANK 4.4.42 Calculation of RWA for investment in fund — approaches
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) There are 3 approaches that may be used (separately or in combination) to calculate the RWA for a banking business firm’s investment in a fund:
(a) the look-through approach (LTA);
(b) the mandate-based approach (MBA); and
(c) the fall-back approach (FBA).
Guidance
1 The LTA assigns risk weights to the fund’s exposures as if they were held directly by the banking business firm concerned. It is the most granular and risk-sensitive approach. However, the necessary information to use it may not be available.
2 The MBA relies on information in a fund’s mandate or the law governing the fund to assign risk weights to the fund’s exposures.
3 The FBA is used only when neither of the other approaches is possible.
(2) If the fund’s RWA was calculated by the LTA or the MBA, the fund’s RWA is subject to a leverage adjustment (see rule 4.4.52) to calculate the RWA for the firm’s investment in the fund.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

However, the necessary information to use it may not be available. 2 The MBA relies on information in a fund’s mandate or the law governing the fund to assign risk weights to the fund’s exposures. 3 The FBA is used only when neither of the other approaches is possible. BANK 4.4.42 Calculation of RWA for investment in fund — approaches
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
Under the LTA or the MBA, the firm calculates the RWA for an investment in a fund by first calculating an RWA for the fund. The RWA for the firm’s investment in the fund is taken (subject to the leverage adjustment) to be the fund’s total RWA multiplied by the percentage of the fund’s total equity that the firm holds.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.44 Applying LTA
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.9 Equity investments in funds
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Under the LTA, risk weights are assigned to the exposures of the fund as if the banking business firm concerned held those exposures directly.
Guidance
Such exposures include, for example, underlying exposure arising from the fund’s derivatives activities for situations in which the underlying receives a risk weighting treatment under Part 4.6A and the associated counterparty credit risk exposure.
(2) In determining the counterparty credit risk for the fund’s exposures to derivatives, the firm must multiply the relevant exposure (calculated in accordance with Part 4.6A) by 1.5 before applying the risk weight associated with the counterparty.
(3) The firm may rely on a third party’s calculations if the conditions in rule 4.4.47 are met.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.46 Applying MBA
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.9 Equity investments in funds
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Under the MBA, the total RWA for a fund’s exposures is the sum of the following:
(a) the total RWA for exposures on the fund’s balance sheet, calculated as set out in subrule (2);
(b) the total RWA for the fund’s derivative exposures and other off-balance-sheet items, calculated as set out in subrule (3);
(c) the total RWA for the fund’s derivative exposures, calculated in accordance with Part 4.6A.
(2) For paragraph (1) (a), the calculation must assume that the fund’s underlying portfolios are invested to the greatest extent allowed under its mandate in assets that attract the highest capital requirements, and then progressively in other assets that attract lower capital requirements. If more than 1 risk weight can be assigned to an exposure, the highest risk weight applicable must be assigned.
(3) For paragraph (1) (b):
(a) in the case of an off-balance-sheet item, if the underlying would receive a risk weight under Division 4.4.C, the notional amount of the item must be assigned a risk weight accordingly; and
(b) in the case of a derivative exposure, if the underlying would receive a risk weight under Part 4.6A the notional amount of the exposure must be assigned a risk weight accordingly.
(4) The firm may rely on a third party’s calculations if the conditions in rule 4.4.47 are met.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.47 Applying LTA or MBA —using third party’s calculations
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.9 Equity investments in funds
BANK 4.4.47 Applying LTA or MBA —using third party’s calculations
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) The conditions under which a banking business firm may use a third party’s calculations of the risk weight of the firm’s investment in a fund are the following:
(a) the party that does the calculation is:
(i) if the fund invests only in securities and deposits the securities at a depository institution — the depository; or
(ii) another entity approved by the Regulatory Authority;
(b) the calculations are done in accordance with the LTA or the MBA;
(c) the firm is given complete access to the calculations and data;
(d) before the firm uses the results of such a calculation in a prudential report, the calculation is reviewed by the firm’s internal audit function;
(e) all the calculations for a year are reviewed by the firm’s external auditor as part of the firm’s annual audit.
(2) If the firm uses a third party’s calculations of the risk weight of the firm’s investment in a fund, the firm must assign, to its exposure to the fund, a risk weight 1.2 times the risk weight that the firm would have assigned if it had held the exposure directly.
(3) However, if the firm has access to the calculations, and the Regulatory Authority so requests, the firm must provide the Authority with details of the calculations. In this case, subrule (2) does not apply.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.51 Treatment of funds’ investments in other funds
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.9 Equity investments in funds
BANK 4.4.51 Treatment of funds’ investments in other funds
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If a banking business firm has an investment in a fund (fund 1) that has an investment in another fund (fund 2), and either the LTA or the MBA was used to calculate the RWA of fund 1, the risk weight to be assigned to fund 2 can be calculated by using the LTA, MBA or FBA (as the available information permits).
(2) For all subsequent layers (such as fund 2’s investment in another fund (fund 3) and so on), the risk weights applied to fund n can be calculated by using the LTA only if the LTA was used for determining the risk weight for fund (n-1). Otherwise, the FBA must be applied.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)
