BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.9 Equity investments in funds
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If a banking business firm has calculated the RWA for a fund using either the LTA or the MBA, it must apply a leverage adjustment to that RWA. The result of applying the leverage adjustment is taken as the RWA for the firm’s investment in the fund.

(2) If LTA or MBA is used to calculate the RWA for a banking business firm’s investment in a fund, the RWA for the investment is calculated by the following formula:

where:
RWAfund is the fund’s total RWA.
Total assetsfund is the fund’s total assets, according to its latest balance sheet.
Lv is:
(a) if the LTA was applied — the fund’s actual leverage (that is, the fund’s total assets divided by its equity, expressed as a percentage);
(b) if the MBA was applied — the highest rate of leverage permitted by the relevant mandate or law.
Eq is the firm’s equity in the fund (that is, the product of the fund’s total equity and the percentage of that equity that the firm holds).

(3) However, the application of a leverage adjustment to an investment in a fund is not to increase the risk weight of the investment higher than 1,250%.

Example
Consider a fund that replicates an equity index. A banking business firm holds 20% of the fund’s shares. Also, assume that:
(1) the firm uses the standardised approach (as set out in Divisions 4.4.B and 4.4.C) when calculating its capital requirements for credit risk, and it uses the standardised approach for determining counterparty credit risk exposures;
(2) the fund holds forward contracts on listed equities that are cleared through a QCCP (with a notional amount of 100); and
(3) the fund presents the following balance sheet:
Assets
Cash20
Government bonds (AAA-rated)30
VM receivable (that is, collateral posted by the firm to the CCP in respect of the forward contracts)50
Liabilities
Notes payable5
Equity
Shares, retained earnings and other reserves95

The fund’s exposures must be risk-weighted as follows:

(1) the RWA for the cash (RWAcash) is the exposure of 20 multiplied by the applicable SA risk weight of 0%. Thus, RWAcash = 0;
(2) the RWA for the government bonds (RWAbonds) is the exposure of 30 multiplied by the applicable SA risk weight of 0%. Thus, RWAbonds = 0;

(3) the RWA for the exposures to the listed equities underlying the forward contracts (RWAunderlying) is the product of the following 3 amounts:

(a) the SA credit conversion factor of 100% that is applicable to forward purchases;
(b) the exposure to the notional amount of $100;
(c) the applicable risk weight for listed equities under the SA which is 100%;
thus, RWAunderlying = 100% × 100 × 100% = 100;
(4) the forward purchase equities expose the bank to counterparty credit risk in respect of the market value of the forwards and the collateral posted that is not held by the CCP on a bankruptcy-remote basis. For the sake of simplicity, assume that the application of Part 4.6A results in an exposure value of $56. The RWA for counterparty credit risk (RWACCR) is the product of the exposure amount and the relevant risk weight for trade exposures to CCPs, which is 2% in this case (see Division 4.6A.D for the capital requirements for bank exposures to CCPs). Thus, RWACCR = $56 × 2% = $1.12. (For the sake of simplicity, this example does not include capital requirements for exposures to CCPs or the credit valuation adjustment framework.)

The total RWA of the fund is therefore $101.12 = (0 + 0 +100 + 1.12).

The leverage of a fund under the LTA is the ratio of the fund’s total assets to its total equity, which in this example is 100/95.

Therefore, the RWA for the bank’s equity investment in the fund is the product of the average risk weight of the fund, the fund’s leverage and the size of the bank’s equity investment — that is:

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
The counterparty credit risk exposure of a netting set of derivatives is calculated by multiplying the sum of the replacement cost and potential future exposure by an alpha factor set at 1.4. Whenever the replacement cost is unknown, the exposure measure for counterparty credit risk will be calculated conservatively by using the sum of the notional amounts of the derivatives in the netting set as a proxy for the replacement cost, and the multiplier used in the calculation of the potential future exposure will be equal to 1. Whenever the potential future exposure is unknown, it will be calculated as 15% of the sum of the notional values of the derivatives in the netting set. The risk weight associated with the counterparty is applied to the counterparty credit risk exposure.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

(1) This Subdivision is about how a banking business firm must assign risk weights to exposures that are secured on real estate and are on its balance sheet.
(2) This Subdivision does not apply to a defaulted exposure, nor to an exposure resulting from an unsettled or failed transaction.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.54 Definitions for Subdivision 4.4.B.10
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.10 Exposures secured on real estate
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
In this Subdivision:

commercial real estate exposure means an exposure that is secured by mortgage over real estate, but is not a residential real estate exposure.

mortgage includes any form of security interest over real estate.

residential real estate exposure means an exposure that is secured by mortgage over real estate, if the real estate:

(a) has (or will, on completion, have) the nature of 1 or more dwellings; and
(b) satisfies all the applicable laws and regulations necessary to enable it to be occupied as housing (or will, on completion, satisfy all such laws and regulations).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) The real estate exposure asset class consists of:
(a) exposures, secured by mortgage over real estate, that are qualifying real estate exposures;
(b) other exposures secured by mortgage over real estate; and
(c) land acquisition, development and construction exposures.
(2) An exposure secured by mortgage over real estate is a qualifying real estate exposure if it meets the requirements in rule 4.4.56.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.56 Prudential requirements
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.10 Exposures secured on real estate
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) The requirements referred to in rule 4.4.55 (2) (the prudential requirements) are the requirements in subrules (2) to (7).
(2) Finished property: the exposure must be secured by either:
(a) a fully completed property; or
(b) residential property under construction, or land upon which residential property will be constructed, but only if:
(i) both of the following are true:
(A) the property is a residential housing unit for 1 to 4 families, and it will be the borrower’s primary residence;
(B) the lending is not, in effect, indirectly financing land acquisition, development and construction; or
(ii) a sovereign or PSE has the legal powers and ability to ensure that the property will be finished.
(3) Legal enforceability: the security must be legally enforceable in all the relevant jurisdictions. The security agreement and the legal process supporting it would allow the firm to realise the value of the property within a reasonable period.
(4) Claims over the property: the firm must hold a first mortgage, or the first mortgage and 1 or more sequentially lower ranking mortgages, over the property (that is, if the firm holds 2 or more mortgages over the property, there is no other mortgage that is intermediate in priority between the firm’s mortgages) — but see rule 4.4.57.
(5) Ability of the borrower to repay: the borrower must meet the requirements referred to in rule 4.4.58.
(6) Prudent value of property: the property must be valued according to the criteria in rules 4.4.59 and 4.4.60 to determine the LTV ratio for the loan. The value of the property must not depend materially on the performance of the borrower.
(7) Required documentation: all the information required at loan origination and for monitoring purposes must be properly documented, including information on:
(a) the borrower’s ability to repay; and
(b) the valuation of the property.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.57 Recognition of second mortgages
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.10 Exposures secured on real estate
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
Despite rule 4.4.56 (4), where the banking business firm concerned does not hold a first mortgage over the relevant property, the Regulatory Authority may approve, as a credit risk mitigant for the purposes of this Subdivision, a second or subsequent mortgage if, under the law of the relevant jurisdiction, all of the following requirements are satisfied:

(a) a second or subsequent mortgage gives the mortgagee a claim that is legally enforceable and constitutes an effective credit risk mitigant;
(b) any mortgagee can initiate the sale of the property independently from the other mortgagees;
(c) if the sale were not carried out by public auction, a mortgagee that held a higher-priority mortgage would be obliged to take reasonable steps to obtain a fair market value (or the best price that could be obtained in the circumstances) when exercising its power of sale.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.58 Underwriting policies
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.10 Exposures secured on real estate
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must have an underwriting policy in relation to the granting of mortgage loans that requires the firm to assess a borrower’s ability to repay such a loan.
(2) The policy must define 1 or more appropriate criteria (such as the loan’s debt service coverage ratio) and must specify the relevant levels for the purpose of that assessment.
(3) The policy must be appropriate even when the repayment of the mortgage loan depends significantly on the cash flows generated by the property, and must take into account relevant measurements such as the property’s occupancy rate.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must calculate the LTV ratio for a proposed real estate loan prudently in accordance with the following requirements:
(a) the loan amount must include any outstanding loan amount and any undrawn committed amount of the loan;
(b) the loan amount must be calculated gross of any provisions and other risk mitigants (except for pledged deposit accounts with the firm that meet all the requirements for netting on the firm’s balance sheet and have been unconditionally and irrevocably pledged for the sole purpose of repaying the loan);
(c) the value must be adjusted to take into account the possibility that the current market price is significantly above the value that would be sustainable over the life of the loan.
(2) The value of the property must continue to be its value at the origination of the loan, unless the Regulatory Authority directs the firm to reduce the value. Modifications made to the property that unequivocally increase its value may be taken into account.
(3) However, the firm may reduce the property’s value if an extraordinary event permanently reduces the property’s value.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) In calculating the amount of an exposure for the purposes of this Subdivision, a banking business firm may take into account financial collateral or a guarantee as a credit risk mitigant if the guarantee or collateral qualifies as eligible collateral or an eligible guarantee (as the case may be) under Part 4.5.
Note For what qualifies as eligible collateral, see rule 4.5.12. For what qualifies as an eligible guarantee, see rule 4.5.27.
(2) The firm may also take into account mortgage indemnity insurance that meets the requirements of Part 4.5 for a guarantee (so far as possible).
(3) However, for the purpose of assigning a risk weight to an exposure, its LTV ratio must be determined without taking any CRM technique into account.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
Qualifying real estate exposures are classified according to whether repayment is dependent on cash flows generated by the property, as follows:

(a) residential exposures repayment of which is not materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property;
(b) residential exposures repayment of which is materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property;
(c) commercial exposures repayment of which is not materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property;
(d) commercial exposures repayment of which is materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property.
Note 1 For the meaning of qualifying real estate exposure, see rule 4.4.55 (2).
Note 2 For the meaning of materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property, see rule 4.4.65.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.65 Meaning of materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.10 Exposures secured on real estate
BANK 4.4.65 Meaning of materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A qualifying real estate exposure (whether residential or commercial) is materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property if the borrower’s prospects of servicing the loan materially depend on the cash flows generated by the property that secures the loan rather than on the borrower’s capacity to do so from other sources (but see subrule (2)).
Guidance
1 The primary source of the cash flows generated by the property would generally be lease or rental payments, or the sale of the property. The distinguishing characteristic of these exposures compared to other qualifying real estate exposures is that both the servicing of the loan and the prospects for recovery in the event of default depend materially on the cash flows generated by the property securing the exposure.
2 The material dependence condition set out above predominantly applies to loans to corporates or SPVs, but is not restricted to such borrowers. For example, a loan might be considered materially dependent if more than 50% of the income from the borrower used in the bank's assessment of its ability to service the loan is from cash flows generated by a residential property.
(2) The following are exceptions to the general rule in subrule (1) (that is, the following types of exposure are not treated as exposures the repayment of which is materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property that secures them):
(a) exposures secured on a property that is the borrower’s primary residence;
(b) exposures, secured on an income-producing residential housing unit, to an individual who has mortgaged fewer than 50% of the properties in the relevant development;
(c) exposures, secured on residential real estate, to an association or cooperative of individuals:
(i) that is regulated under national law; and
(ii) whose only purpose is granting its members the use of a primary residence in the property;
(d) exposures, secured on residential real estate, to a public housing company or not-for-profit association that:
(i) is regulated under national law; and
(ii) exists to serve social purposes and to offer tenants long-term housing.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.72 Risk weights — land acquisition, construction and development exposures
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.10 Exposures secured on real estate
BANK 4.4.72 Risk weights — land acquisition, construction and development exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This rule deals with land acquisition, construction and development (ACD) exposures — that is, exposures resulting from loans to companies or special purpose vehicles to finance the acquisition of land for construction and development purposes, or the construction and development of residential or commercial property.
(2) Such an exposure may be assigned a risk weight of 100% if:
(a) the real estate concerned is residential real estate;
(b) the prudential requirements in rule 4.4.56 are complied with (so far as possible) in relation to the property; and
(c) all of the following requirements are complied with:
(i) pre-sale or pre-lease contracts have been signed that amount to a significant portion of the total contracts or equity at risk;
(ii) those contracts are legally binding written contracts;
(iii) each buyer or lessee has paid a substantial cash deposit that is subject to forfeiture if the contract is terminated;
(iv) equity at risk was determined as an appropriate amount of borrower-contributed equity to the real estate’s appraised value as completed.
Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.
(3) An ACD exposure that does not fall within subrule (2) must be assigned a risk weight of 150%.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.74 Meaning of covered bond and eligible covered bond
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.11 Exposures to covered bonds
BANK 4.4.74 Meaning of covered bond and eligible covered bond
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A covered bond is a bond that is issued by a bank or mortgage institution and is subject by law to public supervision designed to protect the bond-holders.
Guidance
Proceeds from the issue of such bonds must be invested, as the law requires, in assets that, throughout the validity of the bonds, are capable of covering claims attached to the bonds and, if the issuer fails, would be used, on a priority basis, to repay the principal and pay the accrued interest.
(2) An eligible covered bond is a covered bond that satisfies subrules (3) and (4).
(3) A covered bond satisfies this subrule if:
(a) the underlying assets (the cover pool) include only assets of the following kinds:
(i) claims on, or guaranteed by, sovereigns, central banks, PSEs or MDBs;
(ii) claims secured by residential real estate in relation to which the prudential requirements in rule 4.4.56 have been complied with, and with an LTV ratio no higher than 80%;
(iii) claims secured by commercial real estate in relation to which those prudential requirements have been complied with, and with an LTV ratio no higher than 60%;
(iv) claims on, or guaranteed by, banks that qualify for a 30% or lower risk weight (but only if such claims make up no more than 15% of the bond issuance); and
(v) additional collateral of the following kinds:
(A) substitution assets (that is, cash or short-term liquid and secure assets held in substitution for the primary assets, to top up the cover pool for management purposes);
(B) derivatives entered into to hedge the risks arising in the bond programme; and
(b) at both the bonds’ issue and throughout their term, the total nominal value of the cover pool is at least 10% more than the total nominal value of outstanding bonds issued.
Guidance
The requirement that the value of the cover pool continue to exceed the total of bond issues implies that that the issuer must actively manage the cover pool, replacing non-performing assets or assets that have been subject to pre-payment with other appropriate assets.
(4) A covered bond issue satisfies this subrule if the banking business firm concerned can produce evidence to satisfy the Regulatory Authority that:
(a) the firm receives portfolio information at least on:
(i) the value of the cover pool and the outstanding covered bonds;
(ii) the geographical distribution and type of assets in the cover pool, loan size, interest rate and currency risks;
(iii) the maturity structure of the cover assets and covered bonds; and
(iv) the percentage of loans that are more than 90 days past due; and
(b) the issuer makes the information referred to in paragraph (a) available to the firm at least once every 6 months.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.content_text: (1) A covered bond is a bond that is issued by a bank or mortgage institution and is subject by law to public supervision designed to protect the bond-holders. Guidance Proceeds from the issue of such bonds must be invested, as the law requires, in assets that, throughout the validity of the bonds, are capable of covering claims attached to the bonds and, if the issuer fails, would be used, on a priority basis, to repay the principal and pay the accrued interest. (2) An eligible covered bond is a covered bond that satisfies subrules (3) and (4). (3) A covered bond satisfies this subrule if: (a) the underlying assets (the cover pool ) include only assets of the following kinds: (i) claims on, or guaranteed by, sovereigns, central banks, PSEs or MDBs; (ii) claims secured by residential real estate in relation to which the prudential requirements in rule 4.4.56 have been complied with, and with an LTV ratio no higher than 80%; (iii) claims secured by commercial real estate in relation to which those prudential requirements have been complied with, and with an LTV ratio no higher than 60%; (iv) claims on, or guaranteed by, banks that qualify for a 30% or lower risk weight (but only if such claims make up no more than 15% of the bond issuance); and (v) additional collateral of the following kinds: (A) substitution assets (that is, cash or short-term liquid and secure assets held in substitution for the primary assets, to top up the cover pool for management purposes); (B) derivatives entered into to hedge the risks arising in the bond programme; and (b) at both the bonds’ issue and throughout their term, the total nominal value of the cover pool is at least 10% more than the total nominal value of outstanding bonds issued. Guidance The requirement that the value of the cover pool continue to exceed the total of bond issues implies that that the issuer must actively manage the cover pool, replacing non-performing assets or assets that have been subject to pre-payment with other appropriate assets. (4) A covered bond issue satisfies this subrule if the banking business firm concerned can produce evidence to satisfy the Regulatory Authority that: (a) the firm receives portfolio information at least on: (i) the value of the cover pool and the outstanding covered bonds; (ii) the geographical distribution and type of assets in the cover pool, loan size, interest rate and currency risks; (iii) the maturity structure of the cover assets and covered bonds; and (iv) the percentage of loans that are more than 90 days past due; and (b) the issuer makes the information referred to in paragraph (a) available to the firm at least once every 6 months. Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

endnotes: Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

BANK 4.4.77 Unsettled or failed transactions in securities, commodities and foreign exchange — general rule
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
A banking business firm must take into account any unsettled or failed transactions in securities, commodities or foreign exchange when calculating its credit risk capital requirement, including:

(a) transactions through recognised clearing houses and central counterparties that are subject to daily marking to market and the payment of daily variation margin; and
(b) transactions that involve a mismatched trade.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.78 Unsettled or failed transactions in securities, commodities and foreign exchange — DvP transactions

BANK 4.4.78 Unsettled or failed transactions in securities, commodities and foreign exchange — DvP transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to a DvP transaction in securities, commodities or foreign exchange if, 5 days or more after the due date for settlement, the transaction has not been settled.
(2) The firm must calculate the resulting capital requirement by multiplying the positive current exposure of the transaction by the appropriate risk multiplier set out in table 4.4.78. The positive current exposure of the transaction is the difference between the transaction’s value at the agreed settlement price and at current market price.

31 to 45 75
46 or more 100
Note For the treatment of unsettled or failed off-balance-sheet transactions, see rule 4.4.91.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.79 Unsettled or failed transactions in securities, commodities and foreign exchange — non-DvP transactions
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
BANK Subdivision 4.4.B.12 Unsettled or failed transactions
BANK 4.4.79 Unsettled or failed transactions in securities, commodities and foreign exchange — non-DvP transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to a non-DvP transaction in securities, commodities or foreign exchange if the first contractual payment or delivery is made but the second contractual payment or delivery is not made by the end of the same business day.
(2) Until the end of 5 business days after the first contractual payment or delivery, the banking business firm that made the first payment or delivery must treat the resulting exposure as a loan, and must assign a risk weight to that exposure commensurate with the risk weight of the counterparty in accordance with the relevant provision of this Division.
(3) However if the exposure is not significant, the firm may assign a risk weight of 100% to it if the Regulatory Authority so approves.
(4) If the second contractual payment or delivery is not made within 5 business days after the first, the firm that made the first contractual payment or delivery must assign a risk weight of 1,250% to the sum of:
(a) the full amount of the value transferred; and
(b) the replacement cost (if any).
(5) The firm must continue to treat the transaction in accordance with subrule (4) until the second payment or delivery is made.
Note For the treatment of an unsettled or failed off-balance-sheet transaction, see rule 4.4.91.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.81 Meaning of defaulted
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
For these rules, an exposure of a banking business firm is defaulted (or is in default) if any of the following paragraphs is true of it:

(a) a material credit obligation is more than 90 days past due;
(b) in the case of an overdraft — the customer concerned has breached a notified limit or has been notified of a limit lower than the amount outstanding;
(c) a significant credit obligation has “non-accrued” status (for example, the firm no longer recognises accrued interest as income, or makes an equivalent amount of provision);
(d) the firm makes a write-off or account-specific provision as a result of a significant perceived decline in credit quality after the firm takes on credit exposure to the counterparty;
(e) the firm sells a credit obligation at a significant credit-related loss;
(f) the firm agrees to a distressed forbearance of a credit obligation;
Guidance
A distressed forbearance is a forbearance (see Division 4.7.C) that reduces a debtor’s financial obligation to a creditor because the creditor significantly forgives or postpones principal, interest or fees.
(g) another creditor of the counterparty has sought an order for the counterparty’s bankruptcy or for the counterparty to be placed in administration;
(h) the counterparty has sought an order for its bankruptcy or similar protection and the result would be to avoid or delay repayment of any of the counterparty’s credit obligations to the firm;
(i) any other situation has arisen in which the firm considers that the counterparty is unlikely to pay its credit obligations in full unless the firm takes action such as realising security.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.82 Risk weights — certain defaulted real estate exposures

BANK 4.4.82 Risk weights — certain defaulted real estate exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must assign a risk weight of 100% to a defaulted exposure that is secured on residential real estate (net of any specific provision or write-off) if the repayment of the loan does not significantly depend on cash flows generated by the property that secures it.
(2) In calculating the exposure, the firm may take into account an eligible guarantee or eligible collateral.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

BANK 4.4.83 Risk weights — other defaulted exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to a defaulted exposure to which rule 4.4.82 does not apply.
(2) A banking business firm must assign a risk weight to the unsecured or unguaranteed portion of a defaulted exposure (net of any specific provision or write-off) as follows:
(a) if specific provisions are less than 20% of the outstanding amount of the loan — 150%;
(b) if specific provisions are 20% of the outstanding amount of the loan or more — 100%.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.85 Risk weights for assets not otherwise provided for — cash and gold

BANK 4.4.85 Risk weights for assets not otherwise provided for — cash and gold
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm may assign a risk weight of 0% to:
(a) cash owned and held at the firm or in transit; and
(b) gold bullion held:
(i) at the firm; or
(ii) in another bank on an allocated basis (to the extent that the gold bullion assets are backed by gold bullion liabilities).
(2) A banking business firm may assign a risk weight of 20% to a cash item that is in the process of collection.
Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.4.90 Treatment of commitments
doc_path: BANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
BANK Division 4.4.C Standardised approach — off-balance-sheet items
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) For this Division, a commitment is an arrangement that has been offered by a banking business firm, and accepted by an obligor, to extend credit, purchase assets or issue credit substitutes, including such an arrangement that the firm can cancel:
(a) unconditionally at any time without notice; or
(b) if the obligor fails to meet a condition (including a condition that must be met before the first or any later drawdown under the arrangement).
(2) A banking business firm must take every commitment into account in calculating its credit risk capital requirement, whether or not a commitment contains a material adverse change clause or other provision that is intended to relieve the firm of its obligations under particular conditions.
(3) An off-balance-sheet undertaking to provide a commitment to an off-balance-sheet item may be assigned the lower of the 2 applicable CCFs.
(4) To calculate the credit equivalent amount of an undrawn (or partly drawn) commitment, a banking business firm must use the undrawn amount of the commitment.
(5) For an irrevocable commitment to provide a facility off the balance sheet, the original maturity must be taken to be the period from the commencement of the commitment until the associated facility expires.
Example
An irrevocable commitment with an original maturity of 6 months with an associated facility that has a 9-month term is taken to have an original maturity of 9 months.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

BANK 4.4.92 How to calculate risk-weighted amounts
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) The risk-weighted amount of an off-balance-sheet item is calculated as follows:
(a) first, convert the notional principal amount of the item to its on-balance-sheet equivalent (that is, the item’s credit equivalent amount) by multiplying the notional principal amount by the relevant credit conversion factor (CCF), as set out in table 4.4.92;
(b) then, multiply the item’s credit equivalent amount by the risk weight applicable to the claim or asset under Division 4.4.B.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.1 Introduction
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
A banking business firm is able to reduce its credit risk capital requirement by using CRM techniques. The use of CRM techniques must be treated as complementary to, rather than a replacement for, thorough credit risk assessment.

Guidance

Although the use of CRM techniques reduces or transfers credit risk, it may at the same time increase other risks (that is, residual risks). Residual risks include legal, operational, liquidity and market risks. Therefore, banking business firms must employ robust procedures and processes to control such risks, including strategy; consideration of the underlying credit; valuation; policies and procedures; systems; control of roll-off risks; and management of concentration risk arising from the firm’s use of CRM techniques and its interaction with the firm’s overall credit risk profile. If such risks are not adequately controlled, the Regulatory Authority may impose additional capital charges or take other supervisory action.

Note Under rule 4.4.5, if a claim or asset to which a banking business firm must assign a risk weight is secured by eligible collateral or a guarantee (or is covered by a credit derivative or a netting agreement), the firm may apply this Part to reduce the firm’s credit risk capital requirement.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-2 (as from 1st January 2015).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.2 Choice of CRM techniques
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) CRM techniques include:
(a) accepting collateral, standby letters of credit and guarantees;
(b) using credit derivatives or other derivative instruments; and
(c) using netting agreements.
Guidance
1 A banking business firm should not rely excessively on collateral or guarantees to mitigate credit risk. Although collateral or a guarantee may provide secondary protection to the firm if the counterparty defaults, the primary consideration for credit approval should be the counterparty’s ability to repay the loan.
2 A banking business firm that provides mortgages at high LTV ratios should consider the need for alternative forms of protection against the risks of such lending, including mortgage indemnity insurance, to protect itself against the risk of a fall in the value of the property.
(2) In choosing a CRM technique, a banking business firm must consider:
(a) the firm’s knowledge of the technique and its experience in using it;
(b) the cost-effectiveness of the technique;
(c) the type and financial strength of the counterparties or issuers;
(d) the correlation of the technique with the underlying credits;
(e) the availability, liquidity and realisability of the technique;
(f) the extent to which documents in common use (for example, the ISDA Master Agreement) can be adopted; and
(g) the degree of recognition of the technique by financial services regulators.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-2 (as from 1st January 2015).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.3 Requirements — use of CRM techniques
doc_path: BANK 4.5.3 Requirements — use of CRM techniques
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm’s credit risk management policy must set out the conditions under which CRM techniques may be used. The policy must enable the firm to manage CRM techniques and the risks associated with their use.
Note For the general requirements about a firm’s credit risk management policy, see Part 4.2.
(2) The firm must analyse the protection given by any proposed CRM technique to ensure that any residual credit risk is identified, measured, evaluated, managed and either controlled or mitigated.
(3) If the firm accepts collateral, its credit risk management policy must state the types of collateral that it will accept, and the basis and procedures for valuing collateral.
(4) If the firm uses netting agreements, it must have a netting policy that sets out its approach to the use of such agreements. The policy must provide for monitoring such agreements and must enable the firm to monitor and report netted transactions on both gross and net bases.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-2 (as from 1st January 2015).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.4 When CRM techniques reduce credit risk capital requirement
doc_path: BANK 4.5.4 When CRM techniques reduce credit risk capital requirement
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm’s use of a CRM technique reduces the firm’s credit risk capital requirement only if the technique and every document that gives effect to it is binding on all parties and is enforceable in all the relevant jurisdictions.
Guidance
When accepting eligible collateral, a banking business firm must ensure that any necessary legal procedures have been followed to ensure that the collateral can be enforced.
(2) A banking business firm must review the enforceability of a CRM technique that it uses. The firm must have a well-founded legal basis for any conclusion about enforceability, and must carry out further reviews to ensure that the technique remains enforceable.
Guidance
A banking business firm should consider whether independent legal advice should be sought on the enforceability of documents. The documents should be ready before the firm enters into a contractual obligation or releases funds.
(3) The effects of a CRM technique must not be double-counted. The firm’s credit risk capital requirement is not reduced if:
(a) the risk weight for a claim or asset is based on an issue-specific rating; and
(b) the ECRA that determined the rating had taken the technique into consideration in doing so.
(4) A transaction in which CRM techniques are used must not receive a higher capital requirement than an otherwise identical transaction in which no such technique is used.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2015-3 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.5 Use of 2 or more CRM techniques for 1 exposure etc
doc_path: BANK 4.5.5 Use of 2 or more CRM techniques for 1 exposure etc
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If a banking business firm has an exposure that is covered by 2 or more CRM techniques (for example, the exposure is covered by both eligible collateral and an eligible guarantee), the firm must divide the exposure into parts covered by each technique (for example, the part covered by the collateral, and the part covered by the guarantee) and must calculate the risk-weighted assets for each part separately.
(2) If credit protection provided for an exposure by a single protection provider has 2 or more maturities, the exposure must be divided into separate parts for each maturity.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2015-3 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.6 Valuing collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
Collateral accepted by a banking business firm must be valued at its net realisable value, taking into account the prevailing market conditions. That value must be monitored at appropriate intervals, and the collateral must be revalued regularly (at least annually).

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.6 Guidance
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
1 The net realisable value of some collateral may be readily available (for example, collateral that is marked to market regularly). Other collateral may be more difficult to value and may require knowledge and consideration of prevailing market conditions.
2 The method and frequency of monitoring and revaluation depend on the nature and condition of the collateral (see rule 4.5.12 (2)). For example, securities accepted as collateral are usually marked to market daily.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.7 Capital relief from collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Collateral reduces a banking business firm’s credit risk capital requirement in relation to an exposure or exposures only if the collateral is eligible collateral.
Note The capital relief that a banking business firm obtains from collateral is calculated by either the simple approach (see Subdivision 4.5.B.2) or the comprehensive approach (see Subdivision 4.5.B.3). The meaning of eligible collateral differs between the simple approach and the comprehensive approach — see respectively rule 4.5.12 and rule 4.5.16.
(2) Collateral may be lodged either by the firm’s counterparty, or by a third party on the counterparty’s behalf.
(3) The firm must enter into a written agreement with the party that lodges the collateral. The agreement must establish the firm’s direct, explicit, irrevocable and unconditional recourse to the collateral.
Guidance
In the case of cash collateral, the recourse may be in the form of a contractual right to set off credit balances. A common-law right of set-off does not, on its own, satisfy this rule.
(4) If collateral is lodged by a third party, the third party must guarantee the counterparty’s obligation to the firm and must indemnify the firm if the counterparty fails to fulfil its obligation. The firm must ensure that the guarantee is legally enforceable.
(5) The mechanism by which collateral is lodged must allow the firm to liquidate, or take possession of, the collateral in a timely way. The firm must do everything necessary to satisfy the legal requirements applicable to its interest in the collateral.
Guidance
1 The firm should have clear and robust procedures for the liquidation of collateral to ensure that the legal conditions for declaring default and liquidating the collateral are observed.
2 The firm should consider whether, in the event of default, notice to the party that lodged the collateral would be needed before the firm could have recourse to it.
(6) There must not be a significant positive correlation between the value of the collateral and the credit quality of the borrower.
Note A positive correlation between the credit quality of the borrower and the value of the collateral is often called “wrong-way risk”.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.8 Holding eligible collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Eligible collateral must be held by:
(a) the banking business firm concerned;
(b) a branch (in or outside the QFC) of the firm;
(c) another member of the firm’s corporate group;
(d) an independent custodian; or
(e) a central counterparty.
(2) The holder of cash collateral in the form of a certificate of deposit or bank bill issued by a banking business firm must keep possession of the instrument while the collateralised exposure exists.
(3) If the collateral is held by an independent custodian or central counterparty, the firm must take reasonable steps to ensure that the holder segregates the collateral from the holder’s own assets.
(4) If collateral is held by a branch of a banking business firm and the branch is outside the QFC, the agreement between the firm and the party lodging the collateral must require the branch to act in accordance with the agreement.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

doc_path: BANK 4.5.9 Approaches to risk weight using eligible collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) When assigning risk weights to exposures that are collateralised by eligible collateral, a banking business firm may use either of the following approaches:
(a) the simple approach (see Subdivision 4.5.B.2);
(b) the comprehensive approach (see Subdivision 4.5.B.3).
(2) However, the firm must apply the same approach for all of the exposures in its banking book that are collateralised by eligible collateral.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.11 When simple approach may be applied
doc_path: BANK 4.5.11 When simple approach may be applied
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) For the simple approach to be applied, the collateral must be lodged for at least the life of the exposure, and must be marked to market at least once a month. The release of collateral must be conditional on the repayment of the exposure, but collateral may be reduced in proportion to the amount of any reduction in the exposure.
(2) A banking business firm must not apply the simple approach if there is a maturity mismatch between an exposure and its collateral.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.12 Eligible collateral in simple approach
doc_path: BANK 4.5.12 Eligible collateral in simple approach
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) In the simple approach, each of the following is eligible collateral:
(a) gold bullion;
(b) cash (including certificates of deposit and similar instruments issued by the banking business firm concerned);
(c) debt securities of the following kinds:
(i) issued by a sovereign or a non-commercial PSE that is rated, by an ECRA, at least BB- or higher;
(ii) issued by an MDB that is eligible for 0% risk weight;
Note For the list of such MDBs, see rule 4.4.16.
(iii) short-term debt securities rated, by an ECRA, at A 3/P-3 or higher;
(iv) any other securities rated, by an ECRA, at BBB- or higher;
(d) debt securities that have not been assigned an issue-specific rating by an ECRA, if:
(i) the securities are issued by a bank (in or outside the QFC) as senior debt and are listed on a recognised exchange;
Note For the list of recognised exchanges, see Schedule 1.
(ii) all rated issues of the same seniority issued by the bank are rated no lower than BBB- (for long-term instruments) or A-3/P-3 (for short-term instruments); and
(iii) the firm and the holder of the collateral have no information suggesting that the securities should be rated at below BBB- or A 3/P-3;
(e) equities (including convertible bonds) that are included in a main index;
(f) units in tracker funds, mutual funds and UCITS, if:
(i) a price for the units is publicly quoted daily; and
(ii) the funds or UCITS are limited to investing in instruments listed in this subrule.
(2) Cash-funded credit-linked notes issued by the bank against exposures in the banking book that fulfil the criteria for credit derivatives are treated as cash-collateralised transactions.
(3) If a debt security issued by a rated sovereign does not have an issue-specific rating, a banking business firm may treat the rating of the issuer as the rating of the security.
(4) A re-securitisation is not eligible collateral.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.13 Risk weight for exposure collateralised by eligible collateral — simple approach
doc_path: BANK 4.5.13 Risk weight for exposure collateralised by eligible collateral — simple approach
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Under the simple approach, the part of an exposure that is collateralised by eligible collateral must be assigned a risk weight of the higher of:

(a) the risk weight of the collateral under Division 4.4.B; and
(b) subject to the exceptions in subrules (3) to (8) — 20%.
(2) Any part of the exposure that is not so collateralised must be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to an unsecured exposure to the counterparty under Division 4.4.B.

(3) Subrule (4) applies to an exposure of a banking business firm if:

(a) the collateral is cash on deposit, or a certificate of deposit or similar instrument issued by the firm;

(b) the collateral:

(i) is held at a third-party bank in a non-custodial arrangement; and
(ii) is openly pledged to the firm; and
(c) the pledge is unconditional and irrevocable.
(4) If this subrule applies to an exposure, the amount of the exposure that is covered by the collateral receives the risk weight of the third-party bank.

(5) Subrule (6) applies to an exposure that arises from an SFT and fulfils all of the following conditions:

(a) both the exposure and the collateral are either cash, or a sovereign or PSE security that qualifies for a 0% risk weight under Division 4.4.B;
(b) the exposure and the collateral are denominated in the same currency;
(c) either the transaction is overnight, or both the exposure and the collateral are marked to market daily and are subject to daily remargining;
(d) if the counterparty were to fail to remargin, the collateral could be liquidated within no more than 4 business days after the last marking to market before the failure;
(e) the transaction is settled across a settlement system proven for transactions of that type;
(f) the documentation covering the transaction is standard market documentation for SFTs in the securities concerned;
(g) under that documentation, if the counterparty fails to satisfy an obligation to deliver cash or securities or to deliver margin, or otherwise defaults, the transaction is immediately terminable;
(h) on the counterparty’s default the firm has the unfettered, legally enforceable right to immediately seize and liquidate the collateral for its own benefit, even if the counterparty is insolvent or bankrupt.

(6) An exposure to which this subrule applies may be assigned a risk weight of:

(a) 10%; or
(b) if the counterparty is a core market participant — 0%.

(7) Subrule (8) applies to a transaction where:

(a) a banking business firm has a credit exposure or potential credit exposure; and
(b) the exposure is wholly or partly hedged by collateral posted by a counterparty or by a third party on the counterparty’s behalf.

(8) A transaction to this subrule applies may be assigned a risk weight of 0% if the exposure and the collateral are denominated in the same currency, and either:

(a) the collateral is cash; or
(b) the collateral is sovereign or PSE securities that would qualify for a 0% risk weight under Division 4.4.B, and its market value has been discounted by 20%.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.15 Description of comprehensive approach
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) To assign a risk weight to an exposure using the comprehensive approach, a banking business firm must calculate its adjusted exposure to the counterparty to take into account the risk-mitigating effect of the collateral.
(2) The firm must use the applicable supervisory haircuts (set out in rule 4.5.18) to adjust both the amount of the exposure to the counterparty and the value of any collateral received in support of that counterparty, to take account of possible future fluctuations in the value of either, caused by market movements.
Guidance
1 Unless either side of the transaction is cash or a zero haircut is applied, the volatility-adjusted exposure amount will be higher than the nominal exposure and the volatility-adjusted collateral value will be lower than the nominal collateral value.
2 The size of a haircut depends on the type of instrument, the type of transaction, its residual maturity and the frequency of marking to market and remargining.
3 Haircuts must be scaled up using the square-root-of-time formula, depending on the frequency of remargining or marking to market. The formula is in rule 4.5.19 (6).
(3) In the case of a maturity mismatch, the value of the collateral must be adjusted in accordance with rule 4.5.20.
(4) If the exposure and collateral are in different currencies, the firm must apply an additional haircut to the volatility-adjusted collateral amount in accordance with rule 4.5.21 to take account of possible future fluctuations in exchange rates.
(5) The effect of a netting agreement covering an SFT may be taken into account in accordance with Division 4.5.E.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.19 Adjustment for different holding periods, non-daily marking to market and non-daily remargining
doc_path: BANK 4.5.19 Adjustment for different holding periods, non-daily marking to market and non-daily remargining
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Subject to this rule, the minimum holding periods and conditions for the purposes of this Subdivision, set out in table 4.5.19, apply to SFTs, other capital-market transactions (such as OTC derivatives transactions and margin lending) and secured lending.
Guidance
For some transactions, depending on the nature and frequency of the revaluation and remargining provisions, different holding periods and thus different haircuts must be applied. The framework for collateral haircuts distinguishes between SFTs, other capital markets-driven transactions (that is, OTC derivatives transactions and margin lending) and secured lending. In capital-market-driven transactions and repo-style transactions, the documentation contains remargining clauses; in secured lending transactions, it generally does not.

Table 4.5.19 Minimum holding periods and conditions

Transaction type Minimum holding period Condition
SFTs 5 business days Daily remargining
Other capital market transactions 10 business days Daily remargining
Secured lending 20 business days Daily revaluation
(2) However, if a netting set includes both SFTs and other capital market transactions, the minimum holding period of 10 business days must be used.
(3) Also, a minimum holding period of 20 business days must be used in the following cases:
(a) if in a quarter the number of trades in a netting set exceeds 5,000 at any time — in the next quarter;
(b) for a netting set that includes 1 or more trades involving illiquid collateral.
(4) For paragraph (3) (b), whether collateral is illiquid must be determined in the context of stressed market conditions. Collateral is illiquid if there is no continuously active market in which a counterparty would, within 2 days or less, obtain multiple price quotations that would not move the market or reflect a market discount.
Guidance
Examples of collateral that would be considered illiquid include:
• collateral that is not marked to market daily
• collateral that is subject to a particular accounting treatment for valuation purposes (for example, SFTs referencing securities whose fair value is determined by models with inputs that are not observed in the market).
(5) If on a particular netting set, over the previous 2 quarters, a banking business firm has experienced more than 2 margin call disputes that have lasted longer than the firm’s estimate of the margin period of risk (that is, the period from the last exchange of collateral covering the netting set with a defaulting counterparty until the counterparty is closed out and the resulting market risk is rehedged) then, for the following 2 quarters, the firm must use a minimum holding period that is twice the period that would apply except for this subrule.
(6) When remargining or revaluation is undertaken less frequently than the minimum specified in table 4.5.19, the haircut that must be applied is:
where:
H+ is the haircut to be applied.
HM is the haircut under the minimum holding period.
NR is the actual number of business days between remarginings (for capital market transactions) or revaluations (for secured transactions).
TM is the minimum holding period for transactions of that type, as set out in table 4.5.19.
(7) However, the firm may apply a haircut of 0% to an SFT with a core market participant, if the transaction satisfies all of the conditions in rule 4.5.13 (5).

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.20 Treatment of maturity mismatches
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A maturity mismatch exists between an exposure and its credit risk mitigation if the residual maturity of the term of lodgement of the credit risk mitigation is shorter than the maturity of the exposure.
(2) The maturity of the exposure and the maturity of the credit risk mitigation must both be defined conservatively. The effective maturity of the underlying must be taken to be the longest possible remaining time before the counterparty is scheduled to fulfil its obligation, taking into account any applicable grace period. For the credit risk mitigation, embedded options that may reduce the term of the credit risk mitigation must be taken into account so that the shortest possible effective maturity is used.
Guidance
For example: if, in the case of a credit derivative, the protection seller has a call option, the maturity is the first call date. Likewise, if the protection buyer owns the call option and has a strong incentive to call the transaction at the first call date, for example because of a step-up in cost from that date on, the effective maturity is the remaining time to the first call date.
(3) If there is a maturity mismatch, the credit risk mitigation may be recognised only if the original maturity of its term of lodgement is 12 months or longer, and its residual maturity is 3 months or longer.
(4) For the purpose of determining the maturity of the exposure and credit risk mitigation:
(a) for the exposure, the effective maturity is taken to be the longest possible remaining time before the counterparty must fulfil its obligation; and
(b) for the credit risk mitigation, the banking business firm concerned must take into account any provision or incentive within the documentation for the transaction that could reduce the term of the credit risk mitigation, so that the shortest possible effective maturity is used.
(5) If there is a maturity mismatch, the firm must adjust the value of the credit risk mitigation as follows:
where:
Pa is the value of the credit risk mitigation, adjusted for the maturity mismatch.
P is the value of the credit risk mitigation after adjustment for any haircuts.
t is min {T, residual maturity of the credit risk mitigation arrangement}, in years.
T is min {5 years, residual maturity of the exposure}, in years.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.23 Haircut minima for certain SFTs — non-eligible counterparties
doc_path: BANK 4.5.23 Haircut minima for certain SFTs — non-eligible counterparties
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Subrule (2) applies to transactions of the following kinds:
(a) SFTs that are not centrally cleared, and in which the banking business firm concerned provides financing against collateral other than securities issued by a sovereign or a PSE;
(b) collateral upgrade transactions;
with a counterparty that is not supervised by a regulator that imposes prudential requirements consistent with the Basel III framework. However, subrule (2) does not apply to transactions of a kind described in subrule (3).
Guidance
A collateral upgrade transaction is one in which the firm lends a security to the counterparty and the counterparty pledges a lower quality security as collateral, thus allowing the counterparty to exchange a lower quality security for a higher quality security.
(2) Subject to subrule (5) and rule 4.5.24, in transactions to which this subrule applies, a banking business firm must apply the haircut minima set out in table 4.5.23.

Table 4.5.23 Haircut minima for SFTs

Type of security and residual maturity Haircut (%)
Corporate and other issuers Securitised products
≤ 1 year debt securities, and floating rate notes (FRNs) 0.5 1
> 1 year ≤ 5 years debt securities 1.5 4
> 5 years ≤ 10 years debt securities 3 6
> 10 years debt securities 4 7
Main index equities 6 6
Other eligible collateral 10 10
(3) Subrule (2) does not apply to transactions of the following kinds:
(a) SFTs with central banks;
(b) cash-collateralised securities lending transactions of either of the following kinds:
(i) transactions in which securities are lent to a banking business firm at long maturities, and the lender of the securities reinvests or employs the cash at the same or shorter maturity, so that no significant maturity or liquidity mismatch occurs;
(ii) transactions in which securities are lent to such a firm at call or at short maturities (giving rise to liquidity risk) but the lender reinvests the cash collateral into a reinvestment fund or account that is subject to regulation or regulatory guidance that meets global minimum standards for the reinvestment of cash collateral by securities lenders.
(4) For the purposes of subparagraph (3) (b) (ii), the firm may rely on a representation by a securities lender that their reinvestment of cash collateral meets the standards referred to in that subparagraph.
(5) If the firm lends securities for a collateral upgrade transaction, it need not apply the minimum if:
(a) the firm is unable to re-use the securities received as collateral against the securities lent; or
(b) the firm represents that it does not intend to, and will not, re-use them in that way.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.25 Capital relief from guarantees
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A guarantee reduces a banking business firm’s credit risk capital requirement in relation to an exposure only if:
(a) the guarantor is an eligible guarantor (see rule 4.5.26);
(b) the guarantee is an eligible guarantee (see rule 4.5.27); and
(c) an unsecured exposure to the guarantor would be assigned a lower risk weight than an unsecured exposure to the counterparty.
(2) Before accepting a guarantee, a banking business firm must consider the guarantor’s legal and financial ability to fulfil the guarantee.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.26 Eligible guarantors
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
Each of the following is an eligible guarantor:

(a) the State of Qatar or any other sovereign;
(b) a PSE or MDB;
(c) a bank, securities firm or other financial institution that is prudentially regulated to a standard similar to that applied by the Regulatory Authority;
(d) if the relevant exposure is a securitisation exposure — an externally-rated entity (including a parent, subsidiary or affiliate of the obligor) that is rated BBB- or better and was rated A- or better when the guarantee was given;

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.27 What is an eligible guarantee?
doc_path: BANK 4.5.27 What is an eligible guarantee?
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A guarantee is an eligible guarantee if it satisfies subrules (2) to (10).
(2) The guarantor is an eligible guarantor.
(3) The guarantee is explicitly documented.
(4) The guarantee is a direct claim on the guarantor and clearly states the extent of the cover. A letter of comfort is not an eligible guarantee.
(5) The guarantee explicitly refers to specific exposures or a specific pool of exposures, so that the extent of the cover is clearly defined and not open to doubt.
(6) The guarantee is irrevocable (other than for non-payment by the protection buyer of money due for the guarantee).
(7) No provision of the guarantee:
(a) would allow the guarantor to cancel the guarantee, or to change its maturity, unilaterally; or
(b) would increase the effective cost of the cover if the credit quality of the exposure deteriorates.
Guidance
Subrule (6) does not require the maturities of the guarantee and the exposure to be matched. However, it does require that the agreed maturity of the guarantee is not to be reduced by the guarantor after the protection buyer accepts the guarantee.
(8) The guarantee is unconditional. It does not include a term (outside the direct control of the protection buyer) that allows the guarantor not to indemnify the protection buyer in a timely way if the counterparty defaults.
(9) On an event of default or non-payment that triggers the guarantee:
(a) the protection buyer has the right to recover any money outstanding under the transaction from the guarantor in a timely manner;
(b) the guarantor may either pay that money to the protection buyer in a lump sum, or assume the counterparty’s future payment obligations; and
(c) the protection buyer has the right to receive such payments from the guarantor without first having to take legal action against the counterparty for payment.
(10) The guarantee covers all types of payments that the counterparty is expected to make under the transaction (for example, the notional amount and the margin payments) — but see rule 4.5.28.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.28 Risk weighting of exposures covered by eligible guarantees
doc_path: BANK 4.5.28 Risk weighting of exposures covered by eligible guarantees
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If a claim on a counterparty is secured by an eligible guarantee, the part of the claim that is covered by the guarantee may be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to an unsecured exposure to the guarantor under Division 4.4.B. The unsecured part of the claim must be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to an unsecured exposure to the counterparty under that Division.
Note If the guarantee provides for a materiality threshold (below which the issuer is not obliged to pay in the event of a loss), the part of the exposure that is below the threshold must be deducted from CET 1 capital — see rule 3.2.38.
(2) If the guarantee covers the payment of principal only, interest and other uncovered payments must be treated as unsecured.
(3) If an eligible guarantee provides that the banking business firm concerned and the guarantor must share any loss, the firm:
(a) may treat, as covered by an eligible guarantee, a proportion of the exposure equal to the proportion of the loss that the guarantor must bear; and
(b) must treat the remainder of the exposure as unsecured.
(4) If:
(a) a banking business firm transfers part (but not all) of the risk of an exposure in 1 or more tranches to 1 or more eligible guarantors; and
(b) the risk transferred and the risk retained are of different seniority;
the firm may obtain credit protection for either the senior portion or the junior portion. The firm is to be treated as having securitised the exposure, and must determine the relevant capital requirement in accordance with Part 4.6.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.29 Treatment of maturity mismatches
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A maturity mismatch between an exposure and a guarantee exists if the residual term of the guarantee is shorter than the maturity of the exposure.
(2) If there is a maturity mismatch, the guarantee may be recognised only if its original term is 12 months or longer, and its residual maturity is 3 months or longer.
(3) For the purpose of determining the maturity of the exposure and guarantee:
(a) for the exposure, the effective maturity is taken to be the longest possible remaining time before the counterparty must fulfil its obligation; and
(b) for the guarantee, the banking business firm concerned must take into account any provision or incentive within its documentation that could reduce the term of the guarantee, so that the shortest possible effective term is used.

P is the value of the guarantee after adjustment for any haircuts.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:

(2) Before purchasing a credit derivative, a banking business firm must consider the issuer’s legal and financial ability to fulfil the derivative.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.34 Eligible credit derivatives
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A credit derivative is an eligible credit derivative if it satisfies subrules (2) to (16).
(2) It is either a credit default swap or (subject to rule 4.5.36) a total return swap. It provides credit protection equivalent to a guarantee.
(3) It is issued by an eligible issuer.
(4) It is a direct claim on the issuer.
(5) It is explicitly referenced to specific exposures or a specific pool of exposures, so that the extent of the cover is clearly defined and incontrovertible.
(6) It is irrevocable (other than for non-payment by the protection buyer of money due for the credit protection contract).
(7) No provision of the contract:
(a) would allow the issuer to cancel the derivative, or to change its maturity, unilaterally; or
(b) would increase the effective cost of the cover if the credit quality of the exposure deteriorates.
Guidance
The irrevocability condition does not require the derivative and the exposure to be maturity matched. However, it does require that the agreed maturity should not be reduced by the issuer after the banking business firm accepts the derivative.
(8) It is unconditional. It does not include a term or condition (outside the direct control of the banking business firm concerned) that allows the issuer not to indemnify the firm in a timely way on the occurrence of a credit event.
(9) It specifies at least the following as credit events:
(a) failure to pay an amount due under the terms of the underlying exposure that is in effect at the time of the failure (however, any grace period under the terms of the underlying must be allowed);
(b) the obligor of the underlying exposure becoming bankrupt or insolvent or unable to pay its debts (and any similar event);
(c) the obligor’s failure to pay, or admitting in writing its inability generally to pay, its debts as those debts become due (and any similar event);
(d) the application of forbearance to the underlying exposure, including any forgiveness or postponement of principal, interest or fees that results in a credit loss event (but see rule 4.5.38).
(10) On the occurrence of a credit event:
(a) the firm has the right to recover any money outstanding under the transaction from the issuer in a timely manner;
(b) the issuer may either pay that money to the firm in a lump sum, or assume the counterparty’s future payment obligations; and
(c) the firm has the right to receive such payments from the issuer without first having to take legal action against the counterparty for payment.
(11) It clearly identifies the parties responsible for deciding whether a credit event has occurred. That decision is not the sole right of the issuer, and the firm has the right and the ability to notify the issuer about such an event.
(12) It does not terminate before the end of any grace period required after a credit event on the underlying obligation as a result of a failure to pay.
(13) If there is a mismatch between the underlying obligation and the reference obligation used to determine the derivative’s cash settlement value:
(a) the reference obligation is equal in seniority to, or is junior to, the underlying obligation; and
(b) the underlying obligation and reference obligation share the same obligor and there are legally enforceable cross-default or cross-acceleration clauses.
(14) If there is a mismatch between the underlying obligation and the obligation used to determine whether a credit event has occurred:
(a) the obligation used to determine whether a credit event has occurred is equal in seniority to, or is junior to, the underlying obligation; and
(b) the underlying obligation and the obligation used to determine whether a credit event has occurred share the same obligor and there are legally enforceable cross-default or cross-acceleration clauses.
(15) If the derivative is based on cash settlement, the banking business firm concerned must have a robust valuation process to reliably estimate losses on the reference obligation, including a defined period for obtaining valuations of that obligation after a credit event.
(16) If the firm buys credit protection in relation to an existing exposure, the terms of the exposure must allow for its transfer to the issuer. If the firm would be required to transfer the underlying exposure to the issuer for settlement, the terms of the exposure must provide that any required consent to the transfer may not be unreasonably withheld.
(17) First-to-default and all other nth-to-default credit derivatives are not eligible credit derivatives.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.35 Risk weighting of exposures covered by eligible credit derivatives
doc_path: BANK 4.5.35 Risk weighting of exposures covered by eligible credit derivatives
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If an exposure is fully covered by an eligible credit derivative, the exposure may be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to an unsecured exposure to the issuer under Division 4.4.B.
(2) If an exposure is partly covered by an eligible credit derivative:
(a) the covered part must be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to an unsecured exposure to the issuer under Division 4.4.B; and
(b) the remainder must be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to an unsecured exposure to the counterparty under that Division.
Note If the derivative provides for a materiality threshold (below which the issuer is not obliged to pay in the event of a loss), the part of the exposure that is below the threshold must be deducted from CET 1 capital — see rule 3.2.38.
(3) If the derivative provides that the banking business firm concerned and the issuer must share any loss, the firm:
(a) may treat, as covered by an eligible credit derivative, a proportion of the exposure equal to the protected portion; and
(b) must treat the remainder of the exposure as unsecured.
(4) If the derivative covers payment of principal only, interest and other uncovered payments must be treated as unsecured.
(5) If:
(a) a banking business firm transfers part (but not all) of the risk of an exposure in 1 or more tranches to 1 or more protection sellers; and
(b) the risk transferred and the risk retained are of different seniority;
the firm may obtain credit protection for either the second-loss portion or the first-loss portion. The firm is to be treated as having securitised the exposure, and must calculate the relevant capital requirement in accordance with Part 4.6.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.content_text: (1) If an exposure is fully covered by an eligible credit derivative, the exposure may be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to an unsecured exposure to the issuer under Division 4.4.B . (2) If an exposure is partly covered by an eligible credit derivative: (a) the covered part must be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to an unsecured exposure to the issuer under Division 4.4.B ; and (b) the remainder must be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to an unsecured exposure to the counterparty under that Division. Note If the derivative provides for a materiality threshold (below which the issuer is not obliged to pay in the event of a loss), the part of the exposure that is below the threshold must be deducted from CET 1 capital — see rule 3.2.38 . (3) If the derivative provides that the banking business firm concerned and the issuer must share any loss, the firm: (a) may treat, as covered by an eligible credit derivative, a proportion of the exposure equal to the protected portion; and (b) must treat the remainder of the exposure as unsecured. (4) If the derivative covers payment of principal only, interest and other uncovered payments must be treated as unsecured. (5) If: (a) a banking business firm transfers part (but not all) of the risk of an exposure in 1 or more tranches to 1 or more protection sellers; and (b) the risk transferred and the risk retained are of different seniority; the firm may obtain credit protection for either the second-loss portion or the first-loss portion. The firm is to be treated as having securitised the exposure, and must calculate the relevant capital requirement in accordance with Part 4.6 . Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.5.36 Non-recognition of certain total return swaps
doc_path: BANK 4.5.36 Non-recognition of certain total return swaps
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
If a banking business firm buys credit protection through a total return swap and records the net payments received on the swap as net income, but does not record the offsetting deterioration in the value of the asset that is protected (either through reductions in fair value or by an addition to reserves), the credit protection will not be recognised.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)
