QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.3 Capital requirements for counterparty credit risk
doc_path: BANK 4.6A.3 Capital requirements for counterparty credit risk
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm that engages in certain classes of transactions that expose it to counterparty credit risk must hold sufficient regulatory capital to cover the counterparty credit risk that arises from those transactions.
(2) A banking business firm’s capital requirement for counterparty credit risk is made up of the following:
(a) the firm’s risk-weighted assets for counterparty credit risk, which is the sum of the following:
(i) the firm’s risk-weighted assets representing credit exposures for counterparty credit default risk (“default risk RWA”);
(ii) the firm’s risk-weighted assets representing credit exposures for counterparty credit default risk arising from trade exposures to a CCP (“trade exposure RWA”); and
(iii) the firm’s risk-weighted assets representing credit exposure arising from a default fund contribution to a non-qualifying CCP (“default fund RWA”);
(b) any applicable credit valuation adjustment (CVA) risk capital charge;
(c) any applicable default fund capital charge for any default fund contributions to a QCCP.
Note The amount of the firm’s total risk-weighted assets for counterparty credit risk is part of the amount of its total risk-weighted assets for credit risk (see rule 4.1.4). The firm’s total risk-weighted assets for credit risk is its credit risk capital requirement, which is part of its risk-based capital requirement (see rule 3.2.5).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.4 Policies — foreign exchange rollovers
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must have policies for entering into and monitoring rollovers on foreign exchange transactions. The policies must restrict the firm’s capacity to enter into such rollovers, and must have been approved by the Regulatory Authority.
(2) The firm must notify the Authority if it enters into a rollover outside the approved policy. The Authority may direct how the rollover is to be treated for capital adequacy purposes.
(3) The firm must not enter into a transaction at an off-market price, unless the transaction is a historical rate rollover on a foreign exchange transaction.
(4) A historical rate rollover on a foreign exchange transaction may be entered into at an off-market price (instead of current market price).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.5 Methods for calculating counterparty credit risk exposures
doc_path: BANK 4.6A.5 Methods for calculating counterparty credit risk exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Division 4.6A.B sets out the modified current exposure method (or modified CEM) for calculating a banking business firm’s default risk RWA. Subject to subrule (2), a banking business firm must use that method.
(2) The Regulatory Authority may direct a banking business firm to use the SA-CCR, or approve such a firm’s use of that method, to calculate its counterparty credit risk capital requirement (or any part of that requirement).
Guidance
The Authority might direct an authorised firm to use the SA-CCR if:
• at the end date of each of the 4 consecutive financial reporting periods (both interim and annual) immediately preceding the date on which the calculation of the CCR exposure is performed, the total notional amount of the firm’s outstanding derivative contracts (regardless of whether the contracts are recorded as assets or liabilities) does not exceed 10% of the aggregate of its total assets and total liabilities reported in its financial statements
• the Authority considers that the use by the firm of the modified current exposure method would not adequately assess and reflect the firm’s CCR exposure, taking into account the nature of the firm’s business.
(3) If the Authority grants an approval or gives a direction under this rule, the Authority may specify parameters or formulas to be used, or assumptions to be made, in applying the SA-CCR.
(4) In this rule:
SA-CCR means the method of calculating counterparty credit risk exposure set out in the document CRE52: Standardised approach to counterparty credit risk, as issued by the BCBS and in force from time to time.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.7 Capital requirements to be calculated
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.B Modified current exposure method
BANK 4.6A.7 Capital requirements to be calculated
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) For bilateral OTC derivative transactions, a banking business firm must calculate each of the following counterparty credit risk requirements:
(a) default risk RWA, which reflects the potential loss arising from a default of a counterparty; and
(b) a CVA risk capital charge.
(2) For bilateral SFTs, a banking business firm must calculate the default risk RWA. To determine default risk RWA for SFTs, the firm:
(a) must calculate the counterparty credit risk exposure amount as the sum of:
(i) the exposure amount for each SFT that is not covered by an eligible netting agreement; and
(ii) the exposure amount for all SFTs covered by an eligible netting agreement;
in accordance with Part 4.5; and
Note 1 Eligible netting agreement is defined in the glossary.
Note 2 In relation to how eligible netting agreements are to be applied for the purposes of this Division, see Subdivision 4.5.E.1.
(b) must apply the appropriate risk weight in accordance with Division 4.4.B.
(3) Bilateral SFTs are not subject to a CVA risk capital charge unless the Regulatory Authority determines that the relevant banking business firm’s CVA loss exposure arising from SFTs is material, and directs the firm to apply a CVA risk capital charge:
(a) of a specified amount; or
(b) calculated in a specified way.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.8 Default risk RWA for OTC derivative transactions
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.B Modified current exposure method
BANK 4.6A.8 Default risk RWA for OTC derivative transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) To determine the default risk RWA for OTC derivative transactions, a banking business firm must calculate a counterparty credit risk exposure amount, and must apply to it the relevant risk weight, determined as set out in Division 4.4.B.
(2) The counterparty credit risk exposure amount is the credit equivalent amount (CEA) for all OTC derivative transactions with a particular counterparty, calculated by adding together:
(a) for each transaction not covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement — the transaction-level CEA calculated as set out in subrule 4.6A.9 (2); and
Note In relation to how eligible netting agreements may be applied for the purposes of this Division, see Subdivision 4.5.E.1.
(b) for transactions that are covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement — the CEA calculated by the method set out in subrule 4.6A.9 (3);
and adjusting the sum for eligible collateral (within the extended meaning given by rule 4.5.16).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.9 Calculating credit equivalent amount
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.B Modified current exposure method
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If a transaction is secured by eligible collateral or is covered by an eligible guarantee, eligible credit derivative or eligible netting agreement, a CRM technique (see Part 4.5) may be used to reduce the amount of the firm’s exposure.
(2) CEA for transactions that are not covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement is calculated as follows:
(a) for margined transactions — by the formula:
CEA=CCE + PFE
(b) for unmargined transactions — by the formula:
CEA=CCE + (3 × PFE)
where:
CCE is the current credit exposure, calculated as the sum of the positive mark-to-market value (or replacement cost) of the transactions.
PFE is the potential future credit exposure of the transactions, determined in accordance with rules 4.6A.10 and 4.6A.12.
(3) CEA for OTC derivative transactions that are covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement is calculated as follows:
(a) for a netting agreement covering only margined transactions — by the formula:
CEA=NCCE + PFEadj
(b) for a netting agreement covering only unmargined transactions — by the formula:
CEA=NCCE + [3 × (PFEadj)]
(c) for a netting agreement covering both margined and unmargined transactions — by either the formula in paragraph (b) or the formula:
CEA=NCCE + [(1 + 2 × A) × (PFEadj)]
where:
NCCE has the meaning given by subrule (4).
A is:
PFEadj is the add-on for PFE based on the notional principal of all the individual underlying contracts (that is, the gross PFE (PFEgross) adjusted to reflect the effects of the netting agreement).
Note For how to calculate PFEadj, see rules 4.6A.13 and 4.6A.14. For PFEgross, see rule 4.6A.13 (2).
(4) For subrule (3), NCCE is the net current credit exposure of all the transactions covered by the relevant netting agreement, calculated as the sum of all the positive and negative mark-to-market values of all the contracts covered by the netting agreement (that is, transactions with positive mark-to-market values may be offset against transactions with negative mark-to-market values). If the net sum of the mark-to-market values is positive, NCCE is equal to that sum, and if the net sum is zero or negative, NCCE is taken to be zero.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

PFE is the potential future credit exposure of the transactions, determined in accordance with rules 4.6A.10 and 4.6A.12 . (3) CEA for OTC derivative transactions that are covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement is calculated as follows: (a) for a netting agreement covering only margined transactions — by the formula: CEA=NCCE + PFE adj (b) for a netting agreement covering only unmargined transactions — by the formula: CEA = NCCE + [3 × ( PFE adj )] (c) for a netting agreement covering both margined and unmargined transactions — by either the formula in paragraph (b) or the formula: CEA = NCCE + [(1 + 2 × A ) × ( PFE adj )] where: NCCE has the meaning given by subrule (4). A is: PFE adj is the add-on for PFE based on the notional principal of all the individual underlying contracts (that is, the gross PFE ( PFE gross ) adjusted to reflect the effects of the netting agreement). Note For how to calculate PFE adj , see rules 4.6A.13 and 4.6A.14 . For PFE gross , see rule 4.6A.13 (2). (4) For subrule (3), NCCE is the net current credit exposure of all the transactions covered by the relevant netting agreement, calculated as the sum of all the positive and negative mark-to-market values of all the contracts covered by the netting agreement (that is, transactions with positive mark-to-market values may be offset against transactions with negative mark-to-market values). If the net sum of the mark-to-market values is positive, NCCE is equal to that sum, and if the net sum is zero or negative, NCCE is taken to be zero. Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

endnotes: Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.10 Calculating PFE — transactions not covered by eligible bilateral netting agreement
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.B Modified current exposure method
BANK 4.6A.10 Calculating PFE — transactions not covered by eligible bilateral netting agreement
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) To calculate PFE for a transaction that is not covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement, a banking business firm must multiply the notional principal amount of the transaction by the relevant credit conversion factor (CCF) specified in table 4.6A.10. The notional (or nominal) principal amount of a contract is the reference amount used to calculate payment streams between the counterparties.

Note In relation to how eligible netting agreements may be applied for the purposes of this Division, see Subdivision 4.5.E.1.

Table 4.6A.10 Modified CEM — CCFs

Description of claim or assetCCF (%)
Interest rate contracts:
•    residual maturity 1 year or less0
•    residual maturity > 1 year to 5 years0.5
•    residual maturity > 5 years1.5
Foreign exchange and gold contracts:
•    residual maturity 1 year or less1
•    residual maturity > 1 year to 5 years5
•    residual maturity > 5 years7.5
Equity contracts:
•    residual maturity 1 year or less6
•    residual maturity > 1 year to 5 years8
•    residual maturity > 5 years10
Precious metal contracts (other than gold):
•    residual maturity 1 year or less7
•    residual maturity > 1 year to 5 years7
•    residual maturity > 5 years8
Other commodity contracts (other than precious metals):
•    residual maturity 1 year or less10
•    residual maturity > 1 year to 5 years12
•    residual maturity > 5 years15
Other market-related contracts: 
•    residual maturity 1 year or less10
•    residual maturity > 1 year to 5 years12
•    residual maturity > 5 years15
(2) PFE must be based on effective rather than apparent notional amounts. If the stated notional amount of a contract is leveraged or enhanced by the structure of the transaction, the firm must use the effective notional amount when calculating PFE.
(3) No PFE is calculated for single currency floating/floating interest rate swaps because the credit exposure on such contracts must be evaluated solely on the basis of their mark-to-market values.

(4) For contracts that are structured to settle outstanding exposures following specified payment dates on which the terms are reset (so that the mark-to-market value of the contract is zero on the specified dates), the residual maturity must be set equal to the time until the next reset date. In the case of interest rate contracts with those features and a remaining maturity of more than 1 year, the CCF is subject to a minimum of 0.5% even if there are reset dates of a shorter maturity.

Guidance
For example, a principal resetting cross-currency swap or a settled-to-market derivative where, at the next reset date, the outstanding exposure is settled and the terms are reset so that the fair value of the contract is zero. A derivative contract with a mandatory break (where there is a legal contractual obligation on both parties to terminate the transaction by the mandatory break date) would also be eligible where the outstanding exposure is settled completely.
(5) For a contract with 2 or more exchanges of principal, the CCF must be multiplied by the number of exchanges of principal still to be made.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.11 CCFs for items with terms subject to reset
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.B Modified current exposure method
BANK 4.6A.11 CCFs for items with terms subject to reset
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) For an item that is structured to settle outstanding exposures after specified payment dates on which the terms are reset (that is, the marked to market value of the item becomes zero on the specified dates), the period to the next reset date must be taken to be the item’s residual maturity.
(2) For an interest rate item of that kind that is taken to have a residual maturity of more than 1 year, the CCF to be applied must not be less than 0.5% even if there are reset dates of a shorter maturity.
(3) For an item with 2 or more exchanges of principal, the CCF must be multiplied by the number of remaining exchanges under the item.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

(2) PFEgross is the sum of the firm’s potential future credit exposures for each transaction covered by a netting agreement (except transactions covered by the definition of NCCE in subrule 4.6A.9 (4)) as if no netting would occur. QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.13 Calculating PFEadj — transactions covered by eligible bilateral netting agreements — net to gross ratio
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.B Modified current exposure method
BANK 4.6A.13 Calculating PFEadj — transactions covered by eligible bilateral netting agreements — net to gross ratio
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) The net to gross ratio (NGR) is the ratio of the net current exposure of all the transactions covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement to the gross current credit exposure (GCCE) of those transactions. GCCE for such a netting agreement is the sum of the mark-to-market values of all the transactions covered by the agreement (except transactions covered by the definition of NCCE in subrule 4.6A.9 (4)) with a positive mark-to-market value, with no offsetting against contracts with a negative mark-to-market value.
Note In relation to how eligible netting agreements may be applied for the purposes of this Division, see Subdivision 4.5.E.1.
(2) NGR reflects the risk-reducing portfolio effects of netted transactions in relation to current credit exposure:
(3) NGR may be calculated either counterparty-by-counterparty or in the aggregate.
(4) A banking business firm must consistently use either the counterparty-by-counterparty approach or the aggregate approach to calculate NGR¸ and must notify the Regulatory Authority of the approach that it intends to use.
(5) In the counterparty-by-counterparty approach, a unique NGR is applied to each counterparty to calculate the CEA of transactions with that counterparty. NGR is the NCCE of all transactions with an individual counterparty covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement (that is, NCCEindividual) divided by the GCCE of all the transactions with that counterparty covered by the netting agreement (that is, GCCEindividual).
(6) In the aggregate approach, a single NGR is calculated and applied to all counterparties to calculate CEA for transactions with each of those counterparties. NGR is the ratio of the sum of all NCCEs of all transactions with all counterparties subject to any eligible bilateral netting agreement (that is, NCCEaggregate) to the sum of all of the GCCEs for all transactions of all counterparties subject to such a netting agreement (that is, GCCEaggregate).
(7) In calculating GCCEindividual or GCCEaggregate, negative mark-to-market values of transactions with a counterparty cannot be used to offset positive mark-to-market values of transactions with that counterparty or any other counterparty included in the aggregate calculations.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

BANK 4.6A.14 Calculating PFE — single-name credit default swaps and single-name total-rate-of-return swaps
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must calculate the counterparty credit risk requirement for single-name credit default swaps and single-name total-rate-of-return swaps in the trading book using the potential future credit exposure CCFs in table 4.6A.14.

Table 4.6A.14 Potential future exposure credit conversion factors

Type of swap
 		 CCF
Protection buyer (%) Protection seller (%)
Credit default swap
Qualifying reference obligation (see subrule (3)) 5 5
Non-qualifying reference obligation 10 10
Total-rate-of-return swap
Qualifying reference obligation (see subrule (3)) 5 5
Non-qualifying reference obligation 10 10
(2) For table 4.6A.14, the protection seller of a credit default swap is subject to the add-on factor only if the credit default swap is subject to closeout on the insolvency of the protection buyer while the underlying asset is still solvent. The add-on must be capped to the amount of unpaid premiums.
(3) In table 4.6A.14:
qualifying reference obligation includes an obligation arising from items relating to:
(a) securities that are rated “investment grade” by at least 2 ECRAs; or
(b) securities that are unrated (or rated “investment grade” by only 1 ECRA), but:
(i) are issued by an issuer whose equity is included in a main index used in a recognised exchange; and
Note For the list of recognised exchanges, see Schedule 1.
(ii) are approved by the Regulatory Authority, on application by the banking business firm concerned, to be of comparable investment quality.
(4) A banking business firm, in calculating the counterparty credit risk requirement for an nth-to-default credit derivative transaction (such as a first-to-default transaction), must use the add-on determined by the nth-lowest credit quality underlying asset in the relevant basket.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.17 CVA risk capital charge to be calculated
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.B Modified current exposure method
BANK 4.6A.17 CVA risk capital charge to be calculated
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must calculate its CVA risk capital charge for the risk of mark-to-market losses on the expected counterparty credit risk (CVA loss) for:
(a) all bilateral OTC derivative transactions; and
(b) centrally cleared transactions that are required to be treated as bilateral.
(2) Subject to any direction under subrule (3) or approval under subrule (4), the firm must set its CVA risk capital charge equal to the amount of capital required for its risk-weighted credit exposure for counterparty credit default risk.
(3) The Regulatory Authority may direct a banking business firm to apply a CVA risk capital charge:
(a) of a specified amount; or
(b) that is calculated in a specified way.
(4) A banking business firm may apply to the Authority for approval to determine its CVA risk capital requirement in accordance with the Basel III Framework, as in effect from time to time.
(5) If the Authority grants an approval under subrule (4), the Authority may specify parameters or formulas to be used, or assumptions to be made, in applying the framework.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.19 Transactions that Division 4.6A.C applies to
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.19 Transactions that Division 4.6A.C applies to
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This Division applies to all transactions that are centrally cleared (including OTC derivative transactions, exchange-traded derivative transactions, SFTs and long settlement transactions).
(2) For the purposes of this Division, a long settlement transaction must be treated as an OTC derivative transaction.
(3) Transactions that result in exposures arising from the settlement of cash transactions only (for example, equities, fixed income, spot foreign exchange and spot commodities) are not subject to the treatment in this Division.
(4) For transactions cleared through a QCCP, a banking business firm must apply:
(a) the counterparty credit risk requirements for exposures to a QCCP and the firm’s clients in rules 4.6A.26 to 4.6A.36; and
(b) the risk management requirements in rule 4.6A.40.
(5) For transactions cleared through a CCP that is not a QCCP, a banking business firm must apply:
(a) the counterparty credit risk capital requirements for exposures to a non-qualifying CCP in rule 4.6A.37; and
(b) the risk management requirements in rule 4.6A.40.
(6) If a CCP ceases to qualify as a QCCP, then, for the purposes of this Subdivision, a banking business firm may continue, for 3 months afterwards, to treat transactions with the CCP as though the CCP were still a QCCP (subject to any direction by the Regulatory Authority). After that period, the firm must treat exposures to the CCP according to rule 4.6A.37.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

(6) If a CCP ceases to qualify as a QCCP, then, for the purposes of this Subdivision, a banking business firm may continue, for 3 months afterwards, to treat transactions with the CCP as though the CCP were still a QCCP (subject to any direction by the Regulatory Authority). After that period, the firm must treat exposures to the CCP according to rule 4.6A.37 . Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

endnotes: Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.20 Key concept — qualifying CCP
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A qualifying central counterparty (or qualifying CCP or QCCP) is an entity for which all of the following are true:
(a) it is authorised or licensed to operate as a CCP (including a licence granted by way of confirming an exemption);
(b) it is permitted by a financial regulator to operate as a CCP with respect to the products offered;
(c) it satisfies either subrule (2) or subrule (3);
(d) it publishes sufficient information about the factors necessary to calculate its regulatory capital:
(i) to allow each of its clearing members to calculate the member’s capital requirement for the member’s contributions to the CCP’s default fund; and
(ii) for the regulatory authority that supervises such a member to review and confirm that calculation.
(2) A CCP satisfies this subrule if it is based and prudentially supervised in a jurisdiction in which the relevant regulatory authority:
(a) has established rules and regulations that are consistent with the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures issued jointly, under that title, by the Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures of the BCBS and the International Organization of Securities Commissions; and
(b) has publicly indicated that it applies those rules and regulations to the CCP on a continuing basis.
(3) A CCP satisfies this subrule if the Regulatory Authority has determined, by notice published on an approved website, that the CCP satisfies the Principles mentioned in paragraph (2) (a).
(4) A non-qualifying CCP is a CCP that is not a QCCP.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.21 Key concept — margin
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) In this Division:
initial margin is the funded collateral posted to a CCP by a clearing member or client to mitigate the CCP’s potential future exposure to the member or client (including collateral in excess of the minimum required amount, but only if there are appropriate arrangements to prevent the clearing member or client withdrawing the excess).
Guidance
Initial margin does not include a contribution to a CCP for a mutualised loss-sharing arrangement (a default fund contribution).
variation margin is funded collateral posted on a daily or intraday basis to a CCP to mitigate movements in ongoing mark-to-market exposure.
(2) For this Division:
(a) a transaction is considered to be margined if variation margin is exchanged; and
(b) a transaction is considered to be unmargined if no variation margin is exchanged;
whether or not there is collateral other than variation margin.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.22 Key concept — trade exposure
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A trade exposure is an exposure that a clearing member, or a client of a clearing member, has to a CCP, reflecting a measure of the current mark-to-market value (replacement cost) and the potential future exposure arising from transactions to which this Division applies (see rule 4.6A.5 (1)).
(2) Trade exposure is calculated on a bilateral basis, and must include the initial margin posted by a banking business firm, and any variation margin due to the firm from the CCP that has not yet been received.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.23 Other definitions for Division 4.6A.C
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) In this Division:
clearing member of a CCP means a member of, or a direct participant in, a CCP that is entitled to enter into transactions with the CCP.
clearing member firm means a banking business firm that is a clearing member of a CCP.
client of a clearing member firm means a party to a transaction with a CCP through the firm, where the firm either:
(a) acts as a financial intermediary; or
(b) guarantees the client’s performance to the CCP.
(2) A banking business firm is a client firm if:
(a) the firm clears through a QCCP indirectly as a client of a clearing member that acts as a financial intermediary (that is, the clearing member completes an offsetting transaction with the QCCP); or
(b) the firm enters into a transaction with a QCCP, and a clearing member firm guarantees the firm’s performance.
(3) In this Division, a reference to collateral posted by a banking business firm to a QCCP includes:
(a) initial margin;
(b) any variation margin due to the firm from the QCCP but not yet received;
(c) cash, securities, and other pledged assets; and
(d) any excess initial or variation margin;
but does not include any default fund contribution.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.24 Transactions settled to market
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm may treat a transaction as settled-to-market, and as being an unmargined transaction with remaining maturity (Mi) equal to the time until the next exchange of variation margin, if:
(a) the outstanding exposure is settled by variation margin and the terms are reset so that the fair value of the contract is zero; and
(b) the firm has a legal opinion to support that treatment.
Guidance
A centrally cleared derivative transaction is said to have been settled-to-market if the variation margin paid constitutes settlement of the exposure, as opposed to the posting of collateral.
(2) However, the remaining maturity of an unmargined transaction is subject to a minimum of 10 business days.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.25 Centrally cleared transactions under bilateral agreements
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.25 Centrally cleared transactions under bilateral agreements
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
For an exchange-traded derivative where the transaction between the clearing member and client is conducted under a bilateral agreement, a banking business firm that is either a clearing member firm or a client firm must treat the transaction as an OTC derivative transaction for the purposes of this Part.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.26 Exposures from transactions cleared through QCCP
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.26 Exposures from transactions cleared through QCCP
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) For transactions cleared through a QCCP, a clearing member firm must calculate each of the following counterparty credit risk requirements:
(a) trade exposure RWA on the firm’s trade exposure to the QCCP according to rules 4.6A.27 to 4.6A.32;
(b) a default fund capital charge on the default fund contribution to the QCCP, according to Division 4.6A.D;
(c) if the firm has provided a guarantee of a client transaction to the QCCP or acts as a financial intermediary between a client and the QCCP (that is, the firm completes an offsetting transaction with the QCCP) — default risk RWA and a CVA risk capital charge on the counterparty credit risk exposure to its client, according to rule 4.6A.41;
(d) if the firm has provided a guarantee to a client by undertaking an obligation to reimburse the client for any losses suffered due to changes in transaction value if a QCCP defaults — trade exposure RWA and a default fund capital charge on the guaranteed transaction.
(2) A banking business firm that is acting as a client of a clearing member to a QCCP must apply the counterparty credit risk requirements set out in rule 4.6A.34.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.27 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.27 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) To calculate trade exposure RWA, a clearing member firm must calculate its trade exposure to the QCCP, and must apply the relevant risk weights, according to rules 4.6A.28 to 4.6A.32.
(2) For the clearing member firm-to-QCCP leg of a transaction cleared through a QCCP, a clearing member firm must calculate its trade exposure to the QCCP:
(a) for derivative transactions — by the modified CEM set out in Division 4.6A.B; and
(b) for SFTs — in accordance with rule 4.6A.7 (2).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.28 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — use of netting
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.28 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — use of netting
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) When a clearing member firm calculates its trade exposure to a QCCP, the firm may take a netting agreement (including a master netting agreement or a netting contract with a counterparty) into account if the agreement is an eligible bilateral netting agreement.
Guidance
If the agreement is an eligible bilateral netting agreement, settlement is legally enforceable on a net basis in an event of default regardless of whether the counterparty is insolvent or bankrupt.
Note In relation to how eligible netting agreements may be applied for the purposes of this Division, see Subdivision 4.5.E.1.
(2) If a clearing member firm cannot demonstrate that a netting agreement meets the requirements in subrule (1), it must treat each single transaction with the QCCP as a netting set of its own for the calculation of trade exposure.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.29 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — use of collateral
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.29 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — use of collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
If a clearing member firm first collects collateral from a client for a client-cleared trade and then passes that collateral on to a QCCP, the firm may recognise the collateral for both the QCCP-to-firm leg and the firm-to-client leg of the transaction.

Note For the meaning of references in this Subdivision to collateral posted to a QCCP, see rule 4.6A.23 (3).

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.30 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — transactions for own purposes
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.30 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — transactions for own purposes
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
If a clearing member firm is transacting with a QCCP for its own purposes, the firm must apply a 2% risk weight to its trade exposure to the QCCP (excluding any posted collateral that is eligible for a zero risk weight under rule 4.6A.36 (3)).

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.31 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — clearing services to clients
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.31 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — clearing services to clients
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
If a clearing member firm offers clearing services to clients, the firm must apply a 2% risk weight to any trade exposure to the QCCP (excluding any posted collateral that is eligible for a zero risk weight under rule 4.6A.36 (3)) that arises from an obligation to reimburse a client for any losses suffered because of changes in transaction value in the event that the QCCP defaults.

doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.32 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — use of collateral

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.33 Clearing member firm’s exposure to clients
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.33 Clearing member firm’s exposure to clients
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
For the firm-to-client leg of a transaction with a QCCP, a clearing member firm must calculate its counterparty credit risk requirements on its exposures to its clients, as set out in rules 4.6A.8 and 4.6A.17 (respectively, default risk RWA and CVA risk capital charge).

doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.34 Client firm’s exposure to clearing member firm and QCCP
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
A client firm of a clearing member firm:

(a) must calculate a trade exposure to the clearing member firm or QCCP, as the case may be, using the modified CEM; and
(b) must assign a risk weight to the trade exposure according to the requirements in rule 4.6A.35.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.35 Client firm’s trade exposure to clearing member — risk weight
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.35 Client firm’s trade exposure to clearing member — risk weight
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A client firm must treat its trade exposure to a clearing member (excluding any posted collateral that is eligible for a zero risk weight under rule 4.6A.36 (3)) as if it were a clearing member firm’s trade exposure to the QCCP, and must apply the requirements set out in rules 4.6A.27 to 4.6A.30, if the following conditions are satisfied:
(a) the QCCP identifies the offsetting transactions as client transactions, and the collateral to support them is held in a way that would prevent any losses to the firm in the event of the default or insolvency of the clearing member concerned or any 1 or more of the clearing member’s other clients;
(b) the collateral to support the offsetting transactions is held in a way that would prevent any losses to the firm in the event of the joint default or insolvency of the clearing member and any of its other clients; and
(c) the relevant laws, regulation, rules, or contractual or administrative arrangements provide that offsetting transactions with a clearing member are highly likely to continue to be indirectly transacted through the QCCP, or by the QCCP, if that member defaults or becomes insolvent.
Guidance
In such circumstances, the client positions and collateral with the QCCP will be transferred at market value unless the client firm requests to close out the position at market value.
Note For the meaning of references in this Subdivision to collateral posted to a QCCP, see rule 4.6A.23 (3).
(2) For paragraph (1) (a):
(a) the firm must have obtained a legal opinion, and must obtain any subsequent opinions it considers necessary, to ensure that the arrangements continue to be enforceable; and
(b) the firm must have a well-founded basis to conclude that, in the event of legal challenge, the relevant courts and administrative authorities would find the arrangements to be legal, valid, binding and enforceable under the laws of the relevant jurisdictions.
(3) If only paragraphs (1) (a) and (c) are satisfied, the firm must apply a risk weight of 4% to its calculated trade exposure to the QCCP (excluding any posted collateral that is eligible for a zero risk weight under rule 4.6A.36 (3)). The applicable risk weight on collateral posted by the firm that is included in the definition of trade exposure must be determined according to rule 4.6A.36.
(4) In any other case, the firm must treat the exposure as bilateral for the purposes of the counterparty credit risk requirements, and must apply the modified current exposure method to calculate both default risk RWA and a CVA risk capital charge).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.content_text: (1) A client firm must treat its trade exposure to a clearing member (excluding any posted collateral that is eligible for a zero risk weight under rule 4.6A.36 (3)) as if it were a clearing member firm’s trade exposure to the QCCP, and must apply the requirements set out in rules 4.6A.27 to 4.6A.30 , if the following conditions are satisfied: (a) the QCCP identifies the offsetting transactions as client transactions, and the collateral to support them is held in a way that would prevent any losses to the firm in the event of the default or insolvency of the clearing member concerned or any 1 or more of the clearing member’s other clients; (b) the collateral to support the offsetting transactions is held in a way that would prevent any losses to the firm in the event of the joint default or insolvency of the clearing member and any of its other clients; and (c) the relevant laws, regulation, rules, or contractual or administrative arrangements provide that offsetting transactions with a clearing member are highly likely to continue to be indirectly transacted through the QCCP, or by the QCCP, if that member defaults or becomes insolvent. QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.36 Exposures arising from collateral posted to QCCP — risk weight
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.36 Exposures arising from collateral posted to QCCP — risk weight
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If a banking business firm has posted collateral to a QCCP (but is not a clearing member of the QCCP), the firm must risk-weight those assets in accordance with the banking book or trading book treatment that would apply to the assets if they had not been posted as collateral.
Note For the meaning of references in this Subdivision to collateral posted to a QCCP, see rule 4.6A.23 (3).
(2) In addition, the posted assets or collateral are subject to counterparty credit risk requirements regardless of whether they are in the banking or the trading book. For collateral posted by a clearing member firm to a QCCP, the firm:
(a) may apply a zero risk weight to all posted collateral that is held by a custodian if the collateral is bankruptcy-remote from the QCCP;, and
(b) must apply a 2% risk weight to all posted collateral held by the QCCP that is not held in a bankruptcy-remote way.
Guidance
A custodian might be a trustee, agent, pledgee, secured creditor or any other person that holds the collateral in a way that does not give the person a beneficial interest in the collateral and would not result in its being subject to legally-enforceable claims by the person’s creditors, or to a court-ordered stay of the return of the collateral, if the person becomes insolvent or bankrupt.
(3) For collateral posted by a client firm to a QCCP, the firm:
(a) may apply a zero risk weight to all posted collateral that is held by a custodian if the collateral is bankruptcy-remote from:
(i) the QCCP;
(ii) the relevant clearing member; and
(iii) the clearing member’s other clients;
(b) must apply a 2% risk weight to all posted collateral held by the QCCP if:
(i) the collateral is not bankruptcy-remote from the QCCP, but
(ii) all of the conditions in paragraphs 4.6A.35 (1) (a), (b) and (c) are satisfied; and
(c) must apply a 4% risk weight to all posted collateral held by the QCCP if:
(i) the collateral is not bankruptcy-remote from the QCCP; and
(i) only the conditions in paragraphs 4.6A.35 (1) (a) and (c) are satisfied.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.37 Exposures arising from transactions cleared through non-qualifying CCP
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.37 Exposures arising from transactions cleared through non-qualifying CCP
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
For transactions with a non-qualifying CCP, a banking business firm must calculate the following counterparty credit risk capital requirements:

(a) trade exposure RWA for:
(i) the firm’s trade exposure to the CCP (including any exposure that arises because the firm has guaranteed a client trade); and
(ii) any exposure to the firm’s clients;
each calculated in accordance with the modified current exposure method and risk-weighted in accordance with Division 4.4.B; and
(b) a CVA risk capital charge for the CCP and any clients, calculated in accordance with the modified current exposure method.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.38 Transactions cleared through non-qualifying CCP — default fund RWA
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.38 Transactions cleared through non-qualifying CCP — default fund RWA
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
For transactions with a non-qualifying CCP, a banking business firm that is a clearing member of the CCP must calculate a default fund RWA as follows:

RWA = 1,250% × DF

where:

RWA is the firm’s risk-weighted assets for its default fund exposure to the CCP.

DF is the firm’s pre-funded contribution to the CCP’s default fund, plus a proportion (directed by the Regulatory Authority) of the firm’s unfunded contributions that are liable to be paid if the CCP so requires.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.39 Cap on capital requirement for exposures to QCCPs
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
If the amount of capital required for a banking business firm’s exposure to a QCCP due to its trade exposure and default fund contribution is higher than it would be if the CCP were a non-qualifying CCP, the required capital is capped at the latter amount.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.40 Risk management requirements for centrally cleared exposures
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.40 Risk management requirements for centrally cleared exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must establish a process for monitoring by, and regular reporting to, the firm’s senior management of all of its exposures to CCPs, including exposures arising from:
(a) trading through a CCP; and
(b) CCP membership obligations such as default fund contributions.
(2) A banking business firm must also establish a process for regularly reporting, to its governing body, material exposures to CCPs.
(3) A banking business firm must ensure that it maintains adequate capital for its exposures to CCPs, regardless of whether any CCP to which the firm is exposed is a QCCP. In particular, a banking business firm must consider whether it might need to hold capital in excess of the minimum capital requirements if, for example:
(a) its dealings with a CCP give rise to higher risk exposure; or
(b) based on the firm’s dealings with a CCP, it is unclear whether the CCP is a QCCP.
(4) For all of its exposures to CCPs, a clearing member firm must assess (through appropriate scenario analysis and stress testing) whether the level of capital held against the exposures adequately addresses the inherent risks of those transactions. The assessment must take into account potential future or contingent exposure resulting from:
(a) future drawings on default fund commitments; and
(b) any secondary commitments to take over or replace offsetting transactions from the clients of another clearing member that defaults or becomes insolvent.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.41 Membership of CCPs
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A clearing member firm must have an appropriate risk management framework to cover its activities as a clearing member. The framework must include:
(a) regular assessment of the risks (financial, operational and reputational) that might arise from its membership of, and conduct of business through, a CCP and from any similar engagement with 2 or more CCPs;
(b) the application of appropriate systems and controls to monitor, on a continuing basis, those risks, and to manage them (including the application of limits on potential risk exposures); and
(c) the maintenance of appropriate capital cover against those risks, including capital cover:
(i) relating to business conducted through a CCP; and
(ii) for any funded support that the firm has provided, or any contingent support that the firm may be committed to provide, to a CCP.
(2) Membership of a CCP must not expose a banking business firm to an unlimited contingent liability to support the CCP.
(3) A banking business firm must notify the Regulatory Authority before applying for membership of a CCP.
(4) A banking business firm that is a member of a CCP must notify the Authority of any proposed changes to:
(a) the contractual provisions or rules governing its membership; or
(b) business undertaken through the CCP;
that may affect the level of exposure incurred from conducting business through the CCP or from any support (funded or unfunded) that has to be provided to the CCP.
(5) A banking business firm must notify the Authority of any operational or financial risks arising from its membership of, and conduct of business through, a CCP that could affect the firm’s operations, financial position or reputation.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.42 Power of Regulatory Authority in relation to exposures to CCPs
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
BANK 4.6A.42 Power of Regulatory Authority in relation to exposures to CCPs
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
The Regulatory Authority may direct a banking business firm to hold, in relation to its exposures to CCPs, more capital than the minimum required by this Part.

Example

The Authority might do so in relation to a banking business firm’s exposures to a particular QCCP if:

• an external assessment has found material shortcomings in the regulation of the QCCP; and
• the QCCP’s regulator has not publicly addressed the shortcomings.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.44 Treatment of shared default funds
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.D Capital charge for default fund exposures to QCCPs
BANK 4.6A.44 Treatment of shared default funds
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If a QCCP’s default fund is shared between products or types of business that give rise only to settlement risk and products or types of business that this Part applies to (see rule 4.6A.5), all contributions to the fund must be treated as set out in this Division, without apportionment to different classes or types of business or products.
(2) If a QCCP’s default fund is segregated by product types and is accessible only for specific product types, the capital charge for the default fund exposures must be calculated for each product type that gives rise to counterparty credit risk.
(3) If a QCCP’s pre-funded own resources are shared among product types, then, in calculating a clearing member firm’s default fund exposure to the QCCP, those resources must be allocated to each of the calculations in proportion to the respective product-specific EADs.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.45 Default fund capital charge for clearing member firm
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.D Capital charge for default fund exposures to QCCPs
BANK 4.6A.45 Default fund capital charge for clearing member firm
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) The default fund capital charge for a clearing member firm’s default fund exposure is obtained by a 2-step process, as follows:
(a) step 1 — calculate a risk-sensitive measure of the exposure that the QCCP has to its clearing members and their clients (see rules 4.6A.46 to 4.6A.49);
(b) step 2 — calculate the default fund capital charge for the firm (see rule 4.6A.50).
(2) A banking business firm that is a clearing member of a QCCP may rely on the QCCP to undertake the calculations required by subrule (1) (a), and to provide the firm with the necessary data to calculate its default fund capital charge, but only if the QCCP’s calculations meet the following conditions:
(a) the calculations are undertaken transparently, and the QCCP shares enough information:
(i) to enable a supervisor of the QCCP to oversee those calculations;
(ii) to enable the firm to calculate the default fund capital charge on its own default fund contributions; and
(iii) to enable the Regulatory Authority to review and confirm the calculations, if it is asked to do so;
(b) all the calculations (that is, both steps and the inputs to both steps) are done:
(i) at least quarterly (or more frequently, if the Authority so directs); and
(ii) after any material change (such as the QCCP starting to clear a new product, a material change to the number or exposure of cleared transactions, or a material change to the QCCP’s financial resources);
(c) the QCCP provides the Authority, at least quarterly or on the Authority’s request, with sufficient aggregate information about the composition of the QCCP’s exposures to its clearing members, and the information provided to the clearing members for calculation purposes (including the calculation for step 1 and the CCP-level inputs used in step 2).
(3) If any condition in subrule (2) is not met, the firm must treat its default fund exposure to the QCCP as if the QCCP were a non-qualifying CCP. Therefore, the firm must calculate its default fund RWA in accordance with rule 4.6A.38.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.6A.46 Calculating default fund capital charge, step 1 —QCCP’s exposure to clearing members
doc_path: BANK Division 4.6A.D Capital charge for default fund exposures to QCCPs
BANK 4.6A.46 Calculating default fund capital charge, step 1 —QCCP’s exposure to clearing members
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Step 1 is to compute KCCP, the hypothetical capital requirement of the QCCP due to its counterparty credit risk exposures to all of its clearing member firms and their clients, as follows:
where:
RW = 20% (or a higher percentage directed by the Regulatory Authority).
EADm is the exposure amount of the QCCP to the mth clearing member, calculated according to rules 4.6A.47 to 4.6A.49.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.1 What Part 4.7 does
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
This Part sets out the obligations of a banking business firm in relation to:

(a) classifying exposures as performing or non-performing (Division 4.7.B);
(b) the application of forbearance (Division 4.7.C); and
(c) making provision for credit losses (Division 4.7.D).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.2 Assets etc that Part 4.7 applies to
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.2 Assets etc that Part 4.7 applies to
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This Part applies in relation to the following assets and items:
(a) loans, debt securities and other amounts due (such as interest) that are on a banking business firm’s balance sheet and that the firm holds in its banking book;
(b) loan commitments and financial guarantees, and similar items, off the balance sheet;
(c) any other items that the firm must take into account in calculating its risk-weighted assets for credit risk.
(2) For this Part, a banking business firm must take into account the whole of the exposure from an asset or item (even if the relevant non-performance is of only part of the obligor’s obligations), and must apply the classification to that whole amount. In particular, unpaid interest must be taken into account.
(3) For an off-balance-sheet item, such as a loan commitment, the exposure must be taken to be the whole uncancellable nominal amount.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.5 Regulatory Authority can direct firm to reclassify assets etc
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) The Regulatory Authority may at any time require a banking business firm to demonstrate that the firm’s classification of its assets, and its provisions, are adequate for prudential purposes.
(2) The Authority may direct the firm to reclassify its assets or increase the levels of its provisions for credit losses if the Authority considers that the asset classifications are inaccurate, or the provisions are inadequate, for prudential purposes.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.5 Guidance
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.5 Regulatory Authority can direct firm to reclassify assets etc
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
If the Regulatory Authority considers that existing or foreseen deterioration in asset quality is of concern or that a banking business firm’s provisions do not fully reflect expected losses, the Authority may require the firm to adjust its classifications of individual assets, increase its levels of provisions or capital and, if necessary, impose other remedial measures.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.6 Information to firm’s governing body
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm’s governing body must obtain timely information on the condition of the firm’s assets, including the classification of assets, the levels of provisions and problem assets.
(2) The information must include summary results of the latest asset review, comparative trends in the overall quality of problem assets, and measurements of existing or anticipated deterioration in asset quality and losses expected.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
1 A review of a firm’s write-offs can help identify whether the firm’s provisioning policy results in over-provisioning or under-provisioning.
2 The Regulatory Authority regularly assesses trends and concentrations in risk and risk build-up across financial entities in relation to problem assets. In making the assessment, the Authority takes into account any observed concentration in the CRM techniques used by firms and the potential effect on the efficacy of those techniques in reducing loss. The Authority would consider the adequacy of provisions for a firm (and the industry in general) in the light of the assessment.
3 The Authority might seek the opinion of external experts in assessing the adequacy of a firm’s policies for grading and classifying its assets and the appropriateness and robustness of the levels of its provisions.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.8 Write-downs and write-offs — defaulted exposures
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.8 Write-downs and write-offs — defaulted exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If a banking business firm is satisfied that payment of a defaulted exposure is unlikely, the firm must write the exposure off in whole or in part, in accordance with the applicable accounting standard.
(2) A banking business firm must have appropriate policies and procedures in relation to the writing off of defaulted exposures. In particular, the policies must provide for such exposures to be written off within a period approved by the Regulatory Authority.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must classify the exposures in relation to which this Part applies (except for the exposure classes mentioned in subrule (2)) as either performing or non-performing.
(2) The excepted exposure classes are the following:
(a) derivatives;
(b) exposures held in the firm’s trading book.
(3) For this Part, an exposure is classified as performing if:
(a) there is no uncertainty about the timely repayment of the outstanding amounts; and
(b) it is currently in regular payment status with prompt payments.
(4) For this Part, an exposure is classified as non-performing if any of the following is true:
(a) it is defaulted (see rule 4.4.81);
(b) it is credit-impaired (that is, its valuation has been reduced because of a deterioration of its creditworthiness) according to the applicable accounting standard;
(c) it is a material exposure and is more than 90 days past due (see subrule (5));
(d) there is reason to believe that full repayment according to the contractual terms is unlikely unless the firm realises collateral, whether or not the exposure is current (and if it is not current, regardless of the number of days it is past due).
Examples of circumstances in which full repayment according to the contractual terms is unlikely
• the firm concerned puts the credit obligation on non-accrued status
• the firm makes a charge-off or account-specific provision resulting from a material perceived decline in credit quality since the firm took on the exposure
• the firm sells other credit obligations from the same counterparty at a material credit-related economic loss
• the firm applies a distressed forbearance to the credit obligation and this is likely to result in a diminished financial obligation because of material forgiveness, or postponement, of principal, interest or fees
• the firm has filed for the counterparty’s bankruptcy or a similar order in relation to the counterparty’s credit obligation to the firm
• the counterparty has sought, or has been placed in, bankruptcy or similar protection and as a result has avoided or delayed the repayment of the obligation.
(5) For the purposes of this Part, an exposure is past due if any amount due under the relevant contract (interest, principal, a fee or any other amount) was not paid in full on the date when it was due. An exposure must be treated as past due from the first day of missed payment, even if the amount of the exposure or the amount unpaid is not material.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.11 Application of classification to off-balance-sheet exposures
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.11 Application of classification to off-balance-sheet exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must classify an off-balance-sheet exposure as non-performing if the firm has reason to believe that the firm is unlikely to recoup, in a timely manner, the full amount that it may be required to advance.
(2) A commitment must be classified as non-performing if the creditworthiness of the borrower has deteriorated to the extent that the timely repayment in full by the borrower of any drawdown or associated interest payments or fees is unlikely.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.12 Application of classification to derivative exposures
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.12 Application of classification to derivative exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If a banking business firm considers it unlikely that it will receive timely repayment, in full, of cash flow entitlements which are or will be due from a counterparty to a derivative transaction, it must classify such an exposure as non-performing.
(2) For the purposes of measuring non-performance, the firm must calculate its derivative exposures to counterparties using the modified current exposure method. Potential exposure add-ons applied in calculating such exposures must reflect the nature of the individual facility involved.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

BANK 4.7.13 Classification independent of accounting treatment
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
The classification of an exposure as performing or non-performing under this Part does not affect its accounting treatment. Also, the accounting treatment of an exposure does not determine its classification under this Part.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.14 Effect of collateral
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) When classifying an exposure, a banking business firm must not treat collateral or other risk-mitigation arrangements as affecting the classification of the exposure.
(2) However, the firm may take collateral into account in assessing the borrower’s economic incentive to pay.
(3) The firm must not treat the collateralisation of an exposure as affecting the exposure’s past-due status or the counting of past-due days.
(4) The firm must classify an exposure as non-performing for this Part if the exposure satisfies the conditions for being so classified in rule 4.7.10 (4), even if the value of collateral held is more than the amount of the past-due exposure.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.15 Level of application
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If a banking business firm has more than 1 exposure to a particular non-retail counterparty, the firm must consider all of its exposures to that counterparty as non-performing if a material exposure to the counterparty is non-performing. That is, non-performing status is applied to the counterparty.
(2) In the case of a banking business firm’s exposure to a retail counterparty, non-performing status is applied to the transaction. However, if the firm has more than 1 exposure to a particular retail counterparty, the firm must, when deciding about the status of 1 such exposure, consider the status of the other exposures.
Guidance
QFC banking business firms are not permitted to undertake retail banking.
(3) If a banking business firm has exposures to 2 or more members of a corporate group, the firm may apply non-performing status to each member. When the firm is deciding about the status of an exposure to such a member, the firm must take into account the status of its exposure to another member.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.16 Reclassification of non-performing exposures as performing
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.16 Reclassification of non-performing exposures as performing
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm may reclassify a non-performing exposure as performing only if all of the following are true:
(a) no exposure of the firm to the relevant counterparty is 90 days or more past due;
(b) subject to subrule (2), the counterparty has made repayments when due over a continuous period of at least:
(i) for a forborne exposure — 12 months (beginning on the first day on which a payment was due under the revised terms) (but see subrule (3)); or
(ii) in any other case — 90 days;
(c) the firm is satisfied, on the basis of an analysis of the counterparty’s financial situation, that full and timely repayment of the exposure is likely (but see subrule (3));
(d) the exposure is not classified as non-performing under rule 4.7.10.
(2) For paragraph (1) (c), the firm must not consider that full and timely repayment is likely unless the counterparty has made regular and timely payments of amounts equal to:
(a) if any amount was past due when the forbearance was applied — that amount; or
(b) if no amount was then past due — any amount that has been written off under the forbearance measures.
(3) In exceptional circumstances and with the Regulatory Authority’s approval, a banking business firm may reclassify a forborne non-performing exposure as performing if repayments have been made when due over a continuous period of less than 12 months, if all of the following conditions are satisfied:
(a) the firm has taken remedial measures to restructure the counterparty’s business;
(b) the measures:
(i) provide for the firm to participate directly in the counterparty’s business;
(ii) are immediately applicable; and
(iii) make the full repayment of the exposure likely.
(4) However, a banking business firm must not automatically reclassify a non-performing exposure as performing in any of the following circumstances:
(a) the firm has written off part of the exposure because it considers that the part written off is uncollectable;
(b) if the firm has taken possession of collateral on the exposure — until the collateral is actually disposed of and the firm has received the proceeds;
(c) the firm applies forbearance to the exposure or extends an existing application of forbearance.
Note For forbearance, see Division 4.7.C.
(5) The reclassification of a non-performing exposure as performing is to be at the same level (that is, at the level of the counterparty or at the level of the transaction) as when the exposure was classified as non-performing.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.16 Guidance — impairment and regulatory treatment of accounting provisions
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning

BANK 4.7.16 Guidance — impairment and regulatory treatment of accounting provisions
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
1 The Regulatory Authority expects authorised firms to adopt the following approach to the three provisioning stages:
• stage 1 (representing 12-month expected credit loss (ECL) provisions on performing loans): allocate to General Provisions (GP), if held against future, presently unidentified losses and, therefore, freely available to meet losses that subsequently materialise
• stage 2 (representing lifetime ECL provisions on underperforming loans): consider as Specific Provision for regulatory purposes. However, any portion that represents an amount for future, presently unidentified losses, would qualify as a GP
• stage 3 (representing lifetime ECL provisions on non-performing loans): consider as Specific Provision for regulatory purposes.
2 The GP amount that may be included in tier 2 capital remains unchanged at 1.25% limit on credit risk-weighted assets.
3 ECL accounting provisions for exposures may be treated as general provisions for regulatory purposes if the firm can satisfactorily demonstrate that:
• the provision amount is a purely forward looking amount for future, presently unidentified losses, set aside in consideration only of the consequences of potential events or scenarios that could lead to identified losses in the future; and
• there is no evidence the provision relates to the identified deterioration of particular assets or covers exposures on which any impairment or default (individually or collectively) has materialised into identified losses.
4 Accounting provisions for exposures not meeting both of the abovementioned criteria should be treated as specific provisions for regulatory purposes.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.16 Guidance — mapping of IFRS 9 expected credit losses to Regulatory Authority’s regulatory classification
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.16 Reclassification of non-performing exposures as performing
BANK 4.7.16 Guidance — mapping of IFRS 9 expected credit losses to Regulatory Authority’s regulatory classification
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
ECL impairment bucket Treatment in prudential returns
Stage 1: Includes exposures at initial recognition, and those where there is no significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition, or exposures that have low credit risk on reporting date. For exposures in Stage 1, interest is accrued on the gross carrying amount of the instrument and a 12-month ECL is factored into profit and loss (P&L) calculations. This correlates to the performing loans category and any provisions are treated as general provisions (GP), held against future, presently unidentified losses and, therefore, freely available to meet losses that subsequently materialise.
Stage 2: Comprises accounts with a significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition, but which have no objective evidence of impairment to date. Interest for accounts in Stage 2 is accrued on the gross carrying amount; however, a lifetime ECL is factored into P&L calculations This is mapped to the special mention category and any provisions are treated as specific provisions for regulatory purposes. However, any portion that represents an amount for future, presently unidentified losses, would qualify as GP.
Stage 3: Includes accounts that demonstrate evidence of impairment on the reporting date. For such assets, interest is accrued but suspended on the net carrying amount (net of provisions) and a lifetime ECL is factored into P&L calculations. This is mapped to the substandard, doubtful and loss categories, and provisions raised are to be treated as specific provisions.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)
