QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.17 Meaning of concession for Division 4.7.B
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.17 Meaning of concession for Division 4.7.B
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) For this Division, a banking business firm grants a concession to a counterparty if the firm grants special contractual terms and conditions (that would not have been granted if the counterparty had not experienced difficulties in meeting its financial commitments) so that the counterparty can sufficiently service its debt.
(2) For the purposes of this Division, there is no concession to the counterparty unless the counterparty is experiencing, or is likely to experience, financial difficulty.
(3) For the purposes of this Division, the counterparty is taken to be experiencing financial difficulty, or to be likely to do so, if the firm reasonably believes that the counterparty is experiencing financial difficulties, or is likely to do so.
Guidance
Financial difficulty can be identified even if an exposure is not in arrears. The following list of indications that a counterparty is in financial difficulty is not intended to be exhaustive:
• the counterparty is currently past due on a material exposure
• no exposure to the counterparty is currently past due, but a material one is likely to be past due in future (for instance, there has been a pattern of delinquency in payments on its material exposures) unless a concession is made
• the counterparty’s outstanding securities have been delisted, are in the process of being delisted, or are under threat of being delisted, from an exchange for non-compliance with the listing requirements or for financial reasons
• on the basis of the counterparty’s actual performance, and estimates and projections that take into account the counterparty’s current capabilities, the firm expects that, for the foreseeable future, the counterparty’s available cash flows will be insufficient to service all its loans or debt securities (both interest and principal) in accordance with the terms of the existing agreements
• the counterparty has already shown that it has difficulty in repaying in accordance with the credit categorisation scheme within the firm’s internal credit rating system
• a material exposure to the counterparty is classified as non-performing or would be so classified without the concessions
• the counterparty cannot obtain funds from other sources at an effective interest rate equal to the current market interest rate for similar loans or debt securities for a non-troubled counterparty.
(4) Refinancing an existing exposure with a new contract because of the counterparty’s financial difficulty is a concession, even if the terms of the new contract are no more favourable to the counterparty than those of the existing one.
(5) The main characteristic of a concession is that the firm would not extend loans or grant commitments to the counterparty, or purchase its debt securities, on such terms and conditions under normal market conditions.
(6) A concession might, but need not, result in a loss for the firm. A concession could be any of the following:
(a) a modification of the terms and conditions of the exposure;
(b) a total or partial refinance of the exposure;
(c) changes in the conditions of the existing exposure, giving more favourable terms for the counterparty;
(d) a supplementary agreement;
(e) the exercise of contractual rights that enable the counterparty to change the terms and conditions of the contract or to take on additional loans, debt securities or off-balance-sheet items at its own discretion.
Examples of concessions
• extending the loan term
• rescheduling the dates of principal or interest payments
• granting new or additional periods of non-payment (grace period)
• reducing the interest rate, resulting in an effective interest rate below the rate that counterparties with similar risk characteristics could obtain in the market
• capitalising arrears
• forgiving, deferring or postponing principal, interest or fees
• changing an amortising loan to an interest payment only
• releasing collateral or accepting lower levels of collateralisation
• allowing the conversion of debt to equity of the counterparty
• deferring recovery or collection action for extended periods
• easing of covenants
• refinancing an existing exposure with a new contract, even if the terms of the new contract are no more favourable for the counterparty than those of the existing exposure.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

(6) A concession might, but need not, result in a loss for the firm. A concession could be any of the following: (a) a modification of the terms and conditions of the exposure; (b) a total or partial refinance of the exposure; (c) changes in the conditions of the existing exposure, giving more favourable terms for the counterparty; (d) a supplementary agreement; (e) the exercise of contractual rights that enable the counterparty to change the terms and conditions of the contract or to take on additional loans, debt securities or off-balance-sheet items at its own discretion. Examples of concessions • extending the loan term • rescheduling the dates of principal or interest payments • granting new or additional periods of non-payment (grace period) • reducing the interest rate, resulting in an effective interest rate below the rate that counterparties with similar risk characteristics could obtain in the market • capitalising arrears • forgiving, deferring or postponing principal, interest or fees • changing an amortising loan to an interest payment only • releasing collateral or accepting lower levels of collateralisation • allowing the conversion of debt to equity of the counterparty • deferring recovery or collection action for extended periods • easing of covenants • refinancing an existing exposure with a new contract, even if the terms of the new contract are no more favourable for the counterparty than those of the existing exposure. Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

endnotes: Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.18 Meaning of forborne exposure and forbearance for Part 4.7
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.18 Meaning of forborne exposure and forbearance for Part 4.7
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) For this Part, an exposure of a banking business firm is a forborne exposure if the firm has granted a concession (see rule 4.7.17) to the counterparty.

Note There is no concession to a counterparty (and therefore no forbearance) unless the counterparty is experiencing, or is likely to experience, financial difficulty — see rule 4.7.17 (2).
(2) In the circumstances described in subrule (1), the firm has granted forbearance to the counterparty, and has applied forbearance to the exposure.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.19 Relationship between performance and forbearance
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.19 Relationship between performance and forbearance
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm may apply forbearance to either a performing or a non-performing exposure.
(2) If a banking business firm applies forbearance to a non-performing exposure, the firm must continue to classify the exposure as non-performing.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.20 Application of forbearance to performing exposures
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.20 Application of forbearance to performing exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This rule applies if a banking business firm applies forbearance to a performing exposure.
(2) The firm must decide whether the exposure meets the definition of a non-performing exposure, even if the forbearance results in a new exposure.
(3) If the firm decides that the original exposure would have been treated as non-performing when the firm applied the forbearance, the new exposure must be treated as non-performing.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.21 Criteria for exit from forbearance
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.21 Criteria for exit from forbearance
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) An exposure to which forbearance has been applied continues to be a forborne exposure until:
(a) all payments, according to the new contractual terms, have been made in a timely manner over a continuous period of at least 1 year; and
(b) the counterparty has resolved its financial difficulty.
(2) The period mentioned in subrule (1) (a) starts at the scheduled start of payments under the new contractual terms, regardless of whether the exposure was classified as performing or non-performing when the forbearance was granted.
(3) If another forbearance is applied to a forborne exposure before its release from the first forbearance, that period starts again with the new forbearance.
(4) Nothing prevents the period mentioned in subrule (1) (a) for an exposure from running concurrently with a period mentioned in rule 4.7.16 (1) for the same exposure.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.22 Meaning of provisioning
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
Provisioning means setting aside an amount to cover expected losses, based on loan-loss probability. Provisioning is made before profit is earned.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.23 Credit risk and accounting for expected credit losses
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.23 Credit risk and accounting for expected credit losses
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must adopt, document and adhere to sound methods that address policies, processes and controls for assessing and measuring credit losses on all the firm’s exposures. The measurement of provisions must build on robust methods and must result in the appropriate and timely recognition of expected credit losses in accordance with the applicable accounting standard.
(2) The firm’s aggregate amount of provisions for credit losses must be adequate and consistent with the applicable accounting standard.
(3) The firm must have sound policies and processes to appropriately validate the models that it uses to assess and measure expected credit losses.
(4) The firm must use experienced credit judgement, particularly in the robust consideration of reasonable and supportable forward-looking information, including macroeconomic factors, in its assessment and measurement of expected credit losses.
(5) The firm must have an appropriate credit risk assessment and measurement process that provides it with a sound basis for common systems, tools and data to assess credit risk and to account for expected credit losses.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.24 Provisioning policy
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
Depending on the nature, scale and complexity of a banking business firm’s business, and of the credit it provides, the firm’s provisioning policy must set out:

(a) the areas of its business to which the policy applies;
(b) whether the firm uses different approaches to those areas, and the significant differences in approach;
(c) who is responsible for regularly monitoring its assets, to identify problem or potential problem assets, and the factors it takes into account in identifying them;
(d) the extent to which the value of any collateral, guarantees or insurance that the firm holds affects the need for, or the level of, provisions;
(e) the basis on which the firm makes its provisions, including the extent to which their levels are left to managerial judgement or to a committee;
(f) the methods, debt management systems or formulae used to set the levels of provisions and the factors that must be considered in deciding whether the provisions are adequate;
(g) the reports to enable the firm’s governing body and senior management to ensure that the firm maintains adequate provisions;
(h) the procedures and responsibilities for arrears management and the recovery of exposures in arrears or exposures that have had provisions made against them;
(i) the procedures for writing off and writing back provisions; and
(j) the procedures for calculating and making provisions for contingent and other liabilities (such as contingent liabilities that have crystallised from acceptances, endorsements, guarantees, performance bonds, indemnities, irrevocable letters of credit and the confirmation of documentary credits).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.25 Making provision for credit losses
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
BANK 4.7.25 Making provision for credit losses
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must ensure that it maintains provisions for credit losses that, taken together, are prudent, reasonable and adequate to absorb such losses, given the relevant facts and circumstances. The losses covered must include:
(a) losses incurred;
(b) losses incurred but not yet reported; and
(c) losses estimated but not certain to arise;
extending over the life of the individual credits that make up its credit portfolio.
(2) The firm must also ensure that provisions and write-offs are timely and reflect realistic repayment and recovery expectations, taking into account market and macroeconomic conditions. The firm must consider all the significant factors that affect the likelihood of collecting on the transactions that make up its credit portfolio and the estimated future credit losses on those transactions.
(3) Provisions may be general (assessed collectively against the whole of a portfolio) or specific (assessed against individual credits), or both.
(4) The firm must take into account off-balance-sheet exposures in provisioning. However, no provisioning is necessary for off-balance-sheet exposures that the firm can unilaterally cancel.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.26 Amount of provisioning
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Subject to any direction under subrule (2), a banking business firm must make provision for credit losses in accordance with the applicable accounting standard.
(2) If the Regulatory Authority considers that the firm’s provisioning for an exposure, or some or all of its exposures, is insufficient, the Authority may direct the firm to apply rule 4.7.27.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.7.27 Prescribed provisioning
doc_path: BANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If the Regulatory Authority considers that a banking business firm’s own practices for identifying provisions are inadequate in view of its credit risk profile, the Authority may direct the firm to implement prescribed provisioning in accordance with this rule.
(2) To implement prescribed provisioning, the firm must classify exposures to which this Part applies (subject to subrule (7)) into the 5 categories in subrule (3).
(3) The classification is as follows:
(a) an exposure is classified as performing if:
(i) there is no uncertainty about the timely repayment of the outstanding amounts; and
(ii) it is currently in regular payment status with prompt payments;
(b) an exposure is classified as special mention if any of the following subparagraphs is true of it:
(i) it is of deteriorating or potentially deteriorating credit quality that may adversely affect the counterparty’s ability to make scheduled payments on time;
(ii) it is 30 to 90 days in arrears;
(iii) it shows weakness arising from the counterparty’s financial position;
(iv) it is affected by market circumstances or any other industry-related concerns;
(c) an exposure is classified as substandard if:
(i) it shows definite deterioration in credit quality and impaired repayment ability of the counterparty; or
(ii) it is 91 to 180 days in arrears;
(d) an exposure is classified as doubtful if:
(i) it shows significant credit quality deterioration, worse than in the substandard category, to the extent that the prospect of fully recovering all the outstanding amounts is questionable and the probability of a loss is high (though the exact amount of loss cannot be determined yet); or
(ii) it is 181 to 270 days in arrears;
(e) an exposure is classified as loss if:
(i) it is assessed as uncollectable;
(ii) the probability of recovering the amount due is very low; or
(iii) it is more than 270 days in arrears.
(4) Nothing prevents the firm from classifying an exposure in a higher category than subrule (3) requires. For this subrule, the highest category is loss, and the lowest is performing.
(5) The firm must classify all of its exposures to a particular counterparty as of the same category unless there is good reason not to do so.
(6) The firm must make provisions for credit losses that in total at least meet the requirements in table 4.7.27.
Note If the result is to increase the firm’s provision for credit losses, the amount of the increase must be deducted from CET 1 capital — see rule 3.2.28.
(7) Prescribed provisioning does not apply to exposures of the following kinds:
(a) forborne exposures (see Division 4.7.C) that meet the criteria to be classified as performing (see rule 4.7.10);
(b) any asset acquired through enforcing a security;
(c) real estate that the firm owns.

Table 4.7.27 Provisioning requirements

Category of exposure minimum provisioning requirement (% of unsecured part of credit)
Performing 0
Special mention 5 (or a lesser percentage directed by the Authority)
Substandard 20
Doubtful 50
Loss 100
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK Part 4.8 Transactions with related parties

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.8.1 Introduction
doc_path: BANK Part 4.8 Transactions with related parties
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) To guard against abuses in lending to related parties and to address conflicts of interest, this Part requires transactions with related parties to be at arm’s length and subject to appropriate supervision and limits.
(2) Related-party transactions must be interpreted broadly. Related party transactions include on-balance-sheet and off-balance-sheet credit exposures, service contracts, asset purchases and sales, construction contracts, lease agreements, derivative transactions, borrowing and write-offs.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-2 (as from 1st January 2015).

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.8.2 Concept of related parties
doc_path: BANK Part 4.8 Transactions with related parties
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) The concept of parties being related to a banking business firm is used in these rules in relation to parties over which the firm exercises control or parties that exercise control over the firm. The concept is primarily used in relation to the requirement that the firm's transactions be at arm's length.
(2) In contrast, the concept of parties being connected to one another (which is discussed with concentration risk in Chapter 5) is used in these rules to measure concentration risk and large exposures.
(3) It is of course possible for connected counterparties to be related to the banking business firm holding the exposure concerned.

Note For purposes of concentration risk, the firm's exposure to connected counterparties (whether related or not) is taken to be a single risk.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-2 (as from 1st January 2015).

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.8.3 Related parties
doc_path: BANK Part 4.8 Transactions with related parties
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
Related parties, of a banking business firm, includes:

(a) any other member of the firm’s corporate group;
(b) any individual who is able to exercise significant influence over the firm;
(c) any affiliate of the firm; and
(d) any entity that the Regulatory Authority directs the firm to include.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.8.3 Guidance
doc_path: BANK Part 4.8 Transactions with related parties
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
Related party is wider than a firm's corporate group in that it includes individuals. Related parties include the banking business firm's subsidiaries and major stock holders; members of its governing body; its senior management and key employees.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.8.4 Role of governing body — related parties
doc_path: BANK Part 4.8 Transactions with related parties
BANK 4.8.4 Role of governing body — related parties
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm’s governing body must ensure that the firm’s policies relating to related-party transactions are complied with and that any exceptions are reported to the appropriate level of the senior management, and, if necessary, to the governing body.
(2) The governing body must also ensure that the firm’s senior management monitors transactions with related parties, takes appropriate steps to control or mitigate the risks from such transactions and writes off exposures to related parties only in accordance with the firm’s policies.
(3) The governing body must approve transactions with related parties, and the write-off of related-party exposures, if such transactions or write-off exceeds specified amounts or otherwise poses any special risk.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-2 (as from 1st January 2015).

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 4.8.5 Policies — transactions with related parties
doc_path: BANK Part 4.8 Transactions with related parties
BANK 4.8.5 Policies — transactions with related parties
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm’s policy must establish:
(a) effective systems to identify, monitor and report individual and total exposures to, and transactions with, related parties;
(b) procedures to prevent a member of the governing body, a member of the firm’s senior management or any other person who stands to gain a benefit from a related-party transaction from being part of the process of granting and managing the transaction;
(c) well-defined criteria for the write-off of exposures to related parties;
(d) prudent and appropriate limits to prevent or address conflicts of interest; and
(e) procedures for tracking and reporting exceptions to, and deviations from, limits or policies.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-2 (as from 1st January 2015).

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.1.1 Introduction
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This Chapter sets out the requirements for a banking business firm’s policies to identify, measure, evaluate, manage and control or mitigate concentration risk. This Chapter also sets limits on the firm’s exposures to individual counterparties and connected counterparties.
(2) Concentration risk is the potential for a loss in value of an investment portfolio or a financial institution when a group of exposures moves together in an unfavourable direction. Concentration risk in a banking business firm’s portfolio arises from concentration on a single counterparty, sector or country.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-2 (as from 1st January 2015).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
The implication of concentration risk is that it generates such a significant loss that recovery is unlikely.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.1.2 Meaning of risk concentration
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A risk concentration is a single exposure, or a group of exposures with a common element, that is capable of producing a loss that is large enough:
(a) to threaten a banking business firm’s viability or its ability to maintain its core operations; or
(b) to produce a material change in its risk profile.
(2) A risk concentration can arise in a banking business firm’s assets, liabilities or off-balance-sheet items through the execution or processing of transactions (either product or service), or through a combination of exposures.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-2 (as from 1st January 2015).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.1.2 Guidance
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
Examples of a common element among a banking business firm’s exposures that could create a risk concentration are the following:

• that the counterparties are connected or related
• that the exposures are disproportionately denominated in a particular currency
• that the counterparties are concentrated in particular geographical locations or particular industry sectors
• that the exposures are concentrated in particular products
• reliance on particular service providers (such as a provider of back-office services).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.1.3 Identification of risk concentrations
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
A banking business firm must identify the risk concentrations in its portfolio, including those arising from:

(a) large exposures to a single counterparty;
(b) exposures to connected counterparties;
(c) exposures to counterparties in the same industry, economic sector, geographical region or country; and
(d) exposures to counterparties whose financial performance depends on the same activity, commodity or product.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-2 (as from 1st January 2015).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.1.4 Policies — risk concentrations — sources and limits
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.1.4 Policies — risk concentrations — sources and limits
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must have a policy on the management of risk concentrations.
(2) The policy must set limits for acceptable risk concentrations, consistent with the firm’s risk appetite, risk profile and capital. The limits must be made known to, and must be understood by, all relevant staff.

(3) The policy must ensure that:

(a) the firm’s information systems identify exposures that create risk concentrations, aggregate those exposures and facilitate their management; and
(b) all significant risk concentrations are reviewed regularly and reported to the firm’s governing body or senior management.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-2 (as from 1st January 2015).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.1.4 Guidance
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.1.4 Policies — risk concentrations — sources and limits
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
A banking business firm’s policies should be flexible to help the firm to identify risk concentrations. To achieve this, the systems should be capable of analysing the firm’s credit portfolio by:

• size of exposure
• exposures to connected counterparties
• product
• geography
• industry or sector (for example, manufacturing and industrial)
• account performance
• internal credit risk assessment
• funding
• outstandings versus commitments
• types and coverage of collateral.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.1.5 Role of governing body — risk concentrations
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.1.5 Role of governing body — risk concentrations
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm’s governing body must ensure that the firm’s policy for the management of risk concentrations gives a comprehensive firm-wide view of the significant sources of risk concentrations (including exposures on and off its balance sheet and from contingent liabilities).
(2) The governing body must also ensure that the firm’s senior management monitors the firm’s large exposures, and that the large exposure limits (see rule 5.2.9) are not exceeded on a solo or consolidated basis.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.1.6 Relationship to stress-testing
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
When carrying out stress-testing or reviewing stress scenarios, a banking business firm must take into account significant risk concentrations and large exposures, and the effects of changes in market conditions and risk factors on them.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.1.7 Regulatory Authority can set different limits and minimum capital adequacy ratios
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.1.7 Regulatory Authority can set different limits and minimum capital adequacy ratios
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Despite anything in these rules, the Regulatory Authority may, in writing, set specific limits on a banking business firm’s exposures to particular counterparties, groups of counterparties, industries, sectors, regions, countries or asset classes on a case-by-case basis.
(2) If a banking business firm has 1 or more large exposures (excluding exempted exposures) or if, in the Authority’s opinion, the firm is exposed to a significant level of risk concentration, the Authority may increase any 1 or more of the firm’s minimum capital adequacy ratios.
(3) In considering whether to increase any of the firm’s minimum capital adequacy ratios, the Authority will take into account:
(a) whether the increased ratio would be consistent with the firm’s risk concentration and large exposure policies;
(b) the number of exposures, and the size and nature of each; and
(c) the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business and the experience of its governing body and senior management.
(4) The Regulatory Authority may also direct the firm to take measures to reduce its level of risk concentration.
Note Under FSR, article 16, the Regulatory Authority may modify or waive the application of a prudential requirement to an authorised firm or firms.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.2 Definitions for Part 5.2
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
In this Part:

exempted counterparty means a counterparty that is any of the following:

(a) a sovereign;
(b) a central bank;
(c) a PSE that is assigned a 0% risk weight under rule 4.4.14;
(d) an MDB that qualifies for 0% risk weight.
Note For the list of such MDBs, see rule 4.4.16.

exempted exposure means an exposure that arises from a claim, commitment or contingent liability of any of the following kinds:

(a) a claim by, or a commitment or contingent liability to, an exempted counterparty;
(b) a claim, commitment or contingent liability the amount of which is deducted from the firm’s regulatory capital (see Division 3.2.D);
Guidance
If the amount of such a claim, commitment or contingent liability were not deducted from the firm’s regulatory capital, it would be added to the firm’s other exposures to the relevant counterparty. (It would be assigned a risk weight of 1,250% for the purpose of calculating the firm’s risk-weighted assets.)
(c) a claim, commitment or contingent liability that is secured by eligible collateral (see rule 4.5.12) that was issued by an exempted counterparty;
(d) a claim, commitment or contingent liability that is covered by an eligible guarantee (see rule 4.5.27) that was given by an exempted counterparty;
(e) an exposure to a QCCP that is related to clearing;
(f) certain net short positions (see rule 5.2.31 (4)).

exposure to a counterparty (or a group of connected counterparties) means the total of all of a banking business firm’s claims, commitments and contingent liabilities arising from transactions with the counterparty or a member or members of the group (whether on or off the firm’s balance sheet, and whether held in the firm’s banking book or its trading book) but does not include an intra-day exposure to another banking business firm or a bank.

group of connected counterparties has the meaning given by rule 5.2.5.

large exposure of a banking business firm means an exposure to a counterparty or group of connected counterparties that is equal to 10% or more of the firm’s tier 1 capital.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.2.4 Policies in relation to large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must establish and implement appropriate policies for the management of large exposures. In particular, the policies must include:

(a) exposure limits, commensurate with the firm’s risk appetite, risk profile and capital, for exposures to:

(i) categories of counterparties (for example, sovereigns, other authorised firms and other financial entities, corporate and individual borrowers);
(ii) single counterparties and groups of connected counterparties;
(iii) particular industries or sectors;
(iv) particular countries; and
(v) asset classes (for example, property holdings);
(b) the circumstances in which the exposure limits may be exceeded, and the processes required for approving such excesses (for example, approval by the firm’s governing body); and
(c) procedures for identifying, measuring, managing and reporting large exposures.

(2) The policies must ensure that the firm:

(a) has adequate systems and controls to identify, measure, monitor and report large exposures and risk concentrations in a timely manner; and
(b) reviews its large exposures and risk concentrations at least annually.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.5 Meaning of group of connected counterparties
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.2.5 Meaning of group of connected counterparties
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
Two or more of a banking business firm’s counterparties (other than exempted counterparties) form a group of connected counterparties if:

(a) they are connected by any 1 or more of the following:
(i) a control relationship (see rule 5.2.6);
(ii) a relationship of economic interdependence (see rule 5.2.7);
(iii) any other connection or relationship that, in the firm’s opinion, requires it to treat the counterparties as constituting a single risk;
(b) in the case of investments in structured vehicles — they have in common a third party (such as an originator, fund manager, liquidity provider or credit protection provider) that should be treated as a common risk factor (see rule 5.2.23).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.5 Guidance
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.2.5 Meaning of group of connected counterparties
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
1 The concept of parties or counterparties being connected to one another is used in these rules in relation to counterparties or issuers to which a banking business firm has exposures. Connected counterparties are the basis for measuring risk concentrations and large exposures.
2 Nothing prevents the members of a group of connected counterparties being connected in 2 or more of the ways mentioned. If counterparties that are part of different control groups are interconnected by economic interdependency, all entities for which there is a “chain of contagion” need to be grouped into one group of connected counterparties. The chain of contagion leading to a possible default of all entities concerned is the relevant factor for the grouping and needs to be assessed in each individual case.
3 In contrast, the concept of parties being related to a banking business firm (which is discussed with credit risk in Chapter 4) is primarily used in relation to the requirement that the firm’s transactions be at arm’s length.
4 It is of course possible for a firm’s related parties to be connected counterparties (such as when the firm has exposures to them).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.6 Connected counterparties — control relationship
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A control relationship exists between 2 counterparties if either has control of the other.
(2) Whether a control relationship exists between 2 counterparties is to be decided in accordance with the applicable accounting standard.
Guidance
1 A control relationship is likely to exist between 2 counterparties if 1 of them owns 50% or more of the voting rights in the other.
2 To decide whether a control relationship exists between 2 counterparties, a banking business firm should take at least the following factors into account:
• the existence of voting agreements (such as control of a majority of voting rights by means of an agreement with other shareholders)
• whether a member (A) is able to exercise significant influence over the appointment or dismissal of another member’s administrative, management or supervisory body (for example, if A has as the right to appoint or remove a majority of members of such a body, or a majority of members of such a body have been appointed solely as a result of A’s exercise of its voting rights)
• whether a member (A) is able to exercise significant influence over the senior management of another (B) (for example, A has the power to exercise a controlling influence over B’s management or policies (such as by A’s having consent rights over significant decisions)).
(3) However, even if control of 1 entity by another is established, the banking business firm concerned need not treat the counterparties as a group of connected counterparties if it can show the Regulatory Authority that, despite the control, the entities do not form a group of connected counterparties (for example, because of particular circumstances or corporate governance safeguards).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.7 Connected counterparties — economic interdependence
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) To decide whether or not 2 counterparties are connected by a relationship of economic interdependence, the firm must take into account at least the following matters:
(a) whether 50% or more of 1 counterparty’s gross receipts or gross expenditures (on an annual basis) is derived from transactions with the other (for example, the owner of a property and a tenant that pays a significant part of the rent);
(b) whether 1 counterparty has fully or partly guaranteed the exposure of the other, or is liable by other means, and the relevant exposure is so significant that the guarantor would be likely to default if a claim were made;
(c) whether a significant part of 1 counterparty’s production or output is sold to the other, and the other could not easily be replaced by other customers within a reasonable period;
(d) whether the expected source of funds to repay the loans of both counterparties is the same and neither has another independent source of income from which loans could be serviced and fully repaid;
(e) whether it is likely that 1 counterparty’s financial problems would cause difficulties for the other in terms of full and timely repayment of the other’s liabilities;
(f) whether 1 counterparty’s insolvency or default would be likely to be associated with the insolvency or default of the other;
(g) if both counterparties rely on the same provider for the majority of their funding — whether, if funding from the common provider were to become unavailable, an alternative provider could not be found.
(2) However, even if it is established, based on subrule (1), that 2 or more of the firm’s counterparties are in a relationship of economic interdependence, the firm need not treat them as a group of connected counterparties if the firm can show the Regulatory Authority that despite the interdependence, either counterparty could overcome financial difficulties, or even the other counterparty’s default, by finding other customers or funding sources within a reasonable period.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.7 Guidance
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
If the sum of all of a banking business firm’s exposures to a particular counterparty is more than 5% of the firm’s tier 1 capital, the firm should investigate the relationships between all of its counterparties (other than exempted counterparties) to determine whether any 2 or more of them form a group of connected counterparties because of a relationship of economic interdependence. For the meaning of tier 1 capital, see rule 3.2.7 (2).

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.8 Regulatory Authority can create relationships
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.2.8 Regulatory Authority can create relationships
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
If the Regulatory Authority considers it necessary or desirable to do so in the interests of the effective supervision of a banking business firm, the Authority may direct the firm to treat a counterparty as connected to another counterparty.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.9 Limits on large exposures
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK Division 5.2.C Management of large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm’s exposure to any 1 counterparty (except an exempted counterparty), or any 1 group of connected counterparties, must not be greater than 25% of the firm’s tier 1 capital.
Note For the meaning of tier 1 capital, see rule 3.2.7 (2).
(2) The total of all of the firm’s net large exposures must not exceed 800% of the firm’s tier 1 capital.
Note The amount of any breach of a large exposure limit must be deducted from CET 1 capital — see rule 3.2.39.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.10 Exposures that would breach limit — approval by Regulatory Authority
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK Division 5.2.C Management of large exposures
BANK 5.2.10 Exposures that would breach limit — approval by Regulatory Authority
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm may apply to the Regulatory Authority for the approval of an exposure that is greater than a large exposure limit.
(2) The Authority will grant the approval only in exceptional circumstances and only after the firm satisfies the Authority that the proposed exposure does not expose the firm to excessive risk.
(3) If the Authority approves the exposure, the Authority may increase any 1 or more of the firm’s minimum capital adequacy ratios to compensate for the additional risk associated with the exposure.
Note 1 For the meaning of minimum capital adequacy ratios, see rule 3.2.6.
Note 2 The firm must deduct, from CET 1 capital, the amount by which the limit was exceeded, unless the Authority has approved the excess — see rule 3.2.39.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.11 Breaches of limits — reporting and rectification
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK Division 5.2.C Management of large exposures
BANK 5.2.11 Breaches of limits — reporting and rectification
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
If a banking business firm breaches a large exposure limit:

(a) it must immediately report the matter to the Regulatory Authority; and
(b) it must take immediate action to rectify the breach.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.12 Periodic reporting of large exposures etc
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK Division 5.2.C Management of large exposures
BANK 5.2.12 Periodic reporting of large exposures etc
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must report the following to the Regulatory Authority:
(a) each of the firm’s exposures (other than exempted exposures) to any 1 counterparty, or any 1 group of connected counterparties, that is equal to 10% or more of the firm’s tier 1 capital;
(b) each of the firm’s exposures (other than exempted exposures) to any 1 counterparty, or any 1 group of connected counterparties, that is equal to 10% or more of the firm’s tier 1 capital if the effect of credit risk mitigation is not taken into account;
(c) every exempted exposure that is equal to 10% or more of the firm’s tier 1 capital;
Guidance
The exposures that must be reported under paragraph (c) include exposures to exempted counterparties.
(d) the firm’s largest 20 exposures (other than exempted exposures) to a single counterparty or a single group of connected counterparties, regardless of the values of those exposures relative to the firm’s tier 1 capital.
(2) The reporting period for subrule (1) is to be as agreed with, or directed by, the Authority.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.13 What claims, commitments and contingent liabilities must be taken into account
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.2.13 What claims, commitments and contingent liabilities must be taken into account
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) When a banking business firm calculates its exposure to a counterparty or group of connected counterparties, the firm must take into account every claim, commitment or contingent liability (other than a claim, commitment or contingent liability that is or gives rise to an exempted exposure) that it would be required to take into account when calculating its risk-based capital requirement.
Note For how to calculate the firm’s risk-based capital requirement, see rule 3.2.5.
(2) The firm must take into account every such claim, commitment or liability on or off the firm’s balance sheet, and whether in the firm’s banking book or its trading book.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.14 Calculating exposure — general rules
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This rule sets out how to calculate, for this Part, a banking business firm’s exposure arising from a claim, commitment or contingent liability.
(2) In general, except in the cases mentioned in subrules (3) to (5), the amount of the exposure is the accounting value (net of specific provisions and value adjustments) of the claim, commitment or liability.
(3) If the exposure arises from an instrument that gives rise to counterparty credit risk and is not an SFT, the firm’s exposure is the exposure at default for the instrument (see Part 4.6A).
(4) If the exposure arises from an SFT, the firm’s exposure is the amount calculated in accordance with the comprehensive approach in Subdivision 4.5.B.3.
(5) If the exposure arises from an off-balance-sheet item, the firm’s exposure is the item’s credit equivalent amount, calculated in accordance with Division 4.4.C. In calculating the item’s credit equivalent amount, however, a minimum CCF of 10% must be used.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.15 Eligible CRM techniques
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) For this Part, when a banking business firm is calculating the amount of its exposure from a claim, commitment or contingent liability:
(a) it must apply any CRM technique that applies to the claim, commitment or liability, and that the firm would apply when calculating its risk-weighted capital requirement; but
(b) it must not take into account any other CRM technique.
Note Under Part 4.5, the firm may apply any of the following CRM techniques:
• eligible collateral (see Division 4.5.B) in either the simple or the comprehensive approach
• an eligible guarantee (see Division 4.5.C)
• an eligible credit derivative (see Division 4.5.D).
(2) The firm must reduce the value of the exposure to the original counterparty by the recognised amount (that is, the amount by which the technique reduced the exposure for risk-based capital requirements purposes).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.15 Guidance
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
The recognised amount is:

• for unfunded credit protection — the value of the protected portion
• for eligible collateral, if the firm uses the simple approach (see Subdivision 4.5.B.2) to calculate its risk-based capital requirement — the value of the part of the claim that is collateralised by the market value of the collateral
• for eligible collateral, if the firm uses the comprehensive approach (see Subdivision 4.5.B.3) to calculate its risk-based capital requirement — the value of the adjusted collateral after applying the haircuts required under the comprehensive approach
• for an instrument that gives rise to counterparty credit risk (such as an OTC derivative) —the value of the collateral (see Part 4.6A).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.16 Exposure to CRM providers
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
If under this Part a banking business firm must recognise the reduction of an exposure by a CRM technique, it must also recognise an exposure to the CRM provider. The amount of the exposure to the CRM provider is the amount by which the exposure to the original counterparty or group is reduced.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.17 Claims etc hedged subject to maturity mismatch
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.2.17 Claims etc hedged subject to maturity mismatch
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) For this Part, if a claim, commitment or contingent liability is hedged but the hedge is subject to a maturity mismatch, the hedge is to be taken into account only if:
(a) the original maturities of both the claim, commitment or contingent liability and the hedge are 1 year or longer; and
(b) the residual maturity of the hedge is at least 3 months.
(2) If a banking business firm has a maturity mismatch in relation to a CRM technique that the firm can apply in calculating its risk-based capital requirement, then, for the purposes of this Part, the firm must adjust the credit protection provided by the technique in the same way as it would when calculating its risk-based capital requirement.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.18 Effect of netting
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
If a banking business firm has legally enforceable netting arrangements for loans and deposits, the firm may calculate the relevant exposure values for the purposes of this Part in the same way as it would to calculate its risk-based capital requirement — that is, on the basis of the net credit exposures, subject to the conditions in Division 4.5.E for netting on the balance sheet.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.19 Investments in collective investment undertakings etc — whether look-through required
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.2.19 Investments in collective investment undertakings etc — whether look-through required
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If a banking business firm has invested in a structure through an entity that itself has exposures to assets, the firm must look through the structure to identify the underlyings unless:
(a) the firm can show that the amount of its exposure to each underlying is less than 0.25% of its tier 1 capital; or
(b) the firm’s whole investment in the structure is less than 0.25% of its tier 1 capital.
Guidance
Such structures include funds, securitisations and other structures with underlying assets.
Note For the meaning of tier 1 capital, see rule 3.2.7 (2).
(2) The firm must be able to show that a decision not to look through the structure was not influenced by considerations of regulatory arbitrage (for example, it must be able to show that it did not circumvent a large exposure limit by investing in several smaller transactions that have identical underlying assets).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.20 Investments in collective investment undertakings etc — counterparty
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.2.20 Investments in collective investment undertakings etc — counterparty
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This rule sets out how a banking business firm must assign an underlying to its investment in a structure.
(2) For this rule:
(a) the firm must consider only exposures to underlyings that result from its investment in the structure itself; and
(b) the value of an exposure is to be calculated as set out in rule 5.2.22.
(3) If, under rule 5.2.19, the firm is not required to look through the structure to identify the underlyings, the firm must treat the structure itself as its counterparty.
(4) If, under rule 5.2.19, the firm is required to look through the structure to identify the underlyings:
(a) for any underlying for which the exposure value is equal to 0.25% or more of the firm’s tier 1 capital, and the counterparty is identifiable, the firm must treat that counterparty as its counterparty;
(b) for any underlying for which the exposure value is less than 0.25% of the firm’s tier 1 capital, the firm may treat the structure itself as its counterparty;
(c) for any underlying for which the firm cannot identify the counterparty, it must assign that total amount to “the unknown client”; and
(d) for any underlying for which the firm cannot calculate the exposure amount, the firm must assign the nominal amount of its exposure to “the unknown client”.
(5) The firm’s exposure to a counterparty under this rule must be added to any other direct or indirect exposure to that counterparty.
(6) Exposures that have been assigned to “the unknown client” must be aggregated as if “the unknown client” were a single counterparty. The large exposure limits apply to exposures to “the unknown client”.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.22 Investments in collective investment undertakings etc — look-through required — value
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.2.22 Investments in collective investment undertakings etc — look-through required — value
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to a banking business firm’s investment in a structure if, under rule 5.2.19, the firm is required to look through the structure to identify the underlying assets.
(2) The exposure value assigned to a counterparty is equal to the pro rata share that the firm holds in the structure multiplied by the value of the underlying asset.
Guidance
Thus, if the firm holds a 1% share of a structure that invests in 20 assets each with a value of 5, it must assign an exposure of 0.05 to each of the counterparties. An exposure to a counterparty must be added to any other direct or indirect exposures the bank has to that counterparty.
(3) In the case of a tranched structure, the firm must measure its exposure value to a counterparty for each tranche within the structure, assuming a pro rata distribution of losses amongst investors in the tranche. To compute the exposure value to the underlying, the firm:
(a) must first find the lower of:
(i) the value of the tranche in which the bank invests; and
(ii) the nominal value of each underlying in the portfolio; and
(b) must then apply the pro rata share of the firm’s investment in the tranche to the value determined in the first step.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.23 Additional risk factors — role of third parties
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.2.23 Additional risk factors — role of third parties
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm must identify any risk inherent in a structure in relation to an exposure (such as having an originator, fund manager, liquidity provider or credit protection provider) in common. The firm must consider:
(a) whether the connection by way of that entity should be treated as an additional risk factor; and
(b) whether the relevant exposures should be treated as exposures to a group of connected counterparties.
Guidance
In some cases, the manager would be regarded as a distinct counterparty so that the sum of a firm’s investments in all of the funds managed by that manager would be subject to the large exposure limits. But in other cases, the commonality of the manager might not be an additional risk factor — for example, the legal framework that governs the fund might separate the legal entity that manages the fund and the legal entity that has custody of its assets. In the case of a structured finance product, the liquidity provider or sponsor of a short-term programme (such as an asset-backed commercial paper conduit or a structured investment vehicle) may need to be considered as an additional risk factor. Similarly, in synthetic financial instruments, a protection provider may be an additional source of risk and a common factor for connecting different structures.
(2) The firm must also consider whether an entity referred to in subrule (1) is connected closely enough to a counterparty of the firm that the entity and the counterparty should be treated as a group of connected counterparties.
Guidance
1 If the firm has investments in a set of structures associated with a third party that constitutes a common risk factor, the firm might have to consider adding the investments to other exposures (such as a loan) to that party. Whether it is necessary to do so depends on a case-by-case consideration of the specific features of the structure and on the role of the third party.
2 In the example of the fund manager, adding together the exposures may not be necessary because fraudulent behaviour by the fund manager would not necessarily affect the repayment of a loan. The assessment may be different where the risk to the value of investments underlying the structures arises in the event of a third-party default. For example, in the case of a credit protection provider, the source of the additional risk for the firm’s investing in a structure is the default of the credit protection provider. The firm should add the investment in the structure to the direct exposures to the credit protection provider since both exposures might crystallise into losses in the event that the protection provider defaults (ignoring the covered part of the exposures may lead to the undesirable situation of a high risk concentration exposure to issuers of collateral or providers of credit protection).
(3) If the firm considers 2 or more third parties to be potential sources of additional risk, the firm must assign the exposure resulting from the investment in each relevant structure to each of the third parties.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.24 Exposure value of covered bonds
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.2.24 Exposure value of covered bonds
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) In this rule:
covered bond has the same meaning as in rule 4.4.74 (1).
qualifying covered bond means a covered bond that meets the following requirements:
(a) the underlying assets (the cover pool) include only assets of the following kinds:
(i) claims on, or guaranteed by, sovereigns, central banks, PSEs or MDBs;
(ii) claims secured by residential real estate in relation to which the prudential requirements in rule 4.4.56 have been complied with, and with an LTV ratio of 80% or lower;
(iii) claims secured by commercial real estate in relation to which those prudential requirements have been complied with, and with an LTV ratio of 60% or lower;
(iv) additional collateral of the following kinds:
(A) substitution assets (that is, cash or short-term liquid and secure assets held in substitution for the primary assets to top up the cover pool for management purposes);
(B) derivatives entered into to hedge the risks arising in the covered bond programme;
(b) the total nominal value of the cover pool is at least 10% more than the total nominal value of outstanding bonds issued (but see subrule (2));
(c) the bonds met the requirements in paragraphs (a) and (b) when they were issued and will continue to do so until their maturity;
(d) for any real estate that is part of the assets in the cover pool, the following requirements are satisfied:
(i) the real estate is valued at no more than the current fair value under which it could be sold under private contract between a willing seller and an arm’s-length buyer on the date of valuation;
(ii) the firm assesses the value of the real estate frequently (at least annually), or more frequently if the market is subject to significant changes in conditions.
(2) For paragraph (b) of the definition of qualifying covered bond, an issue is taken to meet the requirement as to the value of the cover pool if:
(a) the legislation that governs the bonds requires the value of the cover pool to meet that requirement; or
(b) if that legislation contains no such requirement — the issuer regularly states publicly that the value of the cover pool meets that requirement.
(3) A banking business firm may assign, to a holding of qualifying covered bonds, an exposure value equal to 20% of the nominal value of the holding.
(4) A banking business firm must assign, to a holding of covered bonds that are not qualifying covered bonds, an exposure value equal to 100% of the nominal value of the holding.
(5) The counterparty to the exposure is the issuer of the bonds.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.25 Exposures to central counterparties that are not QCCPs
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK 5.2.25 Exposures to central counterparties that are not QCCPs
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This rule relates to a banking business firm’s exposures to central counterparties that are not QCCPs.
Note 1 Exposures to QCCPs that are related to clearing are exempted exposures — see rule 5.2.2, definition of exempted exposures, paragraph (e).
Note 2 For the meaning of QCCP, see the Glossary.
(2) A banking business firm must measure its exposure to such a central counterparty as the sum of the firm’s clearing exposures and non-clearing exposures to the central counterparty.
(3) For the purpose of deciding whether a QCCP is part of a group of connected counterparties, exposures that are related only to clearing activities are to be disregarded. However, non-clearing exposures are to be taken into account for that purpose.
(4) A banking business firm must identify its exposures to a QCCP that are related to clearing activities and must add those exposures together. The types of exposures that are related to clearing activities, and the value to be assigned to each, are as set out in table 5.2.25.

Table 5.2.25 Exposures related to clearing — values

Type of exposure Value
Trade exposures the value calculated according to the relevant provisions of Divisions 4.4.B and 4.4.C for the type of exposure
Segregated initial margin 0
Non-segregated initial margin the nominal amount posted
Pre-funded default fund contributions the nominal amount of the contribution
Unfunded default fund contributions 0
Equity stakes the nominal amount
(5) For an exposure that is directly related to clearing activities (such as the firm acting as a clearing member or being a client of a clearing member), the firm must determine the counterparty to which the exposure must be assigned by applying the relevant provisions of Part 4.6A.
(6) For an exposure to a QCCP that is not directly related to a clearing service provided by the QCCP (such as a funding facility, credit facility or guarantee), the value must be determined, according to the rules in this Part, in the same way as for any other counterparty.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.26 Exposures in both banking and trading book to same counterparty
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures

BANK 5.2.26 Exposures in both banking and trading book to same counterparty
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
If a banking business firm has exposures to a particular counterparty in both its banking book and trading book, the firm must add all of the exposures to the counterparty to calculate its total exposure to that counterparty.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.27 Values of exposures for trading book positions
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK Subdivision 5.2.D.2 Exposures in trading book
BANK 5.2.27 Values of exposures for trading book positions
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) The exposures considered in this rule correspond to the risk concentrations associated with the default of a single counterparty for exposures in the trading book. Therefore, positions in financial instruments such as bonds and equities are subject to the large exposure limits, but positions in a particular commodity or currency are not.
(2) The exposure value of a debt or equity instrument is the market value of the instrument.

(3) Instruments such as swaps, futures, forwards and credit derivatives held in the trading book must be converted into positions in the same way as when calculating the firm’s risk-based capital requirement. Such instruments must be decomposed into their individual legs, and a leg is to be disregarded if it represents an exposure that need not, under rule 5.2.13, be taken into account for this Part.

Guidance
A stock futures contract on stock X, for example, is decomposed into a long position in stock X and a short position in a risk-free interest rate exposure in the funding currency. A typical interest rate swap is decomposed into a long position in a fixed interest rate exposure and a short position in a floating one, or vice versa.

(4) For a credit derivative that represents sold protection, the exposure to the referenced name is the difference between the amount that would be due if the protection were triggered and the absolute market value of the credit protection.

Guidance
If the market value of a credit derivative is positive for the protection seller, that value should also be added to the protection seller’s exposure to the protection buyer. Such a situation could occur if the present value of agreed but unpaid premiums exceeded the absolute market value of the credit protection.
(5) For a credit-linked note for which the firm is the protection seller, the firm must consider positions in both the issuer and the underlying that the note references.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.28 Exposure values of options in trading book
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK Subdivision 5.2.D.2 Exposures in trading book
BANK 5.2.28 Exposure values of options in trading book
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) For this Part, the exposure value of an option held in the trading book is the change in price that would result from a default of the underlying instrument.
(2) For a call option, the exposure value is the market value of the option. For a long call, the value is positive and for a short call it is negative.
(3) For a put option, the exposure value is the option’s strike price minus its market value. For a short put, the value is positive and for a long put it is negative.
(4) The firm must add the resulting positions to its other exposures. After aggregation, negative net exposures must be treated as being zero.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.29 Exposure values of investments in transactions in trading book
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures

BANK 5.2.29 Exposure values of investments in transactions in trading book
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This rule deals with how a banking business firm must decide the exposure value of an investment in a transaction (such as an index position, a securitisation, a hedge fund or an investment fund) that is held in the firm’s trading book.
(2) The firm must calculate the exposure value of such an investment in the same way as for a similar instrument in the firm’s banking book.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.30 Treatment of long and short positions in trading book — positions in same issue
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK Subdivision 5.2.D.2 Exposures in trading book
BANK 5.2.30 Treatment of long and short positions in trading book — positions in same issue
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
For this Part, a banking business firm may offset long and short positions in the same issue (for this rule, 2 issues are the same if the issuer, coupon, currency and maturity are identical). The firm may treat the net position as being its exposure to the issuer.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.31 Treatment of long and short positions in trading book — positions in different issues from same counterparty
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK Subdivision 5.2.D.2 Exposures in trading book
BANK 5.2.31 Treatment of long and short positions in trading book — positions in different issues from same counterparty
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm may offset positions in different issues by the same counterparty only if:
(a) the short position is junior to the long position; or
(b) the positions are of the same seniority.
(2) To determine the relative seniority of positions, the firm may allocate positions to broad classes based on seniority — for example, “equity”, “subordinated debt” and “senior debt”.
(3) If the firm chooses not to allocate its positions to classes as set out in subrule (2), it must not offset long and short positions in different issues by the counterparty.
(4) If the result of the offsetting is a net short position with a single counterparty, that net position need not be treated as an exposure for the purposes of this Part.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 5.2.32 Treatment of hedged positions in trading book
doc_path: BANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
BANK Subdivision 5.2.D.2 Exposures in trading book
BANK 5.2.32 Treatment of hedged positions in trading book
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) If a banking business firm’s position is hedged by a credit derivative, the firm may take the hedge into account if, for the underlying and the position hedged, the short position is junior to the long position, or the positions are of the same seniority. Subrules 5.2.31 (2) and (3) apply.
(2) If a banking business firm’s exposure is hedged by a credit derivative, any reduction in exposure to the original counterparty is also an exposure to the credit protection provider, in accordance with rule 5.2.16, except in the case mentioned in subrule (3).
(3) If the hedge takes the form of a credit default swap (CDS) and either the CDS provider or the referenced entity is not a financial entity, the amount to be assigned to the CDS provider is, instead, the counterparty credit risk exposure value calculated according to Part 4.6A.
(4) In subrule (3):
financial entity means:
(a) a regulated financial institution (that is, a corporate group in which an entity is supervised by a financial regulator that imposes prudential requirements consistent with international standards); or
Guidance
Regulated financial institutions include, but are not limited to, prudentially regulated insurance companies, broker/dealers, banks, thrifts and futures commission merchants.
(b) a legal entity whose main business is the management of financial assets, lending, factoring, leasing, the provision of credit enhancements, securitisation, investments, financial custody, central counterparty services, proprietary trading and any other financial service activity specified by the Regulatory Authority by notice published on an approved website.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2023-5 (as from 1st July 2024)

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 6.1.1 Introduction
doc_path: BANK Division 6.1.A Management of market risk generally
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) This Chapter sets out the requirements for a banking business firm's market risk management policy to identify, measure, evaluate, manage and control or mitigate market risk. This Chapter also sets out how to calculate the firm's market risk capital requirement.
(2) A banking business firm that operates in a market incurs risks from potential movements in market prices.
(3) The market risk capital requirement for a banking business firm is made up of capital charges for:
(a) foreign exchange risk in the banking book and trading book;
(b) options risk in the banking book and trading book;
(c) commodities risk in the banking book and trading book;
(d) traded equity position risk; and
(e) traded interest rate risk.
Note The measurements of the risks mentioned in subrule (3) are set out in Part 6.2 to Part 6.6.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2015-3 (as from 1st January 2016).

(2) The firm must also have robust market risk measurement and risk management.

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 6.1.3 Standard method to be used
doc_path: BANK Division 6.1.A Management of market risk generally
BANK 6.1.3 Standard method to be used
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) Unless the Regulatory Authority has approved the use of an internal model by a banking business firm, market risk is, as a general rule, measured using the standard method. The standard method comprises a range of approaches that a firm may use to calculate capital charges from its trading activities.

Note For approval of the use of internal models — see rule 3.1.6.
(2) In the standard method, capital requirement is the sum of the capital charges, calculated in accordance with this Chapter, for the risks included in market risk.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-2 (as from 1st January 2015).

QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.title: BANK 6.1.6 Policies — market risk environment
doc_path: BANK Division 6.1.A Management of market risk generally
QFCRA Rules :: Banking Business Prudenti.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm’s market risk management policy must establish:

(a) effective systems for the accurate and timely identification, measurement, evaluation, management and control or mitigation of market risk, and reporting to the firm’s governing body and senior management;
(b) prudent and appropriate market risk limits that are consistent with the firm’s risk appetite, risk profile and capital, and with the management’s ability to manage;
(c) who is responsible for identifying, measuring and reporting market risk;
(d) procedures for tracking and reporting exceptions to, and deviations from, limits or policies; and
(e) procedures for including positions and exposures in the trading book.
(2) The policy must ensure that all of the firm’s transactions are identified and recorded in a timely way and that their valuations are consistent and prudent. The firm must use reliable market data that have been verified by a function that is independent of the function that assumed or incurred the risk.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-2 (as from 1st January 2015).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)
