QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 4.1.1 What is an authorised firm’s senior management?
doc_path: CTRL 4.1.1 What is an authorised firm’s senior management?
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
An authorised firm’s senior management is made up of:

(a) each individual (if any) who is approved to exercise any of the following controlled functions for the firm:
(i) the senior executive function;
(ii) the finance function;
(iii) the senior management function;
(iv) the MLRO function;
(v) the risk management function;
(vi) the compliance oversight function;
(vii) the internal audit function;
(viii) the actuarial function; and
(b) any other individual who, in the Regulatory Authority’s opinion, has overall responsibility for the day-to-day management of the part or parts of the firm’s business in or from the QFC.

 

Derived from QFCRA RM/2012-4 (as from 1st July 2013)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 4.1.2 Senior management’s role
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
The members of an authorised firm’s senior management are collectively responsible for implementing the corporate governance framework and risk management framework approved by the firm’s governing body, and for overseeing the firm’s daily operations. The members of the senior management:

(a) must ensure that the implementation of the frameworks is in accordance with these rules;
(b) must discharge their management responsibilities conscientiously and prudently;
(c) must maintain clear decision-making procedures to the extent appropriate to the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business;
(d) must actively promote a strong governance and risk management culture throughout the firm; and
(e) must establish and maintain policies and procedures that enable them to be satisfied that any individual who is to act for the firm is suitable, having regard to:
(i) the role that he or she is to have in the firm; and
(ii) the law applicable in the QFC.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 4.1.3 Duties of individuals towards firm
doc_path: CTRL 4.1.3 Duties of individuals towards firm
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
Each member of an authorised firm’s senior management owes the following duties to the firm:

(a) to act for the firm’s benefit;
(b) to avoid any conflict between his or her interests and those of the firm (or, if it is not possible to avoid such a conflict, to mitigate it);
(c) to have, and to maintain, the knowledge and skills that are reasonably expected of an individual who holds a similar appointment, and carries out similar functions, in the senior management of the firm;
(d) to carry out his or her functions diligently.

 

Derived from QFCRA RM/2012-4 (as from 1st July 2013)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 4.1.5 Requirement for firms to have finance function
doc_path: CTRL 4.1.5 Requirement for firms to have finance function
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm, or an Islamic banking business firm, and a QFC insurer (other than a QFC captive insurer) that is incorporated under the Companies Regulations, must have an individual who is approved to exercise the finance function for the firm.

(2) Any other authorised firm must either:

(a) have an individual who is approved to exercise the finance function; or

Note INDI, Part S1.6 contains rules about the competencies required for the finance function.
(b) with the permission of the Regulatory Authority, appoint a suitably qualified third party to exercise the finance function for the firm.
(3) Where a firm proposes to appoint a suitably qualified third party to exercise the firm’s finance function, the firm must satisfy the Regulatory Authority that the third party has sufficient knowledge, experience and authority to exercise the function.
(4) When giving permission for the appointment of a third party to exercise a firm’s finance function, the Regulatory Authority may impose such conditions as it considers appropriate on the appointment, including, in particular, conditions related to the employees of the third party.

(5) Where a third party appointed to exercise a firm’s finance function is not established in the QFC, or in the State:

(a) the third party must identify the individual employed by it who is to exercise the finance function for the firm; and
(b) that individual must have sufficient knowledge, experience and authority to exercise the function.

(6) The appointment of a third party to exercise a firm’s finance function is a material outsourcing arrangement (see Part 8.4).

Note By virtue of rule 8.4.2 (2) (d), the appointment of a group employee to exercise a controlled function is not an outsourcing arrangement.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 5.1.1 Exercise of 2 or more controlled functions by same individual
doc_path: CTRL 5.1.1 Exercise of 2 or more controlled functions by same individual
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) Subject to subrule (2), an individual may exercise 2 or more controlled functions for an authorised firm if (but only if):

(a) the firm’s governing body confirms to the Regulatory Authority in writing that it is satisfied that:

(i) the individual’s exercise of those controlled functions in combination:

(A) does not give rise to any internal or external conflict of interest; and
(B) does not compromise the independence, objectivity and effectiveness of the exercise of any of the functions;
(ii) the individual’s combined exercise of the functions will not increase the firm’s risk of non-compliance with the law applicable in the QFC or any other applicable law; and
(iii) it is not inappropriate, having regard to the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business, for the individual to exercise both or all of the controlled functions; and

(b) the Authority is satisfied that:

(i) the conditions in subparagraphs (a) (i), (ii) and (iii) have been met; and
(ii) the individual can adequately exercise the functions in combination.
(2) An authorised firm must not combine the internal audit function with any other controlled function.

(3) At least once in every year, the firm’s senior management must review:

(a) the firm’s policies, procedures and controls for combining the functions, including its procedures for assessing:

(i) whether it is feasible to continue to combine the functions;
(ii) the risk in doing so; and
(iii) the likely effect of doing so on the firm’s business; and

(b) the combined exercise of the functions, to satisfy itself that:

(i) the combined exercise does not compromise the independence, objectivity and effectiveness of the exercise of each function;
(ii) no internal or external conflict of interest arises;
(iii) the combined exercise has not increased, and will not increase, the firm’s risk of non-compliance with the law applicable in the QFC or any other applicable law; and
(iv) the combined exercise continues to be appropriate, having regard to the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business.
(4) The senior management must report the results of a review under subrule (3) to the firm’s governing body within 30 days after the review is completed.

(5) If the Regulatory Authority is satisfied that it is no longer appropriate for 2 or more controlled functions to be exercised for an authorised firm by the same individual, the Authority may, by written notice, direct the firm to do either or both of the following:

(a) stop combining the functions;
(b) appoint 1 or more individuals to exercise any of the functions.

(6) In particular, the Authority may give a direction under subrule (5) if the Authority considers that:

(a) the continued performance by the individual of both or all the functions:

(i) is no longer appropriate, having regard to the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business;
(ii) has given rise, or is likely to give rise, to an internal or external conflict of interest; or
(iii) has compromised, or is likely to compromise, the independence, objectivity and effectiveness of the performance of any of the functions;
(b) the individual is performing any of the functions at a standard that is below the standard at which a reasonable person having the necessary skills, knowledge and experience would be expected to perform that function; or
(c) the combined performance of the functions by the individual has impaired, or is likely to impair, the firm’s compliance with the requirements applicable to the conduct of its business in or from the QFC.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2025-1 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
Note for Chapter 6

An authorised firm’s internal controls and assurance framework is made up of the policies, processes, tasks, behaviours and other aspects of its organisation that, taken together:

• enable the firm to respond appropriately to business, operational, financial, compliance and other risks, and so facilitate its effective operation
• safeguard the firm’s assets and ensure that its liabilities are identified and managed
• ensure the quality of the firm’s internal and external reporting (which requires proper records and processes that generate a flow of timely, relevant and reliable information from internal and external sources)
• ensure that the firm complies with applicable laws and regulations and with its internal policies.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.1.1 Objectives of internal controls and assurance framework
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.1.1 Objectives of internal controls and assurance framework
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
An authorised firm must establish and maintain an internal controls and assurance framework to ensure that:

(a) the firm’s business is conducted efficiently;
(b) the firm’s assets are safeguarded;
(c) fraud and other unlawful acts are prevented or detected;
(d) risk is managed effectively;
(e) the firm’s financial records are accurate and complete; and
(f) the preparation of the firm’s financial statements is timely.

 

Derived from QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.1.2 Independence of internal control and assurance functions etc
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.1.2 Independence of internal control and assurance functions etc
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must ensure that each individual who exercises an internal control and assurance function is sufficiently free from influence to be effective in achieving the function’s purpose.
(2) The requirement in subrule (1) is satisfied if reasonable measures have been taken to ensure that:
(a) no such individual is remunerated in a way that would tend to undermine his or her independence and objectivity in exercising the function;
Note For the requirements relating to a firm’s remuneration policy, see rule 3.1.16.
(b) no such individual is involved in performing a function that generates, or is intended to generate, revenue for the firm;
(c) no such individual is limited or restricted as to the matters that he or she can investigate or report on in the exercise of his or her function;
(d) the reports and conclusions of such an individual can be honest and candid, without fear of reprisal; and
(e) pressure or influence is not applied to such an individual to modify his or her reports or conclusions.
Guidance
An internal control and assurance function cannot be effective unless its exercise is independent. Independent means, broadly, that the individual who exercises the function is not subjected to pressure to mould or manipulate his or her conclusions or results. An internal control and assurance function that produces only results that are convenient to the firm’s governing body or management would not be regarded as satisfying rule 6.1.1.
(3) An authorised firm must ensure that:
(a) each individual who exercises an internal control and assurance function; and
(b) each employee who is allocated responsibilities within the firm’s corporate governance framework and its risk management framework;
has all of the following:
(c) the necessary authority to exercise the function or carry out his or her duties;
(d) access to all necessary information, documents and records of the firm;
(e) appropriate access to the firm’s governing body and senior management.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.1.3 Direct access to governing body by certain individuals
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.1.3 Direct access to governing body by certain individuals
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
An authorised firm’s policies, procedures and controls must provide that an individual who is approved to exercise an internal control and assurance function for the firm is entitled to raise matters directly with the firm’s governing body, the chair of the body, or any relevant committee of the body, and to do so privately (that is, without the presence of any representative of the firm’s senior management).

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.1.4 Certain individuals’ obligation to raise matters promptly
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.1.4 Certain individuals’ obligation to raise matters promptly
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
An authorised firm’s policies, procedures and controls must provide that an individual who is approved to exercise an internal control and assurance function for the firm:

(a) must promptly raise significant matters directly with the firm’s governing body, the chair of the body, or any relevant committee of the body; and
(b) must promptly tell any other individual to whom this rule applies if the first individual becomes aware of a risk that might have (or a number of risks that, taken together, might have) a significant effect on:
(i) the firm’s risk management strategy; or
(ii) the other individual’s functions.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.1.5 Reports about internal control and assurance functions
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.1.5 Reports about internal control and assurance functions
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must ensure that each internal control and assurance function makes periodic written reports to the firm’s governing body, or a relevant committee of the body, about the matters in subrule (2).

(2) The matters are the following:

(a) how each internal control and assurance function is performing against the firm’s policies, procedures and controls for the function;
(b) the shorter-term and longer-term objectives of each internal control and assurance function, and the progress made in achieving those objectives;
(c) resources of staff, equipment, time and budget allocated to the internal controls and assurance framework and an analysis of the adequacy of those resources;

(d) any material deficiency, material weakness or material failure of an internal control and assurance function, and the response to the deficiency, weakness or failure.
Guidance
The body or committee could also have regard to:

• reports by the internal audit function that cover the other internal control and assurance functions
• reports commissioned from third parties in relation the internal control and assurance functions.

(3) The body or committee must determine:

(a) how often such a report must be made; and
(b) how serious a deficiency, weakness or failure must be to require reporting under subrule (2) (d).
Note Under GENE, Part 4.2 an authorised firm must notify the Regulatory Authority if the firm becomes aware of (or believes that there may be) a material weakness in, or failure of, either of the firm’s internal control functions (see GENE, rule 4.2.2 (1) (d))

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.2.2 What makes up authorised firm’s risk management function?
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.2.2 What makes up authorised firm’s risk management function?
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm’s risk management function is made up of:

(a) the individual (if any) who is approved to perform the risk management function for the firm;
(b) any other employees allocated to the function;
(c) the firm’s risk management strategy;
(d) the part of the firm’s resources (other than staff) allocated to the function; and
(e) the firm’s risk management policies and procedures.
(2) The purpose of an authorised firm’s risk management function is to monitor and control the firm’s risk exposure.
(3) The risk management function must provide for timely monitoring of, advising on, investigating and reporting on all reasonably foreseeable material risks.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.2.3 Which firms must have individual to exercise risk management function?
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.2.3 Which firms must have individual to exercise risk management function?
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm, or an Islamic banking business firm, must have an individual who is approved to exercise the risk management function for the firm.
(2) A QFC insurer (other than a QFC captive insurer) must have an individual who is approved to exercise the risk management function for the firm.
Note Banking business firm, or an Islamic banking business firm, QFC insurer and QFC captive insurer are defined in the Glossary.
(3) Any other authorised firm must have an individual who is approved to exercise the risk management function for the firm if it is appropriate to do so because of the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business.

(4) The individual who is approved to exercise the risk management function for the following firms must be ordinarily resident in Qatar:

(a) a banking business firm, or an Islamic banking business firm;
(b) a QFC insurer (other than a QFC captive insurer) that is incorporated under the Companies Regulations.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.3.2 Who can exercise a firm’s compliance oversight function?
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.3.2 Who can exercise a firm’s compliance oversight function?
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm, or an Islamic banking business firm, and a QFC insurer (other than a QFC captive insurer) that is incorporated under the Companies Regulations, must have an individual who is approved to exercise the compliance oversight function for the firm.
(2) The individual who is approved to exercise the compliance oversight function for a banking business firm, or an Islamic banking business firm, or a QFC insurer (other than a QFC captive insurer) that is incorporated under the Companies Regulations, must be ordinarily resident in Qatar.

(3) Any other authorised firm must either:

(a) have an individual who is approved to exercise the compliance oversight function; or
(b) with the permission of the Regulatory Authority, appoint a suitably qualified third party to exercise the compliance oversight function for the firm.
(4) Where a firm proposes to appoint a suitably qualified third party to exercise the firm’s compliance oversight function, the firm must satisfy the Regulatory Authority that the third party has sufficient knowledge, experience and authority to exercise the function.
(5) When giving permission for the appointment of a third party to exercise a firm’s compliance oversight function, the Regulatory Authority may impose such conditions as it considers appropriate on the appointment, including, in particular, conditions related to the employees of the third party.

(6) Where a third party appointed to exercise a firm’s compliance oversight function is not established in the QFC, or in the State:

(a) the third party must identify the individual employed by it who is to exercise the compliance oversight function for the firm; and
(b) that individual must have sufficient knowledge, experience and authority to exercise the function.

(7) The appointment of a third party to exercise a firm’s compliance oversight function is a material outsourcing arrangement (see Part 8.4).

Note By virtue of rule 8.4.2 (2) (d), the appointment of a group employee to exercise a controlled function is not an outsourcing arrangement.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.3.3 What makes up authorised firm’s compliance oversight function?
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.3.3 What makes up authorised firm’s compliance oversight function?
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm’s compliance oversight function is made up of:
(a) the individual who is approved to exercise the compliance oversight function for the firm;
(b) any other employees allocated responsibilities within the function;
(c) the part of the firm’s resources (other than staff) allocated to the function;
(d) the firm’s compliance policies and procedures; and
(e) the records that the firm keeps in relation to compliance matters.
Note Appropriate records must be kept of policies and procedures — see GENE, rule 6.1.1.
(2) The purposes of an authorised firm’s compliance oversight function are the following:
(a) to ensure that the firm complies with:
(i) decisions of the Regulatory Authority;
(ii) the firm’s internal policies, procedures and controls; and
(iii) requirements and standards applicable to the firm under the law applicable in the QFC or any other applicable law;
(b) to ensure that the firm’s business is conducted ethically and responsibly;
(c) to minimise the risk of the firm or its facilities being used in the furtherance of financial crime.
Guidance
The compliance oversight function includes:
• monitoring and assessing the adequacy and effectiveness of the firm’s compliance policies and procedures
• participating in the process of approving new products or significant changes to existing products
• monitoring and assessing the extent to which it complies with those policies and procedures
• monitoring and assessing the adequacy and effectiveness of measures taken to correct any deficiencies
• reporting to the firm’s governing body as necessary
• maintaining and updating the firm’s compliance policies and procedures in conjunction with the firm’s senior executive function and senior management
• providing advice and support to the firm’s senior executive function and senior management about compliance issues.
Note For the meaning of financial crime, see the Glossary.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.4.1 Which firms must have internal audit function?
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.4.1 Which firms must have internal audit function?
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm, or an Islamic banking business firm, or a QFC insurer (other than a QFC captive insurer) must establish and maintain an internal audit function.
(2) An authorised firm that is not required by subrule (1) to have an internal audit function must establish and maintain such a function if it is appropriate to do so because of the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business.
(3) The Regulatory Authority may direct an authorised firm to establish and maintain an internal audit function.

(4) An authorised firm’s internal audit function must be appropriate to:

(a) the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business; and
(b) the firm’s risk profile and legal status.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.4.2 Which firms must have internal auditor?
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.4.2 Which firms must have internal auditor?
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) A banking business firm, or an Islamic banking business firm, must have an individual who is approved to exercise the internal audit function for the firm.

(2) A QFC insurer (other than a QFC captive insurer):

(a) must have an individual who is approved to exercise the internal audit function for the firm; or
(b) may, with the permission of the Regulatory Authority, appoint a suitably qualified third party as internal auditor.
(3) For Part 8.4, the appointment of a third party by a QFC insurer is a material outsourcing arrangement.
(4) Any other authorised firm must have an individual who is approved to exercise the internal audit function for the firm if it is appropriate to do so because of the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business.

(5) The Authority may direct an authorised firm to appoint an individual who is approved to exercise the internal audit function for the firm.

Guidance
For a firm that is part of a corporate group, the corporate group internal audit function may be used to perform the function for the firm. This means that the firm is not required to have a dedicated resource for the internal audit function. The work to be undertaken by the internal audit function would depend on the agreed risk-based audit plan for the firm and the corporate group-wide auditor would be best placed to decide that work.
Note Nothing in this rule prevents a firm from appointing a corporate group employee to the internal audit function.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.4.3 What makes up authorised firm’s internal audit function?
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.4.3 What makes up authorised firm’s internal audit function?
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm’s internal audit function is made up of:
(a) the firm’s internal auditor (if any);
(b) any other employees who are allocated responsibilities within the function;
(c) the part of the firm’s resources (other than staff) allocated to the function;
(d) the firm’s audit charter and risk-based audit plan; and
(e) the records that the firm keeps in relation to internal audit.
Note For other audit requirements for firms, see GENE, Part 9.5.
(2) The purpose of an authorised firm’s internal audit function is to provide independent assurance of:
(a) the adequacy and effectiveness of the firm’s policies and procedures, and the documentation about them, for the firm as a whole, its corporate group, each subsidiary (if any) and each part of the firm (such as a business unit, business area or department);
(b) the reliability and integrity of information and the means used to identify, measure, classify and report such information;
(c) the accuracy and currency of the identification of risks and the agreed actions to address them;
(d) the safeguarding of the firm’s assets and the assets of its depositors, policyholders, clients and other stakeholders;
(e) the existence of those assets;
(f) whether the firm’s assets are appropriately segregated from the assets of its depositors, policyholders, clients and other stakeholders; and
(g) the performance of the firm’s external auditors, to the extent requested by its governing body and consistent with applicable law.
(3) The internal audit function must carry out regular assessments of the firm’s internal audit policies, procedures and controls and incorporate any necessary improvements.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.4.4 Authority of internal auditor
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
An authorised firm’s internal audit policies, procedures and controls must provide that:

(a) the firm’s internal auditor, and any employee allocated responsibilities within the internal audit function, must have access to, and must review, any information, documents and records of the firm that he or she considers necessary to carry out an audit or other review; and
(b) the internal auditor has the authority:
(i) to undertake, on his or her own initiative, a review of any area or any function of the firm consistently with the internal audit function’s purpose;
(ii) to require an appropriate management response to an internal audit report, including the development of a suitable remediation or mitigation plan or other follow-up plan; and
(iii) to decline to undertake an audit or review, or take on any other duty, that he or she believes is inconsistent with the internal audit function’s purpose or the firm’s internal audit policies and procedures.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.5.1 Which QFC insurers must have actuarial function?
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.5.1 Which QFC insurers must have actuarial function?
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to a QFC insurer if:
(a) the insurer conducts long term insurance business (within the meaning given by PINS, rule 1.2.5 (2)); or
(b) the insurer conducts general insurance business (within the meaning given by PINS, rule 1.2.5 (1)), and:
(i) more than 15% of the insurer’s gross outstanding liabilities are attributable to contracts of insurance for general insurance business in PINS category 1; or
(ii) more than 20% of the insurer’s gross outstanding liabilities are attributable to contracts of insurance for general insurance business in PINS category 4.
(2) However, this rule does not apply to a QFC captive insurer.
Note For the obligations of a QFC captive insurer in relation to the actuarial function, see CAPI, Chapter 7.
(3) A QFC insurer to which this rule applies must establish and maintain an actuarial function that is appropriate to the nature, scale and complexity of the insurer’s business.
(4) In subrule (1):
PINS category 1 and PINS category 4 have the respective meanings given by PINS, rule 1.2.8.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.5.2 Which QFC insurers must have individual to exercise actuarial function?
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.5.2 Which QFC insurers must have individual to exercise actuarial function?
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) A QFC insurer to which rule 6.5.1 applies must have an individual who is approved to exercise the actuarial function for the firm (an approved actuary).
(2) The individual must not be one who:
(a) exercises the senior executive, executive governance or non-executive governance function for the insurer or a related body corporate (except a related body corporate that is a subsidiary of the insurer); or
(b) is an employee or director of an approved auditor (under the Companies Regulations, article 85 (1)) for the insurer.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.5.3 What makes up QFC insurer’s actuarial function?
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.5.3 What makes up QFC insurer’s actuarial function?
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) A QFC insurer’s actuarial function is made up of:
(a) each approved actuary for the insurer;
(b) any other employees who are allocated responsibilities within the actuarial function;
(c) the part of the insurer’s resources (other than staff) allocated to the function;
(d) the insurer’s actuarial policies and procedures; and
(e) the records that the insurer keeps in relation to actuarial matters.
Note See PINS, Chapter 9, for an insurer’s obligations in relation to actuarial reporting.
(2) The purpose of the actuarial function of a QFC insurer is to advise the insurer on, and to monitor, investigate and report on, risks that materially affect:
(a) the insurer’s ability to meet its liabilities to policyholders;
(b) its capital requirements and solvency position;
(c) its technical provisions; and
(d) the setting of its premiums or prices.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.5.3 Guidance
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.5.3 What makes up QFC insurer’s actuarial function?
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
The matters about which an insurer’s actuary might advise the insurer include:

• the insurer’s actuarial and financial risks
• its investment policies and the valuation of its assets
• its solvency position, including the calculation of the minimum capital required for regulatory purposes and liability and loss provision
• its prospective solvency position
• its risk management strategy, and its risk assessment and management policies, procedures and controls relevant to actuarial matters or the financial condition of the firm
• distribution of policy dividends or other benefits
• underwriting policies
• reinsurance arrangements
• product development and design, including the terms and conditions of insurance contracts
• the sufficiency and quality of data used to calculate technical provisions
• risk modelling in the insurer’s own risk and solvency assessment
• the insurer’s use of internal models.

(2) The notice must set out the reasons for the removal.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.5.5 QFC insurer to give notice if appointment of approved actuary ends

CTRL 6.5.5 QFC insurer to give notice if appointment of approved actuary ends
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:

(a) that the appointment has ended; and
(b) the reasons for the ending of the appointment.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 6.5.8 Regulatory Authority may appoint actuary in certain circumstances
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.5.8 Regulatory Authority may appoint actuary in certain circumstances
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) If no individual is approved to exercise the actuarial function for a QFC insurer to which rule 6.5.1 applies within 28 days after a vacancy arises, the Regulatory Authority may appoint an actuary, or 2 or more actuaries, to exercise any part of the actuarial function for the insurer on the following terms:
(a) the insurer is to remunerate the actuary or actuaries on a basis agreed between the insurer and the actuary or, if there is no agreement, on a reasonable basis;
(b) each actuary is to hold office until he or she resigns or an actuary is approved for the insurer;
(c) each actuary has the same authority within the insurer that he or she would have as an approved actuary.
(2) The insurer must comply with, and is bound by, the terms on which the Authority appoints an actuary under subrule (1).
(3) An actuary appointed by the Authority under subrule (1) is not an approved actuary.

doc_path: CTRL Chapter 6 Internal controls and assurance
CTRL 6.5.8 Regulatory Authority may appoint actuary in certain circumstances
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
1 Rule 6.5.8 allows, but does not require, the Regulatory Authority to appoint an actuary if no actuary has been approved for the insurer within the 28-day period referred to in rule 6.5.8 (1). In considering whether to use that power, the Authority would take into account the likely delay until the insurer can make an appointment, and the urgency of any pending duties of the actuary.
2 The Authority would not normally seek to appoint an actuary under rule 6.5.8 if the insurer concerned has applied for the approval of an individual to exercise the actuarial function and that application is still being considered.
3 If the Authority appoints an actuary, the insurer remains obliged to appoint an individual to the actuarial function and must seek the Authority’s approval of the individual (even if the individual it proposes to appoint is the actuary appointed by the Authority).

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 7.1.2 What is a risk management framework?
doc_path: CTRL 7.1.2 What is a risk management framework?
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm’s risk management framework is the totality of systems, structures, policies, procedures and people within the firm that identifies, measures, evaluates, monitors, reports on and controls or mitigates all internal and external sources of material risk.
(2) Material risks are risks that could have a material financial or non-financial effect on the firm, or on the interests of its customers or other stakeholders.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 7.1.3 Firms to have risk management framework
doc_path: CTRL 7.1.3 Firms to have risk management framework
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must have a documented risk management framework.

(2) The risk management framework must:

(a) enable the firm to appropriately develop and implement strategies, policies, procedures and controls to identify and manage different types of material risks; and

(b) provide the firm’s governing body with a comprehensive firm-wide view of material risks.

Guidance
1 In identifying material risks, an authorised firm’s risk management framework should be forward looking to ensure new and emerging risks that could materialise are identified.
2 Some emerging risks that may become material may also require consideration of time horizons longer than the normal business and strategic planning of the firm; for example, financial risks related to climate change.
(3) The framework must be appropriate to the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business.
(4) An authorised firm that is a branch may rely on the risk management framework of its head office if the firm has assessed the head office’s framework and decided that it appropriately addresses the firm’s internal and external sources of material risk.

(5) The firm’s risk management framework must reflect the firm’s business objectives and business plan, and must include:

(a) a risk appetite statement;
(b) a risk management strategy;
(c) a risk management function dedicated to the framework;
(d) a BCP;
(e) a management information system to support the effectiveness of the framework;
(f) a robust review process to ensure that the framework remains effective;
(g) for a banking business firm, or an Islamic banking business firm, an internal capital adequacy assessment process (or ICAAP) required under BANK or IBANK; and
(h) for a QFC insurer (other than a QFC captive insurer or a QFC insurer that is a branch), an own risk and solvency assessment (or ORSA) required under PINS.

Note These rules require the governing body of an authorised firm to approve:

(a) the strategic and business plan, see rule 3.1.14 (1) (a);
(b) the risk appetite statement, see rule 7.1.5 (4);
(c) the risk management strategy, see rule 7.1.6 (3); and
(d) the BCP, see rule 8.6.3 (1).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 7.1.4 Risks to be addressed
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) Every authorised firm must ensure that its risk management framework addresses:

(a) liquidity risk;
(b) operational risk (including legal risk and ICT and information security risks);
Guidance

1 Legal risk is the risk of loss arising from:

(a) regulatory or legal action;
(b) disputes; or
(c) failure to comply with, or the inadequate management of, legal or regulatory obligations.

2 An authorised firm’s risk management policies and procedures should include processes for identifying, assessing, managing and mitigating legal risk. The policies should include:

(a) processes for identifying events that might generate legal risk (for example, new products or processes, new documentation), the likelihood of those events occurring and their consequences; and

(b) procedures to ensure that:

(i) all contractual, legal, regulatory and other documents are accurate and complete;
(ii) the firm complies with all its legal, regulatory, contractual and prudential requirements and obligations; and
(iii) all the firm’s insurances (for example, professional indemnity) are renewed in good time and remain effective.
Note For additional requirements on operational risk, see Chapter 8.
(c) compliance, reputational and regulatory risk;
(d) money laundering and terrorism financing risk; and

(e) every other risk (whether singly or in combination with another risk) that:

(i) is material to the firm; or

(ii) may have a material impact on the firm.

Examples
group risk
climate related risk
Guidance
For a firm that is not a banking business firm, an Islamic banking business firm, or a QFC insurer, the risks mentioned in subrule (2) may need to be addressed in the firm’s risk management framework if the risks are material to the firm or may have a material impact on the firm.

(2) An authorised firm that is a banking business firm, an Islamic banking business firm, or a QFC insurer (other than a QFC captive insurer) must ensure that its risk management framework also addresses:

(a) asset-liability management risk;

Guidance
Asset-liability management risk is the risk of an adverse movement in the relative values of assets and liabilities of a bank or insurer due to changes in general market factors, such as interest rates, inflation and, if relevant, foreign exchange rates.

(b) concentration risk;

Guidance
Concentration risk is the risk of over-reliance on, or excessive exposure to, a type of risk, counterparty, asset class, industry or region as a result of credit, balance sheet and market, reserving, insurance, reinsurance, operational and group risks.
(c) credit risk;
(d) market and investment risk (including derivative risk);
(e) market conduct risk; and
(f) strategy and planning risk.

(3) A QFC insurer (other than a QFC captive insurer) must ensure that its risk management framework addresses, in addition to the risks in subrules (1) and (2):

(a) insurance risk;
(b) reserving risk; and
(c) reinsurance risk.
Guidance
1 Insurance risk is the risk that inadequate or inappropriate underwriting, claims management, product design and pricing will expose an insurer to financial loss and the consequent inability to meet its liabilities.
2 Reserving risk is the risk that the reserves set aside by the insurer for its insurance liabilities (net of reinsurance and other recoveries for those liabilities) will be inadequate to meet the net amount payable when the insurance liabilities crystallise.
3 Reinsurance risk is the risk that the reinsurance cover obtained by the insurer is inadequate.
Note PINS, Schedule 1 gives additional guidance on the above risks faced by a QFC insurer. The Parts of Schedule 1 that are relevant are Part S1 credit risk; Part S2 Balance sheet and market risk; Part S3 reserving risk; Part S4 insurance risk; Part S5 reinsurance risk; Part S7 concentration risk and Part S8 group risk.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 7.1.5 Risk appetite statement
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must have a documented risk appetite statement. A risk appetite statement is a high-level statement that clearly captures the firm’s attitude to, and its level of acceptance of, the material risks the firm is exposed to.

(2) The firm’s risk appetite is the level of risk that the firm is willing to assume to achieve its strategic objectives and business plan.

Guidance
In setting its risk appetite, the firm must take account of its prudential and other regulatory requirements.

(3) The statement must, for each material risk, identify the maximum level of risk that the firm is willing to operate within, expressed as a risk limit and based on its risk appetite, risk profile and capital strength (risk tolerance).

Guidance
Risk tolerances are usually quantitative and support the translation of the risk appetite by senior management into operational limits for the day-to-day management of material risks.

(4) The firm’s governing body must review and approve the statement annually.

Guidance
1 An authorised firm should consider using qualitative and quantitative measures in its statement as appropriate. The qualitative statement and quantitative measures referred to in this rule should reflect those expressed in the firm’s risk management strategy (see rule 7.1.6 (2) (c)).
2 For the purposes of setting risk tolerances, the firm may wish to utilise a taxonomy that divides a material risk into more granular risks. For example, a firm may wish to have specific risk tolerances for different risks that fall within the broad definition of operational risk, such as ICT and information security risks.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 7.1.6 Risk management strategy
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm’s risk management strategy must be appropriate to the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business.

(2) The strategy must:

(a) identify each material risk to which the firm is exposed, and the approach to managing those risks;
(b) clearly define and categorise material risks;
(c) include both quantitative and qualitative considerations;
(d) set out the approach to monitoring for significant changes to the firm’s risk profile;
(e) list and summarise the policies and procedures dealing with risk management;
(f) include objectives, principles and a well-defined, transparent and consistent allocation of responsibility for dealing with material risks across the firm, including any branches;

(g) include an assessment of whether the firm’s financial resources are adequate to address material risks, as well as an overview of the mechanisms for monitoring, and ensuring compliance with, its capital requirements; and

Guidance
For a banking business firm, an Islamic banking business firm, or a QFC insurer this requirement can be addressed by referring to its ICAAP or ORSA.

(h) outline the firm’s approach:

(i) to ensuring that all its staff have awareness of the risk management framework as it relates to their role; and
(ii) for establishing an appropriate risk culture across the firm.

(3) The firm’s governing body must review and approve the strategy annually. The firm must have:

(a) a process for obtaining and recording the governing body’s approval for a material change to, or deviation from, the strategy; and
(b) a process for obtaining a direction by the governing body settling any major question about the interpretation of the strategy.

(4) The firm must ensure that the strategy is:

(a) recorded in writing; and
(b) kept up to date to take into account new internal and external circumstances.
(5) If the firm is part of a corporate group, the firm’s governing body must know the implications for the firm of any group-wide risk management strategy.
(6) The firm must give to the Regulatory Authority a copy of its risk management strategy, and any subsequent amended version of that strategy, within 10 business days after its approval.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 7.1.7 Policies and procedures
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm’s risk management policies and procedures required under rule 7.1.6 (2) (e) must be appropriate to the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business and the risks to which it is exposed.

(2) The policies and procedures must include processes for:

(a) identifying and assessing material risks;
(b) establishing, implementing and testing mitigation measures and control mechanisms for material risks;
(c) assessing risk positions, risk exposures, the steps being taken to manage them and, if the firm’s risk profile changes, reviewing risk limits;
(d) reporting risk management information in both normal and stressed market conditions to the firm’s governing body and senior management in a timely way, including escalation processes for reporting material events, issues and incidents;
(e) establishing and maintaining appropriate contingency arrangements (including robust and credible disaster recovery plans where warranted) to address risks that may materialise and actions to be taken, including in stressed conditions;
(f) developing and maintaining effective risk management communication within the firm;
(g) ensuring material risks are appropriately accounted for in the firm’s internal pricing, performance measurement and new product approval processes for all significant business activities; and
(h) reviewing the adequacy and effectiveness of the firm’s risk management policies, procedures and controls, including the triggers for commencing reviews.

(3) A banking business firm or an Islamic banking business firm must ensure that its policies and procedures also include a policy that specifies the nature, role and extent of asset-liability management activities and their relationship with the firm’s banking business model.

Note A banking business firm, or an Islamic banking business firm, is also required to have policies and procedures in relation to certain material risks under BANK or IBANK. Refer to BANK Part 1.2 and IBANK Part 1.2.

(4) A QFC insurer (other than a QFC captive insurer) must ensure that its policies and procedures also include:

(a) a policy that specifies the nature, role and extent of asset-liability management activities and their relationship with product development, pricing and investment management;
(b) a policy that specifies the nature, role and extent of the insurer’s investment activities (including credit exposures) and how the insurer complies with regulatory requirements relating to investment;
(c) a policy that specifies the risks to be accepted by the insurer as part of its insurance business, the processes for underwriting, product design, pricing and claims settlement and how the policy interacts with the insurer’s reinsurance policy; and

(d) a policy that sets out processes for ensuring that its reinsurance arrangements are prudently and soundly managed, including that any reinsurance contract to which the insurer is a party is finalised and the material documents supporting the contract are completed:

(i) before the start of reinsurance cover (the start date); or
(ii) as soon as possible after the start date (but in no case later than 60 days after the start date).
Note The policies and procedures must deal with the risks faced by a QFC insurer. For guidance on what those risks might be, see PINS, Schedule 1, Parts S1 to S5, S7 and S8.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 7.1.8 Firms must provide appropriate training
doc_path: CTRL 7.1.8 Firms must provide appropriate training
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) The senior management of an authorised firm must ensure that appropriate risk management training is available to staff at all levels throughout the firm. The training must be appropriate to the seniority, role and responsibilities of staff.

(2) The senior management must ensure that staff:

(a) have an awareness of the risk management framework as it relates to their role; and
(b) understand the material risks that the firm is exposed to;
so that each member of staff can identify, assess, manage, and mitigate those risks effectively.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 7.1.9 Independence of certain employees
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must ensure that each employee who is allocated responsibilities within the firm’s risk management framework is sufficiently free from influence for the framework to be effective in achieving its purposes.
(2) The requirement in subrule (1) is satisfied if reasonable measures have been taken to ensure that:
(a) no such employee is remunerated in a way that would tend to undermine his or her independence and objectivity in performing the duties;
Note For the requirements relating to a firm’s remuneration policy, see rule 3.1.16.
(b) no such employee is involved in performing a function that generates, or is intended to generate, revenue for the firm;
(c) no such employee is limited or restricted as to the matters that he or she can investigate or report on in the exercise of his or her function;
(d) the reports and conclusions of such an employee can be honest and candid, without fear of reprisal; and
(e) pressure or influence is not applied to such an employee to modify his or her reports or conclusions.

 

Derived from QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
Notes for Chapter 8

1 This Chapter expands the requirements addressed in general, and at a high level, in Chapter 7 as they relate to operational risk. The expanded provisions reflect:

(a) the wide scope of operational risk;
(b) the increasing complexity and interconnectivity of the business environment;
(c) the growing dependence of firms on ICT, third parties and longer supply chains; and
(d) the need for greater focus on operational resilience on the part of authorised firms.
2 This Chapter also sets out requirements for operational resilience, outsourcing, ICT and information security risks, and business continuity.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.1.1 Application of Chapter 8
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) This Chapter applies to all authorised firms.

Guidance
1 An authorised firm should meet the requirements in Chapter 8 in a proportionate way. For example, firms with less complex operations (such as one with lower reliance on third parties or ICT or with less sensitive information assets) may have simpler approaches to meeting them.

2 Because of the principles-based approach adopted by the Regulatory Authority, an authorised firm is allowed to determine how to meet the requirements, depending on the nature, scale and complexity of its business. In particular, each firm’s approach:

(a) should reflect the assessment of its operational risk and operational resilience;
(b) should be aligned to its corporate governance framework, risk appetite and risk management framework; and
(c) should be reviewed and approved by the governing body.
(2) If an authorised firm that is a branch or subsidiary considers it suitable, the firm may rely on the policies, processes and procedures of its head office or parent entity to meet the requirements of this Chapter.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)
Amended by QFCRA_RM2023-3 (as from 1st August 2023).

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.1.2 Risk event reporting
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must give the Regulatory Authority written notice of an operational risk event or near miss that has, or could have had, a material financial, business or reputational impact on the firm’s operations.

Example
A cyber-attack or similar incident.

(2) The notice must be given within 1 business day after the event, near miss, attack or incident occurs and must set out:

(a) the nature and details of the event, near miss, attack or incident and its impact, or likely impact, on the firm’s operations;
(b) the disruption (if any) to the firm’s operations; and
(c) if disruption occurred, the action taken, and to be taken, by the firm to return to normal operations, together with a timeframe for doing so.
(3) If the firm undertakes a root cause analysis of a disruption, it must give the Authority an outline of the procedure and result of the analysis and details of actions taken to prevent a reoccurrence. The outline and details must be given as soon as practicable after the analysis.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.2.1 Definition of operational risk
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) Operational risk is the risk of loss arising from:

(a) inadequate or failed internal processes or systems;
(b) the inactions or actions of people; or
(c) external drivers or events.

(2) Operational risk is inherent in all products, activities, processes and systems. It includes the risk of fraud, legal risk and ICT and information security risks but does not include strategic and reputational risks.

Note Part 8.2 does not list specific risks that fall within the scope of operational risk. An authorised firm should identify for itself those specific risks that are most relevant to its business.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.2.2 Obligations relating to operational risk
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.2.2 Obligations relating to operational risk
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must identify, assess and manage operational risk.

Guidance
1 The identification and assessment of risks is fundamental to effective operational risk management. It directly contributes to the operational resilience of authorised firms.
2 Effective risk identification considers both internal and external factors. Sound risk assessment allows the firm to better understand its risk profile, allocate resources and implement strategies.
3 This rule enhances rule 7.1.5. (3) on the requirement for an authorised firm to identify the maximum level of risk (risk tolerance) based on its risk appetite, risk profile and capital strength.
Examples of tools to identify and assess operational risk
• event management
• operational risk event data gathering
• self-assessments
• control monitoring and assurance framework
• metrics
• scenario analysis

• benchmarking and comparative analysis

Note For guidance on each of the above tools, see the Principles for the sound management of operational risk published by the BCBS, as amended from time to time. See also guidance and principles of other standards-setting bodies such as IAIS and IOSCO regarding identification and assessment of operational risk.

(2) The firm must have a documented operational risk framework that is integrated into its risk management framework. The firm must develop and implement:

(a) governance arrangements for the oversight of operational risk (including reporting lines and roles and responsibilities);
(b) monitoring, analysis and reporting of operational risk and escalation processes for operational risk events; and
(c) internal controls that are designed and used effectively for the management of operational risk.
Guidance

Internal controls should be designed to provide reasonable assurance that an authorised firm will:

(a) have efficient and effective operations;
(b) safeguard its assets and adequately manage liabilities;
(c) produce reliable financial reports; and
(d) comply with its own policies and procedures and with applicable laws and regulations.
Examples of controls
• segregation of duties
• dual controls
• clearly established authorities or processes for approval
• close monitoring of adherence to risk thresholds
• safeguards for access to, and use of, assets and records
• appropriate staffing and training to maintain technical expertise
• ongoing processes to identify business units or products when returns appear to be out of line with reasonable expectations
• regular verification and reconciliation of transactions and accounts
Note Under rule 7.1.4, operational risk is one of the risks that an authorised firm’s risk management framework must address.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.2.3 Operational risk change management processes
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.2.3 Operational risk change management processes
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm’s operational risk framework must include a process for managing changes in its products, activities, systems, markets, locations and jurisdictions (OR change management process).

(2) The firm’s OR change management process must:

(a) include identifying, managing, challenging, approving, and monitoring change on the basis of objective criteria;
(b) ensure that operational risk arising from changes is promptly identified, assessed and managed; and
(c) be subject to independent and regular review and update.
Guidance

1 An authorised firm’s operational risk exposure generally evolves when the firm initiates change by, for example:

(a) engaging in a new activity;
(b) developing a new service or product;
(c) entering into an unfamiliar market or jurisdiction;
(d) implementing new business processes or modifying them; or
(e) engaging in a business that is geographically distant from its head office.
2 As part of the general role and obligations of a firm’s governing body (as set out in Division 3.1.C of Chapter 3) the Regulatory Authority expects the governing body, or an appropriate committee of the governing body, to approve any changes that significantly affect the firm’s risk management process.
3 Change management should assess the evolution of associated risks from start to finish (for example, throughout the full life cycle of a product).
4 The firm’s OR change management process should be able to deal with changes resulting from other sources of operational risk, such as those that may arise from mergers and acquisitions, issues of corporate strategy, and major projects and investments.
Note For management of changes in ICT systems, see Part 8.5.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.2.4 Operational risk reports
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must, from time to time, prepare operational risk reports for the purposes of the monitoring, analysis and reporting required under rule 8.2.2 (2) (b). Each report:

(a) must be comprehensive, accurate, consistent and actionable across business units and products;
(b) must be timely and capable of being produced in both normal and stressed market conditions;
(c) must be manageable in scope and volume;
(d) must give an outlook of the firm’s operational risk profile; and
(e) must not impede decision-making by reason of excessive or inadequate data.
Guidance
The frequency of reporting should reflect the risks that might arise, and the pace and nature of changes, in an authorised firm’s business. The results of monitoring should be included in regular reports to the firm’s governing body and senior management, as should any assessments of its operational risk framework and operational resilience approach.
(2) An operational risk report must describe the firm’s operational risk profile by providing internal financial, operational and compliance indicators, together with external market or environmental information about events and conditions that are relevant to decision making.

(3) The following must be included in the report:

(a) breaches of the firm’s risk appetite and risk tolerance for operational risk (including details of action taken, or planned, to mitigate the effect of any such breaches);
(b) a discussion and assessment of key and emerging risks;
(c) details of recent significant internal operational risk events and losses (including root-cause analysis); and
(d) relevant external events or regulatory changes and their potential impact on the firm.
Guidance
Under this rule, the reports received by the governing body of an authorised firm may include reports on ICT and information security risks, major ICT projects and significant security breaches, as required by rule 8.5.2 (1) (f). Alternatively, the governing body may receive a separate report on those matters.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)
Amended by QFCRA_RM2023-3 (as from 1st August 2023).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.2.4A Amendments to a material outsourcing arrangement
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.2.4A Amendments to a material outsourcing arrangement
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) Other than cases where the Regulatory Authority must give prior permission for a material outsourcing arrangement, an authorised firm must not amend a material outsourcing arrangement unless it gives the Regulatory Authority written notice of the amendment at least 30 business days before the amendment takes effect.
(2) If a material outsourcing arrangement is one which requires the prior permission of the Regulatory Authority, an authorised firm must not amend the arrangement unless it has the Authority’s permission to do so.
 
Inserted by QFCRA_RM2023-3 (as from 1st August 2023).

doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.2.5 Additional information about material outsourcing arrangements
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) The Regulatory Authority may, by written notice to an authorised firm, require the firm to give the Authority, within a stated reasonable period, information about a material outsourcing arrangement (or proposed material outsourcing arrangement) that the Authority reasonably needs to enable it to decide whether the arrangement complies with this Chapter.
(2) The power given by this rule is additional to the Authority’s other powers.
Note See for example FSR, article 48 (Powers to obtain documents and information).

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.2.6 Contingency arrangements
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm that enters into a material outsourcing arrangement must make comprehensive contingency arrangements to allow its business to continue in the event of a significant loss of services from the service provider.
(2) The contingency arrangements must include:
(a) an exit strategy; and
(b) if appropriate, provision for partial exit and step-in.
(3) The contingency arrangements must cover at least the following:
(a) a significant loss of resources at the service provider;
(b) financial failure of the service provider;
(c) unexpected termination of the outsourcing arrangement.

doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience

2 The requirements address the growing risks to operational resilience from the interconnectedness of the financial system and the complex and dynamic environment in which a firm operates.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.3.2 When is an operation critical and what is operational resilience?
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.3.2 When is an operation critical and what is operational resilience?
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An operation is critical if it is a service, product or function identified by an authorised firm as one which, if disrupted, is likely to have a significant impact on the firm, its customers or its role in the financial system.
(2) Operational resilience, of an authorised firm, is the ability of the firm to deliver critical operations in the event of a disruption. It includes the ability of the firm to prevent, adapt to, respond to, recover from, and learn from operational disruption.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.3.2 When is an operation critical and what is operational resilience?
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
1 Operational resilience requires an authorised firm to look at, from end-to-end, each of the activities required to deliver a particular operation. This differs from the more traditional focus of business continuity management on protecting individual systems, processes and functions.
2 The firm’s ICT policies, processes and procedures should identify the ICT dependencies for its critical operations.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.3.3 Approach to operational resilience
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must align its operational resilience approach to its corporate governance framework and operational risk framework.

Guidance

As part of its approach to operational resilience, an authorised firm should:

(a) leverage change management capabilities in accordance with its OR change management process as a way to assess potential effects on the delivery of critical operations and on their interconnections and interdependencies; and
(b) ensure its existing corporate governance framework and committee structures include responsibilities for operational resilience.
Note The governing body of an authorised firm is responsible for overseeing an effective approach to the firm’s operational resilience (see rule 3.1.17).
(2) The firm must have sound, effective and comprehensive processes and systems to enable it to comply with its obligations under this Part.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.3.4 Obligations relating to critical operations
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.3.4 Obligations relating to critical operations
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must identify its critical operations and determine the systems, infrastructure and resources needed to support each operation.

(2) In identifying critical operations, the firm must consider:

(a) the impact a disruption would pose to the firm and its customers;
(b) the soundness of the firm and its ability to continue operating; and
(c) the firm’s role in the financial system.

(3) The governing body must review and approve all operations identified as critical at least once a year.

Guidance
1 Because business differs from firm to firm, an authorised firm should take an outcomes-based approach in identifying critical operations. The firm’s critical operations will usually be a short list of services, products or functions, for which the firm has chosen to build high levels of operational resilience in anticipation of disruption.

2 The firm should consider whether the number of critical operations is appropriate to the nature, scale and complexity of its business. It should also consider the practicalities of identifying critical operations, so that:

(a) the firm’s governing body and senior management can prioritise the operations and make investment decisions; and
(b) the impact tolerance set for an operation can be applied to, and tested on, the operation.
Examples of operations
• payments
• deposit-taking and management
• custody
• settlements
• clearing
• claims processing
• customer enquiries
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.3.5 Impact tolerance
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) Impact tolerance, in relation to a critical operation, is the maximum tolerable level of disruption at which any further disruption to the operation:

(a) will have a significant impact on the soundness of the firm or its ability to continue operating; or
(b) will cause significant adverse impact on an authorised firm’s customers; or
(c) will pose a risk to the soundness, stability or resilience of the financial system or to the orderly operation of the financial markets.

(2) An impact tolerance must have a clear metric identifying the maximum level of disruption the firm is willing to tolerate in relation to the critical operation. At a minimum, there must be a time-based metric indicating the maximum acceptable period a critical operation can withstand a disruption.

Guidance

1 A time-based metric ensures that an authorised firm focuses its response to a disruption on the continuity of its critical operations. To be prepared to withstand more than one type of disruption, an authorised firm should consider having additional impact tolerance metrics that are, for example, based on:

(a) the maximum acceptable number of customers effected by a disruption;
(b) the maximum number of transactions affected by a disruption;
(c) the maximum extent of data loss the firm would tolerate as a result of a disruption; or
(d) the maximum value of transactions impacted.
2 Impact tolerance metrics should be clear and measurable and can be both qualitative and quantitative. They should refer to specific outcomes and measurements, so that the firm can determine the outcome if the impact tolerances are exceeded.
3 While impact tolerances should be aligned to an authorised firm’s risk appetite, they are separate and distinct measurements. Risk appetite and risk tolerances focus on the impact and probability of a risk event occurring and are typically set with references to the firm’s strategic and business plans.
4 The Regulatory Authority’s expectation is that impact tolerances will be set on assumptions that severe but plausible disruptions will occur. The firm should not consider the cause or probability of disruption when setting their impact tolerances.
5 Impact tolerances should be used as a planning tool for the firm (rather than as a tool to measure regulatory compliance) to enable the firm to understand its level of operational resilience in the event of a disruption.
6 In setting impact tolerances, the firm may leverage any appropriate pre-determined and approved criteria used as part of other practices. For example, these may include processes used for business impact analysis (BIA), recovery time objectives (RTOs), recovery point objectives (RPOs) and maximum tolerable outage (MTO) where these metrics that measure disruption of single points of failure feed into the delivery of a critical operation.
(3) An authorised firm must set, in relation to each critical operation, an impact tolerance that has been approved by the firm’s governing body.
(4) The firm must ensure that it can remain below its impact tolerance for each critical operation in the event of a severe but plausible disruption.
(5) Subrule (4) has effect on and after 1 October 2026.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.3.6 Resources and processes for critical operations
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.3.6 Resources and processes for critical operations
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must identify the resources and processes needed to deliver each critical operation.

(2) Identifying the resources and processes needed to deliver a critical operation, includes:

(a) identifying:

(i) resources (including financial and human resources, ICT and other information assets);
(ii) key steps in business activities and processes; and
(iii) organisational structures;
needed to deliver the operation;
(b) setting out interdependencies across the matters identified under paragraph (a); and
(c) identifying risks, obligations, key data and controls associated with delivering the operation.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.3.6 Guidance
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.3.6 Resources and processes for critical operations
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
1 An authorised firm should determine the appropriate methodology and assumptions for identifying the resources and processes needed to deliver critical operations that best fit its business, depending on its nature, scale and complexity.

2 Identification should be conducted with a level of detail that enables the firm to:

(a) identify resources that contribute to the delivery of each stage of the operation, and their importance;
(b) ascertain whether the resources are fit for purpose;
(c) consider what would happen if resources were to become unavailable;
(d) identify vulnerabilities and key dependencies; and
(e) test the firm’s ability to deliver critical operations while remaining below the impact tolerances.
3 The firm should ensure that when identifying the resources and processes needed to deliver critical operations, the firm takes account of dependencies on outsourcing. Particular care should be taken in maintaining updated details of information assets.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.3.7 Testing impact tolerances
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) The firm must periodically test its ability to remain below its impact tolerances and carry on critical operations in the event of a severe but plausible disruption (scenario testing). In conducting scenario testing, the firm must:

(a) identify a range of adverse circumstances of varying nature, severity and duration relevant to its business and operational risk profile; and
(c) consider the risks to delivery of the firm’s critical operations in those circumstances.
(2) The governing body of the firm must review the results of all scenario testing of critical operations.

(3) If scenario testing identifies a situation where impact tolerances may be breached:

(a) the firm must assess whether the test has identified weaknesses or vulnerabilities that require the firm to develop and implement a remediation plan to ensure that the firm can remain below its impact tolerances;
(b) the governing body must approve any remediation plan required to be developed under paragraph (a) and review its implementation; and
(c) the senior management and governing body may take any other action to improve the resilience of the firm’s critical operations and focus investment where needed.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)
