QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.3.7 Guidance
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
1 To design scenarios and understand their full implication, the firm should consider previous breaches or near misses within the firm, across the financial sector, and in other sectors and jurisdictions.
2 Impact tolerance assumes a disruption has occurred, and so testing the ability to remain below impact tolerances should not focus on preventing risk events from occurring. Rather, the Regulatory Authority expects the firm to focus on response and recovery.
3 The type, extent and frequency of testing should be appropriate to the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business. The firm should also consider testing if there is a material change to its business, critical operations or impact tolerances. The firm may choose to conduct this testing alongside its BCP testing.
4 A scenario test should identify any vulnerabilities or reliance on third parties. Testing should evolve as the firm learns from previous testing.
5 If a particular scenario causes the firm to exceed an impact tolerance and the governing body and senior management consider this is tolerable, they will need to be able to explain their reasoning to the Authority.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.3.8 Incident management, response and recovery
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.3.8 Incident management, response and recovery
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must develop and implement response and disaster recovery plans and procedures to manage incidents that disrupt, or that may potentially disrupt, the firm’s critical operations. The plans must be in writing, integrated into the firm’s operational risk framework and aligned to the firm’s operational resilience approach, risk appetite and impact tolerances.
(2) To enhance the firm’s ability to adapt and respond to future incidents, a lessons-learned exercise must be conducted after a disruption to a critical operation.
(3) After each lessons-learned exercise is conducted, the firm must make the necessary improvements to address identified weaknesses or vulnerabilities to ensure that it can remain below its impact tolerance for each critical operation in the event of a severe but plausible disruption.

(4) Root causes of disruptions must be identified and managed to prevent or minimise serial recurrence. The firm must maintain an inventory of:

(a) incident response and recovery;
(b) internal and third-party resources to support the firm’s response;
(c) recovery capabilities; and
(d) communication plans to report incidents to both internal and external stakeholders.
(5) Incident management, response and recovery procedures should be reviewed and tested periodically.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.3.8 Guidance
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.3.8 Incident management, response and recovery
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
1 Operational resilience requires an authorised firm to have an approach that covers the full life cycle of an incident, from the classification of incidents that trigger approved response and recovery procedures through to reflecting on lessons learned.
2 The incident management plan must consider how a disruption resulting from an incident can affect the firm’s risk appetite and impact tolerances.
3 Lessons learned from previous incidents, including incidents experienced by others, should be reflected when updating the incident management, response and disaster recovery plans and procedures.
4 The connections of the firm’s incident management and response plans to its BCP and disaster recovery plans should be clear.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.4.1 Application of Part 8.4
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
This Part does not apply to the outsourcing of a function by an authorised firm if the function is outsourced by the firm under COLL or CAPI.

Note 1 This Part, however, applies to outsourcing by an authorised firm to which PROF applies.
Note 2 Each of COLL and CAPI contains separate outsourcing rules for the outsourcing of functions by authorised firms to which those rules apply.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.4.1 Guidance
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
1 Financial services firms increasingly rely on service providers to support their operations. Firms look to external providers to perform not only functions, services or activities that would normally be performed in-house (that is, outsourcing) but also for new services, capabilities and expertise that extend its offerings to the market.
2 The expanded use of service providers gives rise to longer and more complex supply chains, often involving a reliance on fourth parties and other downstream providers.
3 While the requirements of this Part only apply to outsourcing arrangements, an authorised firm should consider applying the policies and controls mentioned in this Part to any third-party arrangement that could pose risks to the firm.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.4.2 Meaning of outsourcing and material outsourcing
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.4.2 Meaning of outsourcing and material outsourcing
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) In these rules:

material outsourcing arrangement, for an authorised firm, means an arrangement, entered into in accordance with rule 8.4.6, that is of such importance that weakness or failure in the performance of the function, service or activity would cast serious doubt on:

(a) the firm’s ability to comply with:

(i) any regulations, rules or principles; or
(ii) any condition, restriction or requirement of its authorisation;
(b) its financial performance or position; or

(c) the continuity of any of its critical operations.

Note See Part 8.3 on the requirement to identify critical operations.
outsourcing, for an authorised firm, means an arrangement between the firm and a separate service provider (including a member of the firm’s corporate group) by which the service provider performs a function, service or activity that would normally be performed by the firm.

(2) For the purposes of this Part, the following do not constitute outsourcing:

(a) an arrangement to provide advisory services (such as the provision of legal advice), audit services, personnel training services, billing services and physical security;
(b) a supply arrangement (including the supply of electricity or water and the provision of catering and cleaning services);
(c) the purchase of standardised services (such as market information services and the provision of prices); and

(d) the appointment of a group employee to perform a controlled function for the firm.

Note For provisions about the appointment of a group employee to perform a controlled function, see INDI, Part 3.2.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.4.3 Responsibility for outsourced functions, services or activities
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.4.3 Responsibility for outsourced functions, services or activities
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) The outsourcing of a function, service or activity by an authorised firm does not relieve the firm’s governing body from any obligation in relation to the function, service or activity under the law applicable in the QFC.

(2) The governing body remains responsible for ensuring:

(a) that all requirements are complied with in relation to the function, service or activity; and
(b) that the function, service or activity is otherwise properly performed.
(3) The governing body must exercise due skill, care and diligence in carrying out its obligations in relation to an outsourced function, service or activity that is performed under an outsourcing arrangement.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.4.4 Obligation to have outsourcing policy
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.4.4 Obligation to have outsourcing policy
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must have a policy for managing material outsourcing arrangements (outsourcing policy). The firm’s governing body must approve the policy.

(2) The policy must at least provide for:

(a) how the firm determines whether an arrangement relating to the performance of a function, service or activity is material to the firm;
(b) the firm’s approach to entering into, managing, monitoring, substituting and exiting material arrangements;
(c) the firm’s approach to managing the risks associated with material arrangements;
(d) clear accountability and roles and responsibility for entering into, monitoring and managing material arrangements; and
(e) the firm’s risk appetite and risk tolerance for outsourcing.
(3) A policy that the firm will not enter into any material outsourcing arrangements is taken to satisfy subrule (1).

(4) The governing body must review, at least once in every 2 years, the firm’s outsourcing policy and procedures, including:

(a) its procedures for:

(i) assessing the feasibility of a proposed material outsourcing arrangement and the risks that the arrangement poses to the firm’s business; and
(ii) costing any such proposal; and
(b) the criteria for selecting service providers.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.4.5 Due skill in material outsourcing arrangements
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.4.5 Due skill in material outsourcing arrangements
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) The senior management of an authorised firm must exercise due skill, care and diligence in selecting, entering into, managing and exiting from a material outsourcing arrangement.

(2) Before entering into a material outsourcing arrangement, the senior management:

(a) must assess the risks that the arrangement poses to the firm’s business; and
(b) must satisfy themselves that the service provider selected has the ability and capacity to perform the relevant function, service or activity reliably and professionally at the start and throughout the life cycle of the arrangement.

(3) For this rule, the senior management must take into account at least the following matters:

(a) whether the service provider is regulated, to what extent, and by whom;
(b) whether the function, service or activity is subject to specific regulation or supervision;
(c) the risk that the service provider’s service may become unavailable because of the number of other persons using the service provider;
(d) any potential impacts on the firm’s level of operational risk;
(e) any potential impacts on the operational resilience of the firm that the arrangement may give rise to (including the firm’s ability to remain below its impact tolerances);
(e) the financial stability and expertise of the service provider; and
(f) any conflict of interest that might arise from the provision of the function, service or activity by the service provider.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.4.5 Guidance
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.4.5 Due skill in material outsourcing arrangements
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
1 Outsourcing can expose an authorised firm to heightened operational risk (particularly ICT and information security risks). Before entering into an outsourcing arrangement, and throughout the life cycle of the arrangement, the firm should conduct risk assessments and due diligence to consider whether the arrangement:

(a) is aligned to the firm’s risk appetite, ICT strategy and approach to operational resilience; and
(b) is integrated into the firm’s operational risk framework.
2 The firm should be satisfied that the service provider (and any other party subcontracted to provide the service) has sufficient resources, skills and controls. This could be achieved through a combination of interviews, service reporting, control testing, certifications, attestations, referrals and independent assurance assessments.
3 The firm should be able to demonstrate that the systems and controls of service providers in relation to information security are at least as strong as the firm’s own.
4 The senior management of the firm should consider the service provider’s capacity to provide functions, services or activities necessary to the firm’s critical operations in the event of a disruption. The senior management should examine the provider’s business continuity and disaster recovery plans (including the quality of such plans and the frequency and results of their testing by the service provider).

5 Operational risk may be heighted because of increased concentration risks from:

(a) outsourcing to a dominant service provider that is not easily substitutable; and
(b) multiple outsourcing arrangements with the same service provider or closely connected service providers.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.4.6 Entering material outsourcing arrangements
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm may enter into a material outsourcing arrangement only if:

(a) the firm’s governing body has approved the firm’s outsourcing policy; and

(b) the arrangement:

(i) is permitted by the policy;
(ii) will not reduce the firm’s ability to fulfil its obligations to depositors, policyholders, clients and other stakeholders;
(iii) will not increase the firm’s risk of non-compliance with the law applicable in the QFC or any other applicable law;

(iv) will not affect the Regulatory Authority’s ability to appropriately supervise the firm; and

Example for paragraph (b) (iv)
The place where the service provider is located, or that place’s legal system, could prevent the Authority from appropriately supervising the firm.
(v) will not weaken the firm’s ability to deliver critical operations in the event of a disruption.

(2) The material outsourcing arrangement must be in writing. It must be legally binding and require the service provider to:

(a) deal with the Regulatory Authority in an open and co-operative way in relation to matters relating to the firm under the arrangement; and
(b) grant the Authority access to the firm’s books, records and data in the possession or control of the service provider.
Guidance
The Regulatory Authority expects an authorised firm to be able to demonstrate that the outsourced function, service or activity is being effectively performed by the service provider. The Authority may seek documentary evidence relating to the service provider’s performance.

(3) If appropriate, the agreement must include provisions on:

(a) the law applicable to the agreement;
(b) the reporting or notification requirements on the service provider;
(c) the means for measuring quantitative and qualitative performance by the service provider;
(d) access by the firm, its internal auditors, external auditors or actuaries to the firm’s books, records and data while they are in the possession or control of the service provider;
(e) the obligation to protect confidential information and personal data (that is, any information relating to an individual who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identification number or to 1 or more factors specific to the individual’s physical, physiological, mental, economic, cultural or social identity);
(f) the rules for subcontracting, if the arrangement permits it;
(g) the termination rights of each party; and
(h) contingency arrangements.
Note Rule 8.4.11 requires contingency arrangements to be made to allow the firm’s business to continue in the event of a significant loss of services from the service provider.
(4) If the authorised firm is a category A firm, the written agreement must require the service provider to grant the Authority access to the provider’s premises (but see subrule (7)).

(5) The agreement must include the requirement that the service provider grants the Authority access to the provider’s premises if:

(a) the authorised firm is a category B firm; and
(b) the Regulatory Authority directs the firm to include that requirement in the agreement.
Guidance
The Regulatory Authority would normally assess whether to issue a direction under subrule (5) (b) during the 30-business day notification period that firms must provide the Authority prior to entering into or amending an arrangement (see rules 8.4.7 (1) and 8.4.8 (1). But if the Authority thinks it is necessary or appropriate to do so, it may give the direction at a later time.
(6) To avoid doubt, the requirement to notify the Regulatory Authority of an amendment to an outsourcing agreement under rule 8.4.8, does not apply if the Authority directs the firm to amend the agreement under subrule (5) (b).
(7) A written agreement entered into by a category A firm before 1 October 2025 must be amended to include the requirement in subrule (4) no later than 30 September 2026.

(8) The firm must maintain an up-to-date register of material outsourcing arrangements.

Guidance

The register should, at a minimum, include:

(a) a brief description of each arrangement and the service provider;
(b) a list of critical subcontracting parties (if any) to each arrangement;
(c) a statement whether the firm is sharing confidential, personal, regulatory or otherwise sensitive data with the service provider and, if so, who is processing that data, where and how.

(9) The register must be provided to the Regulatory Authority annually and at any other time as the Authority may direct.

Guidance
Clear and consistent identification of material outsourcing arrangements can support an authorised firm in effectively monitoring and managing third-party risks. It can also provide to financial regulators useful data to identify possible concentration risks from outsourcing arrangements that may pose systemic risks.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.4.7 Regulatory Authority to be notified of certain matters
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.4.7 Regulatory Authority to be notified of certain matters
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) Other than cases where the Regulatory Authority must give prior permission for a material outsourcing arrangement, an authorised firm must not enter a material outsourcing arrangement unless it gives the Regulatory Authority written notice of its intention to enter into the arrangement at least 30 business days before it enters into the arrangement.

(2) If a material outsourcing arrangement (including one which requires the Regulatory Authority’s prior permission) permits subcontracting to another third party, the firm must give the Authority notice of that fact.

Note For the requirement to obtain the Regulatory Authority’s permission before outsourcing certain controlled functions, see for example:

(a) rule 4.1.5 on the outsourcing of the finance function by authorised firms other than banking business firms, Islamic banking business firms and QFC insurers (except QFC captive insurers);
(b) rule 6.3.2 on the outsourcing of the compliance oversight function by authorised firms other than banking business firms, Islamic banking business firms and QFC insurers (except QFC captive insurers); and
(c) rule 6.4.2 on the outsourcing of the internal audit function by QFC insurers (except QFC captive insurers).
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.4.8 Amendments to material outsourcing arrangement
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.4.8 Amendments to material outsourcing arrangement
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) Other than cases where the Regulatory Authority must give prior permission for a material outsourcing arrangement, an authorised firm must not amend a material outsourcing arrangement unless it gives the Regulatory Authority written notice of the amendment at least 30 business days before the amendment takes effect.
(2) If a material outsourcing arrangement is one which requires the prior permission of the Regulatory Authority, an authorised firm must not amend the arrangement unless it has the Authority’s permission to do so.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.4.9 Review of outsourcing of controlled functions
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.4.9 Review of outsourcing of controlled functions
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) This rule applies if an authorised firm outsources a controlled function to a third party.
(2) The outsourcing of a controlled function is taken to be a material outsourcing arrangement.

(3) The senior management of the firm must:

(a) review each such arrangement annually to ensure that the independence, objectivity and effectiveness of the performance of the function are not adversely affected; and
(b) report the results of the review to the firm’s governing body.
Note The appointment of a group employee to perform a controlled function for the firm does not, of its own, constitute a material outsourcing arrangement, see rule 8.4.2 (2) (d).
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.4.10 Additional information about material outsourcing arrangements
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.4.10 Additional information about material outsourcing arrangements
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) The Regulatory Authority may, by written notice to an authorised firm, require the firm to give the Authority, within a stated reasonable period, information about a material outsourcing arrangement (or proposed material outsourcing arrangement) that the Authority reasonably needs to enable it to decide whether the arrangement complies with this Part.

(2) The power given by this rule is additional to the Authority’s other powers.

Note See for example FSR, article 48 (powers to obtain documents and information).

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.4.11 Contingency arrangements
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm that enters into a material outsourcing arrangement must make comprehensive contingency arrangements to allow its business to continue in the event of a significant loss of services from the service provider.

(2) The contingency arrangements must include:

(a) an exit strategy; and
(b) if appropriate, provision for partial exit and step-in.

(3) The contingency arrangements must, at a minimum, cover scenarios involving:

(a) a significant loss of resources at the service provider;
(b) the financial failure of the service provider;
(c) an unexpected termination of the outsourcing arrangement;
(d) the service provider posing ICT and information security risks outside of the firm’s risk appetite;
(e) the service provider posing risks that weaken the firm’s ability to remain below its impact tolerances; and
(e) the Regulatory Authority being unable to effectively supervise the firm because of the conditions or circumstances of the material outsourcing arrangement.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL Part 8.5 ICT and information security risks
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL Part 8.5 ICT and information security risks
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
Note for Part 8.5

The purpose of this Part is to enhance aspects of the operational risk framework and operational resilience approach that apply to ICT and information security risks. This Part should be applied proportionately to the nature, scale and technological complexity of an authorised firm’s business and the sensitivity and value of its information assets.

Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.5.1 Definition of ICT and information security risks
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL Part 8.5 ICT and information security risks
CTRL 8.5.1 Definition of ICT and information security risks
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) ICT (or Information and communication technology) and information security risks means the risks of loss arising from:

(a) breach of confidentiality;
(b) failure of integrity of systems and data;
(c) inappropriateness or unavailability of systems and data; or
(d) inability to change ICT within a reasonable period and with reasonable costs when the environment or business requirements change.
(2) ICT and information security risks include risks arising from inadequate or failed internal processes, people or systems, or from external events (such as cyber-attacks) and inadequate physical security.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.5.2 ICT and information security policies, etc
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL Part 8.5 ICT and information security risks
CTRL 8.5.2 ICT and information security policies, etc
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must ensure its operational risk framework includes policies, processes and procedures for managing ICT and information security risks, in particular to:

(a) determine risk tolerances for ICT and information security risks, in accordance with the risk appetite of the firm;
(b) identify and assess the ICT and information security risks to which the firm is exposed, including those associated with legacy ICT assets;

(c) maintain an up-to-date ICT and information security risks register;

Guidance
The register should include, in relation to each risk recorded, the kind of risk, risk owner, materiality of the risk, controls applied to the risk and whether any residual risk remains after controls have been applied.
(d) implement mitigation measures consistent with assessed risks;
(e) monitor the effectiveness of mitigation measures (including through regular testing), as well as the number of reported incidents, and take action to correct the measures where necessary;
(f) report to the governing body on the ICT and information security risks and controls; and
(g) identify and assess whether there are ICT and information security risks arising from any major change in ICT systems or ICT services, processes or procedures, or after any significant security breach.
Guidance
1 The ICT and information security policies, processes and procedures should be appropriately informed by relevant industry, national and international standards and guidelines. Regular reviews should assess the completeness of the policies, processes and procedures against those standards and guidelines, against best practice and against evolving threats and evolving or new technologies.
2 Robust oversight and engagement on ICT matters by an authorised firm’s governing body and senior management play a leading role in promoting an ICT and information security risks-conscious culture within the firm. To ensure this, the governing body and senior management should possess sufficient knowledge and understanding of the ICT and information security risks facing the firm and take steps so that these risks are well understood and properly managed throughout the firm.
3 The firm should clearly define and allocate to a sufficiently senior position within the firm, roles and responsibilities in managing ICT and information security risks (including in emergency or crisis decision-making). The roles and responsibilities should be documented and communicated to relevant staff.
4 Because roles and responsibilities for ICT and information security are often located across business areas and functions, the firm should avoid unclear accountabilities, lack of ownership and ineffective oversight and prevent fragmented practices.
5 For larger and more complex firms, consideration should be given to allocating responsibility for managing and overseeing ICT and information security to a controlled function.
6 An authorised firm should consider gaining assurance of the effectiveness of its governance and control frameworks for ICT and information security risks, either through audit reviews by its internal audit function (if this function has sufficient knowledge, skills and expertise in ICT and information security risks) or by independent experts. The frequency and focus of such audits should be commensurate with the relevant ICT and information security risks.

7 Depending on the nature, scale and technological complexity of an authorised firm’s business, the firm’s ICT policies, processes and procedures should:

(a) maintain an up-to-date inventory of information assets (including configuration of those assets and the links and interconnections between different assets to enable proper configuration and change management);
(b) monitor and manage the life cycles of ICT assets to ensure they meet and support business and risk management requirements;
(c) carry on performance and capacity planning to prevent, detect and respond to important performance issues in ICT systems and services, and in capacity shortages, in a timely manner;
(d) set up data and ICT systems backup and restoration procedures to ensure that they can be recovered as required; and
(e) manage incidents and problems to monitor and log operational risk events and security ICT incidents and to enable the firm to continue or resume, in a timely manner, critical operations when disruptions occur.

8 The scope and frequency of data and ICT systems backup and restoration procedures in guidance 7 (d) should be:

(a) set in line with business recovery requirements and the criticality of the data and the ICT systems; and
(b) evaluated according to the current risk assessment.

9 Incident and problem management in guidance 7 (e) should include:

(a) procedures to identify, track, log, categorise and classify incidents according to criticality;
(b) the roles and responsibilities for different incident scenarios (for example, errors, malfunctioning, cyber-attacks);
(c) problem management procedures to identify, analyse and solve the root cause behind one or more incidents;
(d) effective internal communication plans, including incident notification and escalation processes (including for security-related customer complaints);
(e) incident response procedures to mitigate the impacts related to the incidents and to ensure that the service becomes operational and secure in a timely manner; and
(f) for critical operations, specific external communication plans.

10 Effective internal communication plans in guidance 9 (d) should ensure that:

(a) incidents with a potentially high adverse impact on critical operations are reported to the relevant senior management; and
(b) the governing body is informed on an ad-hoc basis in the event of significant incidents and, at least, informed of the impact, the response and the additional controls to be defined as a result of the incidents.

11 The specific external communication plans for critical operations in guidance 9 (f) are required in order:

(a) to collaborate with relevant stakeholders to effectively respond to and recover from the incident; andv
(b) to provide timely information to external parties (for example, customers, other market participants, the Regulatory Authority, other State agencies) as appropriate and in line with any applicable regulatory requirements.
(2) The ICT and information security policies, processes and procedures of an authorised firm must be aligned to its operational resilience approach to ensure the effective and prudent management of ICT and information security risks.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.5.3 Guidance
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL Part 8.5 ICT and information security risks
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
1 For most authorised firms, ICT is a core enabler of the business with most, if not all, of the critical operations and systems supported by ICT. It is important that an authorised firm has an ICT strategy that is comprehensive and aligned to its business strategy so that it can deliver on objectives to support the current and future strategic direction of the firm.

2 An authorised firm’s ICT strategy should address:

(a) how the firm’s ICT should evolve to effectively support and participate in its business strategy, including the evolution of the organisational structure, ICT system changes and key dependencies (including third parties);
(b) the planned strategy and evolution of the architecture of ICT; and
(c) clear information security objectives, focusing on ICT systems, services, staff and processes.
3 The governing body should ensure that sufficient resources are allocated to implement the ICT strategy, including an adequate ICT budget, staff levels and expertise.
4 There should be clear roles and responsibilities for implementing, managing and overseeing the effectiveness of the ICT strategy.  This is particularly important for ICT and information security risks since roles and responsibilities are often located or spread across business areas and functions.
5 There should also be plans to identify and address any resourcing and capability gaps that could obstruct the achievement of the wider strategic objectives, including those relating to the execution of change management on a present and forward-looking basis.
6 An authorised firm that is part of a group should ensure that any group-driven ICT strategies and governance arrangements are appropriately tailored from a regulatory and operational perspective for the firm.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2025-1 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.5.4 Project and change management processes
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL Part 8.5 ICT and information security risks
CTRL 8.5.4 Project and change management processes
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must have:

(a) a process for managing projects relating to ICT and information security (ICT project management process); and
(b) a process for managing changes relating to ICT and information security (ICT change management process).

(2) The firm’s ICT project management process must include:

(a) project objectives;
(b) project risk assessments;
(c) project plans, timeframes and steps; and
(d) key milestones.

(3) The firm’s ICT change management process must:

(a) include identifying, managing, challenging, approving and monitoring change on the basis of objective criteria; and
(b) ensure that ICT and information security risks arising from new or modified products, activities, processes and systems are promptly identified, assessed and managed.

(4) The firm’s ICT project and change management processes:

(a) must include sufficient testing and consideration of security requirements in all stages of system or product design, development and testing;
(b) must ensure that they effectively address ICT and information security risks associated with the upgrade or the development or acquisition and implementation of new ICT systems or software; and
(c) must be subject to independent and regular review and update.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.5.5 Information security policy
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL Part 8.5 ICT and information security risks
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must have an information security policy setting out the high-level principles to protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of data and information belonging to the firm or its customers.

(2) The firm’s information security policy must:

(a) include a description of the main roles and responsibilities of information security management;

(b) set out how the firm identifies and classifies its information assets (including those managed by third parties) by criticality and sensitivity;

Guidance
Criticality refers to the potential impact of a loss of availability while sensitivity refers to the potential impact of a loss of confidentiality or integrity.
(c) set out the requirements for staff and contractors, processes and technology in relation to information security, recognising that staff and contractors at all levels have responsibilities in ensuring the firm’s information security; and
(d) be communicated to all staff and contractors of the firm.

(3) The firm must ensure it mitigates the ICT and information security risks that it is exposed to and that could impact its ability to meet its information security policy. The mitigation must be commensurate with:

(a) vulnerabilities and threats to the data assets;
(b) the criticality and sensitivity of the data assets;
(c) the stage at which the data assets are within their life cycle; and
(d) the potential consequences of an information security breach.
Guidance

1 Depending on the nature, scale, technological complexity of an authorised firm’s business and the criticality and sensitivity of its information and data assets, the firm’s mitigation measures should include:

(a) procedures for logical access control (that is, identity and access management);

Example of techniques for access control

• user accountability
• need to know, least privilege and segregation of duties
• privileged access rights
• logging of user activities
• access management and rectification
• authentication methods
(b) physical security measures to protect the firm’s premises, data centres and sensitive areas from unauthorised access and from environmental hazards;

(c) ICT security procedures to prevent the occurrence of security issues in ICT systems and services and minimise their impact on ICT service delivery;

Examples of security procedures
• identification of potential vulnerabilities, which should be evaluated and remediated by ensuring that software and firmware are up to date (including the software provided by firms to their internal and external users) by deploying security patches or by implementing compensating controls
• implementation of secure configuration baselines of all network components
• implementation of network segmentation, data loss prevention systems and the encryption of network traffic (in accordance with its classification)
• implementation of protection of endpoints including servers, workstations and mobile devices
• evaluation of whether endpoints meet the security standards defined before they are granted access to the corporate network
• use of mechanisms to verify the integrity of software, firmware and data
• encryption of data at rest and in transit (in accordance with data classification)

(d) security monitoring processes to detect errors and anomalous activities that may impact the firm’s information security and to respond to them appropriately;

Examples of matters to be covered by monitoring processes
• relevant internal and external factors, including business and ICT administrative functions
• transactions to detect misuse of access by third parties or other entities
• internal misuse of access
• potential internal and external threats (for example, information leakages, malicious code and other security threats, and publicly known vulnerabilities in software and hardware)
• technological developments to ensure awareness of security risks

(e) information security review, assessment and testing to ensure the effective identification of vulnerabilities in its ICT systems and services; and

Examples of review, assessment and testing
• gap analysis against information security standards
• compliance reviews
• internal and external audits of information systems
• physical security reviews
• source code reviews
• vulnerability assessments
• penetration tests
• red team exercises
(f) information security training and awareness to provide information on good ICT security practices, common types of threat and the firm’s policies and procedures regarding the appropriate use of applications, systems and networks.
2 Staff with privileged access rights should be aware of good ICT security behaviour and all staff should have an appreciation of the importance of security.
(4) The governing body of an authorised firm must approve the firm’s information security policy and any mitigation of ICT and information security risks under subrule (3).
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.6.1 Definition of business continuity plan
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.6.1 Definition of business continuity plan
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
The business continuity plan (BCP), of an authorised firm, is a comprehensive plan of action, prepared in accordance with rule 8.6.2, that sets out the processes and procedures necessary to continue or restore the operation of the firm in the event of a disruption.

Note Rule 8.6.3 requires an authorised firm’s governing body to approve the firm’s BCP.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

Note Rule 8.6.3 requires an authorised firm’s governing body to approve the firm’s BCP. Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.6.2 Obligations relating to BCP
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An authorised firm must have a robust BCP.

Guidance for all authorised firms
The firm may have more than one BCP and a BCP may include separate crisis management plans and disaster recovery plans.

(2) The BCP must include processes and procedures necessary to keep its critical operations below the firm’s impact tolerances through severe but plausible disruptions.

Guidance

1 BCPs have traditionally focused on single points of failure (such as individual systems, people or processes). For subrule (2), an authorised firm is expected to have processes and procedures:

(a) to ensure that its BCP addresses wider operational resilience objectives; and
(b) to determine points of failure that have the potential to affect the end-to-end delivery of its critical operations.
2 Tools such as business impact analysis (BIA) and testing undertaken for the BCP of the firm would likely inform, or be run alongside, the mapping of its critical operations, development of response and disaster recovery plans and procedures, and testing of its ability to remain below its identified impact tolerances through severe but plausible scenarios.

(3) The firm’s BCP must be in writing and integrated into its operational risk framework and aligned to its operational resilience approach. It must, at a minimum, include:

(a) triggers to identify a disruption and prompt activation of the BCP, and arrangements to direct resources in the event of activation;
(b) roles and responsibilities for managing operational disruptions, with clear guidance on the succession of authority in the event of a disruption impacting key personnel;
(c) actions it would take to recover and restore operations in the event of disruption and maintain critical operations within its impact tolerances;
(d) an assessment of the execution risks, required resources and preparatory measures, including key internal and external dependencies, needed to support the implementation of the BCP; and
(e) a communications strategy to support implementation of the BCP.
Guidance
This rule does not preclude an authorised firm from using metrics targeting more specific BCP objectives (such as recovery time objectives for critical operations and systems), as well as other forms of BCP testing (such as basic call-cascade tests, crisis management exercises or data restoration testing).
(4) The firm must develop and implement a training programme to ensure all staff who have a role in the firm’s BCP are familiar with their roles and responsibilities. The firm must ensure that all staff have an appropriate awareness of the firm’s BCP.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 8.6.3 Approval, review and testing of BCP
doc_path: CTRL Chapter 8 Operational risk and resilience
CTRL 8.6.3 Approval, review and testing of BCP
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) The governing body of an authorised firm must approve the firm’s BCP.
(2) The governing body must ensure that the firm’s BCP is periodically reviewed and tested. The governing body must keep the plan under review and must ensure that it is tested at intervals determined by the body.

(3) The governing body must ensure that the firm’s BCP is reviewed:

(a) annually by the firm’s internal audit function or an independent external reviewer; and
(b) every 3 years by an independent external reviewer.
Guidance
If the same external reviewer is conducting both the 3-year review and the annual review in the third year, they may be conducted as a single process. In this case, the Regulatory Authority would not require separate reviews and reports to be provided to a firm’s governing body and senior management in the third year.

(4) The 3-year review:

(a) must take account of any tests and changes to the BCP in the 3 years; and
(b) may form part of a review carried out under rule 3.1.19 by an independent external reviewer.
(5) The interval between tests must be appropriate to the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business but must not be longer than 18 months. The Regulatory Authority may direct the firm to test the plan at any time and in a way that the Authority considers appropriate.
(6) The BCP must be updated as a result of reviews and tests to address identified shortcomings or reflect changes (for example, to the firm’s legal or organisational structure, business mix, strategy or risk profile).
(7) Results from reviews and tests of the BCP must be reported to the governing body and senior management.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.content_text: (1) The governing body of an authorised firm must approve the firm’s BCP. (2) The governing body must ensure that the firm’s BCP is periodically reviewed and tested. The governing body must keep the plan under review and must ensure that it is tested at intervals determined by the body. (3) The governing body must ensure that the firm’s BCP is reviewed: (a) annually by the firm’s internal audit function or an independent external reviewer; and (b) every 3 years by an independent external reviewer. Guidance If the same external reviewer is conducting both the 3-year review and the annual review in the third year, they may be conducted as a single process. In this case, the Regulatory Authority would not require separate reviews and reports to be provided to a firm’s governing body and senior management in the third year. (4) The 3-year review: (a) must take account of any tests and changes to the BCP in the 3 years; and (b) may form part of a review carried out under rule 3.1.19 by an independent external reviewer. (5) The interval between tests must be appropriate to the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business but must not be longer than 18 months. The Regulatory Authority may direct the firm to test the plan at any time and in a way that the Authority considers appropriate. (6) The BCP must be updated as a result of reviews and tests to address identified shortcomings or reflect changes (for example, to the firm’s legal or organisational structure, business mix, strategy or risk profile). (7) Results from reviews and tests of the BCP must be reported to the governing body and senior management. Inserted by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 9.2.1 Policies — compliance with Shari’a
doc_path: CTRL Part 9.2 Policies, procedures, systems and controls
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
An Islamic financial institution must establish and implement policies to ensure that its business is conducted in accordance with Shari’a. The policies must include effective and comprehensive procedures to ensure that the firm complies with:

(a) Shari’a (in general and in relation to the requirements for Islamic financial contracts); and
(b) the fatwas, rulings and guidelines issued by its Shari’a supervisory board.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 9.2.2 Policy and procedures manual for Islamic financial business
doc_path: CTRL Part 9.2 Policies, procedures, systems and controls
CTRL 9.2.2 Policy and procedures manual for Islamic financial business
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
An Islamic financial institution must establish, implement and maintain a policy and procedures manual for Islamic financial business. The manual must address the following matters:

(a) how the compliance oversight function will be undertaken in relation to compliance with Shari’a;
(b) how the institution’s Shari’a supervisory board will oversee and advise it in regard to the institution’s business;
(c) how fatwas, rulings and guidelines of the Shari’a supervisory board will be recorded, disseminated and implemented and the internal Shari’a review undertaken;
(d) how disputes and differences of opinion between the Shari’a supervisory board and the institution’s governing body in relation to Shari’a compliance will be addressed;
(e) the process for approving the internal policies, procedures, systems and controls to ensure that:
(i) the institution’s business is conducted in accordance with Shari’a; and
(ii) information is disseminated to customers and investors appropriately;
(f) how conflicts of interest and potential conflicts of interest will be identified and managed.

CTRL 9.2.3 Evaluation of information given to firm
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm’s governing body must evaluate the suitability and effectiveness of the information and reports that it and the firm’s senior management receive under this Chapter. The test of suitability and effectiveness is whether the information and reports are suitable for effectively overseeing and implementing the principles and requirements set out in this Chapter.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 9.3.1 Composition of Shari’a supervisory board
doc_path: CTRL Division 9.3.A Appointment and operation of Shari’a supervisory boards
CTRL 9.3.1 Composition of Shari’a supervisory board
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An Islamic financial institution must have a Shari’a supervisory board. The board must have at least 3 members.
(2) Each member must be capable of exercising strong and independent oversight of, and adequate objective judgment about, Shari’a-related matters.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 9.3.2 Appointment etc of members of Shari’a supervisory board
doc_path: CTRL Division 9.3.A Appointment and operation of Shari’a supervisory boards
CTRL 9.3.2 Appointment etc of members of Shari’a supervisory board
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An individual must not be appointed as a member of an Islamic financial institution’s Shari’a supervisory board unless the individual is suitable to exercise the functions of such a member.
(2) The following are not eligible for appointment as a member of the Shari’a supervisory board of an Islamic financial institution:
(a) a controller (within the meaning of GENE, rule 8.1.3 (1)) of the institution;
(b) a member of the institution’s governing body.
(3) Any appointment, dismissal or other change of a member of the Shari’a supervisory board must be approved by the institution’s governing body.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 9.3.3 Assessing suitability of proposed members of Shari’a supervisory board
doc_path: CTRL Division 9.3.A Appointment and operation of Shari’a supervisory boards
CTRL 9.3.3 Assessing suitability of proposed members of Shari’a supervisory board
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
When the governing body of an Islamic financial institution is assessing an individual’s suitability for appointment as a member of the institution’s Shari’a supervisory board, the governing body must take into account:

(a) the individual’s good character (honesty, integrity, fairness and reputation);
(b) the individual’s competence, diligence, capability and soundness of judgment; and
(c) anything else that the governing body considers relevant.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 9.3.4 Assessing good character of proposed members of Shari’a supervisory board
doc_path: CTRL Division 9.3.A Appointment and operation of Shari’a supervisory boards
CTRL 9.3.4 Assessing good character of proposed members of Shari’a supervisory board
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
In assessing an individual’s good character for rule 9.3.3, an Islamic financial institution’s governing body must consider:

(a) whether the individual:

(i) has ever been convicted of a criminal offence, particularly an offence relating to dishonesty, fraud or financial crime;

Note For the meaning of financial crime, see the Glossary.
(ii) has been the subject of any adverse findings or any settlement in civil proceedings, particularly in connection with banking or other financial business, misconduct or fraud;

(iii) has been the owner, manager or director of a company, partnership or other entity that:

(A) has been refused registration, authorisation, membership or a licence to conduct a trade, business or profession; or
(B) has had that registration, authorisation, membership or licence revoked, withdrawn or terminated;
resulting in the individual being refused the right to carry on a trade, business or profession requiring such a licence, registration or other authorisation;
(iv) has been a director, partner or otherwise involved in the management of a business that has gone into receivership, insolvency or compulsory liquidation while the individual was connected with that business or within 1 year after the individual’s departure from it;
(v) has ever been disciplined by a professional, trade or regulatory body, or dismissed or asked to resign, or has resigned, from employment or office or from a position of trust, fiduciary appointment or similar position because of negligence, incompetence, fraud, mismanagement or questions about the individual’s honesty or integrity;
(vi) has ever been disqualified from acting as a director or serving in a managerial capacity because of wrongdoing; or
(vii) has not been fair, truthful and forthcoming in dealings with customers, superiors, auditors and regulatory authorities in the past and has been the subject of any justified complaint relating to regulated activities;
(b) whether the individual shows readiness and willingness to comply with the requirements and standards of the regulatory system in the QFC and other legal, regulatory, or professional requirements and standards;
(c) whether the individual (or any business in which he or she is a controlling shareholder or has a controlling interest or exercises significant influence) has been investigated and disciplined or suspended by a regulatory or professional body, a court or a tribunal, whether publicly or privately; and
(d) anything else that the governing body considers relevant.

 

Derived from QFCRA RM/2020-4 (as from 1st July 2021)

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 9.3.5 Assessing competence of proposed members of Shari’a supervisory board
doc_path: CTRL Division 9.3.A Appointment and operation of Shari’a supervisory boards
CTRL 9.3.5 Assessing competence of proposed members of Shari’a supervisory board
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) To be suitable for appointment as a member of the Shari’a supervisory board of an Islamic financial institution, an individual must be able to demonstrate the competence and ability to understand:
(a) the technical requirements of the institution’s business;
(b) the risks inherent in the institution; and
(c) the processes required to conduct the institution’s operations effectively.
(2) In making the assessment required by subrule (1), the institution’s governing body must consider:
(a) whether the individual has demonstrated, through qualifications and experience, the capacity to successfully undertake the responsibilities of the position;
(b) whether the individual is physically, mentally and emotionally fit to perform the duties of the position;
(c) whether the individual has a sound knowledge of the institution’s business and the responsibilities of the position; and
(d) anything else that the governing body considers relevant.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 9.3.5 Guidance
doc_path: CTRL Division 9.3.A Appointment and operation of Shari’a supervisory boards
CTRL 9.3.5 Assessing competence of proposed members of Shari’a supervisory board
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
1 The Regulatory Authority expects an Islamic financial institution to carry out background checks, and to verify that a person to be appointed as a member of the institution’s Shari’a supervisory board has at least the minimum qualifications and experience set out in Appendix 4 of IFSB 10: Guiding Principles on Shari’a Governance Systems for Institutions offering Islamic Financial Services.
2 So far as possible, such an institution should use the suitability criteria and factors in this Division when appointing an individual to exercise the Shari’a compliance function and internal Shari’a review function. In addition, such an individual is expected to have:
• adequate training in Shari’a
• additional qualifications in finance
• good communication skills to enable him or her to liaise and work effectively with the Shari’a supervisory board
• organisational skills.

CTRL 9.3.6 Policy in relation to appointments etc to Shari’a supervisory boards

An Islamic financial institution must document its policy in relation to:

(a) how appointments, dismissals or changes to the institution’s Shari’a supervisory board will be made;
(b) the process through which the suitability of the members will be considered; and
(c) the remuneration of the members.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 9.3.7 Records of assessment of suitability of Shari’a supervisory board members
doc_path: CTRL Division 9.3.A Appointment and operation of Shari’a supervisory boards
CTRL 9.3.7 Records of assessment of suitability of Shari’a supervisory board members
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An Islamic financial institution must retain a record, for each individual who is or has been a member of its Shari’a supervisory board, of:
(a) its assessment of the individual’s suitability to be such a member; and
(b) the agreed terms of engagement of the individual as such a member.
(2) The record for a member must include:
(a) the factors that were taken into account when assessing the member’s suitability;
(b) the qualifications and experience of the member;
(c) the basis upon which the institution considered that the member was suitable; and
(d) details of any other Shari’a supervisory boards of which the member is, or has been, a member.
(3) The institution must retain the record for a former member of its Shari’a supervisory board for at least 6 years after the date on which he or she ceased to be such a member.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 9.3.8 Islamic financial institution’s obligations to Shari’a supervisory board
doc_path: CTRL Division 9.3.A Appointment and operation of Shari’a supervisory boards
CTRL 9.3.8 Islamic financial institution’s obligations to Shari’a supervisory board
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An Islamic financial institution must take reasonable steps to ensure that the members of its Shari’a supervisory board are independent of the institution, and not subject to any conflict of interest with it.
Guidance
An Islamic financial institution’s Shari’a supervisory board can be considered independent only if none of its members has a blood or close relationship with the institution, the institution’s officers or related parties, that could interfere (or be reasonably perceived as interfering) with the exercise by the board of independent judgment.
(2) The institution and its employees:
(a) must give the Shari’a supervisory board any assistance that it reasonably requires to perform its duties;
(b) must give the board right of access at all reasonable times to relevant records and information;
(c) must not interfere with the board’s ability to perform its duties; and
(d) must not provide false or misleading information to the board.

CTRL 9.3.10 Annual Shari’a supervisory board report
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An Islamic financial institution must commission, from its Shari’a supervisory board, an annual report that complies with AAOIFI Standards on Governance, GSIFI No 1.
(2) The institution must give the Regulatory Authority a copy of each such annual report within 3 months after the day the relevant financial year of the institution ends.
Example
If a financial year of an Islamic financial institution ends on 31 December in a year, the annual report of the institution’s Shari’a supervisory board must be given to the Regulatory Authority before 1 April in the next year.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 9.3.12 Islamic financial institutions to carry out internal Shari’a reviews
doc_path: CTRL 9.3.12 Islamic financial institutions to carry out internal Shari’a reviews
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(1) An Islamic financial institution must from time to time carry out an internal Shari’a review to assess the extent to which the institution complies with Shari’a and with the fatwas, rulings and guidelines issued by its Shari’a supervisory board.
(2) The interval between reviews must be determined by the institution’s Sharia supervisory board, taking into account the nature, scale and complexity of the institution’s business.
(3) The objective of such a review is to ensure that the governing body and senior management of the institution carry out their responsibilities in relation to Shari’a (as determined by the firm’s Shari’a supervisory board).

(4) The review must be carried out, in accordance with the AAOIFI standards relating to Shari’a governance, by:

(a) the institution as part of its internal audit function; or
(b) an independent entity that is competent to do so.

Guidance

1 For the purposes of assessing the competency of personnel or entities that carry out the internal Shari’a review, the institution should consult the AAOIFI Standards on Governance (GSIFI No. 3) and Appendix 4 of IFSB 10: Guiding Principles on Shari’a Governance Systems for Institutions offering Islamic Financial Services.

2 IFSB 3 states that fatwas, rulings, pronouncements and resolutions issued by the Shari’a supervisory board should be strictly adhered to. A person should not be assigned to carry out an internal Shari’a review unless the person:

• is adequately trained in Shari’a compliance
• has a competent grasp of the review process.

3 The Shari’a supervisory board should give a copy of the report or reports prepared by it (including the report on the internal Shari’a review carried out under this rule) to the governing body sufficiently in advance of the firm’s next Annual Financial Report to:

(a) allow the governing body a reasonable opportunity to rectify any non- compliance, if possible; and
(b) consider and use the report or reports in preparing the next report.
(5) The results of each review (including any instance of non-compliance) must be documented, and the institution must ensure that any non-compliance is rectified, so far as possible.
(6) The function or entity that carried out the review or reviews during a period must report on its findings in time for the next meeting of the Shari’a supervisory board. If the function or entity did not conduct any review during the period preceding a meeting, it must notify the board of the fact.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
An Islamic financial institution must give the Regulatory Authority a copy of the report or reports prepared by the institution’s Shari’a supervisory board. The report or reports must be given within 3 months after the day the relevant financial year of the institution ends.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL 9.4.4 Guidance
doc_path: CTRL Part 9.4 Conduct of Islamic financial business
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
1 An important matter that an Islamic financial institution must disclose under AAOIFI FAS 13, as applied by rule 9.4.4 (b), is how the institution would treat an insurance deficit or surplus. Appendix B to AAOIFI FAS 13 provides some guidance as to how to treat a deficit or surplus.
2 That appendix states that there are a number of ways to treat a deficit, including:
(a) settling the deficit from the reserve of policyholders, if any;
(b) borrowing the amount of the deficit from the shareholders’ funds or from others (and paying it back from future surpluses);
(c) asking the policyholders to meet the deficit pro rata; and
(d) increasing the future premium contribution of policyholders on a pro-rata basis.
3 That appendix also states that there are a number of ways to allocate a surplus, including:
(a) allocating the surplus to all policyholders, regardless of whether or not they have made claims on the policy during the relevant financial period;
(b) allocating the surplus only among policyholders who have not made any claims during that financial period;
(c) allocating the surplus among policyholders who have not made any claims and those who have made claims of amounts less than their insurance contributions, provided that the latter category of policyholders should receive only the difference between their insurance contributions and their claims during the financial period;
(d) allocating the surplus between policyholders and shareholders; and
(e) allocating the surplus in other ways.

QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.title: CTRL Glossary
QFCRA Rules :: Governance and Controlled.document_html:
(see rule 1.1.3)

actuarial function has the meaning given by rule 1.2.15.

AML/CFTR means the Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism Rules 2019.

AMLG means the Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism (General Insurance) Rules 2019.

approved actuary of a QFC insurer means the individual who is approved to exercise the actuarial function for the insurer.

approved individual means an individual who is approved under FSR, article 41, to exercise 1 or more controlled functions.

authorisation means an authorisation granted under FSR, Part 5.

authorised firm (or firm) means a person that has been granted an authorisation in accordance with FSR, Part 5.

BANK means the Banking Business Prudential Rules 2014.

banking business firm has the meaning given in BANK, rule 1.3.1.

board of directors (or board) of an authorised firm that is incorporated in the QFC has the meaning given by rule 3.3.3.

business continuity plan or BCP has the meaning given by rule 8.6.1.

business day means a day that is not a Friday, Saturday, or a public or bank holiday in Qatar.

branch means the local office in the QFC of a company or limited liability partnership that is incorporated in a jurisdiction outside the QFC.

CAPI means the Captive Insurance Business Rules 2011.

category A firm has the meaning given by rule 3.3.2.

category B firm has the meaning given by rule 3.3.2.

COLL means the Collective Investment Schemes Rules 2010.

company means:

(a) a company that is incorporated under the Companies Regulations; or
(b) a legal person that is incorporated under the law of a jurisdiction outside the QFC, in which the liability of each member (in its capacity as a member) is limited to the amount of the member’s contribution to the company’s capital.

Companies Regulations means the Companies Regulations 2005 of the QFC.

compliance oversight function has the meaning given by rule 1.2.13.

contract of insurance means the specified product described in FSR, Schedule 3, Part 3, paragraph 10.

controlled function has the meaning given by rule 1.2.5 (2).

corporate governance framework has the meaning given by rule 1.2.2.

corporate group: an entity’s corporate group is made up of:

(a) the entity itself;
(b) any parent entity of the entity; and
(c) any subsidiary (direct or indirect) of that entity or of any parent entity of the entity.

critical operation means a service, product or function identified as such under rule 8.3.2 (1).

director of an authorised firm that is incorporated in the QFC has the meaning given by rule 3.3.3.

document means a record of information in any form (including electronic form), and includes, for example:

(a) anything in writing or on which there is writing; and
(b) anything on which there are figures, marks, numbers, perforations, symbols or anything else having a meaning for individuals qualified to interpret them; and
(c) a drawing, map or photograph or plan; and
(d) any other item or matter (in whatever form) that is, or could reasonably be considered to be, a record of information.

employee: an individual is an employee of a person (the employer) if:

(a) the individual is employed or appointed by the employer in connection with the employer’s business, whether under a contract of service or for services or otherwise; or
(b) the employee’s services are placed at the employer’s disposal, and under the employer’s control, under an arrangement between the employer and a third party.

entity means any kind of entity, and includes, for example, any person.

executive governance function has the meaning given by rule 1.2.6.

exercise a function includes perform the function.

finance function has the meaning given by rule 1.2.9.

financial crime means the use of the financial system in the QFC for criminal, fraudulent or dishonest purposes, including, for example, insider trading, market abuse, handling the proceeds of crime, money laundering and terrorist financing.

firm (or authorised firm) means a person that has been granted an authorisation in accordance with FSR, Part 5.

FSR means the Financial Services Regulations of the QFC.

function includes power.

GENE means the General Rules 2005.

governing body of an authorised firm has the meaning given by rule 1.2.1.

IBANK means the Islamic Banking Business Prudential Rules 2015.

ICT means information and communication technology.

ICT and information security risks has the meaning given by rule 8.5.1.

IFSB means the Islamic Financial Services Board.

impact tolerance, in relation to a critical operation, has the meaning given by rule 8.3.5.

information asset means information and information technology including software, hardware and data (whether in soft or hard copy).

information security means the preservation of information assets’ confidentiality, integrity and availability.

independent non-executive director of an authorised firm has the meaning given by rule 3.3.4.

INDI means the Individuals (Assessment, Training and Competency) Rules 2014.

INMA means the Investment Management and Advisory Rules 2014.

insurer (or QFC insurer) means an authorised firm that has an authorisation to conduct insurance business.

insurance business has the meaning given by PINS, rule 1.2.4.

internal auditor means:

(a) in the case of an authorised firm that has an individual who is approved to exercise the internal audit function — that individual; and
(b) in the case of a QFC insurer that does not have such an individual — the firm of auditors appointed in accordance with paragraph 6.4.2 (2) (b).

internal audit function has the meaning given by rule 1.2.14.

internal control and assurance function has the meaning given by rule 1.2.4 (2).

internal controls and assurance framework has the meaning given by rule 1.2.4.

Islamic banking business firm has the meaning given in IBANK, rule 1.1.9.

Islamic financial institution means an authorised firm whose authorisation includes a condition that the whole of the firm’s business must be conducted in accordance with Shari’a.

limited liability partnership means a partnership:

(a) that is incorporated under the LLP Regulations; or
(b) that is incorporated under the law of a jurisdiction outside the QFC by which the liability of each partner (in its capacity as a partner) is limited to the amount of the partner’s contribution to the partnership’s capital.

LLP Regulations means the Limited Liability Partnerships Regulations 2005 of the QFC.

material outsourcing arrangement has the meaning given by rule 8.4.2.

MLRO function has the meaning given by rule 1.2.11.

month means calendar month — that is, the period beginning at the start of any day of one of the 12 named months of the year and ending:

(a) at the end of the day before the corresponding day on the next named month; or
(b) if there is no corresponding day — at the end of the last day of next named month.

non-executive director of an authorised firm has the meaning given by rule 3.3.4.

non-executive governance function has the meaning given by rule 1.2.7.

outsourcing has the meaning given by rule 8.4.2 (1).

outsourcing policy has the meaning given by rule 8.4.4.

operational resilience has the meaning given by rule 8.3.2 (2).

operational risk has the meaning given by rule 8.2.1 (1).

person means:

(a) an individual (including an individual occupying an office or position from time to time); or
(b) a legal person — that is, an entity, other than an individual, on which the legal system of a jurisdiction confers rights and imposes duties (including, for example, any entity that can own, deal with or dispose of property).

PINS means the Insurance Business Rules 2006.

QFC means the Qatar Financial Centre.

QFC captive insurer has the meaning given by CAPI, rule 1.2.1.

QFC entity means either:

(a) a company incorporated under the Companies Regulations; or
(b) a limited liability partnership incorporated under the LLP Regulations.

QFC insurer (or insurer) has the meaning given by PINS, rule 1.2.3.

regulated activity means an activity that is a regulated activity under FSR.

Regulatory Authority means the Qatar Financial Centre Regulatory Authority established under Law No. (7) of 2005 of the State of Qatar, article 9.

related: a person (the second person) is related to another person (the first person) if:

(a) the second person is a subsidiary, associate or holding company of the first person;
(b) the second person is a subsidiary or associate of the holding company of the first person;
(c) the second person is a director or officer of the first person, or of a person related to the first person because of paragraph (a) or (b);
(d) the second person is the spouse or minor child of an individual mentioned in paragraph (c);
(e) the second person is a company that is a subsidiary of, or subject to significant influence by or from, an individual mentioned in paragraph (c) or (d).

risk appetite has the meaning given by rule 7.1.5 (2).

risk appetite statement has the meaning given by rule 7.1.5 (1).

risk management framework has the meaning given by rule 1.2.3.

risk management function has the meaning given by rule 1.2.12.

risk management strategy means a strategy prepared by an authorised firm in accordance with rule 7.1.6.

risk tolerance has the meaning given by rule 7.1.5 (3).

scenario testing means the testing described by rule 8.3.7 (1).

senior executive function has the meaning given by rule 1.2.8.

senior management of an authorised firm has the meaning given by rule 4.1.1.

senior management function has the meaning given by rule 1.2.10.

Shari’a supervisory board, of an authorised firm, means the board appointed for the firm under rule 9.3.1.

specified product means a product that is a specified product under FSR, Schedule 3, Part 3.

subsidiary: an entity is a subsidiary of another entity if that other entity is the parent entity of the first entity.

writing means any form of writing, and includes, for example, anyway of representing or reproducing words, numbers or symbols or anything else in legible form (for example, by printing or photocopying).

year means a year of the Gregorian calendar.

QFCRA Rules :: Individuals (Assessment,.title: INDI 1.1.1 Introduction
QFCRA Rules :: Individuals (Assessment,.document_html:
(1) These rules are the Individuals (Assessment, Training and Competency) Rules 2014 (or INDI).
(2) These rules set out:
(a) the principles of conduct for individuals who perform controlled functions or the customer-facing function for authorised firms; and
(b) the principles and framework under which:
(i) authorised firms assess the competence, and the fitness and propriety, of individuals who perform controlled functions or the customer-facing function;
(ii) the Regulatory Authority approves individuals to perform controlled functions; and
(iii) authorised firms establish training and competency programmes for individuals who perform controlled functions or the customer-facing function.
Note There are 10 controlled functions, which are described in CTRL, Division 1.2.B. The controlled functions are:
•   the non-executive governance function
•   the executive governance function
•   the senior executive function
•   the finance function
•   the senior management function
•   the MLRO function
•   the risk management function
•   the compliance oversight function
•   the internal audit function
•   the the actuarial function.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2014-5 (as from 1st January 2015)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2021-1 (as from 1st July 2021)
