QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 2.1.8 Firm to Notify Authority
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must notify the Regulatory Authority if it becomes aware, or has reasonable grounds to believe, that the firm has breached, or is about to breach, a prudential requirement.
(2) In particular, the firm must notify the authority as soon as practicable of:
(a) any breach (or foreseen breach) of its minimum capital requirement;
(b) any concern (including because of projected losses) it has about its capital adequacy;
(c) any indication of significant adverse change in the market pricing of, or trading in, the capital instruments of the firm or its financial group (including pressure on the firm to purchase its own equity or debt);
(d) any other significant adverse change in its capital; and
(e) any significant departure from its ICAAP.

Note For an Islamic banking business firm's ICAAP, see rule 3.1.5.
(3) The firm must also notify the authority of any measures taken or planned to deal with any breach, prospective breach or concern.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK Chapter 3 Capital Adequacy
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: IBANK Chapter 3 Capital Adequacy

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK Part 3.1 General
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: IBANK Part 3.1 General

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1.1 Introduction
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This Chapter sets out capital adequacy requirements.
(2) An Islamic banking business firm's total regulatory capital is the sum of its tier 1 capital and tier 2 capital. The categories and elements of regulatory capital, and the limits, restrictions and adjustments to which they are subject are set out in this Chapter.
(3) Capital supports the firm's operation by providing a buffer to absorb losses from its activities and, in the event of problems, it enables the firm to continue to operate in a sound and viable manner while the problems are resolved. Capital management must be an integral part of the firm's credit risk management process and must align the firm's risk appetite and risk profile with its capacity to absorb losses.

Note For the governing body's responsibilities in relation to capital management and capital adequacy, see rule 3.1.3.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1.2 Chapter 3 and its Application to Branches
doc_path: IBANK 3.1.2 Chapter 3 and its Application to Branches
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This Chapter does not apply to an Islamic banking business firm that is a branch insofar as this Chapter would require the branch to hold capital.
(2) A branch is required to comply with the reporting requirements under this Chapter. In relation to the branch's ICAAP, the branch may rely on the head office's ICAAP (if available) to demonstrate compliance.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1.3 Governing Body's Responsibilities
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm's governing body must consider whether the minimum financial resources required by these rules are adequate to ensure that there is no significant risk that the firm's liabilities cannot be met as they fall due. The firm must obtain additional financial resources if its governing body considers that the minimum required does not adequately reflect the risks of its business.

(2) The governing body is also responsible for:

(a) ensuring that capital management is part of the firm's overall risk management and is aligned with its risk appetite and risk profile;
(b) ensuring that the firm has, at all times, financial resources of the kinds and amounts required by these rules;

Note Financial resources is a broader concept than capital resources. Financial resources could include liquid assets (such as cash in hand), irrevocable lines of credit and irrevocable guarantees.
(c) ensuring that the firm has capital, of adequate amount and appropriate quality, for the nature, scale and complexity of its business and for its risk profile;
(d) ensuring that the amount of capital it has exceeds its minimum capital requirement;
(e) approving the firm's ICAAP and any significant changes to it; and
(f) monitoring the adequacy and appropriateness of the firm's systems and controls and the firm's compliance with them.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1.4 Systems and Controls
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must have adequate systems and controls to allow it to calculate and monitor its minimum capital requirement.
(2) The systems and controls must be in writing and must be appropriate for the nature, scale and complexity of its business and for its risk profile.
(3) The systems and controls must enable the firm to show, at all times, whether it complies with this Chapter.
(4) The systems and controls must enable the firm to manage available capital in anticipation of events or changes in market conditions.
(5) The systems and controls must include ICAAP, and the firm must have contingency arrangements to maintain or increase its capital in times of stress.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1.5 Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm's internal capital adequacy assessment process or ICAAP is the process by which the firm continuously demonstrates that it has implemented methods and procedures to ensure that it has adequate capital resources to support the nature and level of its risks.
(2) A firm's ICAAP (and any significant changes to it) must be in writing and must have been approved by the firm's governing body. A copy of the ICAAP must be given to the Regulatory Authority on request.

(3) An ICAAP must reflect the nature, scale and complexity of the firm's operations and must include:x

(a) adequate policies and staff to continuously identify, measure, evaluate, manage and control or mitigate the risks arising from its activities, and monitor the capital held against such risks;
(b) a strategy for ensuring that adequate capital is maintained over time, including specific capital targets set out in the context of its risk appetite, risk profile and capital requirements;
(c) plans for how capital targets are to be met and the means available for obtaining additional capital, if required;
(d) procedures for monitoring its compliance with its capital requirements and capital targets;
(e) triggers to alert senior management to, and specified actions to avert and rectify, possible breaches of capital requirements;
(f) procedures for reporting on the ICAAP and its outcomes to the firm's governing body and senior management, and for ensuring that the ICAAP is taken into account in making business decisions;
(g) policies about the effect on capital of significant risks not covered by explicit capital requirements;
(h) triggers, scope and procedures for reviewing the ICAAP under rule 1.1.14(3) and in the light of changed conditions and factors affecting the firm's risk appetite, risk profile and capital;
(i) procedures for reporting the results of reviews;
(j) an adequate recovery plan for restoring the firm's financial situation after a significant deterioration; and
(k) procedures for stress-testing and the review of stress scenarios.
(4) In addition to the periodic review under rule 1.1.14(3), a firm's ICAAP must be reviewed by an appropriately qualified person at least once every 3 years. The person must be independent of the conduct of the firm's capital management.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

(3) An ICAAP must reflect the nature, scale and complexity of the firm's operations and must include:x (a) adequate policies and staff to continuously identify, measure, evaluate, manage and control or mitigate the risks arising from its activities, and monitor the capital held against such risks; (b) a strategy for ensuring that adequate capital is maintained over time, including specific capital targets set out in the context of its risk appetite, risk profile and capital requirements; (c) plans for how capital targets are to be met and the means available for obtaining additional capital, if required; (d) procedures for monitoring its compliance with its capital requirements and capital targets; (e) triggers to alert senior management to, and specified actions to avert and rectify, possible breaches of capital requirements; (f) procedures for reporting on the ICAAP and its outcomes to the firm's governing body and senior management, and for ensuring that the ICAAP is taken into account in making business decisions; (g) policies about the effect on capital of significant risks not covered by explicit capital requirements; (h) triggers, scope and procedures for reviewing the ICAAP under rule 1.1.14 (3) and in the light of changed conditions and factors affecting the firm's risk appetite, risk profile and capital; (i) procedures for reporting the results of reviews; (j) an adequate recovery plan for restoring the firm's financial situation after a significant deterioration; and (k) procedures for stress-testing and the review of stress scenarios. (4) In addition to the periodic review under rule 1.1.14 (3), a firm's ICAAP must be reviewed by an appropriately qualified person at least once every 3 years. The person must be independent of the conduct of the firm's capital management. Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1.6 Use of Internal Models
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The Regulatory Authority's requirements for Islamic banking business firms to maintain adequate capital and manage risk are based on the approaches set out by the IFSB in its standards and guidelines on capital adequacy and the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision in the Basel Accords. The standards, guidelines and Accords allow firms to use internal models to assess capital adequacy and risk, and this rule governs the use of such models.
(2) A firm must not use its own model to assess capital adequacy or risk unless the Regulatory Authority has approved the model. The authority may approve a model subject to 1 or more conditions.
(3) In making its decision, the authority will take into account:
(a) the nature, scale and complexity of the firm's business;
(b) the standards proposed by the firm, the rigour of its compliance with them, and the ease with which the authority can assess that compliance;
(c) whether the model can be relied on as a reasonable reflection of the risks undertaken by the firm; and
(d) anything else the authority considers relevant.
(4) The authority may revoke the approval if it is satisfied that the firm has failed to comply with any condition specified by the authority or any standard proposed by the firm.
(5) The firm must not stop using an approved model, or make significant changes to it, without the authority's approval.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1A.1 What banking book and trading book are
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.1A Boundary between banking book and trading book
IBANK 3.1A.1 What banking book and trading book are
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm’s trading book consists of the firm’s holdings of instruments and transactions that, under this Part, either must be held in the trading book or are transferred into the trading book.
(2) Every other instrument that the firm holds is taken to be held in its banking book.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1A.2 Firms that must have trading book
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.1A Boundary between banking book and trading book
IBANK 3.1A.2 Firms that must have trading book
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Subject to subrule (2), an Islamic banking business firm must have a trading book if it has positions that, under this Part, must be held in the trading book.
(2) An Islamic banking business firm may apply to the Regulatory Authority for approval to hold positions referred to in subrule (1) in its banking book if, at any time in the previous 12 months, the total value of such positions (whether on or off the firm’s balance sheet) has been less than 5% of the total value of the firm’s positions on and off its balance sheet.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

IBANK 3.1A.3 Instruments to be held in trading book only if no impediment to sale etc

Despite anything else in this Part, an Islamic banking business firm may hold an instrument in the trading book only if there is no legal impediment to the firm’s selling the instrument or fully hedging it in a Shari’a-compliant way.

IBANK 3.1A.4 Instruments in trading book to be fair-valued daily etc
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm must fair-value every instrument in the trading book daily, and must recognise any value change in the firm’s profit and loss account.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1A.5 Meaning of trading intent
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.1A Boundary between banking book and trading book
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
For this Part, an Islamic banking business firm holds an instrument with trading intent if it holds the instrument for any 1 or more of the following purposes:

(a) short-term resale;
(b) profiting from actual or expected short-term price movements;
(c) locking-in arbitrage profits;
(d) Shari’a-compliant hedging of the risks from an instrument that is held for a purpose mentioned in paragraph (a), (b) or (c).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1A.6 Instruments that must be held in trading book
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.1A Boundary between banking book and trading book
IBANK 3.1A.6 Instruments that must be held in trading book
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) In general, if an Islamic banking business firm holds an instrument with trading intent it must hold the instrument in the trading book unless these rules provide otherwise.
(2) An Islamic banking business firm that holds any of the instruments mentioned in subrule (3) is presumed to do so with trading intent. Therefore, unless these rules provide otherwise, such an instrument must be held in the trading book.

(3) The instruments are the following:

(a) instruments held as accounting trading assets or liabilities;
(b) instruments resulting from market-making activities;
(c) equity investments in a fund (other than instruments that must be held in the banking book (see rule 3.1A.7 (1) (d));

(d) listed equities;

Guidance
With the Regulatory Authority’s approval, certain listed equities may be excluded from the market risk framework. The following are examples of equities that may be approved for exclusion:
• equity positions arising from deferred compensation plans
• convertible debt securities
• equities taken as a debt previously contracted
• bank-owned life takaful products
• legislated programmes.

(e) trading-related SFTs (that is, transactions that are entered into for the purposes of market-making, locking in arbitrage profits or creating short credit or equity positions);

Guidance
SFTs that are entered for liquidity management and are valued at accrual for accounting purposes are not presumed to be held for trading purposes.

(f) instruments that include embedded SCHIs from instruments:

(i) that the firm issued out of the banking book; and
(ii) that relate to credit or equity risk.
Note For the meaning of SCHI, see the Glossary.
Guidance
An embedded SCHI is a part of a hybrid contract that includes a non-SCHI host, such as liabilities issued out of the firm’s own banking book that contain embedded SCHIs. The embedded SCHI associated with the host should be bifurcated and separately recognised on the firm’s balance sheet.
This means that the firm should split the liability into two components:
• the embedded SCHI, which is assigned to the trading book
• the residual liability, which is retained in the banking book.
No internal risk transfers are necessary for the bifurcation. If such a liability is unwound, or an embedded option is exercised, both the trading and banking book components are conceptually unwound simultaneously and instantly retired; no transfers between trading and banking book are necessary.

(4) The following instruments must be held in the trading book, unless a rule specifically provides otherwise:

(a) instruments in the firm’s correlation trading portfolio (see subrules (5) to (7));

(b) instruments that would give rise to a net short credit or equity position in the banking book;

Guidance
The firm will have a net short risk position for equity risk or credit risk in the banking book if the present value of the banking book increases when an equity price decreases or when a credit spread on an issuer or group of issuers of debt increases.
(c) instruments resulting from securities underwriting commitments.

(5) An Islamic banking business firm’s correlation trading portfolio comprises the firm’s holdings of securitisation exposures and nth-to-default SCHIs that meet the following criteria:

(a) the positions are neither of the following:

(i) re-securitisation positions;
(ii) SCHIs of securitisation exposures that do not provide a pro-rata share in the proceeds of a securitisation tranche;
Guidance
Therefore, options on a securitisation tranche, or a synthetically leveraged super-senior tranche, are excluded.

(b) all the reference obligations are single-name products (including single-name SCHIs) for which there is a liquid two-way market (see subrule (8)).

Guidance
The instruments referred to in paragraph (b) include commonly traded indices based on such reference obligations.

(6) An Islamic banking business firm may also include, in the correlation trading portfolio, positions:

(a) that hedge positions described in subrule (5); and
(b) that are neither securitisation exposures nor nth-to-default SCHIs;
if there is a liquid two-way market (see subrule (8)) for the instrument or its underlyings.

(7) An Islamic banking business firm must not include in the correlation trading portfolio:

(a) positions that reference an underlying that would be treated as a retail exposure, a residential mortgage exposure or a commercial mortgage exposure under the standardised approach to credit risk (see Part 4.4); or

(b) positions that reference a claim on a special purpose entity.

Note Special purpose entity is defined in the glossary.
(8) For this rule, there is a liquid two-way market for an instrument or underlying if there are independent bona-fide offers to buy and sell, so that a price that is reasonably related to the last sale price or current bona-fide competitive bid and offer quotation can be determined within 1 day and settled at that price within a relatively short period that conforms to trade custom.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1A.7 Instruments that must be held in banking book
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.1A Boundary between banking book and trading book
IBANK 3.1A.7 Instruments that must be held in banking book
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must hold instruments and investments of the following kinds in the banking book:

(a) unlisted equities;
(b) instruments designated for securitisation warehousing;
(c) instruments that represent direct holdings of real estate or Shari’a-compliant hedging of such holdings;
(d) equity investments in a fund (including a hedge fund in which an Islamic banking business firm is unable to look through the fund to obtain daily valuations for the equity investments or is otherwise unable to obtain daily price quotes for those investments) (other than investments to which subrule (2) applies);
(e) equity investments in funds that have instruments of a type mentioned in any of paragraphs (a) to (d) as assets;
(f) instruments held for Shari’a-compliant hedging of a particular risk of a position in instruments of a type mentioned in any of paragraphs (a) to (e).

(2) This subrule applies to an investment in a fund if:

(a) both of the following are true:

(i) the firm is able to look through the fund to its individual components;
(ii) the firm receives sufficient and frequent information, independently verified, about the fund’s composition; or

(b) both of the following are true:

(i) the firm obtains daily price quotes for the fund;
(ii) the firm has access to the information in the fund’s mandate or in the national regulations governing the fund.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1A.8 Continuous evaluation of allocation between banking and trading books
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.1A Boundary between banking book and trading book
IBANK 3.1A.8 Continuous evaluation of allocation between banking and trading books
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If an Islamic banking business firm has a trading book, the firm must ensure that its risk management function continually evaluates the allocation of instruments between the banking and trading books to assess whether the instruments in which the firm takes positions are initially being correctly allocated.

doc_path: IBANK Part 3.1A Boundary between banking book and trading book

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1A.10 Transfer of instruments between books
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.1A Boundary between banking book and trading book
IBANK 3.1A.10 Transfer of instruments between books
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm that has a trading book may transfer an instrument from the trading book to the banking book (or vice versa) only in accordance with this rule.

(2) In particular, the firm must not transfer an instrument from either book to the other for reasons of regulatory arbitrage.

Note See rule 3.1A.13 for the consequences of a transfer for the firm’s risk-based capital requirement.

(3) Before the transfer takes place:

(a) it must be reviewed by the firm’s risk management function to ensure that it complies with the firm’s policies;
(b) it must be thoroughly documented;
(c) it must be approved by the firm’s senior management; and

(d) subject to subrule (6), it must have been approved by the Regulatory Authority.

Guidance
The Authority will allow instruments to be transferred between banking and trading books only in extraordinary circumstances. Examples of situations that might qualify as “extraordinary circumstances” are the following:
• a major publicly announced event, such as a bank restructuring that results in the permanent closure of trading desks and the termination of the business activity applicable to the relevant instrument or portfolio
• a change in an applicable accounting standard that allows an item to be fair-valued through the P&L account.
Market events, changes in the liquidity of a financial instrument, or a change of trading intent alone are not valid reasons for transferring an instrument.
(4) The firm must provide appropriate supporting evidence with its application to the Authority.
(5) The firm must publicly disclose the transfer.
(6) The Authority’s approval is not required for a transfer that is necessary because the instrument concerned has been reclassified as a result of a change in an applicable accounting standard.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1A.11 Policies etc — trading book
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.1A Boundary between banking book and trading book
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm that has a trading book must have clear policies for keeping the trading book up to date and the positions and exposures accurate.

(2) In particular, the firm must have policies on:

(a) what positions to include, and not to include, in the trading book;
(b) managing and reporting trading positions;

(c) how to value positions, including:

(i) clearly defined responsibilities of the staff involved in the valuation;
(ii) sources of market information, and the review of their reliability;
(iii) the frequency of independent valuations;
(iv) the timing of closing prices;
(v) procedures for adjusting valuations between periods;
(vi) ad hoc verification procedures; and
(vii) reporting lines for the valuation function that are independent of the function that gave rise to the position; and
(d) distinguishing between the firm’s trading activities and banking activities.
Note The firm must also have policies in relation to transfers between the banking book and trading book — see rule 3.1A.12.

(3) The firm must also have adequate procedures for monitoring:

(a) compliance with the policies; and
(b) the size of the trading book.
(4) The policies (and any amendment of them) must have been approved by the firm’s governing body.
(5) The firm must notify the Regulatory Authority promptly if the firm’s governing body approves an amendment to the policies.
(6) The firm must document its compliance with the policies and procedures.
(7) The firm’s internal audit function must review the record of compliance periodically (at least annually). The firm must make the results of such a review available to the Authority.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1A.12 Policies in relation to transfers between banking and trading books
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.1A Boundary between banking book and trading book
IBANK 3.1A.12 Policies in relation to transfers between banking and trading books
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an Islamic banking business firm has a trading book, the firm’s policies in relation to the trading book must cover the following matters:

(a) the firm’s policies about transfers of instruments between banking and trading books (taking into account that transfers will be allowed only in extraordinary circumstances);
(b) a description of the circumstances in which a transfer might be considered;
(c) how the firm would identify extraordinary circumstances;
(d) the procedures for obtaining the approval of the firm’s senior management and the Regulatory Authority for such a transfer;
(e) the public disclosure, as soon as possible, of such a transfer.
(2) The policies must be updated at least annually, taking into account all the events that the firm identified during the previous year as giving rise to extraordinary circumstances.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1A.13 Effect on firm’s risk-based capital requirement of transferring instruments between books
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.1A Boundary between banking book and trading book
IBANK 3.1A.13 Effect on firm’s risk-based capital requirement of transferring instruments between books
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm that has a trading book, and proposes to transfer an instrument from the banking book to the trading book (or vice versa) must first calculate:

(a) its risk-based capital requirement before the transfer; and
(b) what its risk-based capital requirement would be after the transfer.

(2) If the effect of the transfer would be to reduce the firm’s risk-based capital requirement, and the transfer takes place, a capital surcharge is applied to the firm — that is, the firm’s risk-based capital requirement is taken to be increased by the amount by which the transfer reduced that requirement. The surcharge continues until the instrument concerned expires or matures.

Guidance
FAQ 1 to RBC25.25 (paragraph 25.25 of the Basel Framework Risk Based Capital Requirements) emphasises that the capital surcharge is to apply even if the transfer is necessary because of a change in an applicable accounting standard.
(3) The firm must notify the Regulatory Authority of any such surcharge.
(4) Subrules (1), (2) and (3) apply without exception in relation to any transfer of an instrument between the banking and trading books, regardless of the reason for the transfer.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1A.14 Regulatory Authority may require evidence that instrument held with trading intent etc
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.1A Boundary between banking book and trading book
IBANK 3.1A.14 Regulatory Authority may require evidence that instrument held with trading intent etc
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The Regulatory Authority may require an Islamic banking business firm to provide evidence that an instrument held in the firm’s trading book is held with trading intent.
(2) If the Authority considers that the firm has not provided enough evidence, or believes that the instrument customarily would be held in the banking book, the Authority may direct the firm to hold the instrument in the banking book.

(3) This rule does not apply to an instrument referred to in rule 3.1A.6 (3).

Note Rule 3.1A.6 (3) specifies certain classes of instruments that are presumed to be held with trading intent.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.1A.16 Regulatory Authority approval to hold instrument in banking book
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.1A Boundary between banking book and trading book
IBANK 3.1A.16 Regulatory Authority approval to hold instrument in banking book
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If an Islamic banking business firm considers that it needs to hold an instrument referred to in rule 3.1A.6 (3) in the banking book rather than the trading book, the firm must apply to the Regulatory Authority for approval to do so. The application must include evidence that the instrument is not held with trading intent.

Note In relation to transferring instruments between banking and trading books, see generally rule 3.1A.10.

doc_path: IBANK Part 3.1A Boundary between banking book and trading book
IBANK 3.1A.17 Regulatory Authority’s power to direct that instrument be held in trading book

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.1 Introduction
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Division 3.2.A Required Capital and Ratios
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm is expected to meet minimum risk-based capital requirements for exposure to credit risk, market risk and operational risk. The firm's capital adequacy ratios (consisting of CET 1 ratio, total tier 1 ratio and total capital ratio) are calculated by dividing its regulatory capital by total risk-weighted assets.
(2) Total risk-weighted assets of an Islamic banking business firm is the sum of:
(a) the firm's risk-weighted on-balance-sheet and off-balance-sheet items calculated in accordance with Part 4.4; and
(b) 12.5 times the sum of the firm's market and operational risk capital requirements (to the extent that each of those requirements applies to the firm).

Note For how to calculate the firm’s market risk and operational risk capital requirements, see rule 6.1.1 (3) and Part 7.4, respectively.
(3) In this Part:

consolidated subsidiary, of an Islamic banking business firm, means:
(a) a subsidiary of the firm; or
(b) a subsidiary of a subsidiary of the firm.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016)
Amended by QFCRA RM/2020-3 (as from 1st January 2021)

IBANK 3.2.2 Required Tier 1 Capital on Authorisation
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An entity must have, at the time it is authorised, tier 1 capital at least equal to:
(a) for an Islamic bank — QR 35 million;
(b) for an Islamic investment dealer — QR 7 million.
(2) The Regulatory Authority will not grant an authorisation unless it is satisfied that the entity complies with this requirement.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.3 Required Ongoing Capital
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Division 3.2.A Required Capital and Ratios
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must have, at all times, capital at least equal to the higher of:
(a) its base capital requirement; and
(b) its risk-based capital requirement.

Note A firm whose minimum capital requirement is its risk-based capital requirement is subject to the additional requirement to maintain a capital conservation buffer — see rule 3.3.2.
(2) The amount of capital that a firm must have is its minimum capital requirement.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.6 Capital Adequacy Ratios
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Division 3.2.A Required Capital and Ratios
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm's capital adequacy is measured against 3 capital ratios expressed as percentages of its total risk-weighted assets.

(2) A firm's minimum capital adequacy ratios are:

(a) a CET 1 capital ratio of 4.5%;
(b) a tier 1 capital ratio of 6%; and
(c) a regulatory capital ratio of 8%.

Note Under rule 3.3.2, at least 2.5% (by way of a capital conservation buffer) must be held by an Islamic banking business firm in addition to the minimum capital adequacy ratios. The firm's CET 1 capital plus capital conservation buffer must therefore be no less than 7% of its total risk-weighted assets.
(3) The Regulatory Authority may, if it believes it is prudent to do so, increase any or all of a firm's minimum capital adequacy ratios. The authority will notify the firm in writing about a new capital adequacy ratio and the timeframe for meeting it.
(4) A firm must maintain, at all times, capital adequacy ratios higher than the required minimum so that adequate capital is maintained in the context of the firm's risk appetite, risk profile and capital requirements, and as an additional buffer to absorb losses and problems from market volatility. These higher ratios are the firm's risk-based capital adequacy ratios.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.7 Regulatory Capital
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Division 3.2.B Elements of Regulatory Capital
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The regulatory capital of an Islamic banking business firm is the sum of its tier 1 capital and tier 2 capital.
(2) Tier 1 capital is the sum of a firm's CET 1 capital and additional tier 1 capital. Tier 1 capital is also known as going-concern capital because it is meant to absorb losses while the firm is viable.

Note For the elements of CET 1 capital and additional tier 1 capital, see rules 3.2.8 and 3.2.10.
(3) Tier 2 capital is the sum of the elements set out in rule 3.2.12. Tier 2 capital is also known as gone-concern capital because it is meant to absorb losses after the firm ceases to be viable.
(4) For these rules, the 3 categories of regulatory capital are CET 1 capital, additional tier 1 capital and tier 2 capital.

Note PSIAs of an Islamic banking business firm do not form part of regulatory capital, because they do not satisfy the criteria for inclusion as either CET 1, additional tier 1 or tier 2 capital. Neither are the PER and IRR part of the regulatory capital of the firm.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.8 Common Equity Tier 1 Capital
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Division 3.2.B Elements of Regulatory Capital
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Common equity tier 1 capital (or CET 1 capital) is the sum of the following elements:

(a) common shares, issued by an Islamic banking business firm, that satisfy the criteria in rule 3.2.9 for classification as common shares (or the equivalent for non-joint stock companies);
(b) share premium (also known as stock surplus) resulting from the issue of instruments included in CET 1 capital;
(c) retained earnings;
(d) accumulated other comprehensive income and other disclosed reserves;
(e) common shares, issued by a consolidated subsidiary of the firm and held by third parties, that satisfy the criteria in rule 3.2.18 for inclusion in CET 1 capital;
(f) regulatory adjustments applied in the calculation of CET 1 capital in accordance with Division 3.2.D.

Note 1 Retained earnings and other comprehensive income include appropriated profit or loss.

Note 2 Even though they are called reserves, the PER and IRR are not part of tier 1 capital of an Islamic banking business firm. They are part of the equity of IAHs and, as such, do not have the requisite loss absorbency.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.9 Criteria for Classification as Common Shares
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Division 3.2.B Elements of Regulatory Capital
IBANK 3.2.9 Criteria for Classification as Common Shares
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An instrument issued by an Islamic banking business firm is classified as a common share and included in CET 1 capital if all of the criteria in subrules (2) to (15) are satisfied.
(2) The instrument is the most subordinated claim in case of the liquidation of the firm.
(3) The holder of the instrument is entitled to a claim on the residual assets that is proportional to its share of issued capital, after all senior claims have been repaid in liquidation. The claim must be unlimited and variable and must be neither fixed nor capped.
(4) The principal amount of the instrument is perpetual and never repayable except in liquidation. Discretionary repurchases and other discretionary means of reducing capital allowed by law do not constitute repayment.

Note Under rule 3.3.6, the Regulatory Authority's approval is required for a reduction in capital.
(5) The firm does nothing to create an expectation at issuance that the instrument will be bought back, redeemed or cancelled. The statutory or contractual terms do not provide anything that might give rise to such an expectation.
(6) Distributions are paid out of distributable items of the firm (including retained earnings) and the amount of distributions:
(a) is not tied or linked to the amount paid in at issuance; and
(b) is not subject to a contractual cap (except to the extent that a firm may not pay distributions that exceed the amount of its distributable items).
(7) There are no circumstances under which the distributions are obligatory. Non-payment of distributions does not constitute default.
(8) Distributions are paid only after all legal and contractual obligations have been met and payments on more senior capital instruments have been made. There are no preferential distributions and in particular none for any other elements classified as the highest quality issued capital.
(9) It is the issued capital that takes the first and proportionately greatest share of any losses as they occur. Within the highest quality capital, each instrument absorbs losses on a going-concern basis proportionately and equally with all the others.

Note This criterion is taken to be satisfied even if the instrument includes a permanent write-down mechanism.
(10) The paid-in amount is recognised as equity capital (rather than as a liability) for determining balance-sheet insolvency.
(11) The paid-in amount is classified as equity in accordance with the relevant accounting standards.
(12) The instrument is directly issued and paid-in, and the firm has not directly or indirectly funded the purchase of the instrument.
(13) The paid-in amount is neither secured nor covered by a guarantee of the firm or a related party, nor subject to any other arrangement that legally or economically enhances the seniority of the holder's claim in relation to the claims of the firm's creditors.
(14) The instrument is issued only with the approval of the owners of the firm, either given directly by the owners or, if permitted by the applicable law, given by its governing body or by other persons authorised by the owners.
(15) The instrument is clearly and separately disclosed on the firm's balance sheet.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.11 Criteria for Inclusion in Additional Tier 1 Capital
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Division 3.2.B Elements of Regulatory Capital
IBANK 3.2.11 Criteria for Inclusion in Additional Tier 1 Capital
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An instrument is included in additional tier 1 capital if all of the criteria in subrules (2) to (15) are satisfied.
(2) The instrument is paid-in.
(3) The instrument is the most subordinated claim after those of depositors, general creditors and holders of the subordinated debt of the firm.
(4) The paid-in amount is neither secured nor covered by a guarantee of the firm or a related party, nor subject to any other arrangement that legally or economically enhances the seniority of the holder's claim in relation to the claims of the firm's creditors.
(5) The instrument is perpetual. It has no maturity date and there are no step-ups or other incentives to redeem.
(6) If the instrument is callable by the firm, it can only be called 5 years or more after the instrument is paid-in and only with the approval of the Regulatory Authority. The firm must not do anything to create an expectation that the exercise of the option will be approved, and, if the exercise is approved, the firm:
(a) must replace the called instrument with capital of the same or better quality and at conditions sustainable for the income capacity of the firm; or
(b) must demonstrate to the authority that its capital will exceed the firm's minimum capital requirement after the option is exercised.
(7) A repayment of principal through repurchase, redemption or other means must be approved by the Regulatory Authority. The firm must not assume, or create a market expectation, that such approval will be given.
(8) The instrument must provide for the firm to have, at all times, discretion not to make a distribution or pay a dividend or profit. The exercise of the discretion must not impose restrictions on the firm (except in relation to distributions to common shareholders) and must not constitute default.
(9) Dividends and profits must be paid out of distributable items.
(10) The instrument must not have a credit-sensitive-dividend feature under which a dividend or profit is periodically reset based (wholly or partly) on the firm's credit standing.
(11) The instrument must not contribute to the firm's liabilities exceeding its assets if such a balance-sheet test forms part of any insolvency law applying in the jurisdiction where the instrument was issued.
(12) An instrument classified as a liability for accounting purposes must have principal loss absorption through conversion to common shares, or a write-down mechanism that allocates losses to the instrument, at a pre-specified trigger point. The conversion must be made in accordance with rule 3.2.15.
(13) Neither the firm nor a related party over which the firm exercises control has purchased the instrument, nor has the firm directly or indirectly funded the purchase of the instrument.
(14) The instrument has no features that hinder recapitalisation. For example, it must not require the firm to compensate investors if a new instrument is issued at a lower price during a specified period.
(15) If the instrument is issued by an SPE, the proceeds are immediately available without limitation to the firm through an instrument that satisfies the other criteria for additional tier 1 capital.

Note For the treatment of instruments issued by an SPE, see rule 3.2.21.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2017-1 (as from 1st April 2017).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.12 Tier 2 Capital
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Division 3.2.B Elements of Regulatory Capital
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Tier 2 capital is the sum of the following elements:

(a) instruments, issued by the firm, that satisfy the criteria in rule 3.2.13 for inclusion in tier 2 capital (and are not included in tier 1 capital);
(b) share premium (also known as stock surplus) resulting from the issue of instruments included in tier 2 capital;
(c) instruments, issued by consolidated subsidiaries of the firm and held by third parties, that satisfy the criteria in rule 3.2.20 for inclusion in tier 2 capital (and are not included in tier 1 capital);
(d) regulatory adjustments applied in the calculation of tier 2 capital in accordance with Division 3.2.D;
(e) general provisions or general reserves held against future, presently unidentified losses (but only up to a maximum of 1.25% of risk-weighted assets for credit risk, calculated using the standardised approach in Part 4.3).

Note 1 General provisions and reserves are freely available to meet losses that subsequently materialise and therefore qualify for inclusion in tier 2 capital. In contrast, provisions for identified deterioration of particular assets or known liabilities, whether individual or grouped, should be excluded because they would not be available to meet losses.

Note 2 Even though they are called reserves, the PER and IRR are not part of tier 2 capital of an Islamic banking business firm. They are part of the equity of IAHs and, as such, do not have the requisite loss absorbency.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

IBANK 3.2.13 Criteria for Inclusion in Tier 2 Capital
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An instrument is included in tier 2 capital if all the criteria in subrules (2) to (11) are satisfied.
(2) The instrument is paid-in.
(3) The instrument is the most subordinated claim after those of depositors, general creditors and holders of the subordinated debt of the firm.
(4) The paid-in amount is neither secured nor covered by a guarantee of the firm or a related party, nor subject to any other arrangement that legally or economically enhances the seniority of the holder's claim in relation to the claims of the firm's depositors and general creditors.
(5) The original maturity of the instrument is at least 5 years.
(6) The recognition in regulatory capital in the remaining 5 years before maturity is amortised on a straight line basis and there are no step-ups or other incentives to redeem.
(7) If the instrument is callable by the firm, it can only be called 5 years or more after the instrument is paid-in and only with the approval of the Regulatory Authority. (8) The holder has no right to accelerate future scheduled payments of profit or principal, except in bankruptcy or liquidation.
(9) The instrument does not have a credit-sensitive-dividend feature under which a dividend or profit is periodically reset based (wholly or partly) on the firm's credit standing.
(10) Neither the firm nor a related party over which the firm exercises control has purchased the instrument, nor has the firm directly or indirectly funded the purchase of the instrument.
(11) If the instrument is issued by an SPE, the proceeds are immediately available without limitation to the firm through an instrument that satisfies the other criteria for tier 2 capital.

Note For the treatment of instruments issued by an SPE, see rule 3.2.21.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.14 Mudarabah Sukuk or Wakalah Sukuk as Tier 2 Capital
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Division 3.2.B Elements of Regulatory Capital
IBANK 3.2.14 Mudarabah Sukuk or Wakalah Sukuk as Tier 2 Capital
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Subject to compliance with Shari'a, an Islamic banking business firm may issue mudarabah sukuk or wakalah sukuk that qualify for inclusion in tier 2 capital under rule 3.2.13. For the sukuk, the receivables from the underlying assets are convertible to common equity at the point of non-viability.
(2) The sukuk contract must state the terms of conversion, trigger point and conversion ratio. The conversion must be made in accordance with rule 3.2.15.

Note For mudarabah sukuk, see rule 10.3.19. For wakalah sukuk, see rule 10.3.21.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.15 Requirements — Loss Absorption at Point of Non-Viability
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Division 3.2.B Elements of Regulatory Capital
IBANK 3.2.15 Requirements — Loss Absorption at Point of Non-Viability
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to an additional tier 1 or tier 2 instrument issued by an Islamic banking business firm. It sets out additional requirements to ensure loss absorption at the point of non-viability.
(2) The terms and conditions of an instrument must give the Regulatory Authority the discretion to direct that the instrument be written-off or converted to common equity on the happening of a trigger event.
(3) The firm must be able to issue the required number of shares specified in the instrument if a trigger event happens. The issuance of any new shares because of a trigger event must happen before any public sector injection of capital so that capital provided by the public sector is not diluted.
(4) Trigger event, in relation to the firm that issued the instrument, is the earliest of:
(a) a decision of the Regulatory Authority that a write-off (without which the firm would become non-viable) is necessary; and
(b) a decision by the relevant authority in Qatar to make a public sector injection of capital, or give equivalent support (without which injection or support the firm would become non-viable, as determined by that authority).
(5) If the firm is a member of a financial group and the firm wishes the instrument to be included in the group's capital in addition to its solo capital, the trigger event must be the earliest of:
(a) the decision in subrule (4) (a);
(b) the decision in subrule (4) (b);
(c) a decision, by the relevant authority in the firm's home jurisdiction, that a write-off (without which the firm would become non-viable) is necessary; and
(d) a decision, by the relevant authority in the jurisdiction of the financial regulator that regulates the parent entity of the firm, to make a public sector injection of capital, or give equivalent support, in that jurisdiction (without which injection or support the firm would become non-viable, as determined by that authority).
(6) Any compensation paid to the holder of an instrument because of a write-off must be paid immediately in the form of common shares (or the equivalent for non-joint-stock companies).
(7) If the firm is a member of a financial group, any common shares paid as compensation to the holder of the instrument must be common shares of the firm or of the parent entity of the group.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The write-off of an instrument using a murabahah contract must be through the investor (as creditor):
(a) making a promise (wa'ad) to waive rights on debts at the point of non-viability; or
(b) agreeing, in the relevant legal documents, to waive rights on debts at the point of non-viability.
(2) The write-off of an instrument using an ijarah contract must be through the investor (as lessor):
(a) making a promise (wa'ad) to transfer ownership of the underlying asset (beneficial or otherwise) to the firm without consideration; or
(b) agreeing, in the relevant legal documents, to waive rights on accrued rental at the point of non-viability.
(3) An Islamic banking business firm may apply to the Regulatory Authority for approval to use a write-off mechanism other than those in subrules (1) and (2).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For rule 3.2.8(e), a common share, issued by a consolidated subsidiary of an Islamic banking business firm and held by a third party as a non-controlling interest, may be included in the firm's CET 1 capital if:
(a) the share would be included in the firm's CET 1 capital had it been issued by the firm; and
(b) the subsidiary that issued the share is itself an Islamic bank or Islamic investment dealer (or an equivalent entity in its home jurisdiction).
(2) The amount to be included in the consolidated CET 1 capital of an Islamic banking business firm is calculated in accordance with the following formula:

NCI — ((CET1s — Min) × SS)

where:

NCI is the total of the non-controlling interests of third parties in a consolidated subsidiary of the firm.

CET1s is the amount of CET 1 capital of the subsidiary.

Min is the lower of:
(a) 1.07 × (minimum CET 1 capital requirement of the subsidiary); and
(b) 1.07 × (the part of the consolidated minimum CET 1 capital requirement that relates to the subsidiary).
SS means the percentage of the shares in the subsidiary (being shares included in CET 1 capital) held by those third parties.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.19 Criteria for Third Party Interests — Additional Tier 1 Capital
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Division 3.2.C Inclusion of Third Parties' Interests
IBANK 3.2.19 Criteria for Third Party Interests — Additional Tier 1 Capital
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For rule 3.2.10(c), an instrument (including a common share) issued by a consolidated subsidiary of an Islamic banking business firm and held by a third party as a non-controlling interest may be included in the firm's additional tier 1 capital if the instrument would be included in the firm's additional tier 1 capital had it been issued by the firm.

Note Any amount already included in CET 1 capital must not be included in additional tier 1 capital — see rule 3.2.10(c).
(2) The amount to be included in the consolidated additional tier 1 capital of an Islamic banking business firm is calculated in accordance with the following formula:

NCI — ((T1s — Min) × SS)

where:

NCI is the total of the non-controlling interests of third parties in a consolidated subsidiary of the firm.

T1s is the amount of additional tier 1 capital of the subsidiary.

Min is the lower of:
(a) 1.07 × (minimum additional tier 1 capital requirement of the subsidiary); and
(b) 1.07 × (the part of the consolidated minimum additional tier 1 capital requirement that relates to the subsidiary).
SS means the percentage of the shares in the subsidiary (being shares included in additional tier 1 capital) held by those third parties.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.20 Criteria for Third Party Interests — Tier 2 Capital
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Division 3.2.C Inclusion of Third Parties' Interests
IBANK 3.2.20 Criteria for Third Party Interests — Tier 2 Capital
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For rule 3.2.12(c), an instrument (including a common share and any other tier 1 capital instrument) issued by a consolidated subsidiary of an Islamic banking business firm and held by a third party as a non-controlling interest may be included in the firm's tier 2 capital if the instrument would be included in the firm's tier 2 capital had it been issued by the firm.

Note Any amount already included in CET 1 capital or additional tier 1 capital must not be included in tier 2 capital — see rule 3.2.12(c).
(2) The amount to be included in the consolidated tier 2 capital of an Islamic banking business firm is calculated in accordance with the following formula:

NCI — ((T2s — Min) × SS)

where:

NCI is the total of the non-controlling interests of third parties in a consolidated subsidiary of the firm.

T2s is the amount of tier 2 capital of the subsidiary.

Min is the lower of:
(a) 1.07 × (minimum tier 2 capital requirement of the subsidiary); and
(b) 1.07 × (the part of the consolidated minimum tier 2 capital requirement that relates to the subsidiary).
SS means the percentage of the shares in the subsidiary (being shares included in tier 2 capital) held by those third parties.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.21 Treatment of third party interests from SPEs
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Division 3.2.C Inclusion of Third Parties' Interests
IBANK 3.2.21 Treatment of third party interests from SPEs
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An instrument issued out of an SPE and held by a third party must not be included in an Islamic banking business firm's CET 1 capital. Such an instrument may be included in the firm's additional tier 1 or tier 2 capital (and treated as if it had been issued by the firm itself directly to the third party) if:
(a) the instrument satisfies the criteria for inclusion in the relevant category of regulatory capital; and
(b) the only asset of the SPE is its investment in the capital of the firm and that investment satisfies the criterion in rule 3.2.11(15) or 3.2.13(11) for the immediate availability of the proceeds.
(2) An instrument described in subrule (1) that is issued out of an SPE through a consolidated subsidiary of an Islamic banking business firm may be included in the firm's consolidated additional tier 1 or tier 2 capital if the instrument satisfies the criteria in rule 3.2.19 or 3.2.20, as the case requires. Such an instrument is treated as if it had been issued by the subsidiary itself directly to the third party.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2017-1 (as from 1st April 2017).

doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Adjustments to an Islamic banking business firm’s regulatory capital may be required to avoid double-counting, or the artificial inflation of its capital. Adjustments may also be required in relation to assets that cannot readily be converted into cash.

IBANK 3.2.25 How adjustments are to be made
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
A regulatory adjustment to an Islamic banking business firm’s regulatory capital may be either a deduction from that capital or the derecognition of an item for the calculation of the capital.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.26 Corresponding deduction approach
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Subdivision 3.2.D.2 Adjustments to Common Equity Tier 1 Capital
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If this Division requires a deduction to be made using the corresponding deduction approach, an Islamic banking business firm must make the deduction from the category of regulatory capital that the holding would qualify as if the firm itself had issued the relevant instrument (or, if the firm does not have sufficient regulatory capital in that category, from the next higher category). For that purpose, CET 1 capital is the highest category of regulatory capital, additional tier 1 capital is the next highest, and tier 2 is the lowest.

Note For these rules, the 3 categories of regulatory capital are CET 1 capital, additional tier 1 capital and tier 2 capital — see rule 3.2.7 (4).

Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.27 Goodwill and intangible assets
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Subdivision 3.2.D.2 Adjustments to Common Equity Tier 1 Capital
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm must deduct, from its CET 1 capital, the amount of its goodwill and other intangible assets (except mortgage servicing rights). The amount must be net of any related deferred tax liability that would be extinguished if the goodwill or assets become impaired or derecognised under IFRS or any other relevant accounting standards.

Note For the treatment of mortgage servicing rights, see rule 3.2.38.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.28 Deferred tax assets that rely on future profitability
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Subdivision 3.2.D.2 Adjustments to Common Equity Tier 1 Capital
IBANK 3.2.28 Deferred tax assets that rely on future profitability
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to deferred tax assets of an Islamic banking business firm if the assets depend on the future profitability of the firm to be realised, but does not apply to such assets that relate to temporary differences.
(2) For each deferred tax asset to which this rule applies, the firm must deduct, from its CET 1 capital, the full amount of the asset net of any deferred tax liability that may be netted against it under subrules (3) to (5).

(3) A deferred tax asset may be netted against a deferred tax liability only if:

(a) the asset and the liability relate to taxes levied by the same taxation authority; and
(b) that authority explicitly permits offsetting.
(4) A deferred tax liability must not be used for netting if it has already been netted against a deduction of goodwill or other intangible assets, or defined benefit pension assets.
(5) A deferred tax liability that may be netted must be allocated pro rata between deferred tax assets deducted under this rule and those to which the treatment in rule 3.2.38 is applied.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

In the calculation of its CET 1 capital, an Islamic banking business firm must derecognise the amount of the cash flow hedge reserve that relates to the hedging of items that are not fair valued on the balance sheet (including projected cash flows).

doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements

IBANK 3.2.31 Gains on sale from securitisations

In the calculation of its CET 1 capital, an Islamic banking business firm must derecognise any increase in equity capital or CET 1 capital from a securitisation or resecuritisation transaction (for example, an increase associated with expected future margin income resulting in a gain-on-sale).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.32 Gains and losses from changes to own credit risk
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Subdivision 3.2.D.2 Adjustments to Common Equity Tier 1 Capital
IBANK 3.2.32 Gains and losses from changes to own credit risk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) In the calculation of an Islamic banking business firm’s CET 1 capital:

(a) the firm must derecognise all unrealised gains and unrealised losses that have resulted from changes in the fair value of liabilities because of changes in the firm’s own credit risk; and
(b) in relation to liabilities arising from SCHIs, the firm must derecognise all accounting valuation adjustments that arise from the firm’s own credit risk.
(2) The firm must not offset valuation adjustments that arise from the firm’s own credit risk against such adjustments that arise from its counterparties’ credit risk.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.33 Defined benefit pension fund assets
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Subdivision 3.2.D.2 Adjustments to Common Equity Tier 1 Capital
IBANK 3.2.33 Defined benefit pension fund assets
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must deduct, from its CET 1 capital, the amount of a defined benefit pension fund that is an asset on the firm’s balance sheet. The amount must be net of any related deferred tax liability that would be extinguished if the asset were to become impaired or derecognised under IFRS or any other relevant accounting standards.
(2) The firm may apply to the Regulatory Authority for approval to offset from the deduction any asset in the fund to which the firm has unrestricted and unfettered access. Such an asset must be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to it if it were owned directly by the firm.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: (1) An Islamic banking business firm must deduct, from its CET 1 capital, the amount of a defined benefit pension fund that is an asset on the firm’s balance sheet. The amount must be net of any related deferred tax liability that would be extinguished if the asset were to become impaired or derecognised under IFRS or any other relevant accounting standards. (2) The firm may apply to the Regulatory Authority for approval to offset from the deduction any asset in the fund to which the firm has unrestricted and unfettered access. Such an asset must be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to it if it were owned directly by the firm. Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.34 Investments in own shares and capital instruments
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Subdivision 3.2.D.2 Adjustments to Common Equity Tier 1 Capital
IBANK 3.2.34 Investments in own shares and capital instruments
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must deduct, from its CET 1 capital, any direct or indirect investment in its own common shares or own capital instruments (except instruments that have been derecognised under IFRS or any other relevant accounting standards). The firm must also deduct any of its own common shares or instruments that it is contractually obliged to purchase.

(2) The firm must apply the corresponding deduction approach to make the deductions required by this rule.

Note For the corresponding deduction approach, see rule 3.2.26.
(3) For this rule, a gross long position may be deducted net of a short position in the same underlying exposure only if the short position involves no counterparty risk.
(4) For this rule, the firm must look through its holdings of index securities to determine its exposures to its own shares. However, if the firm finds it operationally burdensome to look through those holdings and monitor its exact exposure to its own shares, the firm may use a conservative estimate of such exposures if the Regulatory Authority so approves.

(5) The firm may net a gross long position in its own shares resulting from a holding of index securities against a short position in those shares resulting from a short position in the same underlying index if the maturity of the short position matches the maturity of the long position.

Guidance
In such cases, the short positions may involve counterparty credit risk (which will be subject to the relevant counterparty credit risk charge).
(6) This rule applies to an investment whether it is held in the firm’s banking book or trading book.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.35 Treatment of reciprocal cross-holdings in banking, financial and takaful entities
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Subdivision 3.2.D.2 Adjustments to Common Equity Tier 1 Capital
IBANK 3.2.35 Treatment of reciprocal cross-holdings in banking, financial and takaful entities
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must deduct, from its regulatory capital, reciprocal cross-holdings in the shares (or other instruments that qualify as capital) of a banking, financial or takaful entity if the firm’s holding has the effect of artificially inflating the firm’s capital position.

Guidance
The firm should seek guidance from the Regulatory Authority as to whether an entity is a financial entity. However, a financial entity might be involved in (for example) financial leasing, issuing credit cards, portfolio management, investment advisory, custodial and safekeeping services and other similar activities that are ancillary to the business of banking.

(2) The firm must apply the corresponding deduction approach to make the deductions required by this rule.

Note For the corresponding deduction approach, see rule 3.2.26.
(3) For this rule, the provision by an Islamic banking business firm of support, by way of a guarantee or some other capital enhancement, to such an entity is to be treated as an investment by the firm in the entity.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.36 Non- significant investments in unconsolidated banking, financial or takaful entities
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Subdivision 3.2.D.3 Deductions from Categories of Regulatory Capital
IBANK 3.2.36 Non- significant investments in unconsolidated banking, financial or takaful entities
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to an investment by an Islamic banking business firm in the capital of a banking, financial or takaful entity that is outside the scope of regulatory consolidation, if the investment is not a significant investment.

Note For the meaning of financial entity, see rule 3.2.35 (1), guidance.

(2) For this rule and rules 3.2.37 and 3.2.38, significant investment means:

(a) an investment representing more than 10% of the issued common shares, or other instruments that qualify as capital, of the entity; or
(b) if the entity is affiliated with the firm, an investment representing any amount of the issued common shares, or other instruments that qualify as capital, of the entity.
Note For the meaning of affiliated, see subrule (10) (b).
(3) For this rule, the firm must look through its holdings of index securities to determine its exposures to such instruments. However, if the firm finds it operationally burdensome to look through those holdings and monitor its exact exposure to such instruments, the firm may use a conservative estimate of such exposures if the Regulatory Authority so approves.
(4) Underwriting positions held for longer than 5 business days must be included in the investments to be deducted. Underwriting positions held for 5 business days or less must be excluded.

(5) The amount to be deducted is the firm’s net long position in the relevant investments (that is, the gross long position net of any short position in the same underlying exposure, if the maturity of the short position either matches the maturity of the long position or has a residual maturity of at least 1 year). The firm may also net gross long positions arising through holdings of index securities against short positions in the same underlying index if the maturity of the short position either matches the maturity of the long position or has a residual maturity of at least 1 year.

Guidance
In such cases, the short positions may involve counterparty credit risk (which will be subject to the relevant counterparty credit risk charge).

(6) If the total of all such holdings, in aggregate and on a net long basis, is more than 10% of the firm’s CET 1 capital (after applying all the adjustments required by rules 3.2.27 to 3.2.35), the amount to be deducted from each category of the firm’s regulatory capital is to be calculated as follows:

(a) the total amount to be deducted under this rule is the excess amount (that is, the amount by which the total of all such holdings, in aggregate and on a net long basis, is more than 10% of the firm’s CET 1 capital, after applying all the adjustments required by rules 3.2.27 to 3.2.35);
(b) the amount to be deducted from the firm’s CET 1 capital is the excess amount multiplied by the percentage of the holding that is made up of instruments that would qualify as CET 1 capital if issued by the firm itself;
(c) the amount to be deducted from the firm’s additional tier 1 capital is the excess amount multiplied by the percentage of the holding that is made up of instruments that would qualify as additional tier 1 capital if issued by the firm itself;
(d) the amount to be deducted from the firm’s tier 2 capital is the excess amount multiplied by the percentage of the holding that is made up of instruments that would qualify as tier 2 capital if issued by the firm itself;
(e) if the firm does not have enough of a particular category of regulatory capital to make a deduction required by any of paragraphs (b) to (d), the deduction must be made from the next higher category of regulatory capital.

(7) Any amount of a holding to which this rule applies that is not deducted from regulatory capital must be risk-weighted.

Note For the risk-weighting of such holdings, see Part 4.4 (standardised approach to credit risk) for amounts held in the banking book and Part 6.5 (market risk, traded equity positions) for amounts held in the trading book.
(8) This rule applies to an investment whether it is held in the firm’s banking book or trading book.
(9) With the Regulatory Authority’s prior written approval, the firm may exclude from the deductions, for a period specified by the Authority, investments made in the course of resolving a distressed institution or providing financial assistance to reorganise such an institution.

(10) For subrule (2):

(a) the definition of affiliate in the Glossary does not apply;

(b) an entity is affiliated with an Islamic banking business firm if:

(i) the firm controls the entity;
(ii) the entity controls the firm; or
(iii) the firm and the entity are under common control; and
(c) control has the meaning given by the applicable accounting standard.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

IBANK 3.2.37 Significant investments in unconsolidated banking, financial or takaful entities
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies in relation to a significant investment by an Islamic banking business firm in the capital of a banking, financial or takaful entity that is outside the scope of regulatory consolidation.

Note For the meaning of financial entity, see rule 3.2.35 (1), guidance.
(2) Underwriting positions held for longer than 5 business days must be included in the investments to be deducted. Underwriting positions held for 5 business days or less must be excluded.
(3) For this rule, the firm must look through its holdings of index securities to determine its exposures to such instruments. However, if the firm finds it operationally burdensome to look through those holdings and monitor its exact exposure to such instruments, the firm may use a conservative estimate of such exposures if the Regulatory Authority so approves.

(4) The total, on a net long basis, of all such holdings that are not common shares is to be deducted from the firm’s regulatory capital. The amount to be deducted from each category of that capital is to be calculated as follows:

(a) the amount to be deducted from the firm’s CET 1 capital is the total amount of the holding multiplied by the percentage of the holding that is made up of instruments that would qualify as CET 1 capital if issued by the firm itself;
(b) the amount to be deducted from the firm’s additional tier 1 capital is the total amount of the holding multiplied by the percentage of the holding that is made up of instruments that would qualify as additional tier 1 capital if issued by the firm itself;
(c) the amount to be deducted from the firm’s tier 2 capital is the total amount of the holding multiplied by the percentage of the holding that is made up of instruments that would qualify as tier 2 capital if issued by the firm itself;
(d) if the firm does not have enough of a particular category of regulatory capital to make a deduction required by any of paragraphs (a) to (c), the deduction must be made from the next higher category of regulatory capital.
(5) The total, on a net long basis, of all such holdings that are common shares are subject to recognition up to a threshold and deduction above the threshold in accordance with rule 3.2.38.
(6) For this rule and rule 3.2.38, a capital instrument issued by the entity must be treated as common shares if the instrument would not meet the criteria for CET 1 capital, additional tier 1 capital or tier 2 capital if issued by the firm itself.

(7) Any amount of a holding to which this rule applies that is not deducted from regulatory capital must be risk-weighted.

Note For the risk-weighting of such holdings, see Part 4.4 (standardised approach to credit risk) for amounts held in the banking book and Part 6.5 (market risk, traded equity positions) for amounts held in the trading book.
(8) This rule applies to an investment whether it is held in the firm’s banking book or trading book.
(9) With the Regulatory Authority’s prior written approval, the firm may exclude from the deductions, for a period specified by the Authority, investments made in the course of resolving a distressed institution or providing financial assistance to reorganise such an institution.
