QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.38 Threshold deductions
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Subdivision 3.2.D.3 Deductions from Categories of Regulatory Capital
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to the following kinds of asset:

(a) a significant investment in the common shares of an Islamic banking, financial or takaful entity that is outside the scope of regulatory consolidation;
(b) mortgage servicing rights;

(c) deferred tax assets that arise from temporary differences (for example, allowance for credit losses).

Note For the treatment of other deferred tax assets, see rule 3.2.28.
(2) When an Islamic banking business firm calculates its CET 1 capital, the firm may recognise each kind of asset to which this rule applies only up to 10% of the firm’s CET 1 capital (calculated after applying all other adjustments) but this is subject to subrule (4).
(3) The firm must deduct, from its CET 1 capital, the amount by which any of the 3 kinds of asset exceeds 10% of its CET 1 capital (after applying all the other regulatory adjustments required to its CET 1 capital).
(4) When an Islamic banking business firm calculates its CET 1 capital, the firm may recognise the total of all 3 kinds of assets to which this rule applies only up to 15% of the firm’s CET 1 capital (calculated after applying all other adjustment including limiting the recognition of any kind of those assets to 10% of the firm’s CET 1 capital).

(5) The firm must deduct, from its CET 1 capital, the amount by which the total of the 3 kinds of asset (after any limitation applied under subrule (2)) exceeds 15% of its CET 1 capital (after applying all the other regulatory adjustments required to its CET 1 capital).

Note 1 Any amount of such assets that is not deducted from CET 1 capital must be risk-weighted at 250% — see rule 4.4.85.
Note 2 For the general treatment of investments in unconsolidated banking, financial or takaful entities, see rules 3.2.36 and 3.2.37.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.39 Higher capital requirement imposed on overseas branch
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Subdivision 3.2.D.3 Deductions from Categories of Regulatory Capital
IBANK 3.2.39 Higher capital requirement imposed on overseas branch
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an Islamic banking business firm has an overseas branch, the firm must deduct, from its CET 1 capital, any capital requirement imposed on the branch by:

(a) the Regulatory Authority; or
(b) the financial regulator in the jurisdiction in which the branch is located.
(2) If both the Authority and the other financial regulator impose such a requirement, the firm must deduct the higher of the 2 requirements from its CET 1 capital.
(3) Subrules (1) and (2) do not apply if the overseas branch is included in the firm’s consolidated returns.
(4) Despite subrule (3), if the financial regulator in the jurisdiction in which an overseas branch of an Islamic banking business firm is located imposes a capital requirement on the branch, the firm must deduct, from its CET 1 capital, the amount of any shortfall between the actual capital held by the branch and that capital requirement.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.40 Certain exposures protected by guarantees
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK Subdivision 3.2.D.3 Deductions from Categories of Regulatory Capital
IBANK 3.2.40 Certain exposures protected by guarantees
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If an exposure of an Islamic banking business firm is covered by an eligible guarantee, but the coverage is subject to a materiality threshold (below which the protection provider is not obliged to pay on the occurrence of a credit event), the firm must deduct, from its CET 1 capital, so much of the exposure as is below the threshold.

Guidance

A guarantee by an Islamic banking business firm’s parent entity may be an eligible guarantee if the parent entity is an eligible guarantor — see rules 4.6.31 and 4.6.32.

Note Eligible guarantee is defined in rule 4.6.32.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:

(a) obtain eligible collateral (in accordance with either the simple approach or the comprehensive approach) for the amount by which the limit was exceeded; or

(b) deduct that amount from its CET 1 capital.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.42 Firms may use Estimates or Exclude Deductions

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If it is impractical for an Islamic banking business firm to examine and monitor the firm's exposures to the capital of entities concerned (including through holdings of indexed securities), the firm may apply to the Regulatory Authority for approval to use an estimate of such exposures. The authority will grant such an approval only after the firm satisfies the authority that the estimate is conservative, well-founded and reasonable.
(2) An Islamic banking business firm may also apply to the Regulatory Authority for approval not to deduct an investment made to resolve, or provide financial assistance to reorganise, a distressed entity.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.2.43 Deductions from Common Equity Tier 1 Capital
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.2 Initial and Ongoing Capital Requirements
IBANK 3.2.43 Deductions from Common Equity Tier 1 Capital
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) In addition to the other deductions to CET 1 capital under this Chapter, deductions may be required to CET 1 capital under the threshold deduction rule.
(2) The threshold deduction rule provides recognition for particular assets that are considered to have some limited capacity to absorb losses. The following items come within the threshold deduction rule:
(a) significant investments in the common shares, or other instruments that qualify as CET 1 capital, of an unconsolidated entity concerned;
(b) mortgage servicing rights;
(c) deferred tax assets that relate to temporary differences (for example, allowance for credit losses).
(3) Instead of full deduction, the items that come within the threshold deduction rule receive limited recognition when calculating CET 1 capital. The total of each of the items in subrule (2) do not require adjustment from CET 1 capital and are risk-weighted at 300% (for items listed on a recognised exchange) or 400% (for items not so listed) provided that:
(a) each item is no more than 10% of the firm's CET 1 capital (net of all regulatory adjustments except those under this Subdivision); or
(b) in total, the 3 items are no more than 15% of the firm's CET 1 capital (net of all regulatory adjustments except those under this Subdivision).
(4) An Islamic banking business firm must deduct from CET 1 capital any amount in excess of the threshold in subrule (3)(a) or (b).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.3.1 Introduction
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.3 Capital Buffers and Other Requirements
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The capital adequacy framework contains 2 additional measures for conserving capital through the capital conservation buffer and the counter-cyclical capital buffer.
(2) The capital conservation buffer promotes the conservation of capital and the build-up of a buffer above the minimum in times of economic growth and credit expansion, so that the buffer can be drawn down in periods of stress. It imposes an obligation to restrict a firm's distributions when capital falls below the capital conservation buffer minimum.
(3) The counter-cyclical capital buffer is a macroprudential tool that can be used to mitigate the build-up of a system-wide risk such as excess aggregate credit growth. It is intended to ensure that the banking system has a buffer of capital to protect it against future potential losses.
(4) These 2 buffers and other requirements on capital are set out in this Part.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.3.2 Capital Conservation Buffer
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.3 Capital Buffers and Other Requirements
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm whose risk-based capital requirement is higher than its base capital requirement must maintain a minimum capital conservation buffer of:
(a) 2.5% of the firm's total risk-weighted assets; or
(b) a higher amount that the Regulatory Authority may, by written notice, set from time to time.
(2) A firm's capital conservation buffer must be made up of CET 1 capital above the amounts used to meet the firm's CET 1 capital ratio, tier 1 capital ratio and regulatory capital ratio in rule 3.2.6(2).

Note Capital raised through the issuance of sukuk cannot form part of the capital conservation buffer because that capital does not qualify as CET 1 capital.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.3.3 Capital Conservation Ratios
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.3 Capital Buffers and Other Requirements
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an Islamic banking business firm's capital conservation buffer falls below the required minimum, the firm must immediately conserve its capital by restricting its distributions.

Note A payment made by a firm that does not reduce its CET 1 capital is not a distribution for the purposes of this Part. Distributions include, for example, dividends, share buybacks and discretionary bonus payments.
(2) This rule sets out, in column 3 of table 3.3.3, the minimum capital conservation ratios for Islamic banking business firms that are required to maintain a capital conservation buffer. Capital conservation ratio is the percentage of earnings that a firm must not distribute if its CET 1 capital ratio falls within the corresponding ratio in column 2 of that table.
(3) Earnings means distributable profits calculated before deducting elements subject to the restrictions on distributions. Earnings must be calculated after notionally deducting the tax that would have been payable had none of the distributable items been paid.

Note The effect of calculating earnings after tax is that the tax consequence of the distribution is reversed out.
(4) An Islamic banking business firm must have adequate systems and controls to ensure that the amount of distributable profits and maximum distributable amount are calculated accurately. The firm must be able to demonstrate that accuracy if directed by the Regulatory Authority.
(5) If the firm is a member of a financial group, the capital conservation buffer applies at group level.

Table 3.3.3 Minimum capital conservation ratios

column 1 item column 2 CET 1 capital ratio column 3 minimum capital conservation ratio (% of earnings)
1 4.5% to 5.125% 100
2 > 5.125% to 5.75% 80
3 > 5.75% to 6.375% 60
4 > 6.375% to 7.0% 40
5 > 7% 0

Examples of application of table

Assume that a firm's minimum CET 1 capital ratio is 4.5% and an additional 2.5% capital conservation buffer (which must be made up of CET 1 capital) is required for a total of 7% CET 1 capital ratio. Based on table 3.3.3:

1 If a firm's CET 1 capital ratio is 4.5% or more but no more than 5.125%, the firm needs to conserve 100% of its earnings.
2 If a firm's CET 1 capital ratio is more than 5.125% or more but no more than 5.75%, the firm needs to conserve 80% of its earnings and must not distribute more than 20% of those earnings by way of dividends, share buybacks and discretionary bonus payments.
3 A firm with a CET 1 capital ratio of more than 7% can distribute 100% of its earnings.
Amended by QFCRA RM/2018-2 (as from 1st May 2018).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.3.4 Powers of Regulatory Authority
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.3 Capital Buffers and Other Requirements
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The Regulatory Authority may impose a restriction on capital distributions by an Islamic banking business firm even if the amount of the firm's CET 1 capital is greater than its CET 1 capital ratio and required capital conservation buffer.
(2) The Regulatory Authority may, by written notice, impose a limit on the period during which an Islamic banking business firm may operate within a specified capital conservation ratio.
(3) An Islamic banking business firm may apply to the Regulatory Authority to make a distribution in excess of a limit imposed by this Part. The authority will grant approval only if it is satisfied that the firm has appropriate measures to raise capital equal to, or greater than, the amount the firm wishes to distribute above the limit.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.3.5 Counter-Cyclical Capital Buffer
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.3 Capital Buffers and Other Requirements
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If imposed by the Regulatory Authority, the counter-cyclical capital buffer would require a firm to have additional CET 1 capital against possible future losses from system-wide risks such as excess credit growth.
(2) The Regulatory Authority may, by written notice, require Islamic banking business firms to have additional CET 1 capital as a countercyclical capital buffer. The buffer set by the authority will not exceed 2.5% of total risk-weighted assets.
(3) The Regulatory Authority will notify firms of any decision to set, or increase, a counter-cyclical capital buffer within a reasonable period of not more than 1 year before the date when the decision takes effect. However, a decision to remove or decrease a counter-cyclical capital buffer will take effect immediately.
(4) If a counter-cyclical capital buffer applies to a firm, the capital conservation ratios (and capital distribution restrictions) in rule 3.3.3 apply to the firm as if its minimum capital conservation buffer were increased by the amount of the counter-cyclical capital buffer.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.3.6 Capital Reductions
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.3 Capital Buffers and Other Requirements
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must not reduce its capital and reserves without the Regulatory Authority's written approval.

Examples of ways to reduce capital
•   a share buyback or the redemption, repurchase or repayment of capital instruments issued by the firm
•   trading in the firm's own shares or capital instruments outside an arrangement agreed with the authority
•   a special dividend.
(2) An Islamic banking business firm planning a reduction must prepare a forecast (for at least 2 years) showing its projected capital after the reduction. The firm must satisfy the authority that the firm's capital will still comply with these rules after the reduction.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.3.7 Authority can Require Other Matters
doc_path: IBANK Part 3.3 Capital Buffers and Other Requirements
IBANK 3.3.7 Authority can Require Other Matters
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Despite anything in these rules, the Regulatory Authority may require an Islamic banking business firm to have capital resources, comply with any other capital requirement or use a different approach to, or method for, capital management. The authority may also require a firm to carry out stress-testing at any time.

Note Under FSR, article 16, the Regulatory Authority may modify or waive the application of a prudential requirement to an authorised firm or firms.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.4.1 Introduction
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
The leverage ratio is a simple, transparent, non-risk-based measure to help restrict the build-up of leverage in the Islamic banking system. Excessive leverage can expose Islamic banking businesses to higher financial risk, with potential damage to the overall financial system, and to the economy if a de-leveraging process takes place.

Inserted by QFCRA RM/2019-7 (as from 1st January 2020).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.4.2 Objectives of leverage ratio requirements
doc_path: IBANK 3.4.2 Objectives of leverage ratio requirements
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
The leverage ratio supplements the risk-based capital requirements of the rest of this Chapter. The objectives of limiting Islamic banking business firms' leverage ratios are as follows:

(a) to constrain the build-up of leverage in the Islamic banking sector, to help avoid destabilising deleveraging that can damage the broader financial system and the economy;
(b) to reinforce the risk-based requirements in Parts 3.1 to 3.3 with a simple, non-risk-based backstop measure;
(c) to serve as a broad measure of the sources of leverage, both on and off the balance-sheet.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2019-7 (as from 1st January 2020).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.4.4 Minimum leverage ratio
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must maintain a leverage ratio of not less than 3%.
(2) The Regulatory Authority may direct an Islamic banking business firm to maintain a leverage ratio higher than 3% if the Authority considers it necessary to do so because of the firm's risk profile or other particular circumstances.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2019-7 (as from 1st January 2020).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.4.5 How to calculate total exposure measure — general
doc_path: IBANK 3.4.5 How to calculate total exposure measure — general
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) When an Islamic banking business firm calculates its total exposure measure, it must treat each exposure in accordance with the normal accounting treatment of the exposure.
(2) It must include all on-balance-sheet non-derivative exposures, net of specific provisions and valuation adjustments.
(3) It must not take into account the effect of credit risk mitigation.
(4) It must not weight on-balance-sheet exposures.
(5) It must not net financing exposures against PSIAs or deposits.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2019-7 (as from 1st January 2020).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.4.6 Modification of calculation
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The Regulatory Authority may, by written notice, modify the calculation of an Islamic banking business firm's total exposure measure by, for example:
(a) allowing the firm not to take account of a particular exposure or class of exposures;
(b) directing the firm to apply a different risk-weight to an exposure or class of exposures;
(c) directing the firm to take account of an exposure or class of exposures that would not otherwise be taken account of.
(2) The Authority may give a notice under subrule (1) on the application of the firm or on the Authority's own initiative.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2019-7 (as from 1st January 2020).
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: (1) The Regulatory Authority may, by written notice, modify the calculation of an Islamic banking business firm's total exposure measure by, for example: (a) allowing the firm not to take account of a particular exposure or class of exposures; (b) directing the firm to apply a different risk-weight to an exposure or class of exposures; (c) directing the firm to take account of an exposure or class of exposures that would not otherwise be taken account of. (2) The Authority may give a notice under subrule (1) on the application of the firm or on the Authority's own initiative. Inserted by QFCRA RM/2019-7 (as from 1st January 2020).

endnotes: Inserted by QFCRA RM/2019-7 (as from 1st January 2020).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.4.9 How to calculate total exposure measure— assets financed by unrestricted PSIAs
doc_path: IBANK 3.4.9 How to calculate total exposure measure— assets financed by unrestricted PSIAs
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) When an Islamic banking business firm calculates its total exposure measure, it must include a proportion of assets (whether on or off the firm's balance-sheet) financed by unrestricted PSIAs.
(2) The proportion is to be calculated by multiplying the carrying value of the assets by the alpha parameter (100%) for capital adequacy purposes.
(3) Assets financed by restricted PSIAs are not to be included.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2019-7 (as from 1st January 2020).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 3.4.8 How to calculate total exposure measure — off-balance-sheet assets
doc_path: IBANK 3.4.8 How to calculate total exposure measure — off-balance-sheet assets
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) When an Islamic banking business firm calculates its total exposure measure, it must include all off-balance-sheet items (for example, letters of credit, guarantees, unconditionally cancellable commitments, liquidity facilities, and Shara'a-compliant repo and securities financing transactions).
(2) A 100% credit conversion factor applies to all off-balance-sheet items, except that a credit conversion factor of 10% applies to a commitment that can be unconditionally cancelled at any time without notice.
(3) Securitised assets that are de-recognised from the balance-sheet of the sponsor or originator are not to be taken into account.
Inserted by QFCRA RM/2019-7 (as from 1st January 2020).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK Part 4.1 General
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: IBANK Part 4.1 General

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.1.1 Introduction
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This Chapter sets out the requirements for an Islamic banking business firm’s credit risk management policy and practice (including credit risk assessments and the use of ratings from ECRAs) to implement the risk-based framework for capital adequacy and the early identification and management of problem assets.

(2) This Chapter also deals with the following means to determine regulatory capital and control or mitigate credit risk:

(a) the standardised approach for calculating the firm’s credit risk capital requirement;

Note The standardised approach was previously called the risk-weighted assets approach.
(b) CRM techniques;
(c) provisioning.
(3) To guard against abuses and to address conflicts of interest, this Chapter requires transactions with related parties to be at arm’s length.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.1.2 Meaning of credit risk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Credit risk is:

(a) the risk of default by a counterparty; and
(b) the risk that an asset will lose value because its credit quality has deteriorated.
 
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.1.2 Guidance
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Credit risk may result from exposures on or off the balance sheet, including financings and advances, investments, inter-bank lending, transactions in SCHIs, SFTs and trading activities. It can exist in both the trading book and the banking book.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.1.3 General requirements — management of credit risk and problem assets
doc_path: IBANK 4.1.3 General requirements — management of credit risk and problem assets
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must manage credit risk by adopting a prudent credit risk management policy that allows its credit risk to be identified, measured, evaluated, managed and controlled or mitigated.

(2) The policy must also provide for problem assets to be recognised, measured and reported. The policy must set out the factors that must be taken into account in identifying problem assets.

Note 1 For the full requirements as to the firm’s credit risk management policy, see Part 4.2.
Note 2 Additional risk management requirements apply to Islamic banking business firms’ exposures to central counterparties — see rules 4.6A.40 and 4.6A.41.
(3) Problem assets includes non-performing assets (see rule 4.7.10) and other assets for which there is reason to believe that the firm may not be able to collect the amounts due in full or in accordance with the assets’ terms.
(4) An Islamic banking business firm must ensure that it has an adequate understanding of the risk profile and characteristics of each of its counterparties, both at origination and regularly (at least annually) afterwards.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.1.4 Capital and credit risk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must have capital to cover credit risk. The necessary amount of capital is the firm’s credit risk capital requirement.

Guidance
1 The firm’s credit risk capital requirement is part of its risk-based capital requirement — see rule 3.2.5.
2 Under rule 3.2.3, an Islamic banking business firm must have, at all times, capital at least equal to its minimum capital requirement (defined in that rule). The firm’s minimum capital requirement cannot be lower than its risk-based capital requirement, of which the credit risk capital requirement is a major part. Therefore, the firm must know its credit risk capital requirement at all times.

(2) An Islamic banking business firm’s credit risk capital requirement is the sum of the following components:

(a) the total of the firm’s risk-weighted assets for each of the following:

(i) exposures in the banking book (except those mentioned in subparagraphs (ii) to (iv)), calculated using the standardised approach (see Divisions 4.4.B and 4.4.C);
(ii) unsettled transactions and failed trades, in both the banking book and the trading book (see Subdivision 4.4.B.12);
(iii) defaulted exposures, in both the banking book and the trading book (see Subdivision 4.4.B.13);
(iv) securitisation exposures in the banking book (see Part 10.4);
(b) the firm’s capital requirements for counterparty credit risk, for exposures in both the banking book and the trading book (see Part 4.6A).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: IBANK Part 4.2 Credit risk management

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.1 Principle 1: governing body’s responsibilities
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm’s governing body is responsible for approving and periodically (at least annually) reviewing the firm’s credit risk strategy and significant credit risk policies. The firm’s credit risk strategy must reflect the firm’s appetite for risk and the level of profit that the firm expects to achieve for incurring various credit risks.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.2 Principle 2: senior management’s responsibilities
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm’s senior management is responsible for implementing the credit risk strategy approved by the firm’s governing body and for developing policies and procedures for identifying, measuring, monitoring and controlling credit risk. The policies and procedures must address credit risk in all of the firm’s activities and at the level of both individual credits and the portfolio.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.2 Guidance
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Depending on the nature, scale and complexity of an Islamic banking business firm's credit risk, and how often it provides credit or incurs credit risk, the firm's credit risk management policy should include:

(a) how the firm defines and measures credit risk;
(b) the firm's business aims in incurring credit risk, including:
•   identifying the types and sources of credit risk that the firm will permit itself to be exposed to (and the limits on that exposure) and those that it will not
•   setting out the degree of diversification that the firm requires, the firm's tolerance for risk concentrations and the limits on exposures and concentrations
•   stating the risk-return trade-off that the firm is seeking to achieve;
(c) the kinds of credit to be offered, and ceilings, pricing, profitability, maximum maturities and ratios for each kind of credit;
(d) a ceiling for the total credit portfolio (in terms, for example, of loan-to-deposit ratio, undrawn commitment ratio, maximum amount or percentage of the firm's capital);
(e) portfolio limits for maximum gross exposures by region or country, by industry or sector, by category of counterparty (such as banks, non-bank financial entities and corporate counterparties), by product, by counterparty and by connected counterparties;
(f) limits, terms and conditions, approval and review procedures and records kept for lending to connected counterparties;
(g) types of collateral, loan-to-value ratios and criteria for accepting guarantees;
(h) the detailed limits for credit risk, and a credit risk structure, that:
•   takes into account all significant risk factors, including intra-group exposures
•   is commensurate with the scale and complexity of the firm's activities
•   is consistent with the firm's business aims, historical performance, and the amount of capital it is willing to risk;
(i) procedures for:
•   approving new products and activities that give rise to credit risk
•   regular risk position and performance reporting
•   approving and reporting exceptions to limits;
(j) allocating responsibilities for implementing the credit risk management policy and monitoring adherence to, and the effectiveness of, the policy; and
(k) the required information systems, staff and other resources.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.3 Principle 3: obligation to manage credit risk
doc_path: IBANK 4.2.3 Principle 3: obligation to manage credit risk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm must identify and manage the credit risk that is inherent in all of the firm’s products and activities. The firm must ensure that the risks of a product or activity new to it:

(a) are subject to adequate risk management procedures and controls before the product is introduced or the activity undertaken; and
(b) are approved in advance by the firm’s governing body or the governing body’s appropriate committee.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.3 Guidance
doc_path: IBANK 4.2.3 Principle 3: obligation to manage credit risk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
1 The level at which credit decisions are made should vary depending on the kind and amount of credit and the nature, scale and complexity of the firm's business. For some firms, a credit committee with formal terms of reference might be appropriate; for others, individuals with pre-assigned limits would do.
2 An Islamic banking business firm should ensure, through periodic independent audits, that the credit approval function is properly managed and that credit exposures comply with prudential standards and internal limits. The results of audits should be reported directly to the governing body, credit committee or senior management, as appropriate.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.4 Principle 4: sound credit-granting criteria
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm must operate within sound, well-defined credit-granting criteria. The criteria must clearly indicate the firm’s target market, a thorough understanding of the borrower or counterparty, the purpose and structure of the credit, and the source of its repayment.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.17 Credit risk management framework
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.1 Establishing appropriate credit risk environment
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm must implement a credit risk management framework that is appropriate to the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business. The framework must include:

(a) a credit risk appetite statement (see rule 4.2.18);
(b) a credit risk management strategy (see rule 4.2.19);
(c) clearly defined and documented roles, responsibilities and formal reporting structures to manage credit risk, and policies and procedures to support those roles, responsibilities and structures;
(d) a designated credit risk management function;
(e) a management information system that is adequate, both under normal circumstances and in periods of stress, to measure, assess and report on credit risk; and
(f) an independent review process to ensure that the framework is effective to identify, measure, evaluate, monitor, report, and control or mitigate credit risk.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.18 Credit risk appetite statement
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.1 Establishing appropriate credit risk environment
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must maintain an appropriate and well-documented credit risk appetite statement. The statement must set out:

(a) the degree of credit risk that the firm is prepared to accept (its credit risk appetite);
(b) the maximum level of credit risk that the firm is willing to operate within (its credit risk tolerance);
(c) the process for ensuring that the credit risk tolerance is set at an appropriate level;
(d) the process for monitoring compliance with the credit risk tolerance and for taking appropriate action if it is breached; and
(e) the timing and process for reviewing the credit risk appetite and tolerance.
(2) The firm need not have a separate credit risk appetite statement if the firm’s overall risk appetite statement (required by CTRL, rule 7.1.6) includes a credit risk appetite statement that complies with subrule (1).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.19 Credit risk management strategy
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.1 Establishing appropriate credit risk environment
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must maintain an appropriate and well-documented credit risk management strategy that describes the objectives guiding the firm’s credit origination, credit assessment and approval activities and adopts the necessary policies and processes for conducting those activities.
(2) The strategy must reflect the firm’s credit risk appetite, credit risk profile and the market and macroeconomic conditions.
(3) The strategy must describe the firm’s willingness to accept credit risk based on exposure type, economic or industry sector, geographical location, currency and maturity, and must include the overall characteristics that the firm wants to achieve in its credit portfolio.
(4) The strategy must take into account the sustainability of earnings from the firm’s credit risk activities, including an acceptable risk/reward trade-off that takes into account estimates of the cost of capital.
(5) The firm need not have a separate credit risk management strategy document if the document that sets out the firm’s overall risk management strategy (required by CTRL, rule 7.1.7) includes a statement of the firm’s credit risk management strategy that complies with subrules (1) to (4).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.20 Role of governing body in credit risk management
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.1 Establishing appropriate credit risk environment
IBANK 4.2.20 Role of governing body in credit risk management
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm’s governing body must review and approve the firm’s credit risk appetite and credit risk management strategy. The governing body must do so at least annually.
(2) The governing body must regularly challenge, and seek assurance and evidence from, the firm’s senior management that the firm’s credit risk policies, processes and practices are consistent with its credit risk appetite and credit risk management strategy.
(3) The governing body must obtain sufficient information to find out whether the firm’s credit risk profile is consistent with the firm’s credit risk management strategy or not, and if it is not must require the firm’s senior management to take appropriate and timely action.
(4) The governing body must ensure that the firm’s senior management has the capability and resources to manage the firm’s credit risk activities appropriately, and that such activities operate within the firm’s credit risk appetite, credit risk management strategy and credit risk policies.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.21 Role of senior management in credit risk management
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.1 Establishing appropriate credit risk environment
IBANK 4.2.21 Role of senior management in credit risk management
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm’s senior management is responsible for implementing the credit risk management strategy approved by the firm’s governing body and for developing and implementing appropriate policies and processes to identify, measure, monitor, report and control or mitigate credit risk.
(2) The policies and processes must address credit risk in all of the firm’s activities and at the level of both individual exposures and the portfolio.

(3) The senior management’s responsibility for implementing the credit risk management strategy and developing and implementing the firm’s credit risk policies includes ensuring:

(a) that the firm’s credit origination, credit assessment and approval activities conform to the strategy and policies;
(b) that written processes are developed that are consistent with the strategy and policies;
(c) that responsibilities for credit origination, credit assessment and credit approval and review are clearly and properly assigned;
(d) that the strategy, policies and processes are effectively communicated throughout the firm;

(e) that all the relevant personnel:

(i) clearly understand the firm’s approach to originating, assessing, approving and managing credit risk; and
(ii) are held accountable for complying with the policies and processes; and
(f) that there is a regular independent internal review of the firm’s credit origination, credit assessment, credit approval and credit management functions.
(4) The reviews required by paragraph (3) (f) must be carried out independently from the business function concerned — for example, by the firm’s independent risk management and compliance function, or an independent internal audit function or qualified external party.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.22 Credit risk policies and processes
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.1 Establishing appropriate credit risk environment
IBANK 4.2.22 Credit risk policies and processes
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must implement prudent and well-documented policies and processes to identify, measure, monitor, report and control or mitigate credit risk. The full credit life-cycle must be considered, including credit origination, the initial and subsequent credit assessment and approval processes and the continuing monitoring and management of the firm’s credit exposures and portfolio.
(2) The policies must address target markets, portfolio mix, price and non-price terms, the structure of limits, approval authorities and overrides, the processing of waivers or exceptions, and reporting.
(3) The policies must be well-documented, clearly defined, consistent with prudent practices and applicable laws and regulations, and adequate for the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s activities.
(4) The firm must implement the policies within the context of the relevant internal and external factors such as the firm’s market position, personnel capabilities and technology.
(5) The firm must have appropriate operational capacity and business systems to support the credit risk management strategy before the strategy is implemented.
(6) The firm must have prudent and well-documented policies and processes for the early identification and management of problem exposures, including non-performing and forborne exposures and other transactions, and the maintenance of adequate provisions.
(7) The firm must have appropriate credit risk practices, including an effective system of internal control, to consistently determine adequate provisions in accordance with the firm’s stated policies and processes and the applicable accounting standard.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.23 Internal risk appetite limits
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.1 Establishing appropriate credit risk environment
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must implement appropriate policies and processes to ensure that its credit portfolio is adequately diversified, given the firm’s target markets and credit risk management strategy.

(2) In particular, the policies must establish targets for the firm’s portfolio mix and must set prudent limits on the firm’s exposures to:

(a) higher-risk borrowers;
(b) higher-risk credit products and activities; and
(c) particular industry sectors and geographical locations.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.24 Country and transfer risk
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.1 Establishing appropriate credit risk environment
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm that originates credit exposures in geographical locations other than Qatar must have prudent policies and processes for identifying, evaluating, measuring, monitoring, reporting and controlling or mitigating country risk and transfer risk.

Guidance
Country risk or sovereign risk covers all the risks arising from the economic, political and social environments of a foreign country that may have potential consequences for foreigners’ debt and equity investments in that country. Transfer risk focuses more specifically on a borrower’s capacity to obtain the foreign exchange necessary to service its cross-border debt and other contractual obligations.

(2) The monitoring of country risk factors must take into account:

(a) the potential for default by foreign borrowers because of country-specific economic factors; and
(b) the enforceability of agreements, including the timing and ability to realise collateral under the relevant legal framework.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.25 Credit assessment and approval process
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.2 Operating under sound credit granting process
IBANK 4.2.25 Credit assessment and approval process
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must establish sound credit assessment and approval criteria. The criteria must set out:

(a) the borrowers that are eligible for credit;
(b) the extent and nature of credit that the firm is willing to provide; and
(c) the terms and conditions that the exposures would be subject to.
(2) The firm must undertake a comprehensive assessment of a borrower’s credit risk that considers, and is proportionate to, the nature, type and size of the exposure. The firm must use experienced credit judgement in adopting a scalable and flexible approach to its assessment of a borrower’s credit risk.
(3) The firm must assess credit risk primarily on the strength of a borrower’s capacity to repay. The firm must not rely unduly on collateral instead of comprehensive credit assessment.
(4) The firm must not rely unduly on external credit ratings. The firm must obtain adequate information about a borrower to undertake a comprehensive credit assessment.
(5) The firm must properly consider a borrower’s integrity and reputation and its legal capacity to assume liability.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.26 Credit assessment — exposures to individuals
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.2 Operating under sound credit granting process
IBANK 4.2.26 Credit assessment — exposures to individuals
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For an exposure to an individual, an Islamic banking business firm’s credit assessment must consider the following matters, so far as relevant:

(a) the purpose and structure of the exposure;
(b) the borrower’s sources of repayment;
(c) the borrower’s current risk profile;
(d) the borrower’s expenses;

(e) the borrower’s repayment history and capacity, assessed under various scenarios such as:

(i) an increase in profit rates;
(ii) a change from a fixed profit rate to a floating profit rate (or vice versa);
(iii) a decrease in the borrower’s income or cash flows, particularly for less stable sources of income or cash flow; and
(iv) for an exposure with a profit-only period that subsequently reverts to principal and profit payments —a principal and profit basis of repayment;
(f) the proposed terms and conditions of the exposure, including covenants designed to limit to an acceptable level the firm’s exposure to changes in the borrower’s risk profile;
(g) if applicable, the adequacy and enforceability of collateral, guarantees and other risk mitigants, under various scenarios.

(2) For paragraphs (1) (b) to (e), the firm must make reasonable inquiries about, and must take reasonable steps to verify:

(a) the borrower’s sources of repayment; and
(b) the borrower’s commitments and total indebtedness.

(3) For paragraph (1) (d), the firm:

(a) must collect reasonable estimates of the borrower’s expenses; and
(b) must not use expense benchmarks as a substitute for reasonable enquiries about the borrower’s expenses.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.27 Credit assessment — exposures other than to individuals
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.2 Operating under sound credit granting process
IBANK 4.2.27 Credit assessment — exposures other than to individuals
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For an exposure other than to an individual, an Islamic banking business firm’s credit assessment must include consideration of the following matters, if relevant:

(a) the purpose and structure of the exposure;
(b) the borrower’s sources of repayment;
(c) the borrower’s current risk profile;

(d) the borrower’s repayment history and capacity, assessed under various scenarios such as:

(i) an increase in profit rates;
(ii) a change from a fixed profit rate to a floating profit rate (or vice versa);
(iii) a decrease in income or cash flows, particularly for less stable sources of income or cash flow; and
(iv) for an exposure with a profit-only period that subsequently reverts to principal and profit payments —a principal and profit basis of repayment;
(e) the proposed terms and conditions of the exposure (including covenants designed to limit to an acceptable level the firm’s exposure to changes in the borrower’s risk profile);
(f) if applicable, the adequacy and enforceability of collateral, guarantees and other risk mitigants, under various scenarios;
(g) the borrower’s business expertise, its economic or industry sector and its position within that sector;
(h) the borrower’s historical financial and future cash flows;
(i) the borrower’s equity capital invested in the business;
(j) the availability and enforceability of risk mitigants other than collateral, such as hedging and takaful.

(2) For paragraphs (1) (b) and (c), the firm must make reasonable inquiries about, and must take reasonable steps to verify:

(a) the borrower’s sources of repayment, income and cash flows; and
(b) the borrower’s commitments and total indebtedness.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.28 Collateral and guarantees
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.2 Operating under sound credit granting process
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must have prudent credit risk policies covering:

(a) the acceptability of various forms of collateral;
(b) appropriate processes for valuing collateral (including valuing before entering into an exposure and the continuing valuing of collateral, if appropriate); and
(c) an appropriate process to ensure that collateral is, and continues to be, enforceable and realisable.
(2) The firm must ensure that all valuations are appraised independently of the firm’s credit origination, assessment and approval process.
(3) The valuation of collateral must reflect fair values, taking into account market conditions such as the time taken to liquidate or realise collateral.
(4) The firm must ensure that the valuation of collateral such as land takes into account, so far as possible, the likelihood of external events that may affect the valuation of the asset taken as collateral.
(5) The firm must have appropriate mechanisms for regularly assessing the value of collateral, guarantees and other risk mitigants.
(6) The firm must establish appropriate limits on FTV ratio to minimise the risk that an asset that has been taken as collateral will be insufficient to cover any repayment shortfall. The firm must ensure that there is appropriate scrutiny of any instances of lending with a high FTV ratio.
(7) In relation to guarantees, the firm must appropriately evaluate the level of coverage that is provided in relation to the credit quality of the guarantor and the legal enforceability of the guarantee. For exposures to individuals in particular, the firm must ensure that a guarantor clearly understands the risks involved.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.29 Credit approval and experienced credit judgement
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.2 Operating under sound credit granting process
IBANK 4.2.29 Credit approval and experienced credit judgement
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must have a clearly established process for:

(a) approving new exposures (including prudent credit standards);
(b) renewing and refinancing existing exposures; and
(c) identifying the appropriate approval authority for an exposure of a particular size and complexity.
(2) The firm must document the credit assessment and approval process and must identify the approval authority for each exposure, so that it is clear which individual is accountable for each credit decision.
(3) The firm must ensure that personnel involved in the credit assessment and approval process have appropriate experience and knowledge to exercise prudent credit judgement commensurate with the nature, scale and complexity of the relevant transaction.

(4) The firm must have prudent credit risk policies and processes in relation to overrides or waivers of, and exceptions to, the firm’s credit risk policies. The policies and processes must provide:

(a) clear identification of approval authorities; and
(b) limits to the maximum level of allowable overrides, waivers or exceptions.
(5) There must be regular reports to the firm’s relevant internal governance bodies and review functions about exposures that originated as overrides or waivers of, or exceptions to, the firm’s credit risk policies, or were otherwise not in compliance with those policies.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.30 Credit administration, measurement and monitoring
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.3 Maintaining appropriate credit administration, measurement and monitoring process
IBANK 4.2.30 Credit administration, measurement and monitoring
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must have an appropriate system to administer its credit portfolio.

(2) The system must take into account:

(a) the efficiency and effectiveness of the firm’s credit administration, including its monitoring of documentation, contractual requirements, covenants and collateral;
(b) the accuracy and timeliness of the information provided to the firm’s management information systems;
(c) the adequate segregation of duties;
(d) the adequacy of controls over all of the firm’s credit administration processes; and
(e) compliance with the firm’s credit risk policies and processes, and with applicable laws and regulations.
(3) The firm must ensure that its credit administration system captures all the information necessary to ascertain a borrower’s current financial condition, and sufficient information to track all credit decisions made and the history of each exposure. The firm’s credit risk review function must determine that credit administration is complete and that all approvals and other necessary documents have been obtained.
(4) The firm must have an appropriate system to monitor the condition of individual exposures, including determining whether the relevant credit loss provisions are sufficient.
(5) The firm must have an appropriate system to monitor the overall composition and quality of the firm’s credit portfolio.
(6) The firm must have an appropriate information system and analytical techniques that enable the firm’s management to measure the credit risk inherent in all of its activities on and off the firm’s balance sheet. The system must provide adequate information on the composition of the firm’s credit portfolio, including identifying any concentrations of risk.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.31 Credit risk grading systems
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.3 Maintaining appropriate credit administration, measurement and monitoring process
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must have an internal credit risk grading system that is appropriate for the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s operations.
(2) The firm must have prudent policies and processes governing the development, validation, operation and oversight of its credit risk grading system.
(3) The credit risk grading system must extend to as much of the firm’s credit portfolio as possible, including off-balance-sheet exposures.
(4) The system must meaningfully assess and differentiate risk and must be able to rank risk consistently and through time. A sufficient number of risk grades must be included to ensure that the system adequately captures gradation of risk.
(5) The definitions and criteria for each risk grade must be plausible and intuitive.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.32 Stress testing
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.3 Maintaining appropriate credit administration, measurement and monitoring process
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must take into consideration potential future changes in economic conditions when assessing individual exposures and its credit portfolio, and must assess its credit risk exposures under stressed conditions.
(2) The firm must undertake regular portfolio-level and risk-specific stress testing of its credit exposures.
(3) The complexity and granularity of the firm’s stress testing must take into account the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s credit portfolio. The firm must carry out stress testing at a sufficiently granular level to be adequately sensitive to the risk characteristics of different types of exposures.
(4) The scenarios used for stress testing must include severe but plausible adverse conditions.
(5) The firm must consider the results of stress testing in its overall limit-setting and monitoring process.
(6) Stress testing analyses must include contingency plans for actions that the firm’s governing body and senior management may take in particular scenarios.
(7) The stress testing arrangements must include well-documented and sound policies and processes governing the stress testing programme. The arrangements must provide for the timely communication of information to the firm’s governing body and senior management about scenarios, key assumptions, results and capital effects.
(8) Stress testing models must be appropriately validated and checked independently or by an appropriately qualified external party.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.33 Controls over credit risk
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.4 Ensuring adequate controls over credit risk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must establish a system of independent, regular reviews of the firm’s credit risk management processes and practices. The results of a review must be communicated directly to the firm’s governing body and senior management.
(2) The firm must ensure that the credit origination, credit assessment and approval function is properly managed and that credit exposures are within levels consistent with the firm’s limits. The firm must establish and enforce internal controls and other practices to ensure that overrides, waivers or exceptions to policies, processes and limits are reported in a timely manner to the appropriate level of management for action.
(3) The firm must have an appropriate system for early remedial action on problem exposures, managing problem exposures and similar workout situations. The firm’s collections systems must bring together a borrower’s arrears profile and must be able to be scaled to manage high volumes in a time of stress.
(4) The firm must have an effective workout programme for problem exposures, and the workout function must be separate from the function that originated the exposures. The firm must have an effective strategy and appropriate organisational resources and personnel to manage problem exposures.
(5) The firm must have prudent policies and processes that assist the firm to recover as much of an exposure as is reasonably possible within the requirements established by applicable law and also having regard to community expectations as to how borrowers are to be treated. The firm must consider the risk to its reputation in such circumstances.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.34 Classification of exposures and provisions
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.4 Ensuring adequate controls over credit risk
IBANK 4.2.34 Classification of exposures and provisions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must have prudent policies and processes to classify its credit risk exposures for prudential reporting purposes and to establish appropriate and robust provisioning levels. The system must take into account exposures both on and off the firm’s balance sheet.
(2) The firm must classify its credit risk exposures as performing or non-performing, and must have adequate documentation to support its classification of exposures and its provisioning levels. The firm must also classify its exposures when payments are past-due for a minimum number of days (for example, 30, 60 and 90 days).
(3) The firm must regularly review its exposures at individual or portfolio level to ensure that exposures are appropriately classified, appropriate provisioning levels are set and appropriate write-offs are applied.
(4) The firm must have sound policies and processes to ensure that provisions and write-offs are timely and reflect realistic expectations as to repayment and recovery, taking into account market and macroeconomic conditions.

(5) The firm’s governing body must obtain timely and appropriate information on the condition of the firm’s credit portfolio, including the classification of exposures as performing and non-performing and the level of provisions. The information must include:

(a) the results of the latest credit risk review process;
(b) comparative trends in the overall quality of exposures; and

(c) measurements of:

(i) deterioration or expected deterioration in asset quality; and
(ii) expected credit losses.
(6) The firm must ensure that valuation, classification and provisioning for material non-performing exposures are done on an individual exposure basis.
(7) The firm must regularly assess any trends and concentrations in risk and risk build-up in relation to credit exposures, and must take into account any observed concentration in the risk mitigation strategies adopted and the potential effect on the efficacy of the mitigant in reducing loss. The firm must consider the adequacy of provisions in the light of that assessment.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.35 Regulatory Authority may set supervisory limits
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.4 Ensuring adequate controls over credit risk
IBANK 4.2.35 Regulatory Authority may set supervisory limits
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If the Regulatory Authority considers that an Islamic banking business firm is taking excessive credit risk relative to its financial or operational capacity to manage or absorb that risk, the Authority:

(a) may set limits on particular exposures or categories of exposures that the firm may hold (including limits on growth or limits on the share of the firm's portfolio); or
(b) may direct the firm to cease a particular type of lending or credit activity.
(2) If the Authority considers that there is an excessive level of, or excessive growth in, higher-risk lending or credit activity, the Authority may set limits, by notice published on an approved website, on particular types of lending, the share of lending, or the growth rate of lending, for all Islamic banking business firms or a specified class of such firms.
(3) In considering whether there is an excessive level of, or excessive growth in, higher-risk lending or credit activity, the Authority will take into account any easing of credit standards and practices and the proportion of Islamic business firms’ higher-risk lending, including whether the lending is high-leverage, high-FTV-ratio or profit-only.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.36 Directions about adequacy of credit risk management and provisions
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.4 Ensuring adequate controls over credit risk
IBANK 4.2.36 Directions about adequacy of credit risk management and provisions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If the Regulatory Authority considers that an Islamic banking business firm’s policies, processes and practices across its credit risk activities do not meet the requirements of this Division, or that the firm’s credit risk management is otherwise deficient, the Authority may direct the firm:

(a) to amend its credit risk management policies, processes, and practices;
(b) to adopt appropriate credit risk management policies, processes and practices;
(c) to increase its levels of provisions or write-offs; or
(d) to increase its regulatory capital.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: If the Regulatory Authority considers that an Islamic banking business firm’s policies, processes and practices across its credit risk activities do not meet the requirements of this Division, or that the firm’s credit risk management is otherwise deficient, the Authority may direct the firm: (a) to amend its credit risk management policies, processes, and practices; (b) to adopt appropriate credit risk management policies, processes and practices; (c) to increase its levels of provisions or write-offs; or (d) to increase its regulatory capital. Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.37 Direction about independent review etc
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.2.B.4 Ensuring adequate controls over credit risk
IBANK 4.2.37 Direction about independent review etc
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The Regulatory Authority may direct an Islamic banking business firm to appoint an independent person to review the firm’s credit risk management (including the firm’s provisioning practices) or a particular aspect of it, and report to the Authority. The Authority may direct the firm to carry out such a review without first consulting the firm.
(2) The Authority may set the terms of the review and may direct the firm to meet the cost of it.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK Division 4.2.C Management of collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: IBANK Division 4.2.C Management of collateral

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK Division 4.2.C Guidance
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Collateral can include guarantees, takaful arrangements and, importantly, security held over various forms of assets. This Division applies to all forms of collateral, including all types of assets taken as security.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

This Division applies to all forms of collateral, including all types of assets taken as security. Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.38 Identification and documentation of collateral
doc_path: IBANK 4.2.38 Identification and documentation of collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must ensure that an asset that is to be taken as security is accurately identified and documented.

(2) The firm must ensure that the relevant legal requirements are met to maintain and enforce the firm’s security position. The firm must confirm that:

(a) the borrower has, or will have when the exposure is extended, clear title to the asset;
(b) the characteristics of the collateral are as they have been represented; and
(c) if appropriate, an asset serving as collateral is appropriately insured at the time of origination and the takaful is maintained under the contractual terms of the exposure.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.39 Valuation of collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must obtain a valuation of the security for an exposure:

(a) before the financing is drawn down; and
(b) if appropriate, on a continuing basis.

(2) If the fair value of a security is based on observable market prices, the firm’s policies and processes must have regard to:

(a) when observable market prices would be used;
(b) the basis for selecting the market prices to be used;
(c) the effect of market liquidity on the pricing of assets and the timing of their disposal; and
(d) the costs of accessing and disposing of assets held as collateral.
(3) In determining the fair value of a security, an Islamic banking business firm may use a valuation by a suitably qualified internal appraiser or by an external valuer, or an alternative valuation method. The firm’s policies and processes covering the fair value of a security must address the circumstances in which such valuations would be sought.

(4) If the firm uses valuations from internal appraisers, it must have policies and processes that address:

(a) when valuations should be provided by internal appraisers to remove the potential for real or perceived conflicts of interests that might affect the valuations; and
(b) the qualifications and experience required of internal appraisers.

(5) If the firm relies on external expertise for security valuations, it must establish robust selection and review mechanisms. Factors that must be considered in the selection process include:

(a) the professional qualifications to be required;
(b) relevant experience, including local knowledge;
(c) breadth of expertise to cover both standard and specialised security assessments; and
(d) appropriate professional takaful cover.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.40 Valuation of collateral — use of alternative methods
doc_path: IBANK 4.2.40 Valuation of collateral — use of alternative methods
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an Islamic banking business firm relies on the use of alternative valuation methods (such as desktop assessments, kerbside assessments and automated valuation methods) to produce a security valuation, it must have appropriate policies and processes that address:

(a) when valuations would be provided by the alternative method;
(b) monitoring, validation and reporting of valuation data; and
(c) asset values including adequate haircuts for conservatism when using automated valuation methods.

(2) An Islamic banking business firm that is considering the use of alternative valuation methods must thoroughly analyse any such proposal and must develop a risk management capability that includes:

(a) a hierarchy of acceptable methods of determining value that is appropriate to the level of risk;
(b) analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of the approaches or models being considered, including an understanding of the methods used, the sources of data employed and how a service provider might be able to assist in re-engineering the firm’s processes;
(c) details of any back-testing of a statistically random sample of alternative methods or auditing arrangements undertaken by a service provider;
(d) clarity of the output to be provided and how it would be integrated with the firm’s processes; and
(e) continuing monitoring of the tools used, processes that capture evidence of action taken when values are considered to be unreliable and periodic back-testing undertaken by the firm to independently validate the reliability of outcomes.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.41 Valuation of collateral — instructions to valuers etc
doc_path: IBANK 4.2.41 Valuation of collateral — instructions to valuers etc
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm’s policies and procedures must include procedures for giving instructions for the conduct of valuations.

(2) Each valuation request must be the subject of specific instructions to the appraiser or valuer. These instructions must cover (as relevant in each case) appropriate issues such as:

(a) the purpose of the valuation;
(b) the valuation basis required;
(c) whether the valuation is for takaful purposes;
(d) the valuation method;
(e) whether a market summary or commentary is required; and
(f) the form of report that is to be provided.

(3) If a party other than the firm instructs the valuer:

(a) the valuation must be appropriately endorsed for the firm’s use; and

(b) the valuation must be confirmed by:

(i) an internal appraiser; or
(ii) an external valuer with the appropriate expertise.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.42 Valuation of collateral — use of panels of valuers etc
doc_path: IBANK 4.2.42 Valuation of collateral — use of panels of valuers etc
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If an Islamic banking business firm relies on a panel of approved valuation professionals, the firm’s credit risk management policy must provide for the firm to review the panel regularly (at least annually).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.43 Valuation of collateral — professional standards
doc_path: IBANK 4.2.43 Valuation of collateral — professional standards
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If an Islamic banking business firm uses valuations to determine the fair value of collateral, the firm must require valuers and appraisers, in preparing their reports, to adopt the standards and practices of a relevant professional body. Reports must be based on the standard format advocated by a relevant professional body.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.44 Valuation of collateral — reliability of processes
doc_path: IBANK 4.2.44 Valuation of collateral — reliability of processes
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm must have policies and processes directed at ensuring that the valuation processes and valuations received for collateral are reliable. There must be independent and regular internal reviews of valuations and the results of automated valuation methods by appropriate management or audit personnel and formal reviews by an independent valuer.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.45 Valuation of collateral — regular reassessment
doc_path: IBANK 4.2.45 Valuation of collateral — regular reassessment
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm’s policies and processes must provide for regular assessment of collateral values so as to ensure that the fair value of collateral that supports provisioning and reserves, and any collateral coverage measures applied to exposures, is kept current and reliably reflects the values that the firm might realise.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.45 Guidance
doc_path: IBANK 4.2.45 Valuation of collateral — regular reassessment
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
This is especially important for exposures that are secured by assets that are susceptible to significant changes in value, or if the margin for diminution in the value of the security is small.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.46 Valuation of real estate as security
doc_path: IBANK 4.2.46 Valuation of real estate as security
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For the purposes of determining the fair value of security involving real estate, an Islamic banking business firm must assume that:

(a) the relevant property is accessible in the near future;
(b) the period for marketing the property will be up to 12 months (but the firm may adopt a period of up to 24 months for a specialised or unusual property if a professional valuer advises that it would be appropriate to do so); and
(c) market conditions and asset values will not change during the marketing period.
(2) The marketing period must be treated as retrospective and must be assumed to have ended at the date of valuation, rather than taking into account any improvement in market conditions.
(3) The valuation of real estate must be based on fair values. In determining fair values, the firm must use conservative estimates in imputing future income streams, such as lease payments that are not already contracted for.
(4) The firm must ensure that the key assumptions used in the valuation approach are appropriate and that there is sufficient evidence to support them. The firm must review the assumptions and must be satisfied that they are reasonable before the valuation is done.
(5) In determining fair values, a valuation that is based on highest and best use rather than existing use must be adequately supported and documented. If applicable, the valuation report must set out how highest and best use was determined.
(6) In circumstances in which it is difficult to determine the fair value of a property that has not yet achieved a stable income, or that is experiencing fluctuations in income, a forecast of expected cash flows must be used to estimate the value of the property.
(7) The discount rates used in calculating the value of security must reflect the opportunity cost of holding the property, determined by way of comparison with prevailing returns on competing investments, and assuming a long-term holding. Capitalisation rates must reflect expectations about the long-term rate of return that investors require under normal, orderly and sustainable market conditions.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.2.47 Valuation of security in other forms
doc_path: IBANK 4.2.47 Valuation of security in other forms
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For collateral in the form of a security interest over assets other than real estate, an Islamic banking business firm must ensure that all relevant security is properly scrutinised.
(2) If a third party supplies information about a security interest held by the firm, asset values must be objectively assessed to ensure that security coverage is adequate. The assessment may include testing the information supplied.
(3) In determining the fair value of security not in the form of real estate, the firm must also take into account market liquidity, legal costs, impediments to realisation and prior charges.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
