QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK Part 4.3 Credit ratings
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: IBANK Part 4.3 Credit ratings

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.3.1 Meaning of ECRA
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
In these rules:

ECRA (or external credit rating agency) means any of the following:

(a) Standard and Poor’s;
(b) Moody’s Investors Service;
(c) Fitch Ratings;
(d) a rating agency that is affiliated with an agency mentioned in paragraph (a), (b) or (c);
(e) Capital Intelligence Ratings Limited;
(f) any other agency approved by the Regulatory Authority.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.3.1 Guidance
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
1 Credit risk assessment under this Part is different from the evaluation (often called credit assessment) made by a firm as part of its credit approval process.
2 Credit assessment is part of the firm's internal commercial decision-making for approving or refusing credit; it consists of the evaluation of a prospective counterparty's repayment ability. In contrast, credit risk assessment is carried out by the firm (using ratings and risk-weights set out in these rules) as part of calculating its credit risk capital requirement.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.3.2 Criteria for approval as ECRA
doc_path: IBANK 4.3.2 Criteria for approval as ECRA
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
For a credit rating agency to be approved by the Regulatory Authority as an ECRA, the agency must meet the criteria in:

(a) the Revised capital adequacy standard for institutions offering Islamic financial services [Banking Segment], section 4.1.4, published by the IFSB in December 2021; and
(b) the guidance note in connection with that standard, “Recognition of ratings by external credit assessment institutions on Shari’a-compliant Financial Instruments”, published by the IFSB in March 2008.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

doc_path: IBANK 4.3.2 Criteria for approval as ECRA

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.3.3 Meaning of rating etc for Chapter 4
doc_path: IBANK 4.3.3 Meaning of rating etc for Chapter 4
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) In this Chapter:

rating means a rating issued by an ECRA.
Guidance
For this Chapter, an instrument or counterparty is rated only if an ECRA has issued a rating of it. If no ECRA has issued a rating of an instrument or a counterparty, the instrument or counterparty is unrated.

(2) A rating is a solicited rating if the rating was requested and paid for by the issuer of the rated instrument, the rated counterparty or another entity in the same corporate group as the issuer or counterparty. Any other rating is an unsolicited rating.

Note Unsolicited ratings are not to be used without the Regulatory Authority’s consent — see rule 4.3.5.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.3.4 Using ratings
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must use ratings consistently and in accordance with these rules and its credit risk management policy.
(2) The firm must ensure that a rating of an instrument takes into account the total amount of the relevant exposure (that is, the financing and any profit due).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.3.5 Only solicited ratings to be used
doc_path: IBANK 4.3.5 Only solicited ratings to be used
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Subject to subrule (2), an Islamic banking business firm must use only a solicited rating in determining risk weights for the firm’s exposures.
(2) An Islamic banking business firm may use an unsolicited rating with the written approval of the Regulatory Authority or in accordance with a direction by the Authority. The Authority may give a written direction setting out conditions that must be satisfied before the firm may use an unsolicited rating.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.3.6 Multiple ratings for same exposure etc
doc_path: IBANK 4.3.6 Multiple ratings for same exposure etc
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If there is only 1 rating for a particular exposure, that rating must be used to assign a risk weight to the exposure.
(2) If there are 2 ratings and the ratings map to different risk weights, the higher risk weight must be applied.

(3) If there are 3 or more ratings for an exposure, and those ratings map to different risk weights, only the ratings that map to the 2 lowest risk weights may be taken into account, and:

(a) the higher of those 2 risk weights must be applied; or
(b) if both ratings map to the same risk weight, that risk weight must be applied.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.3.7 Choosing between issuer ratings and issue ratings
doc_path: IBANK 4.3.7 Choosing between issuer ratings and issue ratings
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an issue to which an Islamic banking business firm is exposed has an issue-specific rating, the firm must use that rating to assign a risk weight to the exposure.
(2) For an exposure to an issue that does not have an issue-specific rating, the firm must assign a risk weight to it as set out in subrules (3) to (5).
(3) If an issuer has a specific rating for an issue, but the firm’s exposure to the issuer is not to that issue, the firm may assign to its exposure a risk weight lower than that for an unrated exposure only if the firm’s claim on the issuer ranks equally with, or is senior to, the rated issue. Otherwise the firm must treat the exposure as unrated.

(4) If the firm’s exposure is to an unrated issue by the issuer and:

(a) either the issuer, or another issue by it, has a low-quality rating (that is, a rating that would map into a risk weight equal to or higher than that for an unrated exposure); and
(b) the issue to which the firm is exposed ranks equally with, or is junior to, either a senior unsecured claim on the issuer or the issue with a low-quality rating;
the firm must assign the same risk weight to the unrated exposure as it would to the issue with the low-quality rating.
Guidance
If the issuer has an issuer rating, that rating typically applies to senior unsecured claims on that issuer. Consequently, only senior claims on that issuer benefit from a high-quality issuer rating. Other unassessed exposures of a highly rated issuer are treated as unrated.
(5) If an issuer has a specific high-quality rating (that is, a rating that would map to a lower risk weight) that applies only to a limited class of its liabilities (such as a deposit assessment or a counterparty risk assessment), the firm may use that rating only for exposures to the issuer that fall within that class.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

doc_path: IBANK 4.3.7 Choosing between issuer ratings and issue ratings

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.3.9 Using foreign currency and domestic currency ratings of similar exposures to same counterparty
doc_path: IBANK 4.3.9 Using foreign currency and domestic currency ratings of similar exposures to same counterparty
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an Islamic banking business firm proposes to assign a risk weight to an unrated exposure based on the rating of a rated (but otherwise similar) exposure to the same counterparty, it may do so if either of the following paragraphs is true:

(a) the rating is a domestic-currency rating and the rated exposure is denominated in the counterparty’s domestic currency;
(b) the rating is a foreign-currency rating and the rated exposure is denominated in a foreign currency.
(2) Subrule (3) applies to an exposure that arises through an Islamic banking business firm’s participation in a financing that has been extended, or has been guaranteed against convertibility and transfer risk, by an MDB, if an exposure to the MDB is to be assigned a risk weight of 0% under rule 4.4.16.
(3) For an exposure to which this subrule applies, the borrower’s domestic currency rating may be used to assign a risk weight to the exposure instead of its foreign currency rating. In the case of a guarantee against convertibility and transfer risk, the local currency rating may be used only for the part that has been guaranteed, and the remainder that does not benefit from the guarantee must be assigned a risk weight based on the borrower’s foreign currency rating.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.3.10 Using short-term ratings
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm may use a short-term rating to assign a risk weight only to a short-term bank exposure or short-term corporate exposure.
(2) For risk-weighting purposes, an Islamic banking business firm must treat a short-term rating as being issue-specific. The firm may use a short-term rating to assign a risk weight only to an exposure arising from the rated facility, and must not apply it to any other short-term exposure.
(3) An Islamic banking business firm must not use a short-term rating to assign a risk weight to an unrated long-term exposure.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.3.11 Using Foreign Currency and Domestic Currency Ratings
doc_path: IBANK 4.3.11 Using Foreign Currency and Domestic Currency Ratings
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If an issuer rating is assigned to a counterparty and an Islamic banking business firm applies a risk-weight to an unrated position based on the rating of an equivalent exposure to the same counterparty:

(a) the firm must use that counterparty's domestic-currency rating for any exposure denominated in the currency of the counterparty's place of residence or incorporation; and
(b) the firm must use that counterparty's foreign-currency rating for any exposure denominated in a foreign currency.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.3.12 Using Short-Term Ratings
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) A short-term credit risk rating must be used only for short-term claims relating to banks and corporations (such as those arising from the issuance of commercial paper). The rating is taken to be issue-specific and must be used only to assign risk-weights for claims arising from a rated facility.
(2) If a short-term rated exposure is assigned a risk-weight of 50%, an unrated short-term exposure to the same counterparty cannot be assigned a risk-weight lower than 100%.
(3) If a short-term facility of an issuer is assigned a risk-weight of 150% based on the facility's credit risk rating, all unrated claims of the issuer (whether long-term or short-term) must be assigned a risk-weight of 150%.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.1 Guidance
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK 4.4.1 What Part 4.4 does — calculation of risk-weighted assets for credit risk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
1 An Islamic banking business firm’s credit risk capital requirement is the sum of:

• its risk-weighted assets for credit risk, as calculated in accordance with this Part (but subject to any capital relief that is available under Part 4.6)
• its risk-weighted assets for securitisation exposures in the banking book (see Part 10.4).

2 For how to calculate the firm’s credit risk capital requirement, see rule 4.1.4. The following components of the credit risk capital requirement are calculated in accordance with this Part:

• RWA for exposures in the banking book (except those mentioned in the next point)
• RWA for the risk posed by unsettled transactions and failed trades, in both the banking book and the trading book.
3 The firm’s RWA for counterparty credit risk for exposures in both the banking book and the trading book also forms part of its credit risk capital requirement. This is dealt with in Part 4.6A.
4 The sum of an Islamic banking business firm’s risk-weighted assets for credit risk, used for calculating its credit risk capital requirement, is not the same as its total risk-weighted assets (see rule 3.2.1), which is used for calculating the firm’s capital adequacy ratios under Chapter 3.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.3 Risk weights to be assigned
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK 4.4.3 Risk weights to be assigned
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must assign risk weights to on-balance-sheet exposures and off-balance-sheet items. This Part sets out how to do so.

Guidance
Risk weights are broadly aligned with the likelihood of the counterparty’s default. If an exposure or item is rated (see rule 4.3.3), the risk weight to be assigned is determined in accordance with the rating; otherwise, the risk weight is determined directly by this Part (but in both cases subject to the outcome of due diligence by the firm (see rules 4.2.25, 4.2.26 and 4.2.27).

(2) The firm must assign the risk weight set out in, or determined in accordance with, this Part to a claim or asset, subject to:

(a) the outcome of the credit assessment required by rules 4.2.25, 4.2.26 and 4.2.27; and
(b) its assessment of the exposure, as required by rule 4.4.4.

(3) Under this Part, risk weights must be assigned to exposures of a particular kind at specified levels (for example, in the case of rated bank exposures (other than certain short-term exposures), the risk weights that can be assigned are 20%, 30%, 50%, 100% and 150%, according to the rating of the counterparty (see rule 4.4.18)). If this Part specifies a set of such levels in relation to a kind of exposure, only risk weights in the set may be assigned to such an exposure.

Guidance
Subrule (3) would prevent an Islamic banking business firm from (for example) assigning an intermediate risk weight (say 60%) to a rated bank exposure.
(4) For the purpose of assigning risk weights, profit is treated as suspended on a non-performing exposure.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.4 Requirement to decide whether risk weight appropriate
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK 4.4.4 Requirement to decide whether risk weight appropriate
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must assess every exposure (whether rated or unrated) to decide whether the risk weight to be assigned to it under this Part is appropriate. The firm’s decision must be based on the exposure’s inherent risk.
(2) If there are reasonable grounds to believe that the inherent risk of an exposure is significantly higher than that implied by the risk weight to be assigned to it under this Part, the firm must consider the higher risk (and assign a higher risk weight) for the purpose of calculating its credit risk capital requirement.

(3) In particular, the firm must use the results of due diligence carried out on the counterparty to decide whether a risk weight that is solely based on a rating would be appropriate and prudent. If the results show that the exposure poses greater risk than is implied by the rating, the firm must assign a higher risk weight to the exposure than the risk weight that would be assigned on the basis of the rating.

Note For the risk weights that can be assigned, see rule 4.4.3 (3).
(4) However, due diligence analysis must never result in the application of a lower risk weight than that determined by the rating.
(5) For an exposure to an entity that is part of a corporate group, the firm must, as far as possible, carry out due diligence at the level of the entity to which there is an exposure. However, in evaluating the entity’s repayment capacity, the firm must take into account the support of the group and the possibility that the support would be adversely affected by problems in the group.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: (1) An Islamic banking business firm must assess every exposure (whether rated or unrated) to decide whether the risk weight to be assigned to it under this Part is appropriate. The firm’s decision must be based on the exposure’s inherent risk. (2) If there are reasonable grounds to believe that the inherent risk of an exposure is significantly higher than that implied by the risk weight to be assigned to it under this Part, the firm must consider the higher risk (and assign a higher risk weight) for the purpose of calculating its credit risk capital requirement. (3) In particular, the firm must use the results of due diligence carried out on the counterparty to decide whether a risk weight that is solely based on a rating would be appropriate and prudent. If the results show that the exposure poses greater risk than is implied by the rating, the firm must assign a higher risk weight to the exposure than the risk weight that would be assigned on the basis of the rating. Note For the risk weights that can be assigned, see rule 4.4.3 (3). (4) However, due diligence analysis must never result in the application of a lower risk weight than that determined by the rating. (5) For an exposure to an entity that is part of a corporate group, the firm must, as far as possible, carry out due diligence at the level of the entity to which there is an exposure. However, in evaluating the entity’s repayment capacity, the firm must take into account the support of the group and the possibility that the support would be adversely affected by problems in the group. Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

IBANK 4.4.6 Regulatory Authority can direct firms as to risk weights and impose requirements
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Despite anything in these rules, the Regulatory Authority may direct an Islamic banking business firm as to the risk weight to be assigned to a particular exposure if the Authority considers that the firm has assigned an inappropriate risk weight to the exposure. The direction must be in writing.
(2) The Authority may also impose specific capital requirements or limits on significant exposures, including any exposure that, in the Authority’s opinion, has not been adequately transferred or mitigated.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to an exposure if:

(a) the exposure and the counterparty’s income are denominated in different currencies; and
(b) the counterparty does not have a sufficient natural or financial hedge against the resulting foreign exchange risk.
Guidance
A counterparty has a natural hedge if the borrower normally receives foreign currency income (such as remittances, rental incomes, or salaries) in the currency of the relevant financing. A financial hedge generally includes a contract with a financial institution.
(2) This rule applies to all exposures referred to in subrule (1) regardless of whether the exposure is to an individual, a corporate body or a sovereign.
(3) The exposure must be assigned a risk weight 1.5 times the risk weight that would otherwise be assigned under this Part, subject to a maximum risk weight of 150%.
Amended from QFCRA RM/2018-2 (as from 1st May 2018). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.9 Types of exposures by counterparty
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
IBANK 4.4.9 Types of exposures by counterparty
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For this Division, an exposure on an Islamic banking business firm’s balance sheet may be classified as of one of the following types:

(a) a sovereign exposure (see subrule (3));
(b) a PSE exposure (see subrule (4));
(c) an MDB exposure (see subrule (5));
(d) a bank exposure (see subrule (6));
(e) a corporate exposure (see subrule (7)).
(2) To avoid any doubt, for this Division, exposure includes a claim by way of financing or investment by way of sukuk.

(3) A sovereign exposure is a claim on a counterparty that is:

(a) a national government (or the government of a body politic that is part of a nation, such as a State or Province);
(b) a national central bank; or
(c) a body whose obligations are implicitly or explicitly guaranteed by a national government or the government of a part of a nation.
(4) A PSE exposure is a claim on a counterparty that is a PSE.
(5) An MDB exposure is a claim on a counterparty that is an MDB.

(6) A bank exposure is a claim on a financial institution that is licensed to take deposits and is subject to standards and a level of supervision compliant with:

(a) the Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision published by the BCBS in April 2024; or

Note The Principles are available at: https://www.bis.org/bcbs/publ/d573.pdf.

(b) IFSB-17 (Core Principles for Islamic Finance Regulation (Banking Segment)) published by the IFSB in April 2015 and the core principles referred to in paragraph (a) in so far as applied by IFSB-17.

Note Some exposures to securities firms may be treated as bank exposures — see rule 4.4.17 (3).
(7) A corporate exposure is a claim that is not a sovereign exposure, a PSE exposure, an MDB exposure, a bank exposure nor a retail exposure.
(8) For this Division, a retail exposure is an exposure that would qualify for inclusion in the regulatory retail portfolio under the criteria in IFSB-23. paragraphs 171 and 172.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to rated bank exposures (other than bank exposures to a specific short-term-rated facility such as a particular issue of commercial paper).
(2) A rated bank exposure must be assigned a risk weight in accordance with table 4.4.18.

(3) In table 4.4.18:

(a) Column A applies only to the following rated bank exposures:

(i) exposures that relate to trade finance activities between banks and have an original maturity of 6 months or less;
(ii) other exposures with an original maturity of 3 months or less; and
(b) Column B applies to all other rated bank exposures.
Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.
(4) For this rule, the rating must be one that makes no implicit assumption of government support for the counterparty.
(5) Despite subrule (4), an Islamic banking business firm may, with the written approval of the Regulatory Authority, use for this rule a rating of a counterparty that assumes implicit government support of the counterparty. This subrule ceases to apply at the end of 31 December 2027.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Table 4.4.19 sets out risk weights that an Islamic banking business firm may assign to a bank exposure to a specific short-term-rated facility, such as a particular issue of commercial paper.

Table 4.4.19 Risk weights for bank exposures — specific short-term ratings

Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.
(2) If a short-term-rated facility is assigned a 50% risk weight, the firm must not assign a risk weight lower than 100% to an unrated short-term exposure to the same issuer.
(3) If an issuer has a short-term-rated facility with an external rating that maps to a risk weight of 150%, the firm must assign a risk weight of 150% to any unrated exposure to the same issuer, whether long-term or short-term, unless the firm uses a CRM technique for such exposures.
(4) If there is a specific short-term rating of such an exposure, and the rating maps to a risk weight that is the same as, or lower than, the rating based on the general treatment, the short-term rating may be used for that exposure (and only for that exposure).
(5) If there is a specific short-term rating of such an exposure, and the rating maps to a risk weight that is higher than the rating based on the general treatment, the general treatment may not be applied to the exposure, and the exposure must receive the risk weight implied by the short-term rating.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.21 Grade A unrated bank exposures — criteria
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
IBANK 4.4.21 Grade A unrated bank exposures — criteria
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An unrated bank exposure is to be classified as grade A if the bank:

(a) meets whichever is the more onerous of:

(i) the minimum regulatory requirements and capital buffers imposed by the counterparty’s national supervisor, as most recently published by the supervisor; and
(ii) the minimum regulatory requirements and capital buffers imposed by the standardised credit risk assessment under IFSB-23; and
(b) has adequate capacity to meet its financial obligations (including repayments of principal and interest) in a timely manner, throughout the projected life of the exposure, regardless of economic cycles and business conditions.
(2) For paragraph (1) (a), a requirement that is specific to the bank, and has been imposed by its supervisor as part of the bank’s supervisory review process, is not to be taken into account.
(3) If the requirements and buffers referred to in paragraph (1) (a) (i) have not been published either by the bank’s supervisor or the bank itself, the exposure must be classified as grade B or grade C.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.22 Grade B unrated bank exposures — criteria
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement

IBANK 4.4.22 Grade B unrated bank exposures — criteria
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An unrated bank exposure is to be classified as grade B if the counterparty bank:

(a) meets whichever is the more onerous of:

(i) the published minimum regulatory requirements (but not the capital buffers) imposed by the counterparty bank’s national supervisor; and
(ii) the minimum regulatory requirements (but not the capital buffers) imposed by the standardised credit risk assessment under IFSB-23; and
(b) is subject to substantial credit risk (for example, its repayment capacity depends on stable or favourable economic or business conditions).
(2) For paragraph (1) (a), a requirement that is specific to the counterparty bank, and has been imposed by its supervisor as part of the bank’s supervisory review process, is not to be taken into account.
(3) If the requirements referred to in paragraph (1) (a) (i) have not been published either by the counterparty bank’s supervisor or by the counterparty bank itself, the exposure must be classified as grade C.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This Subdivision is about how an Islamic banking business firm must assign risk weights to general corporate exposures that are on its balance sheet. A general corporate exposure is a corporate exposure that is not any of the following:

(a) a specialised lending exposure (see Subdivision 4.4.B.7);
(b) an exposure to subordinated debt, equity or other capital instruments (see Subdivision 4.4.B.8);
(c) an equity investment in an investment fund (see Subdivision 4.4.B.9);
(d) an exposure secured on real estate (see Subdivision 4.4.B.10);
(e) an exposure to covered sukuk (see Subdivision 4.4.B.11).

(2) This Subdivision does not apply to a defaulted exposure, nor to an exposure resulting from an unsettled or failed transaction.

Note For the treatment of exposures resulting from unsettled or failed transactions and defaulted exposures, see Subdivisions 4.4.B.12 and 4.4.B.13 respectively.
(3) An exposure to a securities firm that is not treated as a bank exposure (see rule 4.4.17 (3)) must be treated as a general corporate exposure.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

IBANK 4.4.27 Using short-term ratings — general corporate exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm may use a short-term rating to assign a risk weight to:

(a) a general corporate exposure that arises from trade finance activities and has an original maturity of 6 months or less; or
(b) any other general corporate exposure with an original maturity of 3 months or less.
(2) Table 4.4.27 sets out the risk weights that the firm may assign to an exposure to a specific short-term facility, such as a particular issue of commercial paper.

Table 4.4.27 Risk weights for specific short-term ratings

RatingRisk weight (%)
A-1/P-120
A-2/P-250
A-3/P-3100
Others150
Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.
(3) If a short-term rated facility is assigned a 50% risk weight, the firm must not assign a risk weight lower than 100% to an unrated short-term exposure to the same issuer.
(4) If an issuer has a short-term facility with an external rating that warrants a risk weight of 150%, the firm must assign a risk weight of 150% to any unrated exposure to the same issuer, whether long-term or short-term, unless the firm uses a CRM technique for such exposures.
(5) If there is a specific short-term rating of such an exposure, and the rating maps to a risk weight that is the same as, or lower than, the rating based on the general treatment, the short-term rating may be used for that exposure (and only for that exposure).
(6) If there is a specific short-term rating of such an exposure, and the rating maps to a risk weight that is higher than the rating based on the general treatment, that treatment must not be applied to the exposure, and the exposure must receive the risk weight implied by the short-term rating.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

IBANK 4.4.28 Scope of Subdivision 4.4.B.7 — specialised lending exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This Subdivision is about how an Islamic banking business firm must assign risk weights to specialised lending exposures that are on its balance sheet. A specialised lending exposure is an exposure to project finance, object finance or commodities finance that:

(a) is not related to real estate; and

(b) has (in legal form or economic substance) 1 or more of the following characteristics:

(i) the relevant obligation is on an entity that was created specifically to finance or operate physical assets;
(ii) that entity has few or no other material assets or activities, and therefore little or no independent capacity to repay the obligation (apart from the income that it receives from those assets) so that the primary source of its repayment capacity is the income generated by those assets rather than its own independent capacity;
(iii) the terms of the obligation give the lender a substantial degree of control over the assets and the income that they generate.

(2) This Subdivision does not apply to:

(a) an exposure resulting from a profit-sharing mode of financing;

Note For the treatment of exposures resulting from profit-sharing modes of financing, see Part 4.5.
(b) a defaulted exposure; or
(c) an exposure resulting from an unsettled or failed transaction.
Note For the treatment of exposures resulting from unsettled or failed transactions and defaulted exposures, see Subdivisions 4.4.B.12 and 4.4.B.13 respectively.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
In this Subdivision:

commodities finance means short-term financing of reserves, inventories, or receivables of exchange-traded commodities (for example, crude oil, metals or crops), where the financing will be repaid from the proceeds of the sale of the commodity and the borrower has no independent capacity to repay the financing.

object finance means financing of the acquisition of equipment (for example, ships, aircraft, satellites, railcars or fleets) in which the repayment of the financing is dependent on the cash flows generated by the specific assets that have been financed and pledged or assigned to the lender.

project finance means financing in which the lender looks primarily to the revenues generated by a single project both as the source of repayment and as security for the financing.

(2) A specialised lending exposure for which no issue-specific rating is available must be assigned a risk weight as follows:

(a) an exposure to project finance while the project is in its pre-operational phase — 130%;
(b) subject to rule 4.4.31, an exposure to project finance while the project is in its operational phase — 100%;
(c) an exposure to object finance or commodities finance — 100%.

(3) For subrule (2) and rule 4.4.31, a project is in its operational phase if the entity that was specifically created to finance the project has:

(a) a positive net cash flow that is sufficient to cover any remaining contractual obligation; and
(b) declining long-term debt.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.31 Risk weights — high-quality specialised lending exposures to project finance
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
IBANK 4.4.31 Risk weights — high-quality specialised lending exposures to project finance
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm may assign a risk weight of 80% to a project finance exposure if the exposure is of high quality and the project is in its operational phase.

Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.

(2) For subrule (1), a project finance exposure is of high quality if the exposure meets all of the following conditions:

(a) the project finance entity (that is, the entity to which the firm is exposed) is able to meet its financial obligations in a timely manner, and its ability to do so is assessed to be robust against adverse changes in the economic cycle and business conditions;
(b) the entity is restricted from acting to the detriment of its creditors (for example, because it cannot issue additional debt without their consent);
(c) the entity has sufficient reserve funds or other financial arrangements to cover contingency funding and the project’s working capital requirements;

(d) the entity’s revenues are availability-based or subject to a rate-of-return regulation or take-or-pay contract;

Guidance
Availability-based revenues means that once construction is completed, the project finance entity is entitled to payments from its contractual counterparties (for example, a government), as long as contract conditions are fulfilled. Availability payments are sized to cover operating and maintenance costs, debt service costs and equity returns as the project finance entity operates the project. Availability payments are not subject to swings in demand, such as traffic levels, and are adjusted typically only for lack of performance or lack of availability of the asset to the public.

(e) the entity’s revenue depends on 1 main counterparty that is:

(i) a sovereign;
(ii) a PSE; or
(iii) a corporate entity that has a risk weight of 80% or lower;
(f) the project’s revenues are sufficient to cover the costs of operation, maintenance and debt-service, and equity returns, as the entity operates the project;
(g) the contractual provisions that govern the exposure give the firm a high degree of protection if the entity defaults;
(h) the main counterparty (or another entity that satisfies paragraph (e)) will protect creditors from the losses that would result from the termination of the project;
(i) all of the assets and contracts necessary to operate the project have been pledged to the creditors to the extent permitted by law;
(j) it will be possible for the project’s creditors to take control of the entity if it defaults.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.33 Definitions for Subdivision 4.4.B.8 — equity exposure and equity instrument
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
IBANK Subdivision 4.4.B.8 Exposures to subordinated debt, equity and other capital instruments
IBANK 4.4.33 Definitions for Subdivision 4.4.B.8 — equity exposure and equity instrument
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Whether an instrument creates an equity exposure is to be determined on the basis of its economic substance.

(2) Equity exposures include both direct and indirect ownership interests (whether voting or non-voting) in the assets and income of a commercial enterprise or of a financial institution that is not consolidated or deducted. An instrument is an equity exposure if it meets all of the following requirements:

(a) it is irredeemable (that is, the return of invested funds can be achieved only by the sale of the investment or sale of the rights to the investment or by the liquidation of the issuer);
(b) it does not embody an obligation on the part of the issuer;
(c) it conveys a residual claim on the assets or income of the issuer.
Guidance
Indirect equity interests include holdings of SCHIs tied to equity interests, and holdings in corporations, partnerships, limited liability companies or other types of enterprises that issue ownership interests and are engaged principally in the business of investing in equity instruments.

(3) An instrument of any of the following kinds is also treated as an equity instrument:

(a) an instrument with the same structure as one permitted as tier 1 capital under rules 3.2.8 to 3.2.11;

(b) an instrument that embodies an obligation on the part of the issuer but satisfies any of the following conditions:

(i) the issuer can defer settling the obligation indefinitely;
(ii) the issuer is required or permitted to settle the obligation by the issue of a fixed number of the issuer’s equity shares;
(iii) if the issuer is required or permitted to settle the obligation by the issue of a variable number of the issuer’s equity shares — other things being equal, a change in the value of the obligation is attributable to, is comparable to, and is in the same direction as, a change in the value of a fixed number of the issuer’s equity shares;
(iv) subject to subrule (4), the holder can require the issuer to settle the obligation in equity shares.

(4) Subrule (3) (b) (iv) does not apply if, on application by the firm, the Regulatory Authority is satisfied that:

(a) in the case of a traded instrument — the instrument trades more like the issuer’s debt than its equity, or
(b) in the case of an instrument that is not traded — the instrument should be treated as a debt position.
(5) In the cases mentioned in paragraphs (4) (a) and (b), the firm may decompose the risks for regulatory purposes, with the Authority’s approval.

(6) A holding in a vehicle that is structured to convey the economic substance of equity ownership is to be treated as creating an equity exposure, including the following:

(a) a debt obligation or other security;
(b) a partnership;
(c) an SCHI;
(d) a liability the return from which is linked to that of equity.
Guidance
The Regulatory Authority may decide not to require that liabilities the return from which is linked to that of equities be included if they are directly hedged by an equity holding, such that the net position does not involve material risk.
(7) However, an equity investment that is structured to convey the economic substance of a debt holding or a securitisation exposure is not to be considered as creating an equity exposure.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: (1) Whether an instrument creates an equity exposure is to be determined on the basis of its economic substance. (2) Equity exposures include both direct and indirect ownership interests (whether voting or non-voting) in the assets and income of a commercial enterprise or of a financial institution that is not consolidated or deducted. An instrument is an equity exposure if it meets all of the following requirements: (a) it is irredeemable (that is, the return of invested funds can be achieved only by the sale of the investment or sale of the rights to the investment or by the liquidation of the issuer); (b) it does not embody an obligation on the part of the issuer; (c) it conveys a residual claim on the assets or income of the issuer. Guidance Indirect equity interests include holdings of SCHIs tied to equity interests, and holdings in corporations, partnerships, limited liability companies or other types of enterprises that issue ownership interests and are engaged principally in the business of investing in equity instruments. (3) An instrument of any of the following kinds is also treated as an equity instrument : (a) an instrument with the same structure as one permitted as tier 1 capital under rules 3.2.8 to 3.2.11 ; (b) an instrument that embodies an obligation on the part of the issuer but satisfies any of the following conditions: (i) the issuer can defer settling the obligation indefinitely; (ii) the issuer is required or permitted to settle the obligation by the issue of a fixed number of the issuer’s equity shares; (iii) if the issuer is required or permitted to settle the obligation by the issue of a variable number of the issuer’s equity shares — other things being equal, a change in the value of the obligation is attributable to, is comparable to, and is in the same direction as, a change in the value of a fixed number of the issuer’s equity shares; (iv) subject to subrule (4), the holder can require the issuer to settle the obligation in equity shares. (4) Subrule (3) (b) (iv) does not apply if, on application by the firm, the Regulatory Authority is satisfied that: (a) in the case of a traded instrument — the instrument trades more like the issuer’s debt than its equity, or (b) in the case of an instrument that is not traded — the instrument should be treated as a debt position. (5) In the cases mentioned in paragraphs (4) (a) and (b), the firm may decompose the risks for regulatory purposes, with the Authority’s approval. (6) A holding in a vehicle that is structured to convey the economic substance of equity ownership is to be treated as creating an equity exposure, including the following: (a) a debt obligation or other security; (b) a partnership; (c) an SCHI; (d) a liability the return from which is linked to that of equity. Guidance The Regulatory Authority may decide not to require that liabilities the return from which is linked to that of equities be included if they are directly hedged by an equity holding, such that the net position does not involve material risk. (7) However, an equity investment that is structured to convey the economic substance of a debt holding or a securitisation exposure is not to be considered as creating an equity exposure. Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.35 Risk weights — subordinated debt, equity investments and other capital instruments
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement

IBANK 4.4.35 Risk weights — subordinated debt, equity investments and other capital instruments
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An exposure to subordinated debt, or a capital instrument that is not an equity investment, must be assigned a risk weight of 150%.

(2) An exposure to an equity investment must be assigned a risk weight as follows:

(a) for an equity investment to which rule 4.4.36 applies — as directed under that rule;
(b) for a speculative unlisted equity investment — 400%;
(c) for any other equity investment — 250%.

(3) For paragraph (2) (b), an exposure is to a speculative unlisted equity investment if the investment is in an unlisted company and is:

(a) held for short-term resale; or
(b) considered venture capital or an investment of a similar kind that is subject to price volatility and is acquired in the expectation of significant future capital gains.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies in relation to equity instruments issued under a law of Qatar that:

(a) provides significant subsidies for investment; and
(b) involves government oversight and restrictions that limit the risk that such an investment presents to an Islamic banking business firm.
Examples of restrictions
Limitations on:
• the size and types of businesses
• allowable amounts of ownership interests
• location.
(2) The Regulatory Authority may, either on its own initiative or on application by an Islamic banking business firm, direct that a part of the firm’s holding of a particular such instrument may be assigned a risk weight of 100% (despite rule 4.4.35).

(3) The firm may treat in that way only so much of the firm’s holding of the instrument as is no more than 10% of the firm’s total regulatory capital.

Note For the meaning of total regulatory capital, see rule 3.1.1 (2).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.37 Certain investments in commercial entities
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
IBANK Subdivision 4.4.B.8 Exposures to subordinated debt, equity and other capital instruments
IBANK 4.4.37 Certain investments in commercial entities
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to an investment by an Islamic banking business firm in a commercial entity (that is, an entity that is not a banking, financial or insurance or takaful entity) if:

(a) the investment is a direct or indirect equity exposure or equity investment: and
(b) it represents more than 10% of the common shares, or other instruments that qualify as capital, of the entity.
Guidance
The operation of this rule in relation to such investments by an Islamic banking business firm depends on 2 materiality thresholds:
• for a single investment — whether or not it represents 15% or more of the firm’s total regulatory capital
• for the total of all such investments by the firm — whether or not the total of all such investments represents 60% or more of the firm’s total regulatory capital.
(2) Such an investment that represents less than 15% of the firm’s total regulatory capital must be assigned a risk weight in accordance with rule 4.4.35.
(3) If such an investment represents 15% or more of the firm’s total regulatory capital, the amount of the excess must be assigned a risk weight of 1,250%.
(4) If the total of such investments by the firm represents 60% or more of the firm’s total regulatory capital, the amount of the excess must be assigned a risk weight of 1,250%.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.42 Calculation of RWA for investment in fund — approaches
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures

IBANK 4.4.42 Calculation of RWA for investment in fund — approaches
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) There are 3 approaches that may be used (separately or in combination) to calculate the RWA for an Islamic banking business firm’s investment in a fund:

(a) the look-through approach (LTA);
(b) the mandate-based approach (MBA); and
(c) the fall-back approach (FBA).
Guidance
1 The LTA assigns risk weights to the fund’s exposures as if they were held directly by the Islamic banking business firm concerned. It is the most granular and risk-sensitive approach. However, the necessary information to use it may not be available.
2 The MBA relies on information in a fund’s mandate or the law governing the fund to assign risk weights to the fund’s exposures.
3 The FBA is used only when neither of the other approaches is possible.

(2) If the fund’s RWA was calculated by the LTA or the MBA, the fund’s RWA is subject to a leverage adjustment (see rule 4.4.51) to calculate the RWA for the firm’s investment in the fund.

Guidance
Under the LTA or the MBA, the firm calculates the RWA for an investment in a fund by first calculating an RWA for the fund. The RWA for the firm’s investment in the fund is taken (subject to the leverage adjustment) to be the fund’s total RWA multiplied by the percentage of the fund’s total equity that the firm holds.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Under the LTA, risk weights are assigned to the exposures of the fund as if the Islamic banking business firm concerned held those exposures directly.

Guidance
Such exposures include, for example, underlying exposures arising from the fund’s activities in SCHIs for situations in which the underlying receives a risk-weighting treatment under Part 4.6A and the associated counterparty credit risk exposure.
(2) In determining the counterparty credit risk for the fund’s exposures to SCHIs, the firm must multiply the relevant exposure (calculated in accordance with Part 4.6A) by 1.5 before applying the risk weight associated with the counterparty.
(3) The firm may rely on a third party’s calculations if the conditions in rule 4.4.47 are met.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.46 Applying MBA
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Under the MBA, the total RWA for a fund’s exposures is the sum of the following:

(a) the total RWA for exposures on the fund’s balance sheet, calculated as set out in subrule (2);
(b) the total RWA for the fund’s exposures to SCHIs and other off-balance-sheet items, calculated as set out in subrule (3);
(c) the total RWA for the fund’s exposures to SCHIs, calculated in accordance with Part 4.6A.
(2) For paragraph (1) (a), the calculation must assume that the fund’s underlying portfolios are invested to the greatest extent allowed under its mandate in assets that attract the highest capital requirements, and then progressively in other assets that attract lower capital requirements. If more than 1 risk weight can be assigned to an exposure, the highest risk weight applicable must be assigned.

(3) For paragraph (1) (b):

(a) in the case of an off-balance-sheet item, if the underlying would receive a risk weight under Division 4.4.C, the notional amount of the item must be assigned a risk weight accordingly; and
(b) in the case of an SCHI exposure, if the underlying would receive a risk weight under Part 4.6A, the notional amount of the exposure must be assigned a risk weight accordingly.
(4) The firm may rely on a third party’s calculations if the conditions in rule 4.4.47 are met.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
IBANK Subdivision 4.4.B.9 Equity investments in funds
IBANK 4.4.47 Applying LTA or MBA — using third party’s calculations
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The conditions under which an Islamic banking business firm may use a third party’s calculations of the risk weight of the firm’s investment in a fund are the following:

(a) the party that does the calculation is:

(i) if the fund invests only in securities and deposits the securities at a depository institution — the depository; or
(ii) another entity approved by the Regulatory Authority;
(b) the calculations are done in accordance with the LTA or the MBA;
(c) the firm is given complete access to the calculations and data;
(d) before the firm uses the results of such a calculation in a prudential report, the calculation is reviewed by the firm’s internal audit function;
(e) all the calculations for a year are reviewed by the firm’s external auditor as part of the firm’s annual audit.
(2) If the firm uses a third party’s calculations of the risk weight of the firm’s investment in a fund, the firm must assign, to its exposure to the fund, a risk weight 1.2 times the risk weight that the firm would have assigned if it had held the exposure directly.
(3) However, if the firm has access to the calculations, and the Regulatory Authority so requests, the firm must provide the Authority with details of the calculations. In this case, subrule (2) does not apply.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.50 Treatment of funds’ investments in other funds
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement

IBANK 4.4.50 Treatment of funds’ investments in other funds
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an Islamic banking business firm has an investment in a fund (fund 1) that has an investment in another fund (fund 2), and either the LTA or the MBA was used to calculate the RWA of fund 1, the risk weight to be assigned to fund 2 can be calculated by using the LTA, MBA or FBA (as the available information permits).
(2) For all subsequent layers (such as fund 2’s investment in another fund (fund 3) and so on), the risk weights applied to fund n can be calculated by using the LTA only if the LTA was used for determining the risk weight for fund (n-1). Otherwise, the FBA must be applied.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an Islamic banking business firm has calculated the RWA for a fund using either the LTA or the MBA, it must apply a leverage adjustment to that RWA. The result of applying the leverage adjustment is taken as the RWA for the firm’s investment in the fund.

(2) If LTA or MBA is used to calculate the RWA for. an Islamic banking business firm’s investment in a fund, the RWA for the investment is calculated by the following formula:

where:
RWAfund is the fund’s total RWA.

Total assetsfund is the fund’s total assets, according to its latest balance sheet.

Lv is:
(a) if the LTA was applied — the fund’s actual leverage (that is, the fund’s total assets divided by its equity, expressed as a percentage);
(b) if the MBA was applied — the highest rate of leverage permitted by the relevant mandate or law.
Eq is the firm’s equity in the fund (that is, the product of the fund’s total equity and the percentage of that equity that the firm holds).

(3) However, the application of a leverage adjustment to an investment in a fund is not to increase the risk weight of the investment higher than 1,250%.

Example
Consider a fund that replicates an equity index. An Islamic banking business firm holds 20% of the fund’s shares. Also, assume that:
(1) the firm uses the standardised approach (as set out in Divisions 4.4.B and 4.4.C) when calculating its capital requirements for credit risk, and it uses the standardised approach for determining counterparty credit risk exposures.
(2) the fund holds forward contracts on listed equities that are cleared through a QCCP (with a notional amount of 100); and
(3) the fund presents the following balance sheet:
Assets 
Cash20
Government sukuk (AAA-rated)30
VM receivable (that is, collateral posted by the firm to the CCP in respect of the forward contracts)50
Liabilities
Notes payable5
Equity
Shares, retained earnings and other reserves95

The fund’s exposures must be risk-weighted as follows:

(1) the RWA for the cash (RWAcash) is the exposure of 20 multiplied by the applicable SA risk weight of 0%. Thus, RWAcash = 0;
(2) the RWA for the government sukuk (RWAsukuk) is the exposure of 30 multiplied by the applicable SA risk weight of 0%. Thus, RWAsukuk = 0;

(3) the RWA for the exposures to the listed equities underlying the forward contracts (RWAunderlying) is the product of the following 3 amounts:

(a) the SA credit conversion factor of 100% that is applicable to forward purchases;
(b) the exposure to the notional amount of $100;
(c) the applicable risk weight for listed equities under the SA which is 100%;
thus, RWAunderlying = 100% × 100 × 100% = 100;
(4) the forward purchase equities expose the bank to counterparty credit risk in respect of the market value of the forwards and the collateral posted that is not held by the CCP on a bankruptcy-remote basis. For the sake of simplicity, assume that the application of Part 4.6A results in an exposure value of $56. The RWA for counterparty credit risk (RWACCR) is the product of the exposure amount and the relevant risk weight for trade exposures to CCPs, which is 2% in this case (see 4.6A.D for the capital requirements for bank exposures to CCPs). Thus, RWACCR = $56 × 2% = $1.12. (For the sake of simplicity, this example does not include capital requirements for exposures to CCPs or the credit valuation adjustment framework.)

The total RWA of the fund is therefore $101.12 = (0 + 0 +100 + 1.12).

The leverage of a fund under the LTA is the ratio of the fund’s total assets to its total equity, which in this example is 100/95.

Therefore, the RWA for the bank’s equity investment in the fund is the product of the average risk weight of the fund, the fund’s leverage and the size of the bank’s equity investment — that is:

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
The counterparty credit risk exposure of a netting set of SCHIs is calculated by multiplying the sum of the replacement cost and potential future exposure by an alpha factor set at 1.4. Whenever the replacement cost is unknown, the exposure measure for counterparty credit risk will be calculated conservatively by using the sum of the notional amounts of the SCHIs in the netting set as a proxy for the replacement cost, and the multiplier used in the calculation of the potential future exposure will be equal to 1. Whenever the potential future exposure is unknown, it will be calculated as 15% of the sum of the notional values of the SCHIs in the netting set. The risk weight associated with the counterparty is applied to the counterparty credit risk exposure.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.53 Definitions for Subdivision 4.4.B.10
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
IBANK Subdivision 4.4.B.10 Exposures secured on real estate
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
In this Subdivision:

commercial real estate exposure means an exposure that is secured by mortgage over real estate, but is not a residential real estate exposure.

mortgage includes any form of security interest over real estate.

residential real estate exposure means an exposure that is secured by mortgage over real estate, if the real estate:

(a) has (or will, on completion, have) the nature of 1 or more dwellings; and
(b) satisfies all the applicable laws and regulations necessary to enable it to be occupied as housing (or will, on completion, satisfy all such laws and regulations).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

(b) other exposures secured by mortgage over real estate; and

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.55 Prudential requirements
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
IBANK Subdivision 4.4.B.10 Exposures secured on real estate
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The requirements referred to in rule 4.4.54 (2) (the prudential requirements) are the requirements in subrules (2) to (7).

(2) Finished property: the exposure must be secured by either:

(a) a fully completed property; or

(b) residential property under construction, or land upon which residential property will be constructed, but only if:

(i) both of the following are true:

(A) the property is a residential housing unit for 1 to 4 families, and it will be the borrower’s primary residence;
(B) the lending is not, in effect, indirectly financing land acquisition, development and construction; or
(ii) a sovereign or PSE has the legal powers and ability to ensure that the property will be finished.
(3) Legal enforceability: the security must be legally enforceable in all the relevant jurisdictions. The security agreement and the legal process supporting it would allow the firm to realise the value of the property within a reasonable period.
(4) Claims over the property: the firm must hold a first mortgage, or the first mortgage and 1 or more sequentially lower ranking mortgages, over the property (that is, if the firm holds 2 or more mortgages over the property, there is no other mortgage that is intermediate in priority between the firm’s mortgages) — but see rule 4.4.56.
(5) Ability of the borrower to repay: the borrower must meet the requirements referred to in rule 4.4.57.
(6) Prudent value of property: the property must be valued according to the criteria in rules 4.4.58 and 4.4.59 to determine the FTV ratio for the financing. The value of the property must not depend materially on the performance of the borrower.

(7) Required documentation: all the information required at financing origination and for monitoring purposes must be properly documented, including information on:

(a) the borrower’s ability to repay; and
(b) the valuation of the property.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

Despite rule 4.4.55 (4), where the Islamic banking business firm concerned does not hold a first mortgage over the relevant property, the Regulatory Authority may approve, as a credit risk mitigant for the purposes of this Subdivision, a second or subsequent mortgage if, under the law of the relevant jurisdiction, all of the following requirements are satisfied:

(a) a second or subsequent mortgage gives the mortgagee a claim that is legally enforceable and constitutes an effective credit risk mitigant;
(b) any mortgagee can initiate the sale of the property independently from the other mortgagees;
(c) if the sale were not carried out by public auction, a mortgagee that held a higher-priority mortgage would be obliged to take reasonable steps to obtain a fair market value (or the best price that could be obtained in the circumstances) when exercising its power of sale.

(1) An Islamic banking business firm must have an underwriting policy in relation to the granting of mortgage financings that requires the firm to assess a borrower’s ability to repay such a financing.
(2) The policy must define 1 or more appropriate criteria (such as the financing’s debt service coverage ratio) and must specify the relevant levels for the purpose of that assessment.
(3) The policy must be appropriate even when the repayment of the mortgage financing depends significantly on the cash flows generated by the property, and must take into account relevant measurements such as the property’s occupancy rate.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.58 Valuation of property
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
IBANK Subdivision 4.4.B.10 Exposures secured on real estate
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The property’s value must be determined independently using prudently conservative valuation criteria. The valuation process must not include any expectations of price increases.
(2) If a market value can be determined for the property, the value of the property for the purposes of the financing must not be higher than that market value.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.59 How to calculate FTV ratio
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
IBANK Subdivision 4.4.B.10 Exposures secured on real estate
IBANK 4.4.59 How to calculate FTV ratio
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must calculate the FTV ratio for a proposed real estate financing prudently in accordance with the following requirements:

(a) the financing amount must include any outstanding financing amount and any undrawn committed amount of the financing;
(b) the financing amount must be calculated gross of any provisions and other risk mitigants (except for pledged deposit accounts with the firm that meet all the requirements for netting on the firm’s balance sheet and have been unconditionally and irrevocably pledged for the sole purpose of repaying the financing);
(c) the value must be adjusted to take into account the possibility that the current market price is significantly above the value that would be sustainable over the life of the financing.
(2) The value of the property must continue to be its value at the origination of the financing, unless the Regulatory Authority directs the firm to reduce the value. Modifications made to the property that unequivocally increase its value may be taken into account.
(3) However, the firm may reduce the property’s value if an extraordinary event permanently reduces the property’s value.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.60 Recognition of collateral and guarantees
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement

IBANK Subdivision 4.4.B.10 Exposures secured on real estate
IBANK 4.4.60 Recognition of collateral and guarantees
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) In calculating the amount of an exposure for the purposes of this Subdivision, an Islamic banking business firm may take into account financial collateral or a guarantee as a credit risk mitigant if the guarantee or collateral qualifies as eligible collateral or an eligible guarantee (as the case may be) under Part 4.6.

Note For what qualifies as eligible collateral, see rule 4.6.12. For what qualifies as an eligible guarantee, see rule 4.6.32.
(2) The firm may also take into account mortgage indemnity takaful that meets the requirements of Part 4.6 for a guarantee (so far as possible).
(3) However, for the purpose of assigning a risk weight to an exposure, its FTV ratio must be determined without taking any CRM technique into account.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.61 Qualifying real estate exposures
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
IBANK Subdivision 4.4.B.10 Exposures secured on real estate
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Qualifying real estate exposures are classified according to whether repayment is dependent on cash flows generated by the property, as follows:

(a) residential exposures repayment of which is not materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property;
(b) residential exposures repayment of which is materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property;
(c) commercial exposures repayment of which is not materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property;
(d) commercial exposures repayment of which is materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property.
Note 1 For the meaning of qualifying real estate exposure, see rule 4.4.54 (2).
Note 2 For the meaning of materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property, see rule 4.4.64.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.62 Meaning of qualifying residential real estate exposure

IBANK 4.4.62 Meaning of qualifying residential real estate exposure
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
A qualifying residential real estate exposure is a qualifying real estate exposure that is secured on a property that has the nature of a dwelling and satisfies (or, for residential property under construction, will, when completed, satisfy) all the applicable laws and regulations to enable it to be occupied for housing.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.64 Meaning of materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
IBANK Subdivision 4.4.B.10 Exposures secured on real estate
IBANK 4.4.64 Meaning of materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) A qualifying real estate exposure (whether residential or commercial) is materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property if the borrower’s prospects of servicing the financing materially depend on the cash flows generated by the property that secures the financing rather than on the borrower’s capacity to do so from other sources (but see subrule (2)).

Guidance
1 The primary source of the cash flows generated by the property would generally be lease or rental payments, or the sale of the property. The distinguishing characteristic of these exposures compared to other qualifying real estate exposures is that both the servicing of the financing and the prospects for recovery in the event of default depend materially on the cash flows generated by the property securing the exposure.
2 The material dependence condition set out above predominantly applies to financings to corporates or SPVs, but is not restricted to such borrowers. For example, a financing might be considered materially dependent if more than 50% of the income from the borrower used in the bank's assessment of its ability to service the financing is from cash flows generated by a residential property.

(2) The following are exceptions to the general rule in subrule (1) (that is, the following types of exposure are not treated as exposures the repayment of which is materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property that secures them):

(a) exposures secured on a property that is the borrower’s primary residence;
(b) exposures, secured on an income-producing residential housing unit, to an individual who has mortgaged fewer than 50% of the properties in the relevant development;

(c) exposures, secured on residential real estate, to an association or cooperative of individuals:

(i) that is regulated under national law; and
(ii) whose only purpose is granting its members the use of a primary residence in the property;

(d) exposures, secured on residential real estate, to a public housing company or not-for-profit association that:

(i) is regulated under national law; and
(ii) exists to serve social purposes and to offer tenants long-term housing.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

IBANK 4.4.69 Risk weights — real estate exposures other than qualifying real estate exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to real estate exposures that are neither qualifying real estate exposures nor land acquisition, development and construction exposures.

(2) The risk weight to be assigned to a real estate exposure to which this rule applies is:

(a) if repayment of the exposure is not materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property — the risk weight of the counterparty (see rule 4.4.70); or
(b) in any other case— 150%.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.71 Risk weights — land acquisition, construction and development exposures
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
IBANK Subdivision 4.4.B.10 Exposures secured on real estate
IBANK 4.4.71 Risk weights — land acquisition, construction and development exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule deals with land acquisition, construction and development (ACD) exposures — that is, exposures resulting from financings to companies or special purpose vehicles to finance the acquisition of land for construction and development purposes, or the construction and development of residential or commercial property.

(2) Such an exposure may be assigned a risk weight of 100% if:

(a) the real estate concerned is residential real estate;
(b) the prudential requirements in rule 4.4.55 are complied with (so far as possible) in relation to the property; and

(c) all of the following requirements are complied with:

(i) pre-sale or pre-lease contracts have been signed that amount to a significant portion of the total contracts or equity at risk;
(ii) those contracts are legally binding written contracts;
(iii) each buyer or lessee has paid a substantial cash deposit that is subject to forfeiture if the contract is terminated;
(iv) equity at risk was determined as an appropriate amount of borrower-contributed equity to the real estate’s appraised value as completed.
Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.
(3) An ACD exposure that does not fall within subrule (2) must be assigned a risk weight of 150%.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

IBANK 4.4.73 Meaning of covered sukuk and eligible covered sukuk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) A covered sukuk is a sukuk issue that is issued by a bank or mortgage institution and is subject by law to public supervision designed to protect the sukuk-holders.

Guidance
Proceeds from the issue of such sukuk must be invested, as the law requires, in assets that, throughout the validity of the sukuk, are capable of covering claims attached to the sukuk and, if the issuer fails, would be used, on a priority basis, to repay the principal and pay the accrued profit.
(2) An eligible covered sukuk is a covered sukuk issue that satisfies subrules (3) and (4).

(3) A covered sukuk satisfies this subrule if:

(a) the underlying assets (the cover pool) include only assets of the following kinds:

(i) claims on, or guaranteed by, sovereigns, central banks, PSEs or MDBs;
(ii) claims secured by residential real estate in relation to which the prudential requirements in rule 4.4.55 have been complied with, and with an FTV ratio no higher than 80%;
(iii) claims secured by commercial real estate in relation to which those prudential requirements have been complied with, and with an FTV ratio no higher than 60%;
(iv) claims on, or guaranteed by, banks that qualify for a 30% or lower risk weight (but only if such claims make up no more than 15% of the sukuk issuance); and

(v) additional collateral of the following kinds:

(A) substitution assets (that is, cash or short-term liquid and secure assets held in substitution for the primary assets, to top up the cover pool for management purposes);
(B) SCHIs entered into to hedge the risks arising in the sukuk programme; and

(b) at both the sukuk’s issue and throughout its term, the total nominal value of the cover pool is at least 10% more than the total nominal value of outstanding sukuk issued.

Guidance
The requirement that the value of the cover pool continue to exceed the total of sukuk issues implies that that the issuer must actively manage the cover pool, replacing non-performing assets or assets that have been subject to pre-payment with other appropriate assets.

(4) A covered sukuk issue satisfies this subrule if the Islamic banking business firm concerned can produce evidence to satisfy the Regulatory Authority that:

(a) the firm receives portfolio information at least on:

(i) the value of the cover pool and the outstanding covered sukuk;
(ii) the geographical distribution and type of assets in the cover pool, financing size, profit rate and currency risks;
(iii) the maturity structure of the cover assets and covered sukuk; and
(iv) the percentage of financings that are more than 90 days past due; and
(b) the issuer makes the information referred to in paragraph (a) available to the firm at least once every 6 months.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

(1) This Subdivision is about how an Islamic banking business firm must assign risk weights to unsettled or failed transactions that are on its balance sheet.

(2) This Subdivision applies to unsettled or failed transactions in both the banking book and the trading book.

Guidance
If an exposure or transaction in the banking book on the firm’s balance sheet were not unsettled or failed, another Subdivision of this Division would apply to it.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.76 Unsettled or failed transactions in securities, commodities and foreign exchange — general rule
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement

IBANK 4.4.76 Unsettled or failed transactions in securities, commodities and foreign exchange — general rule
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm must take into account any unsettled or failed transactions in securities, commodities or foreign exchange when calculating its credit risk capital requirement, including:

(a) transactions through recognised clearing houses and central counterparties that are subject to daily marking to market and the payment of daily variation margin; and
(b) transactions that involve a mismatched trade.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
