QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.77 Unsettled or failed transactions in securities, commodities and foreign exchange — DvP transactions

IBANK 4.4.77 Unsettled or failed transactions in securities, commodities and foreign exchange — DvP transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to a DvP transaction in securities, commodities or foreign exchange if, 5 days or more after the due date for settlement, the transaction has not been settled.
(2) The firm must calculate the resulting capital requirement by multiplying the positive current exposure of the transaction by the appropriate risk multiplier set out in table 4.4.77. The positive current exposure of the transaction is the difference between the transaction’s value at the agreed settlement price and at current market price.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.78 Unsettled or failed transactions in securities, commodities and foreign exchange — non-DvP transactions
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
IBANK Subdivision 4.4.B.12 Unsettled or failed transactions
IBANK 4.4.78 Unsettled or failed transactions in securities, commodities and foreign exchange — non-DvP transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to a non-DvP transaction in securities, commodities or foreign exchange if the first contractual payment or delivery is made but the second contractual payment or delivery is not made by the end of the same business day.
(2) Until the end of 5 business days after the first contractual payment or delivery, the Islamic banking business firm that made the first payment or delivery must treat the resulting exposure as a financing, and must assign a risk weight to that exposure commensurate with the risk weight of the counterparty in accordance with the relevant provision of this Division.
(3) However if the exposure is not significant, the firm may assign a risk weight of 100% to it if the Regulatory Authority so approves.

(4) If the second contractual payment or delivery is not made within 5 business days after the first, the firm that made the first contractual payment or delivery must assign a risk weight of 1,250% to the sum of:

(a) the full amount of the value transferred; and
(b) the replacement cost (if any).

(5) The firm must continue to treat the transaction in accordance with subrule (4) until the second payment or delivery is made.

Note For the treatment of an unsettled or failed off-balance-sheet transaction, see rule 4.4.90.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.80 Meaning of defaulted
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.B Standardised approach — on-balance-sheet exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
For these rules, an exposure of an Islamic banking business firm is defaulted (or is in default) if any of the following paragraphs is true of it:

(a) a material credit obligation is more than 90 days past due;
(b) in the case of an overdraft — the customer concerned has breached a notified limit or has been notified of a limit lower than the amount outstanding;
(c) a significant credit obligation has “non-accrued” status (for example, the firm no longer recognises accrued profit as income, or makes an equivalent amount of provision);
(d) the firm makes a write-off or account-specific provision as a result of a significant perceived decline in credit quality after the firm takes on credit exposure to the counterparty;
(e) the firm sells a credit obligation at a significant credit-related loss;

(f) the firm agrees to a distressed forbearance of a credit obligation;

Guidance
A distressed forbearance is a forbearance (see Division 4.7.C) that reduces a debtor’s financial obligation to a creditor because the creditor significantly forgives or postpones principal, profit or fees.
(g) another creditor of the counterparty has sought an order for the counterparty’s bankruptcy or for the counterparty to be placed in administration;
(h) the counterparty has sought an order for its bankruptcy or similar protection and the result would be to avoid or delay repayment of any of the counterparty’s credit obligations to the firm;
(i) any other situation has arisen in which the firm considers that the counterparty is unlikely to pay its credit obligations in full unless the firm takes action such as realising security.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.81 Risk weights — certain defaulted real estate exposures
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement

IBANK 4.4.81 Risk weights — certain defaulted real estate exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must assign a risk weight of 100% to a defaulted exposure that is secured on residential real estate (net of any specific provision or write-off) if the repayment of the exposure does not significantly depend on cash flows generated by the property that secures it.
(2) In calculating the exposure, the firm may take into account an eligible guarantee or eligible collateral.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

IBANK 4.4.82 Risk weights — other defaulted exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to a defaulted exposure to which rule 4.4.81 does not apply.

(2) An Islamic banking business firm must assign a risk weight to the unsecured or unguaranteed portion of a defaulted exposure (net of any specific provision or write-off) as follows:

(a) if specific provisions are less than 20% of the outstanding amount of the exposure — 150%;
(b) if specific provisions are 20% of the outstanding amount of the exposure or more — 100%.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.84 Risk weights for assets not otherwise provided for — cash and gold
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement

IBANK 4.4.84 Risk weights for assets not otherwise provided for — cash and gold
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm may assign a risk weight of 0% to:

(a) cash owned and held at the firm or in transit; and

(b) gold bullion held:

(i) at the firm; or
(ii) in another bank on an allocated basis (to the extent that the gold bullion assets are backed by gold bullion liabilities).

(2) An Islamic banking business firm may assign a risk weight of 20% to a cash item that is in the process of collection.

Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

IBANK 4.4.85 Risk weights for assets not otherwise provided for — certain investments in common shares, mortgage servicing rights and certain deferred tax assets
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to the following items:

(a) investments, to which rule 3.2.38 (1) (a) applies, in common shares;
(b) mortgage servicing rights;
(c) deferred tax assets that arise from temporary differences.
Note Rule 3.2.38 permits the limited recognition of such items when calculating CET 1 capital.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.14 Risk weights — PSE exposures

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm may assign a risk weight of 0% to an exposure to a non-commercial PSE in Qatar that is denominated in Qatari riyals.

Guidance — deciding whether a PSE is commercial
1 The following examples outline how PSEs might be categorised when focusing on one specific feature, namely revenue-raising powers. However, there may be other ways of determining the different treatments applicable to different types of PSEs; for instance, by focusing on the extent of guarantees provided by the central government.
2 A claim on a regional government or local authority could qualify for the same treatment as a claim on its sovereign or central government if the government or authority has revenue-raising powers and institutional arrangements the effect of which is to reduce its risk of default.
3 A claim on an administrative body that is responsible to a central government, regional government or local authority, or on another non-commercial undertaking owned by a government or local authority, may not warrant the same treatment as a claim on the sovereign if the body does not have revenue-raising powers or other arrangements as described. If strict lending rules apply to such a body or a declaration of bankruptcy is not possible because of its special public status, it may be appropriate to treat the body as a PSE.
4 A commercial undertaking owned by a central government, regional government or local authority may be treated as a normal commercial enterprise. In particular, if such an undertaking functions as a corporate in competitive markets even though the central government, a regional authority or a local authority is the major shareholder, the undertaking should be treated as a corporate and exposures to it should be assigned risk weights accordingly.

(2) The firm must assign a risk weight to any other PSE exposure in accordance with table 4.4.14.

Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.

Table 4.4.14 Risk weights for PSE exposures

Rating of relevant sovereignRisk weight (%)
AAA to AA-20
A+ to A-50
BBB+ to BBB-50
BB+ to B-100
Below B-150
Unrated50

Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.16 Risk weight — MDB exposures
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.C Standardised approach — off-balance-sheet items
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm may assign a risk weight of 0% to an exposure to any of the following MDBs:

(a) the African Development Bank (AfDB);
(b) the Asian Development Bank (ADB);
(c) the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank;
(d) the Caribbean Development Bank (CDB);
(e) the Council of Europe Development Bank (CEDB);
(f) the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD);
(g) the European Investment Bank (EIB);
(h) the European Investment Fund (EIF);
(i) the Inter-American Development Bank (IADB);
(j) the International Finance Facility for Immunization;
(k) the Islamic Development Bank (IDB);
(l) the Nordic Investment Bank (NIB);
(m) the World Bank Group (comprising the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA) and the International Development Association (IDA)).

(2) The firm must assign a risk weight to an exposure to any other MDB in accordance with table 4.4.16, but may assign a risk weight of 0% if the Regulatory Authority so approves.

Guidance
The Authority will evaluate eligibility for 0% risk weight case by case. The eligibility criteria for MDBs to be risk-weighted at 0% are as follows:
• very high quality long-term issuer ratings — the majority of the MDB’s external assessments must be AAA
• its shareholder structure is made up of a significant proportion of sovereigns with long-term issuer credit ratings of AA- or better, or the majority of its fund-raising is in the form of paid-in equity/capital and there is little or no leverage
• strong shareholder support demonstrated by the amount of paid-in capital contributed by the shareholders; the amount of further capital the MDB has the right to call, if required, to repay its liabilities; and continued capital contributions and new pledges from sovereign shareholders
• adequate level of capital and liquidity (a case-by-case approach is necessary in order to assess whether the MDB’s capital and liquidity are adequate)
• strict statutory lending requirements and conservative financial policies, including a structured approval process, internal creditworthiness and risk concentration limits (per country, sector, and individual exposure and credit category), approval of large exposures by the board or a committee of the board, fixed repayment schedules, effective monitoring of use of proceeds, status review process, and rigorous assessment of risk and provisioning.

Table 4.4.16 Risk weights for MDB exposures

RatingRisk weight (%)
AAA to AA-20
A+ to A-30
BBB+ to BBB-50
BB+ to B-100
Below B-150
Unrated50
Note Exposures that have an unhedged currency mismatch may be subject to a risk weight multiplier — see rule 4.4.7.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.89 Treatment of commitments
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement
IBANK Division 4.4.C Standardised approach — off-balance-sheet items
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For this Division, a commitment is an arrangement that has been offered by an Islamic banking business firm, and accepted by an obligor, to extend credit, purchase assets or issue credit substitutes, including such an arrangement that the firm can cancel:

(a) unconditionally at any time without notice; or
(b) if the obligor fails to meet a condition (including a condition that must be met before the first or any later drawdown under the arrangement).
(2) An Islamic banking business firm must take every commitment into account in calculating its credit risk capital requirement, whether or not a commitment contains a material adverse change clause or other provision that is intended to relieve the firm of its obligations under particular conditions.
(3) An off-balance-sheet undertaking to provide a commitment to an off-balance-sheet item may be assigned the lower of the 2 applicable CCFs.
(4) To calculate the credit equivalent amount of an undrawn (or partly drawn) commitment, an Islamic banking business firm must use the undrawn amount of the commitment.

(5) For an irrevocable commitment to provide a facility off the balance sheet, the original maturity must be taken to be the period from the commencement of the commitment until the associated facility expires.

Example
An irrevocable commitment with an original maturity of 6 months with an associated facility that has a 9-month term is taken to have an original maturity of 9 months.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.4.91 How to calculate risk-weighted amounts
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.4 Standardised approach to calculating credit risk capital requirement

IBANK 4.4.91 How to calculate risk-weighted amounts
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The risk-weighted amount of an off-balance-sheet item is calculated as follows:

(a) first, convert the notional principal amount of the item to its on-balance-sheet equivalent (that is, the item’s credit equivalent amount) by multiplying the notional principal amount by the relevant credit conversion factor (CCF), as set out in table 4.4.91;
(b) then, multiply the item’s credit equivalent amount by the risk weight applicable to the claim or asset under Division 4.4.B.

(2) For securities referred to in table 4.4.91, item 3, the Islamic banking business firm concerned must also apply the risk-weighting treatment for counterparty credit risk (see Part 4.6A) if the credit risk of the securities remains with the firm. However, this subrule does not apply to lodged collateral, related to SCHI transactions, that is treated in accordance with the counterparty credit risk standards.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.5.1 Introduction
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.5 Risk-Weightings for Islamic Financial Contracts
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This Part describes and sets out the risk-weights applicable to the main kinds of Islamic financial contracts.
(2) The risk-weight to be applied to the exposure under a contract of a particular type may differ:
(a) at different stages of the contract; or
(b) depending on the enterprise or asset to which the contract relates.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.5.3 Treatment of Murabahah and Related Contracts
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.5 Risk-Weightings for Islamic Financial Contracts
IBANK 4.5.3 Treatment of Murabahah and Related Contracts
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm is exposed to credit risk under a murabahah contract if the obligor fails to pay the agreed selling price under the contract. Therefore, the firm is subject to a capital charge for credit risk exposure once the asset is sold and payment is due to the firm.
(2) For an MPO contract, the firm is exposed to credit risk if the obligor (purchase orderer) defaults on its obligation to purchase the asset. Because the firm has recourse against the obligor to purchase the asset at the agreed price, the credit risk exposure commences once the firm acquires the asset.
(3) In an MPO contract, the firm is also exposed to credit risk if the obligor fails to pay the agreed price in accordance with the agreed terms.
(4) Bai bithaman ajil and musawamah contracts are treated in the same way as murabahah contracts.

asset has been sold and title transferred, and selling price is due to the firm based on the customer's type and rating under Part 4.4

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.5.4 Treatment of Salam and Related Contracts
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.5 Risk-Weightings for Islamic Financial Contracts
IBANK 4.5.4 Treatment of Salam and Related Contracts
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Under a salam contract, an Islamic banking business firm is exposed to credit risk if the obligor fails to deliver the relevant commodity in accordance with the agreed terms.
(2) An Islamic banking business firm undertaking parallel salam contracts is exposed to credit risk if the purchaser fails to pay for the relevant commodity. Nevertheless, if the seller under the first salam contract fails to deliver the commodity, the firm is not relieved of its obligation to deliver the commodity to the purchaser under the parallel salam contract.
(3) The firm must not net a salam exposure against a parallel salam exposure.

Table 4.5.4A Credit risk-weights for salam without parallel salam

stage of contract credit risk-weight
firm is expecting delivery of the commodity after purchase price has been paid to salam customer (seller)
Note The parallel salam does not extinguish the requirement for capital from the first salam contract. 		based on the customer's type and rating under Part 4.4

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.5.5 Treatment of Istisna and Related Contracts
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.5 Risk-Weightings for Islamic Financial Contracts
IBANK 4.5.5 Treatment of Istisna and Related Contracts
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Under an istisna contract, an Islamic banking business firm is exposed to credit risk if the obligor fails to pay the price, whether during the manufacturing or construction stage, or on completion of the asset.
(2) Under a parallel istisna contract, the firm, as the purchaser of the asset, is exposed to credit risk if the seller fails to deliver the asset at the agreed time and in accordance with the initial istisna buyer's specification.
(3) The parallel istisna seller's failure to deliver the asset does not discharge the firm's obligation to deliver the asset to the obligor under the initial istisna contract. Thus, the firm is also exposed to the potential loss of making good the shortcoming or acquiring the asset elsewhere.
(4) The firm must not net an istisna exposure against a parallel istisna exposure.

Table 4.5.5A Credit risk-weights for istisna without parallel istisna

stage of contract credit risk-weight
unbilled work-in-process based on the ultimate counterparty's type and rating under Part 4.4
unpaid billed work-in-process based on the ultimate counterparty's type and rating under Part 4.4

Table 4.5.5B Credit risk-weights for istisna with parallel istisna

stage of contract credit risk-weight
unbilled work-in-process based on the ultimate counterparty's type and rating under Part 4.4
unpaid billed work-in-process based on the ultimate counterparty's type and rating under Part 4.4

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.5.6 Treatment of Ijarah and Related Contracts
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.5 Risk-Weightings for Islamic Financial Contracts
IBANK 4.5.6 Treatment of Ijarah and Related Contracts
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm that is the lessor under an ijarah contract is exposed to credit risk if the lessee fails to pay the rental amount in accordance with the agreement to lease.
(2) In addition, the firm is exposed to credit risk if the lessee (lease orderer) defaults on its obligation to lease the asset. In this situation, the firm may lease or dispose of the asset to another party, but the firm is also exposed to credit risk if the lessee is not able to compensate it for the losses incurred arising from the disposal of the asset.
(3) In an ijarah contract, the underlying asset is not eligible collateral for purposes of credit risk mitigation.
(4) An IMB contract is treated as a financing agreement and must be risk-weighted in accordance with table 4.5.6.

Table 4.5.6 Credit risk-weights for IMB contracts

stage of contract credit risk-weight
asset available for lease and on firm's balance sheet based on the lessee's type and rating under Part 4.4, with the applicable risk-weight applied to the acquisition cost
lease contract has become binding and rental payments due from lessee based on the lessee's type and rating under Part 4.4, with the applicable risk-weight applied to net receivables (that is, total estimated value of lease receivables for the remaining period plus the residual value of the leased asset at the end of the contract)
(5) An operating ijarah is treated as an investment and must be risk-weighted in accordance with subrule (6), (7), (8) or (9), depending on the leased asset and how the investment is made.
(6) If the investment is made by the firm itself (direct investment exposure), the risk-weighted amount of the direct investment exposure must be calculated by multiplying the carrying value of the asset by 150%.
(7) If the investment is made by the firm indirectly (indirect investment exposure) through a subsidiary, its share or equity investment in the capital of the subsidiary must be risk-weighted at 150% and any financing provided by the firm to the subsidiary must be risk-weighted at the same rate.
(8) If the investment is made by the firm indirectly (indirect investment exposure) through a joint venture or partnership, the indirect investment exposure must be risk-weighted at:
(a) 300% if the firm has majority ownership over the asset and can exit the investment at any time; or
(b) 400% if the firm does not have majority ownership over the asset or cannot exit the investment at any time.
(9) If the investment is in physical assets (such as commercial vehicles, passenger cars, ships, aircraft, railway machinery, computers, business machines and other types of equipment), the exposure must be risk-weighted at:
(a) 300% if the firm has majority ownership over the asset and can exit the investment at any time; or
(b) 400% if the firm does not have majority ownership over the asset or cannot exit the investment at any time.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA_RM2023-3 (as from 1st August 2023).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.5.7 Treatment of Musharakah
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.5 Risk-Weightings for Islamic Financial Contracts
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For the purpose of determining the minimum capital requirement, there are 4 categories of musharakah:
(a) private commercial enterprise to undertake trading activities in foreign exchange, shares or commodities;
(b) private commercial enterprise to undertake a business venture other than trading in foreign exchange, shares or commodities;
(c) joint ownership of real estate or movable assets through musharakah with murabahah subcontract; and
(d) joint ownership of real estate or movable assets through musharakah with ijarah subcontract
(2) Except in the case of diminishing musharakah contracts, all musharakah investments are treated as equity investments.
(3) As an equity investment, a musharakah investment must be risk-weighted in accordance with table 4.5.7A.

(4) The lower risk-weight of 300% applies to an investment that would normally be risk-weighted at 400% if, under the musharakah contract, the Islamic banking business firm is allowed to withdraw its participation within 5 business days after giving notice of withdrawal. In any other case, the firm may apply a risk-weight of 300% if it can demonstrate:
(a) that the lower risk-weight is appropriate for the nature, scale and complexity of the firm's business;
(b) that the firm can effectively participate in the management of the investment and that such participation would not unduly increase operational risk;
(c) the firm's ability to monitor the operations and performance of the investment;
(d) that the valuation methods and exit strategies used by the firm are appropriate; and
(e) that the firm has effective reporting and information-sharing systems.

Table 4.5.7A Credit risk-weights for musharakah (non-diminishing) column 1 item column 2 description of investment column 3 risk-weight % 1 investments in funds (a) rated funds based on ECRA rating in table 4.5.7B (b) unrated funds that are listed 100 (c) unrated funds that are unlisted 150 2 equity exposures (a) equity exposures that are not deducted from capital and are listed on a recognised exchange 300 (b) equity exposures that are not deducted from capital and are not listed on a recognised exchange 400, except if rule 4.5.7(4) applies 3 investment in real estate 150 4 investment in physical assets (such as commercial vehicles, passenger cars, ships, aircraft, railway machinery, computers, business machines and other types of equipment) (a) if the firm has majority ownership over the asset and can exit the investment at any time 300 (b) if the firm does not have majority ownership over the asset or cannot exit the investment at any time 400, except if rule 4.5.7(4) applies Table 4.5.7B Risk-weights for investments in rated funds based on ECRA ratings Note In the table, the ratings are given according to Standard & Poor's conventions. If a claim or asset is not rated by Standard & Poor's, its ratings must be mapped to the equivalent Standard & Poor's rating. AAA to AA- A+ to A- BBB+ to BBB- BB+ to BB- B+ to B- below B- 20 50 100 100 150 150 (4) The lower risk-weight of 300% applies to an investment that would normally be risk-weighted at 400% if, under the musharakah contract, the Islamic banking business firm is allowed to withdraw its participation within 5 business days after giving notice of withdrawal. In any other case, the firm may apply a risk-weight of 300% if it can demonstrate: (a) that the lower risk-weight is appropriate for the nature, scale and complexity of the firm's business; (b) that the firm can effectively participate in the management of the investment and that such participation would not unduly increase operational risk; (c) the firm's ability to monitor the operations and performance of the investment; (d) that the valuation methods and exit strategies used by the firm are appropriate; and (e) that the firm has effective reporting and information-sharing systems. QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.1 Introduction
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm is able to obtain capital relief by using Shari’a-compliant CRM techniques. The use of such techniques must be treated as complementary to, rather than a replacement for, thorough credit risk assessment.

Guidance

Although the use of CRM techniques reduces or transfers credit risk, it may at the same time increase other risks (that is, residual risks). Residual risks include legal, operational, liquidity and market risks. Therefore, Islamic banking business firms must employ robust procedures and processes to control such risks, including strategy; consideration of the underlying credit; valuation; policies and procedures; systems; control of roll-off risks; and management of concentration risk arising from the firm’s use of CRM techniques and its interaction with the firm’s overall credit risk profile. If such risks are not adequately controlled, the Regulatory Authority may impose additional capital charges or take other supervisory action.

Note Under rule 4.4.5, if a claim or asset to which an Islamic banking business firm must assign a risk weight is secured by eligible collateral or a guarantee (or is covered by an SCHI or a netting agreement), the firm may apply this Part to reduce the firm’s credit risk capital requirement.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.2 Choice of CRM techniques
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) CRM techniques include:

(a) accepting collateral, standby letters of credit and guarantees;
(b) using SCHIs; and
(c) using netting agreements.
Guidance
1 An Islamic banking business firm should not rely excessively on collateral or guarantees to mitigate credit risk. While collateral or guarantees may provide secondary protection to the firm if the counterparty defaults, the primary consideration for credit approval should be the counterparty’s repayment ability.
2 An Islamic banking business firm that provides mortgages at high FTV ratios should consider the need for alternative forms of protection against the risks of such lending, in order to protect itself against the risk of a fall in the value of the property.

(2) In choosing a CRM technique, the firm must consider:

(a) the firm’s knowledge of, and experience in using, the technique;
(b) the cost-effectiveness of the technique;
(c) the type and financial strength of the counterparties or issuers;
(d) the correlation of the technique with the underlying credits;
(e) the availability, liquidity and realisability of the technique;
(f) the extent to which documents in common use can be adopted; and
(g) the degree of recognition of the technique by financial services regulators.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.3 Requirements — CRM techniques
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm’s credit risk management policy must set out the conditions under which CRM techniques may be used. The policy must enable the firm to manage CRM techniques and the risks associated with their use.
(2) The firm must analyse the protection given by CRM techniques to ensure that any residual credit risk is identified, measured, evaluated, managed and controlled or mitigated.

(3) The policy must include procedures for:

(a) setting mark-up rates according to the risk rating of the counterparties;
(b) taking account of governing laws for contracts relating to financing transactions; and
(c) assessing the risks and obligations from the firm’s own exposures in parallel transactions such as those in salam and istisna.
(4) If the firm accepts collateral, its policy must state the types of collateral that it will accept, and the basis and procedures for valuing collateral.
(5) If the firm uses netting agreements, it must have a netting policy that sets out its approach. The netting policy must provide for monitoring netting agreements and must enable the firm to monitor and report netted transactions on both gross and net bases.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.4 When CRM techniques reduce credit risk capital requirement
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.4 When CRM techniques reduce credit risk capital requirement
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm’s use of a CRM technique reduces the firm’s credit risk capital requirement only if the technique and every document that gives effect to it are binding on all parties and enforceable in all the relevant jurisdictions.

Guidance
When accepting collateral, an Islamic banking business firm must ensure that any necessary legal procedures have been followed, to ensure that the collateral can be enforced.

(2) An Islamic banking business firm must review the enforceability of a CRM technique that it uses. The firm must have a well-founded legal basis for any conclusion about enforceability, and must carry out further reviews to ensure that the technique remains enforceable.

Guidance
An Islamic banking business firm should consider whether independent legal opinion should be sought on the enforceability of documents. The documents should be ready before the firm enters into a contractual obligation or releases funds.

(3) The effects of a CRM technique must not be double-counted. The firm is not allowed to obtain capital relief if:

(a) the risk weight for the claim or asset is based on an issue-specific rating; and
(b) the ECRA that determined the rating had taken the technique into consideration in doing so.
(4) A transaction in which CRM techniques are used must not receive a higher capital requirement than an otherwise identical transaction in which no such technique is used.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.5 Use of 2 or more CRM techniques for 1 exposure etc
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.5 Use of 2 or more CRM techniques for 1 exposure etc
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an Islamic banking business firm has an exposure that is covered by 2 or more CRM techniques (for example, the exposure is covered by both eligible collateral and an eligible guarantee), the firm must divide the exposure into parts covered by each technique (for example, the part covered by the collateral, and the part covered by the guarantee) and must calculate the risk-weighted assets for each part separately.
(2) If credit protection provided for an exposure by a single protection provider has 2 or more maturities, the exposure must be divided into separate parts for each maturity.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2022-2 (as from 1st April 2022).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK Division 4.6.B Collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: IBANK Division 4.6.B Collateral

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.6 Capital relief from collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm may obtain capital relief by accepting Shari’a-compliant eligible collateral.

Note The capital relief that an Islamic banking business firm obtains from collateral is calculated by either the simple approach (see Subdivision 4.6.B.2) or the comprehensive approach (see Subdivision 4.6.B.3). The meaning of eligible collateral differs between the simple approach and the comprehensive approach — see respectively rule 4.6.12 and rule 4.6.16.
(2) Collateral may be lodged by the firm’s counterparty, or by a third party on behalf of the counterparty.

(3) The firm must enter into a written agreement with the party lodging the collateral. The agreement must establish the firm’s direct, explicit, irrevocable and unconditional recourse to the collateral.

Guidance
In the case of cash collateral, the recourse may be in the form of a contractual right of set-off on credit balances. A common-law right of set-off is, on its own, insufficient to satisfy this rule.
(4) If collateral is lodged by a third party, the third party must guarantee the counterparty’s obligation to the firm and must indemnify the firm if the counterparty fails to fulfil its obligation. The firm must ensure that the guarantee does not fail for lack of consideration.

(5) The mechanism by which collateral is lodged must allow the firm to liquidate or take possession of the collateral in a timely way. The firm must take all steps necessary to satisfy the legal requirements applicable to its interest in the collateral.

Guidance
1 The firm should have clear and robust procedures for the liquidation of collateral to ensure that the legal conditions for declaring default and liquidating the collateral are observed.
2 The firm should consider whether, in the event of default, notice to the party that lodged the collateral would be needed before the firm could have recourse to it.

(6) There must not be a significant positive correlation between the value of the collateral and the credit quality of the borrower.

Note A positive correlation between the credit quality of the borrower and the value of the collateral is often called “wrong-way risk”.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

The firm must take all steps necessary to satisfy the legal requirements applicable to its interest in the collateral. Guidance 1 The firm should have clear and robust procedures for the liquidation of collateral to ensure that the legal conditions for declaring default and liquidating the collateral are observed. 2 The firm should consider whether, in the event of default, notice to the party that lodged the collateral would be needed before the firm could have recourse to it. (6) There must not be a significant positive correlation between the value of the collateral and the credit quality of the borrower. Note A positive correlation between the credit quality of the borrower and the value of the collateral is often called “wrong-way risk”. Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.7 Valuing collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Collateral accepted by an Islamic banking business firm must be valued at its net realisable value, taking into account prevailing market conditions. That value must be monitored at appropriate intervals, and the collateral must be regularly revalued.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.7 Guidance
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
1 The net realisable value of some collateral may be readily available (for example, collateral that is marked-to-market regularly). Other collateral may be more difficult to value and may require knowledge and consideration of prevailing market conditions.

2 The method and frequency of monitoring and revaluation depend on the nature and condition of the collateral. For example:

• securities accepted as collateral are usually marked-to-market daily while physical assets that are accepted as eligible collateral are valued less often
• commercial property might be valued every year while residential property might not need to be valued as often.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.8 Holding eligible collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Eligible collateral must be held by:

(a) the Islamic banking business firm concerned;
(b) a branch (in or outside the QFC) of the firm;
(c) another member of the firm’s corporate group;
(d) an independent custodian; or
(e) a central counterparty.
(2) The holder of cash collateral in the form of a certificate of deposit or bank bill issued by an Islamic banking business firm must keep possession of the instrument while the collateralised exposure exists.
(3) If the collateral is held by an independent custodian or central counterparty, the firm must take reasonable steps to ensure that the holder segregates the collateral from the holder’s own assets.
(4) If collateral is held by a branch of an Islamic banking business firm and the branch is outside the QFC, the agreement between the firm and the party lodging the collateral must require the branch to act in accordance with the agreement.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2022-2 (as from 1st April 2022).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.9 Approaches to risk weight using eligible collateral
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.9 Approaches to risk weight using eligible collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) When assigning risk weights to exposures that are collateralised by eligible collateral, an Islamic banking business firm may use either of the following approaches:

(a) the simple approach (see Subdivision 4.6.B.2);
(b) the comprehensive approach (see Subdivision 4.6.B.3).
(2) However, the firm must apply the same approach for all of the exposures in its banking book that are collateralised by eligible collateral.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.10 Definition for Division 4.6.B — core market participant
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.10 Definition for Division 4.6.B — core market participant
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
In this Division:

core market participant means any of the following:

(a) the State of Qatar;
(b) the Qatar Central Bank;
(c) any other sovereign or central bank that qualifies for a 0% risk weight under Division 4.4.B;
(d) a bank;

(e) any other financial entity that is subject to capital or leverage requirements and qualifies for a 20% risk weight under Division 4.4.B;

Note For example, a CCP, regulated mutual fund or regulated pension fund that is subject to capital or leverage requirements may qualify for a 20% risk weight under Division 4.4.B.
(g) a QCCP.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.11 When simple approach may be applied
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.11 When simple approach may be applied
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For the simple approach to be applied, the collateral must be lodged for at least the life of the exposure, and must be marked to market at least once a month. The release of collateral must be conditional on the repayment of the exposure, but collateral may be reduced in proportion to the amount of any reduction in the exposure.
(2) An Islamic banking business firm must not apply the simple approach if there is a maturity mismatch between an exposure and its collateral.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.12 Eligible collateral in simple approach
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.12 Eligible collateral in simple approach
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The following are eligible collateral if they satisfy the criteria in subrule (2):

(a) gold bullion;
(b) cash;

(c) hamish jiddiyah or refundable security deposit taken by the firm against damages if:

(i) a purchase orderer in an MPO contract defaults on its obligation to purchase the asset; or
(ii) a lease orderer in an ijarah contract defaults on its obligation to lease the asset;
(d) urbun or earnest money held by a firm as collateral to guarantee contract performance;

(e) sukuk that are assigned, by an ECRA, a rating of:

(i) for sovereign or non-commercial public sector enterprise securities that are eligible for 0% risk weight—at least BB ;
(ii) for short-term securities—at least A-3/P-3; or
(iii) for any other securities—at least BBB ;

(f) sukuk that have not been assigned a rating by an ECRA, if:

(i) the securities are issued by an Islamic banking business firm (or by a conventional bank that is outside the QFC and that has an Islamic window or subsidiary operation) as senior securities and are listed on a recognised exchange;
(ii) all rated issues of the same seniority issued by that firm or bank have a credit rating of at least BBB- (for long-term debt instruments) or A-3/P-3 (for short-term instruments); and
(iii) the firm or bank and the holder of the collateral have no information suggesting that the securities should have a rating below BBB- or A 3/P-3;
(g) Shari’a-compliant equities (including convertible sukuk) that are included in a main index;
(h) units in investment funds;

(i) tracker funds, mutual funds and undertakings for collective investments in transferable securities (UCITS) if:

(i) a price for the units is publicly quoted daily; and
(ii) the funds or UCITS are limited to investing in instruments listed in this subrule;
(j) Shari’a-compliant equities (including convertible sukuk) that are not included in a main index but are listed on a recognised exchange, and funds and UCITS described in paragraph (i) that include such equities.
Note Under certain Islamic transactions (such as murabahah, salam, istisna’ and ijarah), the underlying physical assets, namely commercial and residential real estate, plant and machinery, are eligible collateral under the comprehensive approach (see rule 4.6.16) but not under the simple approach.
(2) For collateral to be eligible collateral, it must be lodged for at least the life of the exposure, and must be marked-to-market at least once a month. The release of collateral must be conditional on the repayment of the exposure, but collateral may be reduced in proportion to the amount of any reduction in the exposure.
(3) Collateral in the form of securities issued by the counterparty or a person connected to the counterparty is not eligible collateral.
(4) Takaful contracts, unilateral promises to buy from counterparties (such as put options), and forward sales contracts or agreements (such as salam and istisna contracts) are not eligible collateral.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.13 Risk weight for exposure collateralised by eligible collateral — simple approach
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.13 Risk weight for exposure collateralised by eligible collateral — simple approach
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Under the simple approach, the part of an exposure that is collateralised by eligible collateral must be assigned a risk weight of the higher of:
(a) the risk weight of the collateral under Division 4.4.B; and
(b) subject to the exceptions in subrules (3) to (10) — 20%.
(2) Any part of the exposure that is not so collateralised must be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to an unsecured exposure to the counterparty under Division 4.4.B.
(3) Subrule (4) applies to an exposure of an Islamic banking business firm if:
(a) the collateral is cash on deposit, or a certificate of deposit or similar instrument issued by the firm;
(b) the collateral:
(i) is held at a third-party bank in a non-custodial arrangement; and
(ii) is openly pledged to the firm; and
(c) the pledge is unconditional and irrevocable.
(4) If this subrule applies to an exposure, the amount of the exposure that is covered by the collateral receives the risk weight of the third-party bank.
(5) Subrule (6) applies to an exposure that arises from an SFT and fulfils all of the following conditions:
(a) both the exposure and the collateral are either cash, or a sovereign or PSE security that qualifies for a 0% risk weight under Division 4.4.B;
(b) the exposure and the collateral are denominated in the same currency;
(c) either the transaction is overnight, or both the exposure and the collateral are marked to market daily and are subject to daily remargining;
(d) if the counterparty were to fail to remargin, the collateral could be liquidated within no more than 4 business days after the last marking to market before the failure;
(e) the transaction is settled across a settlement system proven for transactions of that type;
(f) the documentation covering the transaction is standard market documentation for SFTs in the securities concerned;
(g) under that documentation, if the counterparty fails to satisfy an obligation to deliver cash or securities or to deliver margin, or otherwise defaults, the transaction is immediately terminable;
(h) on the counterparty’s default the firm has the unfettered, legally enforceable right to immediately seize and liquidate the collateral for its own benefit, even if the counterparty is insolvent or bankrupt.
(6) An exposure to which this subrule applies may be assigned a risk weight of:
(a) 10%; or
(b) if the counterparty is a core market participant — 0%.
(7) Subrule (8) applies to an exposure that arises from an SCHI of a kind that is normally traded OTC and fulfils all of the following conditions:
(a) both the exposure and the collateral are either cash, or a sovereign or PSE sukuk that qualifies for a 0% risk weight under Division 4.4.B;
(b) the exposure and the collateral are denominated in the same currency;
(c) both the exposure and the collateral are marked to market daily.
(8) An exposure to which this subrule applies may be assigned a risk weight of:
(a) if the collateral is cash — 0%; or
(b) if the collateral is a sovereign or PSE sukuk that qualifies for a 0% risk weight under Division 4.4.B — 10%.
(9) Subrule (10) applies to a transaction where:
(a) an Islamic banking business firm has a credit exposure or potential credit exposure; and
(b) the exposure is wholly or partly hedged by collateral posted by a counterparty or by a third party on the counterparty’s behalf.
(10) A transaction to this subrule applies may be assigned a risk weight of 0% if the exposure and the collateral are denominated in the same currency, and either:
(a) the collateral is cash; or
(b) the collateral is sovereign or PSE securities that would qualify for a 0% risk weight under Division 4.4.B, and its market value has been discounted by 20%.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

If SFTs are covered by an eligible netting agreement, an Islamic banking business firm must calculate the exposure value of the netting set as follows:

where:

E* is the exposure value of the netting set after risk mitigation.

Ei is the current value of all cash and securities lent to, sold (with an agreement to repurchase) to, or otherwise lodged with the counterparty under the netting agreement.

Cj is the current value of all cash and securities borrowed by, purchased (with an agreement to resell) by, or otherwise held by the firm under the netting agreement.

N is the number of security issues in the netting set (excluding issuances whose value Es is less than one-tenth of the value of the largest Es in the netting set).

Efx is the absolute value of the net position in each currency fx that is not the settlement currency.

Hfx is the haircut appropriate for the currency mismatch of currency fx.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.28 Haircut minima for certain SFTs — non-eligible counterparties
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.28 Haircut minima for certain SFTs — non-eligible counterparties
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Subrule (2) applies to transactions of the following kinds:

(a) SFTs that are not centrally cleared, and in which the Islamic banking business firm concerned provides financing against collateral other than securities issued by a sovereign or a PSE;
(b) collateral upgrade transactions;
with a counterparty that is not supervised by a regulator that imposes prudential requirements consistent with the Basel III framework. However, subrule (2) does not apply to transactions of a kind described in subrule (3).
Guidance
A collateral upgrade transaction is one in which the firm lends a security to the counterparty and the counterparty pledges a lower quality security as collateral, thus allowing the counterparty to exchange a lower quality security for a higher quality security.
(2) Subject to subrule (5) and rule 4.6.29, in transactions to which this subrule applies, an Islamic banking business firm must apply the haircut minima set out in table 4.6.28.

(3) Subrule (2) does not apply to transactions of the following kinds:

(a) SFTs with central banks;

(b) cash-collateralised securities lending transactions of either of the following kinds:

(i) transactions in which securities are lent to an Islamic banking business firm at long maturities, and the lender of the securities reinvests or employs the cash at the same or shorter maturity, so that no significant maturity or liquidity mismatch occurs;
(ii) transactions in which securities are lent to such a firm at call or at short maturities (giving rise to liquidity risk) but the lender reinvests the cash collateral into a reinvestment fund or account that is subject to regulation or regulatory guidance that meets global minimum standards for the reinvestment of cash collateral by securities lenders.
(4) For the purposes of subparagraph (3) (b) (ii), the firm may rely on a representation by a securities lender that their reinvestment of cash collateral meets the standards referred to in that subparagraph.

(5) If the firm lends securities for a collateral upgrade transaction, it need not apply the minimum if:

(a) the firm is unable to re-use the securities received as collateral against the securities lent; or
(b) the firm represents that it does not intend to, and will not, re-use them in that way.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.15 Description of comprehensive approach
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) To assign a risk weight to an exposure using the comprehensive approach, an Islamic banking business firm must calculate its adjusted exposure to the counterparty to take into account the risk-mitigating effect of the collateral.

(2) The firm must use the applicable supervisory haircuts (set out in rule 4.6.23) to adjust both the amount of the exposure to the counterparty and the value of any collateral received in support of that counterparty, to take account of possible future fluctuations in the value of either, caused by market movements.

Guidance
1 Unless either side of the transaction is cash or a zero haircut is applied, the volatility-adjusted exposure amount will be higher than the nominal exposure and the volatility-adjusted collateral value will be lower than the nominal collateral value.
2 The size of a haircut depends on the type of instrument, the type of transaction, its residual maturity and the frequency of marking to market and remargining.
3 Haircuts must be scaled up using the square-root-of-time formula, depending on the frequency of remargining or marking to market. The formula is in rule 4.6.24 (6).
(3) In the case of a maturity mismatch, the value of the collateral must be adjusted in accordance with rule 4.6.25.
(4) If the exposure and collateral are in different currencies, the firm must apply an additional haircut to the volatility-adjusted collateral amount in accordance with rule 4.6.26 to take account of possible future fluctuations in exchange rates.
(5) The effect of a netting agreement covering an SFT may be taken into account in accordance with rule 4.6.27 and Division 4.6.E.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

(a) equities and convertible sukuk that are not included in a main index but are listed on a recognised exchange;

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.30 Capital relief from guarantees
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) A guarantee reduces an Islamic banking business firm’s credit risk capital requirement in relation to an exposure only if:

(a) the guarantor is an eligible guarantor (see rule 4.6.31);
(b) the guarantee is an eligible guarantee (see rule 4.6.32); and
(c) an unsecured exposure to the guarantor would be assigned a lower risk weight than an unsecured exposure to the counterparty.
(2) Before accepting a guarantee, an Islamic banking business firm must consider the guarantor’s legal and financial ability to fulfil the guarantee.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.31 Eligible guarantors
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Each of the following is an eligible guarantor:

(a) the State of Qatar or any other sovereign;
(b) a PSE or MDB;
(c) a bank, securities firm or other financial institution that is prudentially regulated to a standard similar to that applied by the Regulatory Authority;
(d) if the relevant exposure is a securitisation exposure — an externally-rated entity (including a parent, subsidiary or affiliate of the obligor) that is rated BBB- or better and was rated A- or better when the guarantee was given;
(e) if the relevant exposure is not a securitisation exposure — any externally-rated entity, including a parent, subsidiary or affiliate of the obligor.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.32 What is an eligible guarantee?
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.32 What is an eligible guarantee?
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) A guarantee is an eligible guarantee if it satisfies subrules (2) to (10).
(2) The guarantor is an eligible guarantor.
(3) The guarantee is explicitly documented.
(4) The guarantee is a direct claim on the guarantor and clearly states the extent of the cover. A letter of comfort is not an eligible guarantee.
(5) The guarantee explicitly refers to specific exposures or a specific pool of exposures, so that the extent of the cover is clearly defined and not open to doubt.
(6) The guarantee is irrevocable (other than for non-payment by the protection buyer of money due for the guarantee).

(7) No provision of the guarantee:

(a) would allow the guarantor to cancel the guarantee, or to change its maturity, unilaterally; or
(b) would increase the effective cost of the cover if the credit quality of the exposure deteriorates.
Guidance
Subrule (6) does not require the maturities of the guarantee and the exposure to be matched. However, it does require that the agreed maturity of the guarantee is not to be reduced by the guarantor after the protection buyer accepts the guarantee.
(8) The guarantee is unconditional. It does not include a term (outside the direct control of the protection buyer) that allows the guarantor not to indemnify the protection buyer in a timely way if the counterparty defaults.

(9) On an event of default or non-payment that triggers the guarantee:

(a) the protection buyer has the right to recover any money outstanding under the transaction from the guarantor in a timely manner;
(b) the guarantor may either pay that money to the protection buyer in a lump sum, or assume the counterparty’s future payment obligations; and
(c) the protection buyer has the right to receive such payments from the guarantor without first having to take legal action against the counterparty for payment.
(10) The guarantee covers all types of payments that the counterparty is expected to make under the transaction (for example, the notional amount and the margin payments) — but see rule 4.6.33.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.33 Risk-weighting of exposures covered by eligible guarantees
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.33 Risk-weighting of exposures covered by eligible guarantees
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If a claim on a counterparty is secured by an eligible guarantee, the part of the claim that is covered by the guarantee may be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to an unsecured exposure to the guarantor under Division 4.4.B. The unsecured part of the claim must be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to an unsecured exposure to the counterparty under that Division.

Note If the guarantee provides for a materiality threshold (below which the issuer is not obliged to pay in the event of a loss), the part of the exposure that is below the threshold must be deducted from CET 1 capital — see rule 3.2.40.
(2) If the guarantee covers the payment of principal only, profit and other uncovered payments must be treated as unsecured.

(3) If an eligible guarantee provides that the Islamic banking business firm concerned and the guarantor must share any loss, the firm:

(a) may treat, as covered by an eligible guarantee, a proportion of the exposure equal to the proportion of the loss that the guarantor must bear; and
(b) must treat the remainder of the exposure as unsecured.

(4) If:

(a) an Islamic banking business firm transfers part (but not all) of the risk of an exposure in 1 or more tranches to 1 or more eligible guarantors; and
(b) the risk transferred and the risk retained are of different seniority;
the firm may obtain credit protection for either the senior portion or the junior portion. The firm is to be treated as having securitised the exposure, and must determine the relevant capital requirement in accordance with Part 10.4.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.34 Treatment of maturity mismatches
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) A maturity mismatch between an exposure and a guarantee exists if the residual term of the guarantee is shorter than the maturity of the exposure.
(2) If there is a maturity mismatch, the guarantee may be recognised only if its original term is 12 months or longer, and its residual maturity is 3 months or longer.

(3) For the purpose of determining the maturity of the exposure and guarantee:

(a) for the exposure, the effective maturity is taken to be the longest possible remaining time before the counterparty must fulfil its obligation; and
(b) for the guarantee, the Islamic banking business firm concerned must take into account any provision or incentive within its documentation that could reduce the term of the guarantee, so that the shortest possible effective term is used.

(4) If there is a maturity mismatch, the firm must adjust the value of the guarantee as follows:

P is the value of the guarantee after adjustment for any haircuts.
t is min {T, residual maturity of the guarantee}, in years.
T is min {5 years, residual maturity of the exposure}, in years.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.17 When physical assets may be eligible collateral
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6.D Sharia Compliant Hedging Instruments
IBANK 4.6.17 When physical assets may be eligible collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm may accept as eligible collateral, by way of pledge, a specified asset that can be lawfully owned, and is saleable and deliverable. The pledge must be enforceable and the asset must be unencumbered.
Note In an ijarah contract, the underlying asset is not eligible collateral for purposes of credit risk mitigation — see rule 4.5.6 (3).
(2) The firm may accept a physical asset as eligible collateral only if:
(a) either:
(i) the firm legally owns the asset; or
Guidance
Therefore ijarah contracts are restricted to operating ijarah only, where the firm bears related costs of asset ownership.
(ii) the asset attracts capital charges other than credit risk before the beginning of, and throughout, the financing period; and
Examples
operating ijarah
inventories under murabahah
(b) the asset meets the relevant criteria in rules 4.6.18 to 4.6.20; and
(c) the firm complies with the conditions in rules 4.6.18 to 4.6.21.
(3) A physical asset accepted as eligible collateral must be valued depending on whether there is an active market for the asset.
(4) If there is such a market, the asset must be valued at least once a month. If there is no active market for the asset, it must be valued:
(a) each time there is a significant change in the market in which the asset operates; and
(b) each time there is a significant change in the condition of the asset.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.36 Capital relief from SCHIs
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6.D Sharia Compliant Hedging Instruments
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm is able to reduce its credit risk capital requirement in relation to an exposure or exposures by purchasing an SCHI only if:

(a) the issuer is an eligible issuer (see rule 4.6.38);
(b) the SCHI is an eligible SCHI (see rule 4.6.39); and
(c) the issuer’s risk weight is lower than that of the counterparty.
(2) Before purchasing an SCHI, an Islamic banking business firm must consider the issuer’s legal and financial ability to fulfil the SCHI.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.38 Eligible issuers
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6.D Sharia Compliant Hedging Instruments
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Each of the following is an eligible issuer:

(a) the State of Qatar or any other sovereign;
(b) a PSE or MDB;
(c) a bank, securities firm or other financial institution that is prudentially regulated;

(d) if the relevant exposure is a securitisation exposure:

(i) the issuer is a parent, subsidiary or affiliate of the obligor; or
(ii) where the issuer is an external entity — the issuer is rated BBB- or better and was rated A- or better when the instrument was issued;
(e) if the exposure is not a securitisation exposure — any externally-rated entity, including a parent, subsidiary or affiliate of the obligor.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.39 Eligible SCHIs
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6.D Sharia Compliant Hedging Instruments
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An SCHI is an eligible SCHI if it satisfies subrules (2) to (15).
(2) It is issued by an eligible issuer.
(3) It is a direct claim on the issuer.
(4) It is explicitly referenced to specific exposures or a specific pool of exposures, so that the extent of the cover is clearly defined and incontrovertible.
(5) It is irrevocable (other than for non-payment by the protection buyer of money due for the credit protection contract).

(6) No provision of the contract:

(a) would allow the issuer to cancel the SCHI, or to change its maturity, unilaterally; or
(b) would increase the effective cost of the cover if the credit quality of the exposure deteriorates.
Guidance
The irrevocability condition does not require the SCHI and the exposure to be maturity matched. However, it does require that the agreed maturity should not be reduced by the issuer after the Islamic banking business firm concerned accepts the SCHI.
(7) It is unconditional. It does not include a term or condition (outside the direct control of the Islamic banking business firm concerned) that allows the issuer not to indemnify the firm in a timely way on the occurrence of a credit event.

(8) It specifies at least the following as credit events:

(a) failure to pay an amount due under the terms of the underlying exposure that is in effect at the time of the failure (however, any grace period under the terms of the underlying must be allowed);
(b) the obligor of the underlying exposure becoming bankrupt or insolvent or unable to pay its debts (and any similar event);
(c) the obligor’s failure to pay, or admitting in writing its inability generally to pay, its debts as those debts become due (and any similar event);
(d) the application of forbearance to the underlying exposure, including any forgiveness or postponement of principal, profit or fees that results in a credit loss event (but see rule 4.6.41).

(9) On the occurrence of a credit event:

(a) the firm has the right to recover any money outstanding under the transaction from the issuer in a timely manner;
(b) the issuer may either pay that money to the firm in a lump sum, or assume the counterparty’s future payment obligations; and
(c) the firm has the right to receive such payments from the issuer without first having to take legal action against the counterparty for payment.
(10) It clearly identifies the parties responsible for deciding whether a credit event has occurred. That decision is not the sole right of the issuer, and the firm has the right and the ability to notify the issuer about such an event.
(11) It does not terminate before the end of any grace period required after a credit event on the underlying obligation as a result of a failure to pay.

(12) If there is a mismatch between the underlying obligation and the reference obligation used to determine the SCHI’s cash settlement value:

(a) the reference obligation is equal in seniority to, or is junior to, the underlying obligation; and
(b) the underlying obligation and reference obligation share the same obligor and there are legally enforceable cross-default or cross-acceleration clauses.

(13) If there is a mismatch between the underlying obligation and the obligation used to determine whether a credit event has occurred:

(a) the obligation used to determine whether a credit event has occurred is equal in seniority to, or is junior to, the underlying obligation; and
(b) the underlying obligation and the obligation used to determine whether a credit event has occurred share the same obligor and there are legally enforceable cross-default or cross-acceleration clauses.
(14) If the SCHI is based on cash settlement, the Islamic banking business firm concerned must have a robust valuation process to reliably estimate losses on the reference obligation, including a defined period for obtaining valuations of that obligation after a credit event.
(15) If the firm buys credit protection in relation to an existing exposure, the terms of the exposure must allow for its transfer to the issuer. If the firm would be required to transfer the underlying exposure to the issuer for settlement, the terms of the exposure must provide that any required consent to the transfer may not be unreasonably withheld.
(16) First-to-default and all other nth-to-default credit SCHIs are not eligible SCHIs.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.40 Risk-weighting of exposures covered by eligible SCHIs
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6.D Sharia Compliant Hedging Instruments
IBANK 4.6.40 Risk-weighting of exposures covered by eligible SCHIs
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an exposure is fully covered by an eligible SCHI, the exposure may be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to an unsecured exposure to the issuer under Division 4.4.B.

(2) If an exposure is partly covered by an eligible SCHI:

(a) the covered part must be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to an unsecured exposure to the issuer under Division 4.4.B; and
(b) the remainder must be assigned the risk weight that would be assigned to an unsecured exposure to the counterparty under that Division.
Note If the SCHI provides for a materiality threshold (below which the issuer is not obliged to pay in the event of a loss), the part of the exposure that is below the threshold must be deducted from CET 1 capital — see rule 3.2.40.

(3) If the SCHI provides that the Islamic banking business firm concerned and the issuer must share any loss, the firm:

(a) may treat, as covered by an eligible SCHI, a proportion of the exposure equal to the protected portion; and
(b) must treat the remainder of the exposure as unsecured.
(4) If the SCHI covers payment of principal only, profit and other uncovered payments must be treated as unsecured.

(5) If:

(a) an Islamic banking business firm transfers part (but not all) of the risk of an exposure in 1 or more tranches to 1 or more protection sellers; and
(b) the risk transferred and the risk retained are of different seniority;
the firm may obtain credit protection for either the second-loss portion or the first-loss portion. The firm is to be treated as having securitised the exposure, and must calculate the relevant capital requirement in accordance with Chapter 10.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.41 Partial recognition of SCHIs when application of forbearance to underlying not covered
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6.D Sharia Compliant Hedging Instruments
IBANK 4.6.41 Partial recognition of SCHIs when application of forbearance to underlying not covered
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an SCHI does not cover the application of forbearance to the underlying obligation, but the SCHI otherwise meets the requirements in rule 4.6.39, the Islamic banking business firm concerned may recognise the SCHI, for the purpose of reducing its credit risk capital requirement, to the extent allowed by this rule.

(2) If the amount of the SCHI is less than or equal to that of the amount of the underlying obligation, the firm may treat, as covered, so much of the obligation as equals 60% of the amount of the hedge.

Guidance
For example. if the amount of the obligation is 100, and the hedge is 80, the firm may treat (60% × 80 = 48) of the obligation as covered.

(3) If the amount of the SCHI is more than that of the underlying obligation, the firm may treat no more than 60% of the amount of the obligation as covered.

Guidance
For example. if the amount of the obligation is 100, and the hedge is 120, the firm may treat (60% × 100 = 60) of the obligation as covered.

doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6.D Sharia Compliant Hedging Instruments

(1) A maturity mismatch between an exposure and the relevant credit protection exists if the residual maturity of the credit protection is shorter than the maturity of the exposure.
(2) If there is a maturity mismatch, the credit protection may be recognised only if its original maturity is 12 months or longer, and its residual maturity is 3 months or longer.

(b) for the credit protection, the Islamic banking business firm concerned must take into account any provision or incentive within the documentation that could reduce the term of the protection, so that the shortest possible effective maturity is used.

P is the value of the protection after adjustment for any haircuts.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.18 When physical assets may be eligible collateral — real estate
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.18 When physical assets may be eligible collateral — real estate
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule sets out the conditions under which an Islamic banking business firm may recognise real estate as eligible collateral in the comprehensive approach, including the criteria that such collateral must satisfy.
(2) The risk of the obligor must not be materially dependent upon the performance of the underlying property or project, but rather on the underlying capacity of the obligor to repay the debt from other sources. Repayment of the facility must not be materially dependent on cash flow generated by the collateral.

(3) The value of the collateral must not be materially dependent on the performance of the obligor.

Guidance
This requirement is not intended to apply to situations where purely macro-economic factors affect both the value of the collateral and the performance of the obligor.

(4) The collateral must meet the following requirements:

(a) any claim on the collateral must be legally enforceable in all the relevant jurisdictions, and any claim on the collateral must be properly filed on a timely basis;
(b) the firm’s interest must be a perfected lien (that is, all legal requirements for establishing the claim must have been fulfilled);
(c) the collateral agreement and the legal process underpinning it must provide for the firm to realise the value of the collateral within a reasonable timeframe;
(d) the collateral must be valued at or less than the current fair value under which the property could be sold under private contract between a willing seller and an arm’s-length buyer on the date of valuation;
(e) a junior lien may be taken into account if there is no doubt that the claim is legally enforceable and constitutes an efficient credit risk mitigant.

(5) In the case of a junior lien, the firm may use only the residual value after taking into account the collateral haircut.

Guidance
In this case, residual value is derived after deducting exposures with other pledgees, using approved limits or total outstanding amount of the exposures with other pledgees whichever is higher.

(6) The firm must monitor the value of the collateral frequently (at least annually).

Guidance
1 More frequent monitoring is suggested where the market is subject to significant changes in conditions.
2 Acceptable statistical methods of evaluation (for example reference to house price indices, sampling) may be used to update estimates or to identify collateral that may have declined in value and that may need re-appraisal.
3 A qualified professional must evaluate the property when there is reason to believe that the value of the collateral may have declined materially relative to general market prices or when a credit event, such as default, occurs.

(7) The firm must also meet the following management requirements:

(a) it must clearly document the types of collateral that it accepts, and its financing policies when this type of collateral is taken;
(b) it must take steps to ensure that property taken as collateral is adequately insured against damage or deterioration;
(c) it must continuously monitor the extent of any permissible prior claims (for example tax) on the property; and
(d) it must appropriately monitor the risk of environmental liability arising in respect of the collateral, such as the presence of toxic material on a property.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
