QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.19 When physical assets may be eligible collateral — other physical assets
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.19 When physical assets may be eligible collateral — other physical assets
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule sets out the conditions under which an Islamic banking business firm may recognise physical collateral (other than real estate) as eligible collateral in the comprehensive approach, including the criteria that such collateral must satisfy.
(2) There must be a liquid market for the disposal of the collateral in an expeditious and economically efficient manner.
(3) There must be well established, publicly available market prices for the collateral.
(4) The firm must comply with the operational requirements set out in rules 4.6.18 (6) and (7) as if those requirements applied to assets that are not real estate.
(5) The firm’s claim over the collateral must be a first lien on, or charge over, the collateral.
(6) The financing agreement must include a detailed description of the collateral and detailed specifications of the manner and frequency of its revaluation.

(7) The firm must also meet the following management requirements:

(a) its internal credit policies must clearly document the types of physical collateral that it accepts and its policies and practices in relation to the appropriate amount of each type of collateral relative to the exposure amount;
(b) that documentation must be available for examination and audit review;

(c) the firm’s credit policies must address appropriate collateral requirements in relation to:

(i) the exposure amount;
(ii) the ability to liquidate the collateral readily;
(iii) the ability to objectively establish a price or market value;
(iv) the frequency with which the value can readily be obtained (including a professional appraisal or valuation), and
(v) the volatility of the collateral’s value;
(d) the periodic revaluation process must pay particular attention to “fashion-sensitive” collateral to ensure that valuations are appropriately adjusted downward for fashion, or model-year, obsolescence as well as physical obsolescence or deterioration; and
(e) in the case of inventory (for example raw materials, finished goods, dealers’ inventories of vehicles) and equipment, the periodic revaluation process must include physical inspection of the collateral.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.20 When physical assets may be eligible collateral — leased assets
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.20 When physical assets may be eligible collateral — leased assets
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule sets out the conditions under which an Islamic banking business firm may recognise a leased asset (that is, an asset used in operating ijarah or IMB) as eligible collateral under the comprehensive approach.
(2) The asset must comply with the relevant requirements of rules 4.6.18 and 4.6.19.
(3) The firm as lessor must exercise robust risk management in relation to the location of the asset, the use to which it is put, its age, and planned obsolescence.
(4) There must be a robust legal framework establishing the lessor’s legal ownership of the asset and its ability to exercise its rights as owner in a timely manner.
(5) The difference between the rate of depreciation of the asset and the rate of amortisation of the lease payments must not be so large as to overstate the CRM attributed to the asset.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.21 When physical assets may be eligible collateral — general conditions in relation to firm’s management of collateral
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.21 When physical assets may be eligible collateral — general conditions in relation to firm’s management of collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule sets out further conditions (in relation to the management of collateral) under which an Islamic banking business firm may recognise a physical asset as eligible collateral under the comprehensive approach.
(2) The firm must collect and retain the relevant data about revaluation and disposal of physical assets as a means to recover from delinquent or defaulted exposures, particularly data on disposal amount and timeline of disposal of the physical assets and the costs incurred for the disposal.
(3) The firm must use the data to verify, at least annually, the appropriateness of the minimum 30% haircut on physical assets. The firm must apply a greater haircut if their data on the disposal of physical assets shows losses of more than the 30% haircut.
(4) The firm must conduct an independent review to find out whether it complies with the requirements of these rules in relation to recognising physical collateral as a credit risk mitigant. The firm must conduct such a review before the firm recognises the physical collateral as a credit risk mitigant and at least annually afterwards.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.24 Adjustment for different holding periods, non-daily marking to market and non-daily remarginings
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.24 Adjustment for different holding periods, non-daily marking to market and non-daily remarginings
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Subject to this rule, the minimum holding periods and conditions for the purposes of this Subdivision, set out in table 4.6.24, apply to SFTs, other capital-market transactions (such as OTC transactions in SCHIs, and margin lending) and secured lending.

Guidance
For some transactions, depending on the nature and frequency of the revaluation and remargining provisions, different holding periods and thus different haircuts must be applied. The framework for collateral haircuts distinguishes between SFTs, other capital markets-driven transactions (that is, OTC transactions in SCHIs and margin lending) and secured lending. In capital-market-driven transactions and repo-style transactions, the documentation contains remargining clauses; in secured lending transactions, it generally does not.

Table 4.6.24 Minimum holding periods and conditions

Transaction typeMinimum holding periodCondition
SFTs5 business daysDaily remargining
Other capital market transactions10 business daysDaily remargining
Secured lending20 business daysDaily revaluation
(2) However, if a netting set includes both SFTs and other capital market transactions, the minimum holding period of 10 business days must be used.

(3) Also, a minimum holding period of 20 business days must be used in the following cases:

(a) if in a quarter the number of trades in a netting set exceeds 5,000 at any time — in the next quarter;
(b) for a netting set that includes 1 or more trades involving illiquid collateral.

(4) For paragraph (3) (b), whether collateral is illiquid must be determined in the context of stressed market conditions. Collateral is illiquid if there is no continuously active market in which a counterparty would, within 2 days or less, obtain multiple price quotations that would not move the market or reflect a market discount.

Guidance
Examples of collateral that would be considered illiquid include:
• collateral that is not marked to market daily
• collateral that is subject to a particular accounting treatment for valuation purposes (for example, SFTs referencing securities whose fair value is determined by models with inputs that are not observed in the market).
(5) If on a particular netting set, over the previous 2 quarters, a banking business firm has experienced more than 2 margin call disputes that have lasted longer than the firm’s estimate of the margin period of risk (that is, the period from the last exchange of collateral covering the netting set with a defaulting counterparty until the counterparty is closed out and the resulting market risk is re-hedged) then, for the following 2 quarters, the firm must use a minimum holding period that is twice the period that would apply except for this subrule.

(6) When remargining or revaluation is undertaken less frequently than the minimum specified in table 4.6.24, the haircut that must be applied is:

where:
H+ is the haircut to be applied.
HM is the haircut under the minimum holding period.
NR is the actual number of business days between remarginings (for capital market transactions) or revaluations (for secured transactions).
TM is the minimum holding period for transactions of that type, as set out in table 4.6.24.
(7) However, the firm may apply a haircut of 0% to an SFT with a core market participant, if the transaction satisfies all of the conditions in rule 4.6.13 (5).

In capital-market-driven transactions and repo-style transactions, the documentation contains remargining clauses; in secured lending transactions, it generally does not. Table 4.6.24 Minimum holding periods and conditions Transaction type Minimum holding period Condition SFTs 5 business days Daily remargining Other capital market transactions 10 business days Daily remargining Secured lending 20 business days Daily revaluation (2) However, if a netting set includes both SFTs and other capital market transactions, the minimum holding period of 10 business days must be used. (3) Also, a minimum holding period of 20 business days must be used in the following cases: (a) if in a quarter the number of trades in a netting set exceeds 5,000 at any time — in the next quarter; (b) for a netting set that includes 1 or more trades involving illiquid collateral. (4) For paragraph (3) (b), whether collateral is illiquid must be determined in the context of stressed market conditions. Collateral is illiquid if there is no continuously active market in which a counterparty would, within 2 days or less, obtain multiple price quotations that would not move the market or reflect a market discount. Guidance Examples of collateral that would be considered illiquid include: • collateral that is not marked to market daily • collateral that is subject to a particular accounting treatment for valuation purposes (for example, SFTs referencing securities whose fair value is determined by models with inputs that are not observed in the market). (5) If on a particular netting set, over the previous 2 quarters, a banking business firm has experienced more than 2 margin call disputes that have lasted longer than the firm’s estimate of the margin period of risk (that is, the period from the last exchange of collateral covering the netting set with a defaulting counterparty until the counterparty is closed out and the resulting market risk is re-hedged) then, for the following 2 quarters, the firm must use a minimum holding period that is twice the period that would apply except for this subrule. (6) When remargining or revaluation is undertaken less frequently than the minimum specified in table 4.6.24, the haircut that must be applied is: where: H + is the haircut to be applied. H M is the haircut under the minimum holding period. N R is the actual number of business days between remarginings (for capital market transactions) or revaluations (for secured transactions). T M is the minimum holding period for transactions of that type, as set out in table 4.6.24. (7) However, the firm may apply a haircut of 0% to an SFT with a core market participant, if the transaction satisfies all of the conditions in rule 4.6.13 (5). QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.25 Treatment of maturity mismatches
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) A maturity mismatch exists between an exposure and its credit risk mitigation if the residual maturity of the term of lodgement of the credit risk mitigation is shorter than the maturity of the exposure.

(2) The maturity of the exposure and the maturity of the credit risk mitigation must both be defined conservatively. The effective maturity of the underlying must be taken to be the longest possible remaining time before the counterparty is scheduled to fulfil its obligation, taking into account any applicable grace period. For the credit risk mitigation, embedded options that may reduce the term of the credit risk mitigation must be taken into account so that the shortest possible effective maturity is used.

Guidance
For example: if, in the case of an SCHI, the protection seller has a call option, the maturity is the first call date. Likewise, if the protection buyer owns the call option and has a strong incentive to call the transaction at the first call date, for example because of a step-up in cost from that date on, the effective maturity is the remaining time to the first call date.
(3) If there is a maturity mismatch, the credit risk mitigation may be recognised only if the original maturity of its term of lodgement is 12 months or longer, and its residual maturity is 3 months or longer.

(4) For the purpose of determining the maturity of the exposure and credit risk mitigation:

(a) for the exposure, the effective maturity is taken to be the longest possible remaining time before the counterparty must fulfil its obligation; and
(b) for the credit risk mitigation, the Islamic banking business firm concerned must take into account any provision or incentive within the documentation for the transaction that could reduce the term of the credit risk mitigation, so that the shortest possible effective maturity is used.

(5) If there is a maturity mismatch, the firm must adjust the value of the credit risk mitigation as follows:

where:
Pa is the value of the credit risk mitigation, adjusted for the maturity mismatch.
P is the value of the credit risk mitigation after adjustment for any haircuts.
t is min {T, residual maturity of the credit risk mitigation arrangement}, in years.
T is min {5 years, residual maturity of the exposure}, in years.

Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.26 Treatment of currency mismatches
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) A currency mismatch exists between an exposure and its credit risk mitigation if the credit risk mitigation is denominated in a different currency from the one in which the exposure is denominated. HFX is the haircut appropriate for the currency mismatch (see subrule (2)).

(2) The haircut for a 10-business-day holding period (assuming daily marking to market) is 8%. For a longer holding period, HFX must be increased as follows:

TM is the minimum holding period for the transaction, as specified in table 4.6.24.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.45 Meaning of eligible netting agreement
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.45 Meaning of eligible netting agreement
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) A netting agreement is an eligible netting agreement if:

(a) it is in writing;
(b) it creates a single obligation covering all the transactions and collateral included in it;
(c) it provides for the netting of gains and losses on transactions (including the value of any collateral) that are terminated and closed out under it so that a single net amount is owed by one party to the other;
(d) it is legally enforceable in each relevant jurisdiction on an event of default, regardless of the counterparty’s insolvency or bankruptcy;

(e) it gives the Islamic banking business firm concerned the following rights:

(i) the right to terminate and close out, in a timely manner, all transactions under the agreement on an event of default (including the counterparty’s insolvency or bankruptcy);

(ii) the right to net the gains and losses on those transactions (including the value of any collateral) so that the firm either has a claim to receive, or an obligation to pay, only the net sum of the close-out values of the individual transactions;

Note For forward contracts, swaps, options and similar instrument transactions, this right would include the positive and negative marked to market values of the individual transactions.
(iii) the right to liquidate or set-off collateral if either party to the agreement fails to meet its obligations because of default, liquidation, bankruptcy or other similar circumstances.
(2) A netting agreement that is subject to a walkaway clause is not an eligible netting agreement.
(3) A netting agreement is not an eligible netting agreement if there is doubt about its enforceability.
(4) An Islamic banking business firm must not treat a netting agreement as an eligible netting agreement if it becomes aware that a financial services regulator of the counterparty is not satisfied that the agreement is enforceable under the law of the regulator’s jurisdiction. This subrule applies regardless of any legal opinion obtained by the firm.
(5) An eligible bilateral netting agreement is an eligible netting agreement to which there is only 2 parties.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.46 Transactions not to be selectively netted
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.46 Transactions not to be selectively netted
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm that has entered into a netting agreement must consistently net all the transactions covered by the agreement. The firm must not selectively pick which transactions to net.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.47 Transactions not covered by appropriate legal opinion not to be netted
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.47 Transactions not covered by appropriate legal opinion not to be netted
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must ensure that a transaction is not netted unless the transaction is covered by a legal opinion that satisfies rule 4.6.48.
(2) In calculating the net sum due to or from a counterparty, the firm must exclude any netted transaction for which it has not obtained a legal opinion that satisfies rule 4.6.48 and applies to the relevant jurisdiction. The firm must report such a transaction on a gross basis.

(3) The firm must report a transaction on a gross basis if:

(a) there is any doubt about the enforceability of the relevant netting agreement; or
(b) any legal development affects the agreement’s enforceability.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.48 Requirements with which legal opinions must comply
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.48 Requirements with which legal opinions must comply
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The requirements with which a legal opinion must comply are set out in subrules (2) and (3).

(2) The opinion must conclude that, in the event of default, liquidation, bankruptcy or other similar circumstances of a party to the netting agreement, the Islamic banking business firm’s claims and obligations are limited to the net sum calculated under the netting agreement in accordance with the applicable law.

Guidance
The Regulatory Authority expects the legal opinion to deal with the issue of which of the following laws applies to the netting:
• the law of the jurisdiction in which the counterparty is incorporated or formed (or, in the case of an individual, resides)
• if an overseas branch of the counterparty is involved — the law of the jurisdiction in which the branch is located
• the law that governs the individual transactions
• the law that governs any contract or agreement necessary to give effect to the netting.

(3) In particular, the opinion must conclude that, if the counterparty becomes insolvent or enters into external administration, a liquidator or administrator of the counterparty will not be able to claim a gross amount from the firm while being liable to pay only a dividend in insolvency to the firm (as separate money flows).

Guidance
In some countries, there is provision for the appointment of an administrator to a troubled bank. Under those provisions, the appointment of an administrator might not constitute a ground for triggering a netting agreement. Such provisions do not prevent the recognition of a netting agreement under this Division if the agreement can still take effect despite the bank under administration not meeting its obligations as they fall due.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.49 Firm’s use of legal opinions
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.49 Firm’s use of legal opinions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Before an Islamic banking business firm uses a legal opinion to support a netting agreement, the firm:

(a) must ensure that none of the assumptions on which the opinion is based, nor any qualification or reservation to which it is subject, is unduly restrictive;
(b) must review the assumptions about the enforceability of the agreement, and must ensure that they are specific and factual, and are adequately explained in the opinion; and
(c) must review and assess the assumptions, qualifications and omissions in the opinion to determine whether they give rise to any doubt about the enforceability of the agreement.
(2) The firm must have procedures to monitor legal developments and to ensure that its netting agreements continue to be enforceable. The firm must update the relevant legal opinions, as necessary, to ensure that the firm continues to have the sound basis referred to in rule 4.6.53 (1) (b).
(3) The firm may rely on a legal opinion obtained on a group basis by another member of its corporate group if the firm and the other member have satisfied themselves that the opinion applies to a netting agreement to which the firm is a counterparty.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.50 Relying on general legal opinions
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.50 Relying on general legal opinions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm may rely on a general legal opinion about the enforceability of netting agreements in a particular jurisdiction if the firm is satisfied that the type of netting agreement is covered by the opinion.
(2) The firm must satisfy itself that the netting agreement with a counterparty and the general legal opinion are applicable to each transaction and product type undertaken with the counterparty, and in all jurisdictions where those transactions are originated.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.51 Netting of positions across books
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.51 Netting of positions across books
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm may net positions across its banking book and trading book only if:

(a) the netted transactions are marked to market daily; and
(b) any collateral used in the transactions satisfies the criteria for eligible collateral (in either the simple approach or the comprehensive approach) in the banking book.

Note For the criteria for eligible collateral in the simple approach, see rule 4.6.12; for the criteria in the comprehensive approach, see rules 4.6.16 to 4.6.20.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.52 Monitoring and reporting of netting agreements
doc_path: IBANK 4.6.52 Monitoring and reporting of netting agreements
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must monitor its netting agreements and must report and manage:

(a) roll-off risks;
(b) exposures on a net basis; and
(c) termination risks;
for all the transactions included in a netting agreement.
(2) The firm must keep adequate records to support its use of netting agreements and to be able to report netted transactions on both gross and net bases.
(3) The firm must demonstrate that its netting policy is consistently implemented, and that its netting agreements continue to be enforceable, if the Regulatory Authority so directs.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6.53 Capital relief from netting agreements
doc_path: IBANK Subdivision 4.6.E.2 Capital relief from netting
IBANK 4.6.53 Capital relief from netting agreements
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm is able to reduce its credit risk capital requirement by means of a netting agreement with a counterparty only if:

(a) the agreement is an eligible netting agreement;
(b) the firm has a sound basis (supported by a legal opinion that satisfies rule 4.6.48) for concluding that the agreement is legally enforceable in each relevant jurisdiction, regardless of whether the counterparty is insolvent or bankrupt; and

(c) the firm:

(i) is able at any time to determine the assets and liabilities that are subject to the agreement;
(ii) monitors and controls its roll-off risks; and
(iii) monitors and controls the exposures on a net basis.

(2) Only the following kinds of transaction may be netted:

(a) financings and deposits on the firm’s balance sheet (but only if they satisfy the conditions in subrule (4));
(b) SFTs;
(c) OTC transactions in SCHIs, as set out in subrule (5).
(3) Structured deposits and restricted PSIAs may not be netted.

(4) For paragraph (2) (a), the conditions are the following:

(a) that at all times the firm is able to determine the assets and liabilities that are subject to netting under the agreement;

(b) that the deposits satisfy the criteria for eligible collateral (in either the simple or the comprehensive approach).

Note For the criteria for eligible collateral in the simple approach, see rule 4.6.12; for the criteria in the comprehensive approach, see rules 4.6.16 to 4.6.20.

(5) OTC transactions in SCHIs may be netted:

(a) across both the banking and trading books of the firm (if the netted transactions satisfy the criteria in rule 4.6.52); and
(b) across different market-related products, to the extent that the products are recognised as market-related transactions.

(5) OTC transactions in SCHIs may be netted: (a) across both the banking and trading books of the firm (if the netted transactions satisfy the criteria in rule 4.6.52 ); and (b) across different market-related products, to the extent that the products are recognised as market-related transactions. QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.1 What is counterparty credit risk?
doc_path: IBANK 4.6A.1 What is counterparty credit risk?
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Counterparty credit risk is the risk that the counterparty to a transaction could default before the final settlement of the transaction’s cash flows.
(2) Counterparty credit risk arises in certain kinds of transactions in which there is a risk of loss to both parties, because of the possibility that a party will default. In such a transaction, if either party defaults at a time when the transaction has a positive economic value to the other party, a loss to the other party results.
(3) The exposure to credit risk through a financing is one-sided — only the lender faces the risk of loss. For the kinds of transaction that create counterparty credit risk, the market value of a transaction varies over time with the movement of underlying market factors, and at a particular time can be positive or negative to either party.

(4) Therefore, both parties to such a transaction face a risk of loss.

Examples

1 A bank provides a financing to a borrower and receives collateral from the borrower.

• The borrower is exposed to the risk that the bank defaults and does not return the collateral. Even in cases where the customer has the legal right to offset the amount it owes on the financing in compensation for the lost collateral, the customer is still exposed to the risk of loss at the outset of the financing because the value of the financing may be less than the value of the collateral the time of default of the bank.

2 A bank borrows cash from a counterparty and posts collateral to the counterparty (or undertakes a transaction that is economically equivalent, such as the sale and repurchase (repo) of a security).

• The bank is exposed to the risk that its counterparty defaults and does not return the collateral that the bank posted.
• The counterparty is exposed to the risk that the bank defaults and the amount the counterparty raises from the sale of the collateral that the bank posted is insufficient to cover the loss on the counterparty’s financing to the bank.

3 A bank borrows a security from a counterparty and posts cash to the counterparty as collateral (or undertakes a transaction that is economically equivalent, such as a reverse repo).

• The bank is exposed to the risk that its counterparty defaults and does not return the cash that the bank posted as collateral.
• The counterparty is exposed to the risk that the bank defaults and the cash that the bank posted as collateral is insufficient to cover the loss of the security that the bank borrowed.

4 A bank enters a transaction in an SCHI with a counterparty (for example, it enters a swap transaction or purchases an option). The value of the transaction may vary over time with the movement of underlying market factors.

• The bank is exposed to the risk that the counterparty defaults when the SCHI has a positive value for the bank.
• The counterparty is exposed to the risk that the bank defaults when the SCHI has a positive value for the counterparty.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.2 Transactions that Part 4.6A applies to
doc_path: IBANK 4.6A.2 Transactions that Part 4.6A applies to
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This Part applies to transactions of the following kinds, whether in the banking book or the trading book, and whether or not settled in cash:

(a) OTC transactions in SCHIs;
(b) exchange-traded SCHIs;
(c) long settlement transactions;
(d) SFTs.
Guidance

1 The transactions referred to in subrule (1) generally have the following characteristics:

• they generate a current exposure or market value
• their future market value is uncertain or unknown, but is affected by market variables
• they generate an exchange of future payments, or an exchange of a financial instrument (or commodities) against payment
• they are with an identified counterparty for which a unique probability of default can be determined.

2 Those transactions often have the following characteristics also:

• collateral may be used to mitigate the risk exposure and is inherent in some transactions
• short-term financing may be a main purpose, in that the transactions mostly consist of an exchange of one asset (cash or securities) for another for a relatively short period, usually for the business purpose of financing; the two sides of the transactions are not the result of separate decisions but form an indivisible whole for a particular purpose
• netting may be used to mitigate the risk
• positions are frequently valued (most commonly daily), according to market variables
• remargining may be employed.
Note Long settlement transaction and SFT (securities financing transaction) are defined in the glossary.

(2) An Islamic banking business firm must calculate counterparty credit risk charges for:

(a) all bilateral transactions (see Division 4.6A.B);
(b) all centrally cleared transactions (see Division 4.6A.C); and
(c) default fund contributions to QCCPs (see Division 4.6A.D), if any.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.3 Capital requirements for counterparty credit risk
doc_path: IBANK 4.6A.3 Capital requirements for counterparty credit risk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm that engages in certain classes of transactions that expose it to counterparty credit risk must hold sufficient regulatory capital to cover the counterparty credit risk that arises from those transactions.

(2) An Islamic banking business firm’s capital requirement for counterparty credit risk is made up of the following:

(a) the firm’s risk-weighted assets for counterparty credit risk, which is the sum of the following:

(i) the firm’s risk-weighted assets representing credit exposures for counterparty credit default risk (“default risk RWA”);
(ii) the firm’s risk-weighted assets representing credit exposures for counterparty credit default risk arising from trade exposures to a CCP (“trade exposure RWA”); and
(iii) the firm’s risk-weighted assets representing credit exposure arising from a default fund contribution to a non-qualifying CCP (“default fund RWA”);
(b) any applicable credit valuation adjustment (CVA) risk capital charge;
(c) any applicable default fund capital charge for any default fund contributions to a QCCP.
Note The amount of the firm’s total risk-weighted assets for counterparty credit risk is part of the amount of its total risk-weighted assets for credit risk (see rule 4.1.4). The firm’s total risk-weighted assets for credit risk is its credit risk capital requirement, which is part of its risk-based capital requirement (see rule 3.2.5).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.4 Policies — foreign exchange rollovers
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must have policies for entering into and monitoring rollovers on foreign exchange transactions. The policies must restrict the firm’s capacity to enter into such rollovers, and must have been approved by the Regulatory Authority.
(2) The firm must notify the Authority if it enters into a rollover outside the approved policy. The Authority may direct how the rollover is to be treated for capital adequacy purposes.
(3) The firm must not enter into a transaction at an off-market price, unless the transaction is a historical rate rollover on a foreign exchange transaction.
(4) A historical rate rollover on a foreign exchange transaction may be entered into at an off-market price (instead of current market price).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.5 Methods for calculating counterparty credit risk exposures
doc_path: IBANK 4.6A.5 Methods for calculating counterparty credit risk exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Division 4.6A.B sets out the modified current exposure method (or modified CEM) for calculating an Islamic banking business firm’s default risk RWA. Subject to subrule (2), such a firm must use that method.

(2) The Regulatory Authority may direct an Islamic banking business firm to use the SA-CCR, or approve such a firm’s use of that method, to calculate its counterparty credit risk capital requirement (or any part of that requirement).

Guidance
The Authority might direct an Islamic banking business firm to use the SA-CCR if:
• at the end date of each of the 4 consecutive financial reporting periods (both interim and annual) immediately preceding the date on which the calculation of the CCR exposure is performed, the total notional amount of the firm’s outstanding SCHI contracts (regardless of whether the contracts are recorded as assets or liabilities) does not exceed 10% of the aggregate of its total assets and total liabilities reported in its financial statements
• the Authority considers that the use by the firm of the modified current exposure method would not adequately assess and reflect the firm’s CCR exposure, taking into account the nature of the firm’s business.
(3) If the Authority grants an approval or gives a direction under this rule, the Authority may specify parameters or formulas to be used, or assumptions to be made, in applying the SA-CCR.

(4) In this rule:

SA-CCR means the method of calculating counterparty credit risk exposure set out in the document CRE52: Standardised approach to counterparty credit risk, as issued by the BCBS and in force from time to time.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.7 Capital requirements to be calculated
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.B Modified current exposure method
IBANK 4.6A.7 Capital requirements to be calculated
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For bilateral OTC transactions in SCHIs, an Islamic banking business firm must calculate each of the following counterparty credit risk requirements:

(a) default risk RWA, which reflects the potential loss arising from a default of a counterparty; and
(b) a CVA risk capital charge.

(2) For bilateral SFTs, an Islamic banking business firm must calculate the default risk RWA. To determine default risk RWA for SFTs, the firm:

(a) must calculate the counterparty credit risk exposure amount as the sum of:

(i) the exposure amount for each SFT that is not covered by an eligible netting agreement; and
(ii) the exposure amount for all SFTs covered by an eligible netting agreement;
in accordance with Part 4.6; and
Note 1 Eligible netting agreement is defined in the glossary.
Note 2 In relation to how eligible netting agreements are to be applied for the purposes of this Division, see Subdivision 4.6.E.1.
(b) must apply the appropriate risk weight in accordance with Division 4.4.B.

(3) Bilateral SFTs are not subject to a CVA risk capital charge unless the Regulatory Authority determines that the relevant Islamic banking business firm’s CVA loss exposure arising from SFTs is material, and directs the firm to apply a CVA risk capital charge:

(a) of a specified amount; or
(b) calculated in a specified way.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.8 Default risk RWA for OTC transactions in SCHIs
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.B Modified current exposure method
IBANK 4.6A.8 Default risk RWA for OTC transactions in SCHIs
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) To determine the default risk RWA for OTC transactions in SCHIs, an Islamic banking business firm must calculate a counterparty credit risk exposure amount, and must apply to it the relevant risk weight, determined as set out in Division 4.4.B.

(2) The counterparty credit risk exposure amount is the credit equivalent amount (CEA) for all OTC transactions in SCHIs with a particular counterparty, calculated by adding together:

(a) for each transaction not covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement — the transaction-level CEA calculated as set out in subrule 4.6A.9 (2); and

Note In relation to how eligible netting agreements may be applied for the purposes of this Division, see Subdivision 4.6.E.1.
(b) for transactions that are covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement — the CEA calculated by the method set out in subrule 4.6A.9 (3);
and adjusting the sum for eligible collateral (within the extended meaning given by rule 4.6.16).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.9 Calculating credit equivalent amount
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.B Modified current exposure method
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If a transaction is secured by eligible collateral or is covered by an eligible guarantee, eligible credit SCHI or eligible netting agreement, a CRM technique (see Part 4.6) may be used to reduce the amount of the relevant firm’s exposure.

(2) CEA for transactions that are not covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement is calculated as follows:

(a) for margined transactions — by the formula:

CEA = CCE + PFE

(b) for unmargined transactions — by the formula:

CEA = CCE + (3 × PFE)
where:
CCE is the current credit exposure, calculated as the sum of the positive mark-to-market value (or replacement cost) of the transactions.
PFE is the potential future credit exposure of the transactions, determined in accordance with rules 4.6A.10 and 4.6A.12.

(3) CEA for OTC transactions in SCHIs that are covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement is calculated as follows:

(a) for a netting agreement covering only margined transactions — by the formula:

CEA = NCCE + PFEadj

(b) for a netting agreement covering only unmargined transactions — by the formula:

CEA = NCCE + [3 × (PFEadj)]

(c) for a netting agreement covering both margined and unmargined transactions — by either the formula in paragraph (b) or the formula:

CEA = NCCE + [(1 + 2 × A) × (PFEadj)]
where:
NCCE has the meaning given by subrule (4).

A is:

PFEadj is the add-on for PFE based on the notional principal of all the individual underlying contracts (that is, the gross PFE (PFEgross) adjusted to reflect the effects of the netting agreement).
Note For how to calculate PFEadj, see rules 4.6A.12 and 4.6A.13. For PFEgross, see rule 4.6A.12 (2).
(4) For subrule (3), NCCE is the net current credit exposure of all the transactions covered by the relevant netting agreement, calculated as the sum of all the positive and negative mark-to-market values of all the contracts covered by the netting agreement (that is, transactions with positive mark-to-market values may be offset against transactions with negative mark-to-market values). If the net sum of the mark-to-market values is positive, NCCE is equal to that sum, and if the net sum is zero or negative, NCCE is taken to be zero.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: (1) If a transaction is secured by eligible collateral or is covered by an eligible guarantee, eligible credit SCHI or eligible netting agreement, a CRM technique (see Part 4.6 ) may be used to reduce the amount of the relevant firm’s exposure. (2) CEA for transactions that are not covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement is calculated as follows: (a) for margined transactions — by the formula: CEA = CCE + PFE (b) for unmargined transactions — by the formula: CEA = CCE + ( 3 × PFE) where: CCE is the current credit exposure, calculated as the sum of the positive mark-to-market value (or replacement cost) of the transactions. PFE is the potential future credit exposure of the transactions, determined in accordance with rules 4.6A.10 and 4.6A.12 . (3) CEA for OTC transactions in SCHIs that are covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement is calculated as follows: (a) for a netting agreement covering only margined transactions — by the formula: CEA = NCCE + PFE adj (b) for a netting agreement covering only unmargined transactions — by the formula: CEA = NCCE + [3 × (PFE adj )] (c) for a netting agreement covering both margined and unmargined transactions — by either the formula in paragraph (b) or the formula: CEA = NCCE + [(1 + 2 × A ) × ( PFE adj )] where: NCCE has the meaning given by subrule (4). A is: PFE adj is the add-on for PFE based on the notional principal of all the individual underlying contracts (that is, the gross PFE ( PFE gross ) adjusted to reflect the effects of the netting agreement). Note For how to calculate PFE adj , see rules 4.6A.12 and 4.6A.13 . For PFE gross , see rule 4.6A.12 (2). (4) For subrule (3), NCCE is the net current credit exposure of all the transactions covered by the relevant netting agreement, calculated as the sum of all the positive and negative mark-to-market values of all the contracts covered by the netting agreement (that is, transactions with positive mark-to-market values may be offset against transactions with negative mark-to-market values). If the net sum of the mark-to-market values is positive, NCCE is equal to that sum, and if the net sum is zero or negative, NCCE is taken to be zero. Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

endnotes: Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.10 Calculating PFE — transactions not covered by eligible bilateral netting agreement
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.B Modified current exposure method
IBANK 4.6A.10 Calculating PFE — transactions not covered by eligible bilateral netting agreement
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) To calculate PFE for a transaction that is not covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement, an Islamic banking business firm must multiply the notional principal amount of the transaction by the relevant credit conversion factor (CCF) specified in table 4.6A.10. The notional (or nominal) principal amount of a contract is the reference amount used to calculate payment streams between the counterparties.

Note In relation to how eligible netting agreements may be applied for the purposes of this Division, see Subdivision 4.6.E.1.

Table 4.6A.10 Modified CEM — market-related CCFs

ItemDescription of claim or assetCCF (%)
1Profit rate contracts:
 •    residual maturity 1 year or less0
 •    residual maturity > 1 year to 5 years0.5
 •    residual maturity > 5 years1.5
2Foreign exchange and gold contracts:
 •    residual maturity 1 year or less1
 •    residual maturity > 1 year to 5 years5
 •    residual maturity > 5 years7.5
3Equity contracts:
 •    residual maturity 1 year or less6
 •    residual maturity > 1 year to 5 years8
 •    residual maturity > 5 years10
4Precious metal contracts (other than gold):
 •    residual maturity 1 year or less7
 •    residual maturity > 1 year to 5 years7
 •    residual maturity > 5 years8
5Other commodity contracts (other than precious metals):
 •    residual maturity 1 year or less10
 •    residual maturity > 1 year to 5 years12
 •    residual maturity > 5 years15
6Other market-related contracts:
 •    residual maturity 1 year or less10
 •    residual maturity > 1 year to 5 years12
 •    residual maturity > 5 years15
(2) PFE must be based on effective rather than apparent notional amounts. If the stated notional amount of a contract is leveraged or enhanced by the structure of the transaction, the firm must use the effective notional amount when calculating PFE.
(3) No PFE is calculated for single currency floating/floating interest rate swaps because the credit exposure on such contracts must be evaluated solely on the basis of their mark-to-market values.

(4) For contracts that are structured to settle outstanding exposures following specified payment dates on which the terms are reset (so that the mark-to-market value of the contract is zero on the specified dates), the residual maturity must be set equal to the time until the next reset date. In the case of interest rate contracts with those features and a remaining maturity of more than 1 year, the CCF is subject to a minimum of 0.5% even if there are reset dates of a shorter maturity.

Guidance
For example, a principal resetting cross-currency swap or a settled-to-market SCHI where, at the next reset date, the outstanding exposure is settled and the terms are reset so that the fair value of the contract is zero. An SCHI contract with a mandatory break (where there is a legal contractual obligation on both parties to terminate the transaction by the mandatory break date) would also be eligible where the outstanding exposure is settled completely.
(5) For a contract with 2 or more exchanges of principal, the CCF must be multiplied by the number of exchanges of principal still to be made.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.11 CCFs for items with terms subject to reset
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.B Modified current exposure method
IBANK 4.6A.11 CCFs for items with terms subject to reset
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For an item that is structured to settle outstanding exposures after specified payment dates on which the terms are reset (that is, the marked to market value of the item becomes zero on the specified dates), the period to the next reset date must be taken to be the item’s residual maturity.
(2) For an interest rate item of that kind that is taken to have a residual maturity of more than 1 year, the CCF to be applied must not be less than 0.5% even if there are reset dates of a shorter maturity.
(3) For an item with 2 or more exchanges of principal, the CCF must be multiplied by the number of remaining exchanges under the item.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.13 Calculating PFEadj — transactions covered by eligible bilateral netting agreements — net to gross ratio
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.B Modified current exposure method
IBANK 4.6A.13 Calculating PFEadj — transactions covered by eligible bilateral netting agreements — net to gross ratio
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The net to gross ratio (NGR) is the ratio of the net current exposure of all the transactions covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement to the gross current credit exposure (GCCE) of those transactions. GCCE for such a netting agreement is the sum of the mark-to-market values of all the transactions covered by the agreement (except transactions covered by the definition of NCCE in subrule 4.6A.9(4)) with a positive mark-to-market value, with no offsetting against contracts with a negative mark-to-market value.

Note In relation to how eligible netting agreements may be applied for the purposes of this Division, see Subdivision 4.6.E.1.

(2) NGR reflects the risk-reducing portfolio effects of netted transactions in relation to current credit exposure:

(3) NGR may be calculated either counterparty-by-counterparty or in the aggregate.
(4) An Islamic banking business firm must consistently use either the counterparty-by-counterparty approach or the aggregate approach to calculate NGR¸ and must notify the Regulatory Authority of the approach that it intends to use.
(5) In the counterparty-by-counterparty approach, a unique NGR is applied to each counterparty to calculate the CEA of transactions with that counterparty. NGR is the NCCE of all transactions with an individual counterparty covered by an eligible bilateral netting agreement (that is, NCCEindividual) divided by the GCCE of all the transactions with that counterparty covered by the netting agreement (that is, GCCEindividual).
(6) In the aggregate approach, a single NGR is calculated and applied to all counterparties to calculate CEA for transactions with each of those counterparties. NGR is the ratio of the sum of all NCCEs of all transactions with all counterparties subject to any eligible bilateral netting agreement (that is, NCCEaggregate) to the sum of all of the GCCEs for all transactions of all counterparties subject to such a netting agreement (that is, GCCEaggregate).
(7) In calculating GCCEindividual or GCCEaggregate, negative mark-to-market values of transactions with a counterparty cannot be used to offset positive mark-to-market values of transactions with that counterparty or any other counterparty included in the aggregate calculations.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

(3) In table 4.6A.14:

qualifying reference obligation includes an obligation arising from items relating to:

(4) An Islamic banking business firm, in calculating the counterparty credit risk requirement for an nth-to-default credit SCHI transaction (such as a first-to-default transaction), must use the add-on determined by the nth-lowest credit quality underlying asset in the relevant basket.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.17 CVA risk capital charge to be calculated
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.B Modified current exposure method
IBANK 4.6A.17 CVA risk capital charge to be calculated
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must calculate its CVA risk capital charge for the risk of mark-to-market losses on the expected counterparty credit risk (CVA loss) for:

(a) all bilateral OTC transactions in SCHIs; and
(b) centrally cleared transactions that are required to be treated as bilateral.
(2) Subject to any direction under subrule (3) or approval under subrule (4), the firm must set its CVA risk capital charge equal to the amount of capital required for its risk-weighted credit exposure for counterparty credit default risk.

(3) The Regulatory Authority may direct an Islamic banking business firm to apply a CVA risk capital charge:

(a) of a specified amount; or
(b) that is calculated in a specified way.
(4) An Islamic banking business firm may apply to the Authority for approval to determine its CVA risk capital requirement in accordance with the Basel III Framework, as in effect from time to time.
(5) If the Authority grants an approval under subrule (4), the Authority may specify parameters or formulas to be used, or assumptions to be made, in applying the framework.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.19 Transactions that Division 4.6A.C applies to
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.19 Transactions that Division 4.6A.C applies to
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This Division applies to all transactions that are centrally cleared (including OTC transactions in SCHIs, exchange-traded transactions in such instruments, SFTs and long settlement transactions).

Note Long settlement transaction and SFT (securities financing transaction) are defined in the glossary.
(2) For the purposes of this Division, a long settlement transaction must be treated as an OTC transaction in an SCHI.
(3) Transactions that result in exposures arising from the settlement of cash transactions only (for example, equities, fixed income, spot foreign exchange and spot commodities) are not subject to the treatment in this Subdivision.

(4) For transactions cleared through a QCCP, an Islamic banking business firm must apply:

(a) the counterparty credit risk requirements for exposures to a QCCP and the firm’s clients in rules 4.6A.26 to 4.6A.36; and
(b) the risk management requirements in rule 4.6A.40.

(5) For transactions cleared through a CCP that is not a QCCP, an Islamic banking business firm must apply:

(a) the counterparty credit risk requirements for exposures to a non-qualifying CCP in rule 4.6A.37; and
(b) the risk management requirements in rule 4.6A.40.
(6) If a CCP ceases to qualify as a QCCP, then, for the purposes of this Division, an Islamic banking business firm may continue, for 3 months afterwards, to treat transactions with the CCP as though the CCP were still a QCCP (subject to any direction by the Regulatory Authority). After that period, the firm must treat exposures to the CCP according to rule 4.6A.37.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

(2) For the purposes of this Division, a long settlement transaction must be treated as an OTC transaction in an SCHI. (3) Transactions that result in exposures arising from the settlement of cash transactions only (for example, equities, fixed income, spot foreign exchange and spot commodities) are not subject to the treatment in this Subdivision. (4) For transactions cleared through a QCCP, an Islamic banking business firm must apply: (a) the counterparty credit risk requirements for exposures to a QCCP and the firm’s clients in rules 4.6A.26 to 4.6A.36 ; and (b) the risk management requirements in rule 4.6A.40 . (5) For transactions cleared through a CCP that is not a QCCP, an Islamic banking business firm must apply: (a) the counterparty credit risk requirements for exposures to a non-qualifying CCP in rule 4.6A.37 ; and (b) the risk management requirements in rule 4.6A.40 . (6) If a CCP ceases to qualify as a QCCP, then, for the purposes of this Division, an Islamic banking business firm may continue, for 3 months afterwards, to treat transactions with the CCP as though the CCP were still a QCCP (subject to any direction by the Regulatory Authority). After that period, the firm must treat exposures to the CCP according to rule 4.6A.37 . Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

endnotes: Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.20 Key concept — qualifying CCP
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) A qualifying central counterparty (or qualifying CCP or QCCP) is an entity for which all of the following are true:

(a) it is authorised or licensed to operate as a CCP (including a licence granted by way of confirming an exemption);
(b) it is permitted by a financial regulator to operate as a CCP with respect to the products offered;
(c) it satisfies either subrule (2) or subrule (3);

(d) it publishes sufficient information about the factors necessary to calculate its regulatory capital:

(i) to allow each of its clearing members to calculate the member’s capital requirement for the member’s contributions to the CCP’s default fund; and
(ii) for the regulatory authority that supervises such a member to review and confirm that calculation.

(2) A CCP satisfies this subrule if it is based and prudentially supervised in a jurisdiction in which the relevant regulatory authority:

(a) has established rules and regulations that are consistent with the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures issued jointly, under that title, by the Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures of the BCBS and the International Organization of Securities Commissions; and
(b) has publicly indicated that it applies those rules and regulations to the CCP on a continuing basis.
(3) A CCP satisfies this subrule if the Regulatory Authority has determined, by notice published on an approved website, that the CCP satisfies the Principles mentioned in paragraph (2) (a).
(4) A non-qualifying CCP is a CCP that is not a QCCP.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.21 Key concept — margin
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) In this Division:

initial margin is the funded collateral posted to a CCP by a clearing member or client to mitigate the CCP’s potential future exposure to the member or client (including collateral in excess of the minimum required amount, but only if there are appropriate arrangements to prevent the clearing member or client withdrawing the excess).
Guidance
Initial margin does not include a contribution to a CCP for a mutualised loss-sharing arrangement (a default fund contribution).
variation margin is funded collateral posted on a daily or intraday basis to a CCP to mitigate movements in ongoing mark-to-market exposure.

(2) For this Division:

(a) a transaction is considered to be margined if variation margin is exchanged; and
(b) a transaction is considered to be unmargined if no variation margin is exchanged;
whether or not there is collateral other than variation margin.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.22 Key concept — trade exposure
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) A trade exposure is an exposure that a clearing member, or a client of a clearing member, has to a CCP, reflecting a measure of the current mark-to-market value (replacement cost) and the potential future exposure arising from transactions to which this Part applies (see rule 4.6A.2 (1)).
(2) Trade exposure is calculated on a bilateral basis, and must include the initial margin posted by an Islamic banking business firm, and any variation margin due to the firm from the CCP that has not yet been received.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.23 Other definitions for Division 4.6A.C
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) In this Division:

clearing member of a CCP means a member of, or a direct participant in, a CCP that is entitled to enter into transactions with the CCP.
clearing member firm means an Islamic banking business firm that is a clearing member of a CCP.
client of a clearing member firm means a party to a transaction with a CCP through the firm, where the firm either:
(a) acts as a financial intermediary; or
(b) guarantees the client’s performance to the CCP.

(2) An Islamic banking business firm is a client firm if:

(a) the firm clears through a QCCP indirectly as a client of a clearing member that acts as a financial intermediary (that is, the clearing member completes an offsetting transaction with the QCCP); or
(b) the firm enters into a transaction with a QCCP, and a clearing member guarantees the firm’s performance.

(3) In this Division, a reference to collateral posted by an Islamic banking business firm to a QCCP includes:

(a) initial margin;
(b) any variation margin due to the firm from the QCCP but not yet received;
(c) cash, securities, and other pledged assets; and
(d) any excess initial or variation margin;
but does not include any default fund contribution.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

(2) An Islamic banking business firm is a client firm if: (a) the firm clears through a QCCP indirectly as a client of a clearing member that acts as a financial intermediary (that is, the clearing member completes an offsetting transaction with the QCCP); or (b) the firm enters into a transaction with a QCCP, and a clearing member guarantees the firm’s performance. QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.24 Transactions settled to market
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm may treat a transaction as settled-to-market, and as being an unmargined transaction with remaining maturity (Mi) equal to the time until the next exchange of variation margin, if:

(a) the outstanding exposure is settled by variation margin and the terms are reset so that the fair value of the contract is zero; and
(b) the firm has a legal opinion to support that treatment.
Guidance
A centrally cleared transaction in an SCHI is said to have been settled-to-market if the variation margin paid constitutes settlement of the exposure, as opposed to the posting of collateral.
(2) However, the remaining maturity (Mi) of an unmargined transaction is subject to a minimum of 10 business days.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.25 Centrally cleared transactions under bilateral agreements
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.25 Centrally cleared transactions under bilateral agreements
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
For an exchange-traded SCHI where the transaction between the clearing member and client is conducted under a bilateral agreement, an Islamic banking business firm that is either a clearing member firm or a client firm must treat the transaction as an OTC transaction in an SCHI for the purposes of this Subdivision.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.26 Exposures from transactions cleared through QCCP
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.26 Exposures from transactions cleared through QCCP
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For transactions cleared through a QCCP, a clearing member firm must calculate each of the following counterparty credit risk requirements:

(a) trade exposure RWA on the firm’s trade exposure to the QCCP according to rules 4.6A.27 to 4.6A.32;
(b) a default fund capital charge on the default fund contribution to the QCCP, according to Division 4.6A.D;
(c) if the firm has provided a guarantee of a client transaction to the QCCP or acts as a financial intermediary between a client and the QCCP (that is, the firm completes an offsetting transaction with the QCCP) — default risk RWA and a CVA risk capital charge on the counterparty credit risk exposure to its client, according to rule 4.6A.33;
(d) if the firm has provided a guarantee to a client by undertaking an obligation to reimburse the client for any losses suffered due to changes in transaction value if a QCCP defaults — trade exposure RWA and a default fund capital charge on the guaranteed transaction.
(2) An Islamic banking business firm that is acting as a client of a clearing member to a QCCP must apply the counterparty credit risk requirements set out in rule 4.6A.34.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.27 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.27 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) To calculate trade exposure RWA, a clearing member firm must calculate its trade exposure to the QCCP, and must apply the relevant risk weights, according to subrules (2) and (3) and rules 4.6A.28 to 4.6A.32.

(2) For the clearing member firm-to-QCCP leg of a transaction cleared through a QCCP, a clearing member firm must calculate its trade exposure to the QCCP in accordance with:

(a) for transactions in SCHIs — the modified CEM set out in Division 4.6A.B; and
(b) for SFTs —rule 4.6A.7 (2).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.28 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — use of netting
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.28 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — use of netting
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) When a clearing member firm calculates its trade exposure to a QCCP, the firm may take a netting agreement (including a master netting agreement or a netting contract with a counterparty) into account if the agreement is an eligible bilateral netting agreement.

Guidance
If the agreement is an eligible bilateral netting agreement, settlement is legally enforceable on a net basis in an event of default regardless of whether the counterparty is insolvent or bankrupt.
Note In relation to how eligible netting agreements may be applied for the purposes of this Division, see Subdivision 4.6.E.1.
(2) If a clearing member firm cannot demonstrate that a netting agreement meets the requirements in subrule (1), it must treat each single transaction with the QCCP as a netting set of its own for the calculation of trade exposure.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.29 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — use of collateral
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.29 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — use of collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If a clearing member firm first collects collateral from a client for a client-cleared trade and then passes that collateral on to a QCCP, the firm may recognise the collateral for both the QCCP-to-firm leg and the firm-to-client leg of the transaction.

Note For the meaning of references in this Division to collateral posted to a QCCP, see rule 4.6A.23 (3).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.30 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — transactions for own purposes
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.30 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — transactions for own purposes
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If a clearing member firm is transacting with a QCCP for its own purposes, the firm must apply a 2% risk weight to its trade exposure to the QCCP (excluding any posted collateral that is eligible for a zero risk weight under rule 4.6A.36 (3)).

Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.31 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — clearing services to clients
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.31 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — clearing services to clients
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If a clearing member firm offers clearing services to clients, the firm must apply a 2% risk weight to any trade exposure to the QCCP (excluding any posted collateral that is eligible for a zero risk weight under rule 4.6A.36 (3)) that arises from an obligation to reimburse a client for any losses suffered because of changes in transaction value in the event that the QCCP defaults.

doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.32 Trade exposure RWA for clearing member firm’s exposure to QCCP — use of collateral
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
The risk weight applied to any collateral posted by a clearing member firm to a QCCP that is included in the definition of trade exposure (see rule 4.6A.22) must be determined in accordance with rule 4.6A.36.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.33 Clearing member firm’s exposure to clients
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.33 Clearing member firm’s exposure to clients
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
For the firm-to-client leg of a transaction with a QCCP, a clearing member firm must calculate its default risk RWA and CVA risk capital charge on its exposures to its clients, as set out in Division 4.6A.B.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.34 Client firm’s exposure to clearing member firm and QCCP
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.34 Client firm’s exposure to clearing member firm and QCCP
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
A client firm of a clearing member firm:

(a) must calculate a trade exposure to the clearing member firm or QCCP, as the case may be, using the modified CEM (see Division 4.6A.B); and
(b) must assign a risk weight to the trade exposure according to the requirements in rule 4.6A.35.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.34 Client firm’s exposure to clearing member firm and QCCP
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.35 Client firm’s trade exposure to clearing member — risk weight
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.35 Client firm’s trade exposure to clearing member — risk weight
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) A client firm must treat its trade exposure to a clearing member (excluding any posted collateral that is eligible for a zero risk weight under rule 4.6A.36 (3)) as if it were a clearing member firm’s trade exposure to the QCCP, and must apply the requirements set out in rules 4.6A.27 to 4.6A.30, if the following conditions are satisfied:

(a) the QCCP identifies the offsetting transactions as client transactions, and the collateral to support them is held in a way that would prevent any losses to the firm in the event of the default or insolvency of the clearing member concerned or any 1 or more of the clearing member’s other clients;
(b) the collateral to support the offsetting transactions is held in a way that would prevent any losses to the firm in the event of the joint default or insolvency of the clearing member and any of its other clients; and

(c) the relevant laws, regulation, rules, or contractual or administrative arrangements provide that offsetting transactions with a clearing member are highly likely to continue to be indirectly transacted through the QCCP, or by the QCCP, if that member defaults or becomes insolvent.

Guidance
In such circumstances, the client positions and collateral with the QCCP will be transferred at market value unless the client firm requests to close out the position at market value.
Note For the meaning of references in this Division to collateral posted to a QCCP, see rule 4.6A.23 (3).

(2) For paragraph (1) (a):

(a) the firm must have obtained a legal opinion, and must obtain any subsequent opinions it considers necessary, to ensure that the arrangements continue to be enforceable; and
(b) the firm must have a well-founded basis to conclude that, in the event of legal challenge, the relevant courts and administrative authorities would find the arrangements to be legal, valid, binding and enforceable under the laws of the relevant jurisdictions.

(3) If only paragraphs (1) (a) and (c) are satisfied, the firm must apply a risk weight of 4% to its calculated trade exposure to the QCCP (excluding any posted collateral that is eligible for a zero risk weight under rule 4.6A.36 (3)). The applicable risk weight on collateral posted by the firm that is included in the definition of trade exposure must be determined according to rule 4.6A.36.

Note For that definition, see rule 4.6A.22.
(4) In any other case, the firm must treat the exposure as bilateral for the purposes of the counterparty credit risk requirements.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: (1) A client firm must treat its trade exposure to a clearing member (excluding any posted collateral that is eligible for a zero risk weight under rule 4.6A.36 (3)) as if it were a clearing member firm’s trade exposure to the QCCP, and must apply the requirements set out in rules 4.6A.27 to 4.6A.30 , if the following conditions are satisfied: (a) the QCCP identifies the offsetting transactions as client transactions, and the collateral to support them is held in a way that would prevent any losses to the firm in the event of the default or insolvency of the clearing member concerned or any 1 or more of the clearing member’s other clients; (b) the collateral to support the offsetting transactions is held in a way that would prevent any losses to the firm in the event of the joint default or insolvency of the clearing member and any of its other clients; and (c) the relevant laws, regulation, rules, or contractual or administrative arrangements provide that offsetting transactions with a clearing member are highly likely to continue to be indirectly transacted through the QCCP, or by the QCCP, if that member defaults or becomes insolvent. Guidance In such circumstances, the client positions and collateral with the QCCP will be transferred at market value unless the client firm requests to close out the position at market value. Note For the meaning of references in this Division to collateral posted to a QCCP, see rule 4.6A.23 (3). (2) For paragraph (1) (a): (a) the firm must have obtained a legal opinion, and must obtain any subsequent opinions it considers necessary, to ensure that the arrangements continue to be enforceable; and (b) the firm must have a well-founded basis to conclude that, in the event of legal challenge, the relevant courts and administrative authorities would find the arrangements to be legal, valid, binding and enforceable under the laws of the relevant jurisdictions. (3) If only paragraphs (1) (a) and (c) are satisfied, the firm must apply a risk weight of 4% to its calculated trade exposure to the QCCP (excluding any posted collateral that is eligible for a zero risk weight under rule 4.6A.36 (3)). The applicable risk weight on collateral posted by the firm that is included in the definition of trade exposure must be determined according to rule 4.6A.36 . Note For that definition, see rule 4.6A.22 . (4) In any other case, the firm must treat the exposure as bilateral for the purposes of the counterparty credit risk requirements.
