QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.36 Exposures arising from collateral posted to QCCP — risk weight
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.36 Exposures arising from collateral posted to QCCP — risk weight
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an Islamic banking business firm has posted collateral to a QCCP (but is not is a clearing member of the QCCP), the firm must risk-weight those assets in accordance with the banking book or trading book treatment that would apply to the assets if they had not been posted as collateral.

Note For the meaning of references in this Division to collateral posted to a QCCP, see rule 4.6A.23 (3).

(2) In addition, the posted assets or collateral are subject to counterparty credit risk requirements regardless of whether they are in the banking or the trading book. For collateral posted by a clearing member firm to a QCCP, the firm:

(a) may apply a zero risk weight to all posted collateral that is held by a custodian if the collateral is bankruptcy-remote from the QCCP;, and
(b) must apply a 2% risk weight to all posted collateral held by the QCCP that is not held in a bankruptcy-remote way.
Guidance
A custodian might be a trustee, agent, pledgee, secured creditor or any other person that holds the collateral in a way that does not give the person a beneficial interest in the collateral and would not result in its being subject to legally-enforceable claims by the person’s creditors, or to a court-ordered stay of the return of the collateral, if the person becomes insolvent or bankrupt.

(3) For collateral posted by a client firm to a QCCP, the firm:

(a) may apply a zero risk weight to all posted collateral that is held by a custodian if the collateral is bankruptcy-remote from:

(i) the QCCP;
(ii) the relevant clearing member; and
(iii) the clearing member’s other clients;

(b) must apply a 2% risk weight to all posted collateral held by the QCCP if:

(i) the collateral is not bankruptcy-remote from the QCCP, but
(ii) all of the conditions in paragraphs 4.6A.35 (1) (a), (b) and (c) are satisfied; and

(c) must apply a 4% risk weight to all posted collateral held by the QCCP if:

(i) the collateral is not bankruptcy-remote from the QCCP; and
(ii) only the conditions in paragraphs 4.6A.35 (1) (a) and (c) are satisfied.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.37 Exposures arising from transactions cleared through non-qualifying CCP
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.37 Exposures arising from transactions cleared through non-qualifying CCP
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
For transactions with a non-qualifying CCP, an Islamic banking business firm:

(a) must calculate its trade exposure RWA for:

(i) its trade exposure to the CCP (including any exposure that arises because it has guaranteed a client trade); and
(ii) any exposure to its clients;
in accordance with Division 4.6A.B, and must risk-weight it in accordance with Division 4.4.B; and
(b) must calculate its CVA risk capital charge for the CCP and any clients, in accordance with Division 4.6A.B.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.38 Transactions cleared through non-qualifying CCP — default fund RWA
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.38 Transactions cleared through non-qualifying CCP — default fund RWA
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
For transactions with a non-qualifying CCP, an Islamic banking business firm that is a clearing member of the CCP must calculate a default fund RWA as follows:

RWA = 1,250% × DF

where:

RWA is the firm’s risk-weighted assets for its default fund exposure to the CCP.

DF is the firm’s pre-funded contribution to the CCP’s default fund, plus a proportion (directed by the Regulatory Authority) of the firm’s unfunded contributions that are liable to be paid if the CCP so requires.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.39 Cap on capital requirement for exposures to QCCPs
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If the amount of capital required for an Islamic banking business firm’s exposure to a QCCP due to its trade exposure and default fund contribution is higher than it would be if the CCP were a non-qualifying CCP, the required capital is capped at the latter amount.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.40 Risk management requirements for centrally cleared exposures
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.40 Risk management requirements for centrally cleared exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must establish a process for monitoring by, and regular reporting to, the firm’s senior management of all of its exposures to CCPs, including exposures arising from:

(a) trading through a CCP; and
(b) CCP membership obligations such as default fund contributions.
(2) An Islamic banking business firm must also establish a process for regularly reporting, to its governing body, material exposures to CCPs.

(3) An Islamic banking business firm must ensure that it maintains adequate capital for its exposures to CCPs, regardless of whether any CCP to which the firm is exposed is a QCCP. In particular, an Islamic banking business firm must consider whether it might need to hold capital in excess of the minimum capital requirements if, for example:

(a) its dealings with a CCP give rise to higher risk exposure; or
(b) based on the firm’s dealings with a CCP, it is unclear whether the CCP is a QCCP.

(4) For all of its exposures to CCPs, a clearing member firm must assess (through appropriate scenario analysis and stress testing) whether the level of capital held against the exposures adequately addresses the inherent risks of those transactions. The assessment must take into account potential future or contingent exposure resulting from:

(a) future drawings on default fund commitments; and
(b) any secondary commitments to take over or replace offsetting transactions from the clients of another clearing member that defaults or becomes insolvent.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.41 Membership of CCPs
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) A clearing member firm must have an appropriate risk management framework to cover its activities as a clearing member. The framework must include:

(a) regular assessment of the risks (financial, operational and reputational) that might arise from its membership of, and conduct of business through, a CCP and from any similar engagement with 2 or more CCPs;
(b) the application of appropriate systems and controls to monitor, on a continuing basis, those risks, and to manage them (including the application of limits on potential risk exposures); and

(c) the maintenance of appropriate capital cover against those risks, including capital cover:

(i) relating to business conducted through a CCP; and
(ii) for any funded support that the firm has provided, or any contingent support that the firm may be committed to provide, to a CCP.
(2) Membership of a CCP must not expose an Islamic banking business firm to an unlimited contingent liability to support the CCP.
(3) An Islamic banking business firm must notify the Regulatory Authority before applying for membership of a CCP.

(4) An Islamic banking business firm that is a member of a CCP must notify the Authority of any proposed changes to:

(a) the contractual provisions or rules governing its membership; or
(b) business undertaken through the CCP;
that may affect the level of exposure incurred from conducting business through the CCP or from any support (funded or unfunded) that has to be provided to the CCP.
(5) An Islamic banking business firm must notify the Authority of any operational or financial risks arising from its membership of, and conduct of business through, a CCP that could affect the firm’s operations, financial position or reputation.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.42 Power of Regulatory Authority in relation to exposures to CCPs
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.C Counterparty credit risk requirements for centrally cleared transactions
IBANK 4.6A.42 Power of Regulatory Authority in relation to exposures to CCPs
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
The Regulatory Authority may direct an Islamic banking business firm to hold, in relation to its exposures to CCPs, more capital than the minimum required by this Part.

Example

The Authority might do so in relation to an Islamic banking business firm’s exposures to a particular QCCP if:

• an external assessment has found material shortcomings in the regulation of the QCCP; and
• the QCCP’s regulator has not publicly addressed the shortcomings.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.44 Treatment of shared default funds
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.D Capital charge for default fund exposures to QCCPs
IBANK 4.6A.44 Treatment of shared default funds
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If a QCCP’s default fund is shared between products or types of business that give rise only to settlement risk and products or types of business that this Part applies to (see rule 4.6A.2), all contributions to the fund must be treated as set out in this Division, without apportionment to different classes or types of business or products.
(2) If a QCCP’s default fund is segregated by product types and is accessible only for specific product types, the capital charge for the default fund exposures must be calculated for each product type that gives rise to counterparty credit risk.
(3) If a QCCP’s pre-funded own resources are shared among product types, then, in calculating a clearing member firm’s default fund exposure to the QCCP, those resources must be allocated to each of the calculations in proportion to the respective product-specific EADs.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.45 Default fund capital charge for clearing member firm
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.D Capital charge for default fund exposures to QCCPs
IBANK 4.6A.45 Default fund capital charge for clearing member firm
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The default fund capital charge for a clearing member firm’s default fund exposure is obtained by a 2-step process, as follows:

(a) step 1 — calculate a risk-sensitive measure of the exposure that the QCCP has to its clearing members and their clients (see rules 4.6A.46 to 4.6A.49);
(b) step 2 — calculate the default fund capital charge for the firm (see rule 4.6A.50).

(2) An Islamic banking business firm that is a clearing member of a QCCP may rely on the QCCP to undertake the calculations required by subrule (1) (a), and to provide the firm with the necessary data to calculate its default fund capital charge, but only if the QCCP’s calculations meet the following conditions:

(a) the calculations are undertaken transparently, and the QCCP shares enough information:

(i) to enable a supervisor of the QCCP to oversee those calculations;
(ii) to enable the firm to calculate the default fund capital charge on its own default fund contributions; and
(iii) to enable the Regulatory Authority to review and confirm the calculations, if it is asked to do so;

(b) all the calculations (that is, both steps and the inputs to both steps) are done:

(i) at least quarterly (or more frequently, if the Authority so directs); and
(ii) after any material change (such as the QCCP starting to clear a new product, a material change to the number or exposure of cleared transactions, or a material change to the QCCP’s financial resources);
(c) the QCCP provides the Authority, at least quarterly or on the Authority’s request, with sufficient aggregate information about the composition of the QCCP’s exposures to its clearing members, and the information provided to the clearing members for calculation purposes (including the calculation for step 1 and the CCP-level inputs used in step 2).
(3) If any condition in subrule (2) is not met, the firm must treat its default fund exposure to the QCCP as if the QCCP were a non-qualifying CCP. Therefore, the firm must calculate its default fund RWA in accordance with rule 4.6A.38.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.6A.46 Calculating default fund capital charge, step 1 — QCCP’s exposure to clearing members
doc_path: IBANK Division 4.6A.D Capital charge for default fund exposures to QCCPs
IBANK 4.6A.46 Calculating default fund capital charge, step 1 — QCCP’s exposure to clearing members
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Step 1 is to compute KCCP, the hypothetical capital requirement of the QCCP due to its counterparty credit risk exposures to all of its clearing member firms and their clients, as follows:

where:
RW = 20% (or a higher percentage directed by the Regulatory Authority).
EADm is the exposure amount of the QCCP to the mth clearing member, calculated according to rules 4.6A.47 to 4.6A.49.
Guidance

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.1 What Part 4.7 does
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
This Part sets out the obligations of an Islamic banking business firm in relation to:

(a) classifying exposures as performing or non-performing (Division 4.7.B);
(b) the application of forbearance (Division 4.7.C); and
(c) making provision for credit losses (Division 4.7.D).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). 
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016). Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.2 Assets etc that Part 4.7 applies to
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.2 Assets etc that Part 4.7 applies to
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This Part applies in relation to the following assets and items:

(a) financings, debt securities and other amounts due (such as profit) that are on an Islamic banking business firm’s balance sheet and that the firm holds in its banking book;
(b) financing commitments and financial guarantees, and similar items, off the balance sheet;
(c) any other items that the firm must take into account in calculating its risk-weighted assets for credit risk.
(2) For this Part, an Islamic banking business firm must take into account the whole of the exposure from an asset or item (even if the relevant non-performance is of only part of the obligor’s obligations), and must apply the classification to that whole amount. In particular, unpaid profit must be taken into account.
(3) For an off-balance-sheet item, such as a financing commitment, the exposure must be taken to be the whole uncancellable nominal amount.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.3 No circumventing of provisioning requirements
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm must not apply forbearance to, refinance or reclassify an asset to circumvent the requirements on provisioning.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning

An Islamic banking business firm must review its non-performing exposures at least once a month. It may do so individually or by class.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.4 Guidance
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
1 A review of a firm's write-offs can help identify whether the firm's provisioning policy results in over-provisioning or under-provisioning.
2 The Regulatory Authority regularly assesses trends and concentrations in risk and risk build-up across financial entities in relation to problem assets. In making the assessment, the authority takes into account any observed concentration in the CRM techniques used by firms and the potential effect on the efficacy of those techniques in reducing loss. The authority would consider the adequacy of provisions for a firm (and the industry in general) in the light of the assessment.
3 The Regulatory Authority might seek the opinion of external experts in assessing the adequacy of a firm's policies for grading and classifying its assets and the appropriateness and robustness of the levels of its provisions.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.5 Regulatory Authority can direct firm to reclassify assets etc
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The Regulatory Authority may at any time require an Islamic banking business firm to demonstrate that the firm’s classification of its assets, and its provisions, are adequate for prudential purposes.
(2) The Authority may direct the firm to reclassify its assets or increase the levels of its provisions for credit losses if the Authority considers that the asset classifications are inaccurate, or the provisions are inadequate, for prudential purposes.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.5 Regulatory Authority can direct firm to reclassify assets etc
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If the Regulatory Authority considers that existing or foreseen deterioration in asset quality is of concern or that an Islamic banking business firm’s provisions do not fully reflect expected losses, the Authority may require the firm to adjust its classifications of individual assets, increase its levels of provisions or capital and, if necessary, impose other remedial measures.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.6 Information to firm’s governing body
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.6 Information to firm’s governing body
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm’s governing body must obtain timely information on the condition of the firm’s assets, including the classification of assets, the levels of provisions and problem assets.
(2) The information must include summary results of the latest asset review, comparative trends in the overall quality of problem assets, and measurements of existing or anticipated deterioration in asset quality and losses expected.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

IBANK 4.7.8 Write-downs and write-offs — defaulted exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an Islamic banking business firm is satisfied that payment of a defaulted exposure is unlikely, the firm must write the exposure off in whole or in part, in accordance with the applicable accounting standard.
(2) An Islamic banking business firm must have appropriate policies and procedures in relation to the writing off of defaulted exposures. In particular, the policies must provide for such exposures to be written off within a period approved by the Regulatory Authority.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.10 Classification of exposures
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must classify the exposures in relation to which this Part applies (except for the exposure classes mentioned in subrule (2)) as either performing or non-performing.

(2) The excepted exposure classes are the following:

(a) SCHIs;
(b) exposures held in the firm’s trading book.

(3) For this Part, an exposure is classified as performing if:

(a) there is no uncertainty about the timely repayment of the outstanding amounts; and
(b) it is currently in regular payment status with prompt payments.

(4) For this Part, an exposure is classified as non-performing if any of the following is true:

(a) it is defaulted (see rule 4.4.80);
(b) it is credit-impaired (that is, its valuation has been reduced because of a deterioration of its creditworthiness) according to the applicable accounting standard;
(c) it is a material exposure and is more than 90 days past due (see subrule (5));

(d) there is reason to believe that full repayment according to the contractual terms is unlikely unless the firm realises collateral, whether or not the exposure is current (and if it is not current, regardless of the number of days it is past due).

Examples of circumstances in which full repayment according to the contractual terms is unlikely
• the firm concerned puts the credit obligation on non-accrued status
• the firm makes a charge-off or account-specific provision resulting from a material perceived decline in credit quality since the firm took on the exposure
• the firm sells other credit obligations from the same counterparty at a material credit-related economic loss
• the firm applies a distressed forbearance to the credit obligation and this is likely to result in a diminished financial obligation because of material forgiveness, or postponement, of principal, profit or fees
• the firm has filed for the counterparty’s bankruptcy or a similar order in relation to the counterparty’s credit obligation to the firm
• the counterparty has sought, or has been placed in, bankruptcy or similar protection and as a result has avoided or delayed the repayment of the obligation.
(5) For the purposes of this Part, an exposure is past due if any amount due under the relevant contract (profit, principal, a fee or any other amount) was not paid in full on the date when it was due. An exposure must be treated as past due from the first day of missed payment, even if the amount of the exposure or the amount unpaid is not material.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.11 Application of classification to off-balance-sheet exposures
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.11 Application of classification to off-balance-sheet exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must classify an off-balance-sheet exposure as non-performing if the firm has reason to believe that the firm is unlikely to recoup, in a timely manner, the full amount that it may be required to advance.
(2) A commitment must be classified as non-performing if the creditworthiness of the borrower has deteriorated to the extent that the timely repayment in full by the borrower of any drawdown or associated profit payments or fees is unlikely.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.12 Application of classification to exposures to SCHIs
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.12 Application of classification to exposures to SCHIs
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an Islamic banking business firm considers it unlikely that it will receive timely repayment, in full, of cash flow entitlements which are or will be due from a counterparty to a transaction in SCHIs, it must classify such an exposure as non-performing.
(2) For the purposes of measuring non-performance, the firm must calculate its exposures to counterparties from SCHIs using the modified current exposure method set out in Division 4.6A.B. Potential exposure add-ons applied in calculating such exposures must reflect the nature of the individual facility involved.

IBANK 4.7.13 Classification independent of accounting treatment

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.14 Effect of collateral
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) When classifying an exposure, an Islamic banking business firm must not treat collateral or other risk-mitigation arrangements as affecting the classification of the exposure.
(2) However, the firm may take collateral into account in assessing the borrower’s economic incentive to pay.
(3) The firm must not treat the collateralisation of an exposure as affecting the exposure’s past-due status or the counting of past-due days.
(4) The firm must classify an exposure as non-performing for this Part if the exposure satisfies the conditions for being so classified in rule 4.7.10 (4), even if the value of collateral held is more than the amount of the past-due exposure.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.15 Level of application
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an Islamic banking business firm has more than 1 exposure to a particular non-retail counterparty, the firm must consider all of its exposures to that counterparty as non-performing if a material exposure to the counterparty is non-performing. That is, non-performing status is applied to the counterparty.

(2) In the case of an Islamic banking business firm’s exposure to a retail counterparty, non-performing status is applied to the transaction. However, if the firm has more than 1 exposure to a particular retail counterparty, the firm must, when deciding about the status of 1 such exposure, consider the status of the other exposures.

Guidance
QFC Islamic banking business firms are not permitted to undertake retail banking.
(3) If an Islamic banking business firm has exposures to 2 or more members of a corporate group, the firm may apply non-performing status to each member. When the firm is deciding about the status of an exposure to such a member, the firm must take into account the status of its exposure to another member.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.16 Reclassification of non-performing exposures as performing
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.16 Reclassification of non-performing exposures as performing
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm may reclassify a non-performing exposure as performing only if all of the following are true:

(a) no exposure of the firm to the relevant counterparty is 90 days or more past due;

(b) subject to subrule (2), the counterparty has made repayments when due over a continuous period of at least:

(i) for a forborne exposure — 12 months (beginning on the first day on which a payment was due under the revised terms) (but see subrule (3)); or
(ii) in any other case — 90 days;
(c) the firm is satisfied, on the basis of an analysis of the counterparty’s financial situation, that full and timely repayment of the exposure is likely (but see subrule (3));
(d) the exposure is not classified as non-performing under rule 4.7.10.

(2) For paragraph (1) (c), the firm must not consider that full and timely repayment is likely unless the counterparty has made regular and timely payments of amounts equal to:

(a) if any amount was past due when the forbearance was applied — that amount; or
(b) if no amount was then past due — any amount that has been written off under the forbearance measures.

(3) In exceptional circumstances and with the Regulatory Authority’s approval, an Islamic banking business firm may reclassify a forborne non-performing exposure as performing if repayments have been made when due over a continuous period of less than 12 months, if all of the following conditions are satisfied:

(a) the firm has taken remedial measures to restructure the counterparty’s business;

(b) the measures:

(i) provide for the firm to participate directly in the counterparty’s business;
(ii) are immediately applicable; and
(iii) make the full repayment of the exposure likely.

(4) However, an Islamic banking business firm must not automatically reclassify a non-performing exposure as performing in any of the following circumstances:

(a) the firm has written off part of the exposure because it considers that the part written off is uncollectable;
(b) if the firm has taken possession of collateral on the exposure — until the collateral is actually disposed of and the firm has received the proceeds;

(c) the firm applies forbearance to the exposure or extends an existing application of forbearance.

Note For forbearance, see Division 4.7.C.
(5) The reclassification of a non-performing exposure as performing is to be at the same level (that is, at the level of the counterparty or at the level of the transaction) as when the exposure was classified as non-performing.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.16 Guidance — impairment and regulatory treatment of accounting provisions
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.16 Reclassification of non-performing exposures as performing
IBANK 4.7.16 Guidance — impairment and regulatory treatment of accounting provisions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
1 The Regulatory Authority expects authorised firms to adopt the following approach to the three provisioning stages:

• stage 1 (representing 12-month expected credit loss (ECL) provisions on performing financings): allocate to General Provisions (GP), if held against future, presently unidentified losses and, therefore, freely available to meet losses that subsequently materialise
• stage 2 (representing lifetime ECL provisions on underperforming financings): consider as Specific Provision for regulatory purposes. However, any portion that represents an amount for future, presently unidentified losses, would qualify as a GP
• stage 3 (representing lifetime ECL provisions on non-performing financings): consider as Specific Provision for regulatory purposes.
2 The GP amount that may be included in tier 2 capital remains unchanged at 1.25% limit on credit risk-weighted assets.

3 ECL accounting provisions for exposures may be treated as general provisions for regulatory purposes if the firm can satisfactorily demonstrate that:

• the provision amount is a purely forward looking amount for future, presently unidentified losses, set aside in consideration only of the consequences of potential events or scenarios that could lead to identified losses in the future; and
• there is no evidence the provision relates to the identified deterioration of particular assets or covers exposures on which any impairment or default (individually or collectively) has materialised into identified losses.
4 Accounting provisions for exposures not meeting both of the abovementioned criteria should be treated as specific provisions for regulatory purposes.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

ECL impairment bucketTreatment in prudential returns
Stage 1: Includes exposures at initial recognition, and those where there is no significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition, or exposures that have low credit risk on reporting date. Stage 3: Includes accounts that demonstrate evidence of impairment on the reporting date. For such assets, interest is accrued but suspended on the net carrying amount (net of provisions) and a lifetime ECL is factored into P&L calculations.This is mapped to the substandard, doubtful and loss categories, and provisions raised are to be treated as specific provisions.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.17 Meaning of concession for Division 4.7.C
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.17 Meaning of concession for Division 4.7.C
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For this Division, an Islamic banking business firm grants a concession to a counterparty if the firm grants special contractual terms and conditions (that would not have been granted if the counterparty had not experienced difficulties in meeting its financial commitments) so that the counterparty can sufficiently service its debt.
(2) For the purposes of this Division, there is no concession to the counterparty unless the counterparty is experiencing, or is likely to experience, financial difficulty.

(3) For the purposes of this Division, the counterparty is taken to be experiencing financial difficulty, or to be likely to do so, if the firm reasonably believes that the counterparty is experiencing financial difficulties, or is likely to do so.

Guidance
Financial difficulty can be identified even if an exposure is not in arrears. The following list of indications that a counterparty is in financial difficulty is not intended to be exhaustive:
• the counterparty is currently past due on a material exposure
• no exposure to the counterparty is currently past due, but a material one is likely to be past due in future (for instance, there has been a pattern of delinquency in payments on its material exposures) unless a concession is made
• the counterparty’s outstanding securities have been delisted, are in the process of being delisted, or are under threat of being delisted, from an exchange for non-compliance with the listing requirements or for financial reasons
• on the basis of the counterparty’s actual performance, and estimates and projections that take into account the counterparty’s current capabilities, the firm expects that, for the foreseeable future, the counterparty’s available cash flows will be insufficient to service all its financings or debt securities (both profit and principal) in accordance with the terms of the existing agreements
• the counterparty has already shown that it has difficulty in repaying in accordance with the credit categorisation scheme within the firm’s internal credit rating system
• a material exposure to the counterparty is classified as non-performing or would be so classified without the concessions
• the counterparty cannot obtain funds from other sources at an effective profit rate equal to the current market profit rate for similar financings or debt securities for a non-troubled counterparty.
(4) Refinancing an existing exposure with a new contract because of the counterparty’s financial difficulty is a concession, even if the terms of the new contract are no more favourable to the counterparty than those of the existing one.
(5) The main characteristic of a concession is that the firm would not extend financings or grant commitments to the counterparty, or purchase its debt securities, on such terms and conditions under normal market conditions.

(6) A concession might, but need not, result in a loss for the firm. A concession could be any of the following:

(a) a modification of the terms and conditions of the exposure;
(b) a total or partial refinance of the exposure;
(c) changes in the conditions of the existing exposure, giving more favourable terms for the counterparty;
(d) a supplementary agreement;
(e) the exercise of contractual rights that enable the counterparty to change the terms and conditions of the contract or to take on additional financings, debt securities or off-balance-sheet items at its own discretion.
Examples of concessions
• extending the financing term
• rescheduling the dates of principal or profit payments
• granting new or additional periods of non-payment (grace period)
• reducing the profit rate, resulting in an effective profit rate below the rate that counterparties with similar risk characteristics could obtain in the market
• capitalising arrears
• forgiving, deferring or postponing principal, profit or fees
• changing an amortising financing to a profit payment only
• releasing collateral or accepting lower levels of collateralisation
• allowing the conversion of debt to equity of the counterparty
• deferring recovery or collection action for extended periods
• easing of covenants
• refinancing an existing exposure with a new contract, even if the terms of the new contract are no more favourable for the counterparty than those of the existing exposure.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: (1) For this Division, an Islamic banking business firm grants a concession to a counterparty if the firm grants special contractual terms and conditions (that would not have been granted if the counterparty had not experienced difficulties in meeting its financial commitments) so that the counterparty can sufficiently service its debt. (2) For the purposes of this Division, there is no concession to the counterparty unless the counterparty is experiencing, or is likely to experience, financial difficulty. (3) For the purposes of this Division, the counterparty is taken to be experiencing financial difficulty, or to be likely to do so, if the firm reasonably believes that the counterparty is experiencing financial difficulties, or is likely to do so. Guidance Financial difficulty can be identified even if an exposure is not in arrears. The following list of indications that a counterparty is in financial difficulty is not intended to be exhaustive: • the counterparty is currently past due on a material exposure • no exposure to the counterparty is currently past due, but a material one is likely to be past due in future (for instance, there has been a pattern of delinquency in payments on its material exposures) unless a concession is made • the counterparty’s outstanding securities have been delisted, are in the process of being delisted, or are under threat of being delisted, from an exchange for non-compliance with the listing requirements or for financial reasons • on the basis of the counterparty’s actual performance, and estimates and projections that take into account the counterparty’s current capabilities, the firm expects that, for the foreseeable future, the counterparty’s available cash flows will be insufficient to service all its financings or debt securities (both profit and principal) in accordance with the terms of the existing agreements • the counterparty has already shown that it has difficulty in repaying in accordance with the credit categorisation scheme within the firm’s internal credit rating system • a material exposure to the counterparty is classified as non-performing or would be so classified without the concessions • the counterparty cannot obtain funds from other sources at an effective profit rate equal to the current market profit rate for similar financings or debt securities for a non-troubled counterparty. (4) Refinancing an existing exposure with a new contract because of the counterparty’s financial difficulty is a concession, even if the terms of the new contract are no more favourable to the counterparty than those of the existing one. (5) The main characteristic of a concession is that the firm would not extend financings or grant commitments to the counterparty, or purchase its debt securities, on such terms and conditions under normal market conditions. (6) A concession might, but need not, result in a loss for the firm. A concession could be any of the following: (a) a modification of the terms and conditions of the exposure; (b) a total or partial refinance of the exposure; (c) changes in the conditions of the existing exposure, giving more favourable terms for the counterparty; (d) a supplementary agreement; (e) the exercise of contractual rights that enable the counterparty to change the terms and conditions of the contract or to take on additional financings, debt securities or off-balance-sheet items at its own discretion. Examples of concessions • extending the financing term • rescheduling the dates of principal or profit payments • granting new or additional periods of non-payment (grace period) • reducing the profit rate, resulting in an effective profit rate below the rate that counterparties with similar risk characteristics could obtain in the market • capitalising arrears • forgiving, deferring or postponing principal, profit or fees • changing an amortising financing to a profit payment only • releasing collateral or accepting lower levels of collateralisation • allowing the conversion of debt to equity of the counterparty • deferring recovery or collection action for extended periods • easing of covenants • refinancing an existing exposure with a new contract, even if the terms of the new contract are no more favourable for the counterparty than those of the existing exposure. Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.18 Meaning of forborne exposure and forbearance for Part 4.7
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.18 Meaning of forborne exposure and forbearance for Part 4.7
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For this Part, an exposure of an Islamic banking business firm is a forborne exposure if the firm has granted a concession (see rule 4.7.17) to the counterparty.

Note There is no concession to a counterparty (and therefore no forbearance) unless the counterparty is experiencing, or is likely to experience, financial difficulty — see rule 4.7.17 (2).
(2) In the circumstances described in subrule (1), the firm has granted forbearance to the counterparty, and has applied forbearance to the exposure.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.19 Relationship between performance and forbearance
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.19 Relationship between performance and forbearance
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm may apply forbearance to either a performing or a non-performing exposure.
(2) If an Islamic banking business firm applies forbearance to a non-performing exposure, the firm must continue to classify the exposure as non-performing.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.20 Application of forbearance to performing exposures
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.20 Application of forbearance to performing exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies if an Islamic banking business firm applies forbearance to a performing exposure.
(2) The firm must decide whether the exposure meets the definition of a non-performing exposure, even if the forbearance results in a new exposure.
(3) If the firm decides that the original exposure would have been treated as non-performing when the firm applied the forbearance, the new exposure must be treated as non-performing.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.21 Criteria for exit from forbearance
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.21 Criteria for exit from forbearance
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An exposure to which forbearance has been applied continues to be a forborne exposure until:

(a) all payments, according to the new contractual terms, have been made in a timely manner over a continuous period of at least 1 year; and
(b) the counterparty has resolved its financial difficulty.
(2) The period mentioned in subrule (1) (a) starts at the scheduled start of payments under the new contractual terms, regardless of whether the exposure was classified as performing or non-performing when the forbearance was granted.
(3) If another forbearance is applied to a forborne exposure before its release from the first forbearance, that period starts again with the new forbearance.
(4) Nothing prevents the period mentioned in subrule (1) (a) for an exposure from running concurrently with a period mentioned in rule 4.7.16 (1) for the same exposure.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.22 Meaning of provisioning
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Provisioning means setting aside an amount to cover expected losses, based on financing-loss probability. Provisioning is made before profit is earned.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.23 Credit risk and accounting for expected credit losses
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.23 Credit risk and accounting for expected credit losses
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must adopt, document and adhere to sound methods that address policies, processes and controls for assessing and measuring credit losses on all the firm’s exposures. The measurement of provisions must build on robust methods and must result in the appropriate and timely recognition of expected credit losses in accordance with the applicable accounting standard.
(2) The firm’s aggregate amount of provisions for credit losses must be adequate and consistent with the applicable accounting standard.
(3) The firm must have sound policies and processes to appropriately validate the models that it uses to assess and measure expected credit losses.
(4) The firm must use experienced credit judgement, particularly in the robust consideration of reasonable and supportable forward-looking information, including macroeconomic factors, in its assessment and measurement of expected credit losses.
(5) The firm must have an appropriate credit risk assessment and measurement process that provides it with a sound basis for common systems, tools and data to assess credit risk and to account for expected credit losses.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.24 Provisioning policy
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Depending on the nature, scale and complexity of an Islamic banking business firm’s business, and of the credit it provides, the firm’s provisioning policy must set out:

(a) the areas of its business to which the policy applies;
(b) whether the firm uses different approaches to those areas, and the significant differences in approach;
(c) who is responsible for regularly monitoring its assets, to identify problem or potential problem assets, and the factors it takes into account in identifying them;
(d) the extent to which the value of any collateral, guarantees or insurance that the firm holds affects the need for, or the level of, provisions;
(e) the basis on which the firm makes its provisions, including the extent to which their levels are left to managerial judgement or to a committee;
(f) the methods, debt management systems or formulae used to set the levels of provisions and the factors that must be considered in deciding whether the provisions are adequate;
(g) the reports to enable the firm’s governing body and senior management to ensure that the firm maintains adequate provisions;
(h) the procedures and responsibilities for arrears management and the recovery of exposures in arrears or exposures that have had provisions made against them;
(i) the procedures for writing off and writing back provisions; and
(j) the procedures for calculating and making provisions for contingent and other liabilities (such as contingent liabilities that have crystallised from acceptances, endorsements, guarantees, performance bonds, indemnities, irrevocable letters of credit and the confirmation of documentary credits).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.25 Making provision for credit losses
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
IBANK 4.7.25 Making provision for credit losses
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must ensure that it maintains provisions for credit losses that, taken together, are prudent, reasonable and adequate to absorb such losses, given the relevant facts and circumstances. The losses covered must include:

(a) losses incurred;
(b) losses incurred but not yet reported; and
(c) losses estimated but not certain to arise;
extending over the life of the individual credits that make up its credit portfolio.
(2) The firm must also ensure that provisions and write-offs are timely and reflect realistic repayment and recovery expectations, taking into account market and macroeconomic conditions. The firm must consider all the significant factors that affect the likelihood of collecting on the transactions that make up its credit portfolio and the estimated future credit losses on those transactions.
(3) Provisions may be general (assessed collectively against the whole of a portfolio) or specific (assessed against individual credits), or both.
(4) The firm must take into account off-balance-sheet exposures in provisioning. However, no provisioning is necessary for off-balance-sheet exposures that the firm can unilaterally cancel.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.26 Amount of provisioning
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Subject to any direction under subrule (2), an Islamic banking business firm must make provision for credit losses in accordance with the applicable accounting standard.
(2) If the Regulatory Authority considers that the firm’s provisioning for an exposure, or some or all of its exposures, is insufficient, the Authority may direct the firm to apply rule 4.7.27.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.7.27 Prescribed provisioning
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.7 Problem assets and provisioning
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If the Regulatory Authority considers that an Islamic banking business firm’s own practices for identifying provisions are inadequate in view of its credit risk profile, the Authority may direct the firm to implement prescribed provisioning in accordance with this rule.
(2) To implement prescribed provisioning, the firm must classify exposures to which this Part applies (subject to subrule (7)) into the 5 categories in subrule (3).

(3) The classification is as follows:

(a) an exposure is classified as performing if:

(i) there is no uncertainty about the timely repayment of the outstanding amounts; and
(ii) it is currently in regular payment status with prompt payments;

(b) an exposure is classified as special mention if any of the following subparagraphs is true of it:

(i) it is of deteriorating or potentially deteriorating credit quality that may adversely affect the counterparty’s ability to make scheduled payments on time;
(ii) it is 30 to 90 days in arrears;
(iii) it shows weakness arising from the counterparty’s financial position;
(iv) it is affected by market circumstances or any other industry-related concerns;

(c) an exposure is classified as substandard if:

(i) it shows definite deterioration in credit quality and impaired repayment ability of the counterparty; or
(ii) it is 91 to 180 days in arrears;

(d) an exposure is classified as doubtful if:

(i) it shows significant credit quality deterioration, worse than in the substandard category, to the extent that the prospect of fully recovering all the outstanding amounts is questionable and the probability of a loss is high (though the exact amount of loss cannot be determined yet); or
(ii) it is 181 to 270 days in arrears;

(e) an exposure is classified as loss if:

(i) it is assessed as uncollectable;
(ii) the probability of recovering the amount due is very low; or
(iii) it is more than 270 days in arrears.
(4) Nothing prevents the firm from classifying an exposure in a higher category than subrule (3) requires. For this subrule, the highest category is loss, and the lowest is performing.
(5) The firm must classify all of its exposures to a particular counterparty as of the same category unless there is good reason not to do so.

(6) The firm must make provisions for credit losses that in total at least meet the requirements in table 4.7.27.

Note If the result is to increase the firm’s provision for credit losses, the amount of the increase must be deducted from CET 1 capital — see rule 3.2.30.

(7) Prescribed provisioning does not apply to exposures of the following kinds:

(a) forborne exposures (see Division 4.7.C) that meet the criteria to be classified as performing (see rule 4.7.10);
(b) any asset acquired through enforcing a security;
(c) real estate that the firm owns.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.8.1 Introduction
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.8 Transactions with Related Parties
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) To guard against abuses in lending to related parties and to address conflicts of interest, this Part requires transactions with related parties to be at arm's length and subject to appropriate supervision and limits.
(2) Related-party transactions must be interpreted broadly. Related party transactions include on-balance-sheet and off-balance-sheet credit exposures, service contracts, asset purchases and sales, construction contracts, lease agreements, borrowing and write-offs.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.8.2 Concept of Related Parties
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.8 Transactions with Related Parties
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The concept of parties being related to an Islamic banking business firm is used in these rules in relation to parties over which the firm exercises control or parties that exercise control over the firm. The concept is primarily used in relation to the requirement that the firm's transactions be at arm's length.
(2) In contrast, the concept of parties being connected to one another (which is discussed with concentration risk in Chapter 5) is used in these rules to measure concentration risk and large exposures.
(3) It is of course possible for connected counterparties to be related to the banking business firm holding the exposure concerned.

Note For purposes of concentration risk, the firm's exposure to connected counterparties (whether related or not) is taken to be a single risk.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.8.3 Related Parties
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.8 Transactions with Related Parties
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Related parties, of an Islamic banking business firm, includes:

(a) any other member of the firm's corporate group;
(b) any individual who is able to exercise significant influence over the firm;
(c) any affiliate of the firm; and
(d) any entity that the Regulatory Authority directs the firm to include.

Guidance

Related party is wider than a firm's corporate group in that it includes individuals. Related parties include the banking business firm's subsidiaries and major stock holders; members of its governing body; its senior management and key employees.

Note Affiliate is defined in the glossary.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: Related parties , of an Islamic banking business firm, includes: (a) any other member of the firm's corporate group; (b) any individual who is able to exercise significant influence over the firm; (c) any affiliate of the firm; and (d) any entity that the Regulatory Authority directs the firm to include. QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.8.4 Role of Governing Body — Related Parties
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.8 Transactions with Related Parties
IBANK 4.8.4 Role of Governing Body — Related Parties
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm's governing body must ensure that the firm's policies relating to related-party transactions are complied with and that any exceptions are reported to the appropriate level of the senior management, and, if necessary, to the governing body.
(2) The governing body must also ensure that the firm's senior management monitors transactions with related parties, takes appropriate steps to control or mitigate the risks from such transactions and writes off exposures to related parties only in accordance with the firm's policies.
(3) The governing body must approve transactions with related parties, and the write-off of related-party exposures, if such transactions or write-off exceeds specified amounts or otherwise poses any special risk.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 4.8.5 Policies — Transactions with Related Parties
doc_path: IBANK Part 4.8 Transactions with Related Parties
IBANK 4.8.5 Policies — Transactions with Related Parties
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm's policy must establish:
(a) effective systems to identify, monitor and report individual and total exposures to, and transactions with, related parties;
(b) procedures to prevent a member of the governing body, a member of the firm's senior management or any other person who stands to gain a benefit from a related-party transaction from being part of the process of granting and managing the transaction;
(c) well-defined criteria for writing-off exposures to related parties;
(d) prudent and appropriate limits to prevent or address conflicts of interest; and
(e) procedures for tracking and reporting exceptions to, and deviations from, limits or policies.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

A transaction with a related party must not be undertaken on terms more favourable to the party than a corresponding transaction with a non-related party.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.1.1 Introduction
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This Chapter sets out the requirements for an Islamic banking business firm’s policies to identify, measure, evaluate, manage and control or mitigate concentration risk. This Chapter also sets limits on the firm’s exposures to individual counterparties and connected counterparties.
(2) Concentration risk is the potential for a loss in value of an investment portfolio or a financial institution when a group of exposures moves together in an unfavourable direction. Concentration risk in an Islamic banking business firm’s portfolio arises from concentration on a single counterparty, sector or country.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
The implication of concentration risk is that it generates such a significant loss that recovery is unlikely.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.1.2 Meaning of risk concentration
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) A risk concentration is a single exposure, or a group of exposures with a common element, that is capable of producing a loss that is large enough:

(a) to threaten an Islamic banking business firm’s viability or its ability to maintain its core operations; or
(b) to produce a material change in its risk profile.
(2) A risk concentration can arise in an Islamic banking business firm’s assets, liabilities or off-balance-sheet items through the execution or processing of transactions (either product or service), or through a combination of exposures.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.1.2 Guidance
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Examples of a common element among an Islamic banking business firm’s exposures that could create a risk concentration are the following:

• that the counterparties are connected or related
• that the exposures are disproportionately denominated in a particular currency
• that the counterparties are concentrated in particular geographical locations or particular industry sectors
• that the exposures are concentrated in particular products
• reliance on particular service providers (such as a provider of back-office services).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.1.3 Identification of risk concentrations
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm must identify the risk concentrations in its portfolio, including those arising from:

(a) large exposures to a single counterparty;
(b) exposures to connected counterparties;
(c) exposures to counterparties in the same industry, economic sector, geographical region or country; and
(d) exposures to counterparties whose financial performance depends on the same activity, commodity or product.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.1.3 Guidance
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
1 Two or more individuals or legal persons would constitute a single risk if they are so connected that, if one of them were to experience financial problems, the other or others would be likely to encounter repayment difficulties.
2 Connected counterparties should be identified and the procedures to manage the combined credit risk considered. An Islamic banking business firm may need to monitor and report the gross exposure to connected counterparties against combined limits in addition to monitoring the exposure to each counterparty.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.1.4 Policies — risk concentrations — sources and limits
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.1.4 Policies — risk concentrations — sources and limits
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must have a policy on the management of risk concentrations.
(2) The policy must set limits for acceptable risk concentrations, consistent with the firm’s risk appetite, risk profile and capital. The limits must be made known to, and must be understood by, all relevant staff.

(3) The policy must ensure that:

(a) the firm’s information systems identify exposures that create risk concentrations, aggregate those exposures and facilitate their management; and
(b) all significant risk concentrations are reviewed regularly and reported to the firm’s governing body or senior management.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.1.4 Guidance
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.1.4 Policies — risk concentrations — sources and limits
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm’s policies should be flexible to help the firm to identify risk concentrations. To achieve this, the systems should be capable of analysing the firm’s credit portfolio by:

• size of exposure
• exposures to connected counterparties
• product
• geography
• industry or sector (for example, manufacturing and industrial)
• account performance
• internal credit risk assessment
• funding
• outstandings versus commitments
• types and coverage of collateral.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.1.5 Role of governing body — risk concentrations
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.1.5 Role of governing body — risk concentrations
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm’s governing body must ensure that the firm’s policy for the management of risk concentrations gives a comprehensive firm-wide view of the significant sources of risk concentrations (including exposures on and off its balance sheet and from contingent liabilities).
(2) The governing body must also ensure that the firm’s senior management monitors the firm’s large exposures, and that the large exposure limits (see rule 5.2.9) are not exceeded on a solo or consolidated basis.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.1.6 Relationship to stress-testing
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
When carrying out stress-testing or reviewing stress scenarios, an Islamic banking business firm must take into account significant risk concentrations and large exposures, and the effects of changes in market conditions and risk factors on them.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.1.7 Regulatory Authority can set different limits and minimum capital adequacy ratios
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.1.7 Regulatory Authority can set different limits and minimum capital adequacy ratios
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Despite anything in these rules, the Regulatory Authority may, in writing, set specific limits on an Islamic banking business firm’s exposures to particular counterparties, groups of counterparties, industries, sectors, regions, countries or asset classes on a case-by-case basis.
(2) If an Islamic banking business firm has 1 or more large exposures (excluding exempted exposures) or if, in the Authority’s opinion, the firm is exposed to a significant level of risk concentration, the Authority may increase any 1 or more of the firm’s minimum capital adequacy ratios.

(3) In considering whether to increase any of the firm’s minimum capital adequacy ratios, the Authority will take into account:

(a) whether the increased ratio would be consistent with the firm’s risk concentration and large exposure policies;
(b) the number of exposures, and the size and nature of each; and
(c) the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business and the experience of its governing body and senior management.

(4) The Regulatory Authority may also direct the firm to take measures to reduce its level of risk concentration.

Note Under FSR, article 16, the Regulatory Authority may modify or waive the application of a prudential requirement to an authorised firm or firms.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.2 Definitions for Part 5.2
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
In this Part:

exempted counterparty means a counterparty that is any of the following:

(a) a sovereign;
(b) a central bank;
(c) a PSE that is assigned a 0% risk weight under rule 4.4.14;

(d) an MDB that qualifies for 0% risk weight.

Note For the list of such MDBs, see rule 4.4.16.
exempted exposure means an exposure that arises from a claim, commitment or contingent liability of any of the following kinds:
(a) a claim by, or a commitment or contingent liability to, an exempted counterparty;

(b) a claim, commitment or contingent liability the amount of which is deducted from the firm’s regulatory capital (see Division 3.2.D);

Guidance
If the amount of such a claim, commitment or contingent liability were not deducted from the firm’s regulatory capital, it would be added to the firm’s other exposures to the relevant counterparty. (It would be assigned a risk weight of 1,250% for the purpose of calculating the firm’s risk-weighted assets.)
(c) a claim, commitment or contingent liability that is secured by eligible collateral (see rule 4.6.12) that was issued by an exempted counterparty;
(d) a claim, commitment or contingent liability that is covered by an eligible guarantee (see rule 4.6.32) that was given by an exempted counterparty;
(e) an exposure to a QCCP that is related to clearing;
(f) certain net short positions (see rule 5.2.28 (6)).
exposure to a counterparty (or a group of connected counterparties) means the total of all of an Islamic banking business firm’s claims, commitments and contingent liabilities arising from transactions with the counterparty or a member or members of the group (whether on or off the firm’s balance sheet, and whether held in the firm’s banking book or its trading book) but does not include an intra-day exposure to another banking business firm or a bank.
group of connected counterparties has the meaning given by rule 5.2.5.
large exposure of an Islamic banking business firm means an exposure to a counterparty or group of connected counterparties that is equal to 10% or more of the firm’s tier 1 capital.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.2 Guidance
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm's policies should be flexible to help the firm to identify risk concentrations. To achieve this, the systems should be capable of analysing the firm's credit portfolio by:

•   size of exposure
•   exposure to connected counterparties
•   product
•   geography
•   industry or sector (for example, manufacturing and industrial)
•   account performance
•   internal credit risk assessment
•   funding
•   outstandings versus commitments
•   types and coverage of collateral.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.4 Policies in relation to large exposures
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.2.4 Policies in relation to large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must establish and implement appropriate policies for the management of large exposures. In particular, the policies must include:

(a) exposure limits, commensurate with the firm’s risk appetite, risk profile and capital, for exposures to:

(i) categories of counterparties (for example, sovereigns, other authorised firms and other financial entities, corporate and individual borrowers);
(ii) single counterparties and groups of connected counterparties;
(iii) particular industries or sectors;
(iv) particular countries; and
(v) asset classes (for example, property holdings);
(b) the circumstances in which the exposure limits may be exceeded, and the processes required for approving such excesses (for example, approval by the firm’s governing body); and
(c) procedures for identifying, measuring, managing and reporting large exposures.

(2) The policies must ensure that the firm:

(a) has adequate systems and controls to identify, measure, monitor and report large exposures and risk concentrations in a timely manner; and
(b) reviews its large exposures and risk concentrations at least annually.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.5 Meaning of group of connected counterparties
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.2.5 Meaning of group of connected counterparties
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Two or more of an Islamic banking business firm’s counterparties (other than exempted counterparties) form a group of connected counterparties if:

(a) they are connected by any 1 or more of the following:

(i) a control relationship (see rule 5.2.6);
(ii) a relationship of economic interdependence (see rule 5.2.7);
(iii) any other connection or relationship that, in the firm’s opinion, requires it to treat the counterparties as constituting a single risk;
(b) in the case of investments in structured vehicles — they have in common a third party (such as an originator, fund manager, liquidity provider or credit protection provider) that should be treated as a common risk factor (see rule 5.2.23).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: Two or more of an Islamic banking business firm’s counterparties (other than exempted counterparties) form a group of connected counterparties if: (a) they are connected by any 1 or more of the following: (i) a control relationship (see rule 5.2.6 ); (ii) a relationship of economic interdependence (see rule 5.2.7 ); (iii) any other connection or relationship that, in the firm’s opinion, requires it to treat the counterparties as constituting a single risk; (b) in the case of investments in structured vehicles — they have in common a third party (such as an originator, fund manager, liquidity provider or credit protection provider) that should be treated as a common risk factor (see rule 5.2.23 ). QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.5 Guidance
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.2.5 Meaning of group of connected counterparties
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
1 The concept of parties or counterparties being connected to one another is used in these rules in relation to counterparties or issuers to which an Islamic banking business firm has exposures. Connected counterparties are the basis for measuring risk concentrations and large exposures.
2 Nothing prevents the members of a group of connected counterparties being connected in 2 or more of the ways mentioned. If counterparties that are part of different control groups are interconnected by economic interdependency, all entities for which there is a “chain of contagion” need to be grouped into one group of connected counterparties. The chain of contagion leading to a possible default of all entities concerned is the relevant factor for the grouping and needs to be assessed in each individual case.
3 In contrast, the concept of parties being related to an Islamic banking business firm (which is discussed with credit risk in Chapter 4) is primarily used in relation to the requirement that the firm’s transactions be at arm’s length.
4 It is of course possible for a firm’s related parties to be connected counterparties (such as when the firm has exposures to them).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.6 Connected counterparties — control relationship
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) A control relationship exists between 2 counterparties if either has control of the other.

(2) Whether a control relationship exists between 2 counterparties is to be decided in accordance with the applicable accounting standard.

Guidance
1 A control relationship is likely to exist between 2 counterparties if 1 of them owns 50% or more of the voting rights in the other.

2 To decide whether a control relationship exists between 2 counterparties, an Islamic banking business firm should take at least the following factors into account:

• the existence of voting agreements (such as control of a majority of voting rights by means of an agreement with other shareholders)
• whether a member (A) is able to exercise significant influence over the appointment or dismissal of another member’s administrative, management or supervisory body (for example, if A has as the right to appoint or remove a majority of members of such a body, or a majority of members of such a body have been appointed solely as a result of A’s exercise of its voting rights)
• whether a member (A) is able to exercise significant influence over the senior management of another (B) (for example, A has the power to exercise a controlling influence over B’s management or policies (such as by A’s having consent rights over significant decisions)).
(3) However, even if control of 1 entity by another is established, the Islamic banking business firm concerned need not treat the counterparties as a group of connected counterparties if it can show the Regulatory Authority that, despite the control, the entities do not form a group of connected counterparties (for example, because of particular circumstances or corporate governance safeguards).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
