QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.7 Connected counterparties — economic interdependence
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) To decide whether or not 2 counterparties are connected by a relationship of economic interdependence, an Islamic banking business firm must take into account at least the following matters:

(a) whether 50% or more of 1 counterparty’s gross receipts or gross expenditures (on an annual basis) is derived from transactions with the other (for example, the owner of a property and a tenant that pays a significant part of the rent);
(b) whether 1 counterparty has fully or partly guaranteed the exposure of the other, or is liable by other means, and the relevant exposure is so significant that the guarantor would be likely to default if a claim were made;
(c) whether a significant part of 1 counterparty’s production or output is sold to the other, and the other could not easily be replaced by other customers within a reasonable period;
(d) whether the expected source of funds to repay the financings of both counterparties is the same and neither has another independent source of income from which financings could be serviced and fully repaid;
(e) whether it is likely that 1 counterparty’s financial problems would cause difficulties for the other in terms of full and timely repayment of the other’s liabilities;
(f) whether 1 counterparty’s insolvency or default would be likely to be associated with the insolvency or default of the other;
(g) if both counterparties rely on the same provider for the majority of their funding — whether, if funding from the common provider were to become unavailable, an alternative provider could not be found.
(2) However, even if economic interdependence between 2 counterparties is established based on subrule (1), the firm need not treat them as a group of connected counterparties if the firm can show the Regulatory Authority that despite the interdependence, either counterparty could overcome financial difficulties, or even the other counterparty’s default, by finding other customers or funding sources within a reasonable period.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html: If the sum of all of an Islamic banking business firm’s exposures to a particular counterparty is more than 5% of the firm’s tier 1 capital, the firm should investigate the relationships between all of its counterparties (other than exempted counterparties) to determine whether any 2 or more of them form a group of connected counterparties because of a relationship of economic interdependence. doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.9 Limits on large exposures
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK Division 5.2.C Management of large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm’s exposure to any 1 counterparty (except an exempted counterparty), or any 1 group of connected counterparties, must not be greater than 25% of the firm’s tier 1 capital.

Note For the meaning of tier 1 capital, see rule 3.2.7 (2).

(2) The total of all of the firm’s net large exposures must not exceed 800% of the firm’s tier 1 capital.

Note The amount of any breach of a large exposure limit must be deducted from CET 1 capital — see rule 3.2.41.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.10 Exposures that would breach limit — approval by Regulatory Authority
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK Division 5.2.C Management of large exposures
IBANK 5.2.10 Exposures that would breach limit — approval by Regulatory Authority
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm may apply to the Regulatory Authority for the approval of an exposure that is greater than a large exposure limit.
(2) The Authority will grant the approval only in exceptional circumstances and only after the firm satisfies the Authority that the proposed exposure does not expose the firm to excessive risk.

(3) If the Authority approves the exposure, the Authority may increase any 1 or more of the firm’s minimum capital adequacy ratios to compensate for the additional risk associated with the exposure.

Note 1 For the meaning of minimum capital adequacy ratios, see rule 3.2.6.
Note 2 The firm must deduct, from CET 1 capital, the amount by which the limit was exceeded, unless the Authority has approved the excess — see rule 3.2.41.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.11 Breaches of limits — reporting and rectification
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK Division 5.2.C Management of large exposures
IBANK 5.2.11 Breaches of limits — reporting and rectification
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If an Islamic banking business firm breaches a large exposure limit:

(a) it must immediately report the matter to the Regulatory Authority; and
(b) it must take immediate action to rectify the breach.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.12 Periodic reporting of large exposures etc
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK Division 5.2.C Management of large exposures
IBANK 5.2.12 Periodic reporting of large exposures etc
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must report the following to the Regulatory Authority:

(a) each of the firm’s exposures (other than exempted exposures) to any 1 counterparty, or any 1 group of connected counterparties, that is equal to 10% or more of the firm’s tier 1 capital;
(b) each of the firm’s exposures (other than exempted exposures) to any 1 counterparty, or any 1 group of connected counterparties, that is equal to 10% or more of the firm’s tier 1 capital if the effect of credit risk mitigation is not taken into account;

(c) every exempted exposure that is equal to 10% or more of the firm’s tier 1 capital;

Guidance
The exposures that must be reported under paragraph (c) include exposures to exempted counterparties.
(d) the firm’s largest 20 exposures (other than exempted exposures) to a single counterparty or a single group of connected counterparties, regardless of the values of those exposures relative to the firm’s tier 1 capital.
(2) The reporting period for subrule (1) is to be as agreed with, or directed by, the Authority.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: (1) An Islamic banking business firm must report the following to the Regulatory Authority: (a) each of the firm’s exposures (other than exempted exposures) to any 1 counterparty, or any 1 group of connected counterparties, that is equal to 10% or more of the firm’s tier 1 capital; (b) each of the firm’s exposures (other than exempted exposures) to any 1 counterparty, or any 1 group of connected counterparties, that is equal to 10% or more of the firm’s tier 1 capital if the effect of credit risk mitigation is not taken into account; (c) every exempted exposure that is equal to 10% or more of the firm’s tier 1 capital; Guidance The exposures that must be reported under paragraph (c) include exposures to exempted counterparties. (d) the firm’s largest 20 exposures (other than exempted exposures) to a single counterparty or a single group of connected counterparties, regardless of the values of those exposures relative to the firm’s tier 1 capital. (2) The reporting period for subrule (1) is to be as agreed with, or directed by, the Authority. Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.13 What claims, commitments and contingent liabilities must be taken into account
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.2.13 What claims, commitments and contingent liabilities must be taken into account
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) When an Islamic banking business firm calculates its exposure to a counterparty or group of connected counterparties, the firm must take into account every claim, commitment or contingent liability (other than a claim, commitment or contingent liability that is, or gives rise to, an exempted exposure) that it would be required to take into account when calculating its risk-based capital requirement.

Note For how to calculate the firm’s risk-based capital requirement, see rule 3.2.5.
(2) The firm must take into account every such claim, commitment or liability on or off the firm’s balance sheet, and whether in the firm’s banking book or its trading book.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.14 Calculating exposure — general rules
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule sets out how to calculate, for this Part, an Islamic banking business firm’s exposure arising from a claim, commitment or contingent liability.
(2) In general, except in the cases mentioned in subrules (3) to (5), the amount of the exposure is the accounting value (net of specific provisions and value adjustments) of the claim, commitment or liability.
(3) If the exposure arises from an instrument that gives rise to counterparty credit risk and is not an SFT, the firm’s exposure is the exposure at default for the instrument (see Part 4.6A).
(4) If the exposure arises from an SFT, the firm’s exposure is the amount calculated in accordance with the comprehensive approach in Subdivision 4.6.B.3.
(5) If the exposure arises from an off-balance-sheet item, the firm’s exposure is the item’s credit equivalent amount, calculated in accordance with Division 4.4.C. In calculating the item’s credit equivalent amount, however, a minimum CCF of 10% must be used.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.15 Eligible CRM techniques
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For this Part, when an Islamic banking business firm is calculating the amount of its exposure from a claim, commitment or contingent liability:

(a) it must apply any CRM technique that applies to the claim, commitment or liability, and that the firm would apply when calculating its risk-weighted capital requirement; but
(b) it must not take into account any other CRM technique.

Note Under Part 4.6, the firm may apply any of the following CRM techniques:

• eligible collateral (see Division 4.6.B) in either the simple or the comprehensive approach
• an eligible guarantee (see Division 4.6.C)
• an eligible SCHI (see Division 4.6.D).
(2) The firm must reduce the value of the exposure to the original counterparty by the recognised amount (that is, the amount by which the technique reduced the exposure for risk-based capital requirements purposes).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.15 Guidance
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
The recognised amount is:

• for unfunded credit protection — the value of the protected portion
• for eligible collateral, if the firm uses the simple approach (see Subdivision 4.6.B.2) to calculate its risk-based capital requirement — the value of the part of the claim that is collateralised by the market value of the collateral
• for eligible collateral, if the firm uses the comprehensive approach (see Subdivision 4.6.B.3) to calculate its risk-based capital requirement — the value of the adjusted collateral after applying the haircuts required under the comprehensive approach
• for an instrument that gives rise to counterparty credit risk (such as an OTC SCHI) —the value of the collateral (see Part 4.6A).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.16 Exposure to CRM providers
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If under this Part an Islamic banking business firm must recognise the reduction of an exposure by a CRM technique, it must also recognise an exposure to the CRM provider. The amount of the exposure to the CRM provider is the amount by which the exposure to the original counterparty or group is reduced.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.17 Claims etc hedged subject to maturity mismatch
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.2.17 Claims etc hedged subject to maturity mismatch
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For this Part, if a claim, commitment or contingent liability is hedged but the hedge is subject to a maturity mismatch, the hedge is to be taken into account only if:

(a) the original maturities of both the claim, commitment or contingent liability and the hedge are 1 year or longer; and
(b) the residual maturity of the hedge is at least 3 months.
(2) If an Islamic banking business firm has a maturity mismatch in relation to a CRM technique that the firm can apply in calculating its risk-based capital requirement, then, for the purposes of this Part, the firm must adjust the credit protection provided by the technique in the same way as it would when calculating its risk-based capital requirement.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.18 Effect of netting
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If an Islamic banking business firm has legally enforceable netting arrangements for financings and deposits, the firm may calculate the relevant exposure values for the purposes of this Part in the same way as it would to calculate its risk-based capital requirement — that is, on the basis of the net credit exposures, subject to the conditions in Division 4.6.E for netting on the balance sheet.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.19 Investments in collective investment undertakings etc — whether look-through required
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.2.19 Investments in collective investment undertakings etc — whether look-through required
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an Islamic banking business firm has invested in a structure through an entity that itself has exposures to assets, the firm must look through the structure to identify the underlyings unless:

(a) the firm can show that the amount of its exposure to each underlying is less than 0.25% of its tier 1 capital; or
(b) the firm’s whole investment in the structure is less than 0.25% of its tier 1 capital.
Guidance
Such structures include funds, securitisations and other structures with underlying assets.
Note For the meaning of tier 1 capital, see rule 3.2.7 (2).
(2) The firm must be able to show that a decision not to look through the structure was not influenced by considerations of regulatory arbitrage (for example, it must be able to show that it did not circumvent a large exposure limit by investing in several smaller transactions that have identical underlying assets).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.20 Investments in collective investment undertakings etc — counterparty
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.2.20 Investments in collective investment undertakings etc — counterparty
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule sets out how an Islamic banking business firm must assign an underlying to its investment in a structure.

(2) For this rule:

(a) the firm must consider only exposures to underlyings that result from its investment in the structure itself; and
(b) the value of an exposure is to be calculated as set out in rule 5.2.22.
(3) If, under rule 5.2.19, the firm is not required to look through the structure to identify the underlyings, the firm must treat the structure itself as its counterparty.

(4) If, under rule 5.2.19, the firm is required to look through the structure to identify the underlyings:

(a) for any underlying for which the exposure value is equal to 0.25% or more of the firm’s tier 1 capital, and the counterparty is identifiable, the firm must treat that counterparty as its counterparty;
(b) for any underlying for which the exposure value is less than 0.25% of the firm’s tier 1 capital, the firm may treat the structure itself as its counterparty;
(c) for any underlying for which the firm cannot identify the counterparty, it must assign that total amount to “the unknown client”; and
(d) for any underlying for which the firm cannot calculate the exposure amount, the firm must assign the nominal amount of its exposure to “the unknown client”.
(5) The firm’s exposure to a counterparty under this rule must be added to any other direct or indirect exposure to that counterparty.
(6) Exposures that have been assigned to “the unknown client” must be aggregated as if “the unknown client” were a single counterparty. The large exposure limits apply to exposures to “the unknown client”.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.22 Investments in collective investment undertakings etc — look-through required — value
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.2.22 Investments in collective investment undertakings etc — look-through required — value
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies to an Islamic banking business firm’s investment in a structure if, under rule 5.2.19, the firm is required to look through the structure to identify the underlying assets.

(2) The exposure value assigned to a counterparty is equal to the pro rata share that the firm holds in the structure multiplied by the value of the underlying asset.

Guidance
Thus, if the firm holds a 1% share of a structure that invests in 20 assets each with a value of 5, it must assign an exposure of 0.05 to each of the counterparties. An exposure to a counterparty must be added to any other direct or indirect exposures the bank has to that counterparty.

(3) In the case of a tranched structure, the firm must measure its exposure value to a counterparty for each tranche within the structure, assuming a pro rata distribution of losses amongst investors in the tranche. To compute the exposure value to the underlying, the firm:

(a) must first find the lower of:

(i) the value of the tranche in which the bank invests; and
(ii) the nominal value of each underlying in the portfolio; and
(b) must then apply the pro rata share of the firm’s investment in the tranche to the value determined in the first step.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.23 Additional risk factors — role of third parties
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.2.23 Additional risk factors — role of third parties
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must identify any risk inherent in a structure in relation to an exposure (such as having an originator, fund manager, liquidity provider or credit protection provider) in common. The firm must consider:

(a) whether the connection by way of that entity should be treated as an additional risk factor; and
(b) whether the relevant exposures should be treated as exposures to a group of connected counterparties.
Guidance
In some cases, the manager would be regarded as a distinct counterparty so that the sum of a firm’s investments in all of the funds managed by that manager would be subject to the large exposure limits. But in other cases, the commonality of the manager might not be an additional risk factor — for example, the legal framework that governs the fund might separate the legal entity that manages the fund and the legal entity that has custody of its assets. In the case of a structured finance product, the liquidity provider or sponsor of a short-term programme (such as an asset-backed commercial paper conduit or a structured investment vehicle) may need to be considered as an additional risk factor. Similarly, in synthetic financial instruments, a protection provider may be an additional source of risk and a common factor for connecting different structures.

(2) The firm must also consider whether an entity referred to in subrule (1) is connected closely enough to a counterparty of the firm that the entity and the counterparty should be treated as a group of connected counterparties.

Guidance
1 If the firm has investments in a set of structures associated with a third party that constitutes a common risk factor, the firm might have to consider adding the investments to other exposures (such as a financing) to that party. Whether it is necessary to do so depends on a case-by-case consideration of the specific features of the structure and on the role of the third party.
2 In the example of the fund manager, adding together the exposures may not be necessary because fraudulent behaviour by the fund manager would not necessarily affect the repayment of a financing. The assessment may be different where the risk to the value of investments underlying the structures arises in the event of a third-party default. For example, in the case of a credit protection provider, the source of the additional risk for the firm’s investing in a structure is the default of the credit protection provider. The firm should add the investment in the structure to the direct exposures to the credit protection provider since both exposures might crystallise into losses in the event that the protection provider defaults (ignoring the covered part of the exposures may lead to the undesirable situation of a high risk concentration exposure to issuers of collateral or providers of credit protection).
(3) If the firm considers 2 or more third parties to be potential sources of additional risk, the firm must assign the exposure resulting from the investment in each relevant structure to each of the third parties.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.24 Exposure value of covered sukuk
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.2.24 Exposure value of covered sukuk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) In this rule:

covered sukuk has the same meaning as in rule 4.4.73 (1).
qualifying covered sukuk means a covered sukuk that meets the following requirements:

(a) the underlying assets (the cover pool) include only assets of the following kinds:

(i) claims on, or guaranteed by, sovereigns, central banks, PSEs or MDBs;
(ii) claims secured by residential real estate in relation to which the prudential requirements in rule 4.4.55 have been complied with, and with an FTV ratio of 80% or lower;
(iii) claims secured by commercial real estate in relation to which those prudential requirements have been complied with, and with an FTV ratio of 60% or lower;

(iv) additional collateral of the following kinds:

(A) substitution assets (that is, cash or short-term liquid and secure assets held in substitution for the primary assets to top up the cover pool for management purposes);
(B) SCHIs entered into to hedge the risks arising in the covered sukuk programme;
(b) the total nominal value of the cover pool is at least 10% more than the total nominal value of outstanding sukuk issued (but see subrule (2));
(c) the sukuk met the requirements in paragraphs (a) and (b) when they were issued and will continue to do so until their maturity;

(d) for any real estate that is part of the assets in the cover pool, the following requirements are satisfied:

(i) the real estate is valued at no more than the current fair value under which it could be sold under private contract between a willing seller and an arm’s-length buyer on the date of valuation;
(ii) the firm assesses the value of the real estate frequently (at least annually), or more frequently if the market is subject to significant changes in conditions.

(2) For paragraph (b) of the definition of qualifying covered sukuk, an issue is taken to meet the requirement as to the value of the cover pool if:

(a) the legislation that governs the sukuk requires the value of the cover pool to meet that requirement; or
(b) if that legislation contains no such requirement — the issuer regularly states publicly that the value of the cover pool meets that requirement.
(3) An Islamic banking business firm may assign, to a holding of qualifying covered sukuk, an exposure value equal to 20% of the nominal value of the holding.
(4) An Islamic banking business firm must assign, to a holding of covered sukuk that are not qualifying covered sukuk, an exposure value equal to 100% of the nominal value of the holding.
(5) The counterparty to the exposure is the issuer of the sukuk.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.25 Exposures to central counterparties that are not QCCPs
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.2.25 Exposures to central counterparties that are not QCCPs
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule relates to an Islamic banking business firm’s exposures to central counterparties that are not QCCPs.

Note 1 Exposures to QCCPs that are related to clearing are exempted exposures — see rule 5.2.2, definition of exempted exposures, paragraph (e).
Note 2 For the meaning of QCCP, see the Glossary.
(2) An Islamic banking business firm must measure its exposure to such a central counterparty as the sum of the firm’s clearing exposures and non-clearing exposures to the central counterparty.
(3) For the purpose of deciding whether a QCCP is part of a group of connected counterparties, exposures that are related only to clearing activities are to be disregarded. However, non-clearing exposures are to be taken into account for that purpose.
(4) An Islamic banking business firm must identify its exposures to a QCCP that are related to clearing activities and must add those exposures together. The types of exposures that are related to clearing activities, and the value to be assigned to each, are as set out in table 5.2.25.

Table 5.2.25 Exposures related to clearing — values

Type of exposureValue
Trade exposuresthe value calculated according to the relevant provisions of Divisions 4.4.B and 4.4.C for the type of exposure
Segregated initial margin0
Non-segregated initial marginthe nominal amount posted
Pre-funded default fund contributionsthe nominal amount of the contribution
Unfunded default fund contributions0
Equity stakesthe nominal amount
(5) For an exposure that is directly related to clearing activities (such as the firm acting as a clearing member or being a client of a clearing member), the firm must determine the counterparty to which the exposure must be assigned by applying the relevant provisions of Part 4.6A.
(6) For an exposure to a QCCP that is not directly related to a clearing service provided by the QCCP (such as a funding facility, credit facility or guarantee), the value must be determined, according to the rules in this Part, in the same way as for any other counterparty.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.26 Exposures in both banking and trading book to same counterparty
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.2.26 Exposures in both banking and trading book to same counterparty
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
If an Islamic banking business firm has exposures to a particular counterparty in both its banking book and trading book, the firm must add all of the exposures to the counterparty to calculate its total exposure to that counterparty.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.27 Values of exposures for trading book positions
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.2.27 Values of exposures for trading book positions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The exposures considered in this rule correspond to the risk concentrations associated with the default of a single counterparty for exposures in the trading book. Therefore, positions in financial instruments such as sukuk and equities are subject to the large exposure limits, but positions in a particular commodity or currency are not.
(2) The exposure value of a sukuk or equity instrument is the market value of the instrument.

(3) Instruments such as SCHIs held in the trading book must be converted into positions in the same way as when calculating the firm’s risk-based capital requirement. Such instruments must be decomposed into their individual legs, and a leg is to be disregarded if it represents an exposure that need not, under rule 5.2.13, be taken into account for this Part.

Guidance
A stock futures contract on stock X, for example, is decomposed into a long position in stock X and a short position in a risk-free profit rate exposure in the funding currency. A typical profit rate swap is decomposed into a long position in a fixed profit rate exposure and a short position in a floating one, or vice versa.

(4) For an SCHI that represents sold protection, the exposure to the referenced name is the difference between the amount that would be due if the protection were triggered and the absolute market value of the credit protection.

Guidance
If the market value of an SCHI is positive for the protection seller, that value should also be added to the protection seller’s exposure to the protection buyer. Such a situation could occur if the present value of agreed but unpaid premiums exceeded the absolute market value of the credit protection.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.28 Exposure values of investments in transactions in trading book
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.2.28 Exposure values of investments in transactions in trading book
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule deals with how an Islamic banking business firm must decide the exposure value of an investment in a transaction (such as an index position, a securitisation, a hedge fund or an investment fund) that is held in the firm’s trading book.
(2) The firm must calculate the exposure value of such an investment in the same way as for a similar instrument in the firm’s banking book.

(3) An Islamic banking business firm may offset positions in different issues by the same counterparty only if:

(a) the short position is junior to the long position; or
(b) the positions are of the same seniority.
(4) To determine the relative seniority of positions, the firm may allocate positions to broad classes based on seniority.
(5) If the firm chooses not to allocate its positions to classes as set out in subrule (4), it must not offset long and short positions in different issues by the counterparty.
(6) If the result of the offsetting is a net short position with a single counterparty, that net position need not be treated as an exposure for the purposes of this Part.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.2.29 Treatment of hedged positions in trading book
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK 5.2.29 Treatment of hedged positions in trading book
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an Islamic banking business firm’s position is hedged by an SCHI, the firm may take the hedge into account if, for the underlying and the position hedged, the short position is junior to the long position, or the positions are of the same seniority.
(2) If an Islamic banking business firm’s exposure is hedged by an SCHI, any reduction in exposure to the original counterparty is also an exposure to the credit protection provider, in accordance with rule 5.2.16.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.3.1 Calculating Exposures
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Large exposure means a gross exposure to a counterparty or connected counterparties that is 10% or more of an Islamic banking business firm's regulatory capital.

Note Regulatory capital is defined in rule 3.2.7.
(2) In this rule:

gross exposure to a counterparty or connected counterparties is the total of the following exposures:
(a) on-balance-sheet and off-balance-sheet exposures;
(b) debt securities held by the firm;
(c) equity exposures.
(3) In calculating the gross exposure, include:
(a) the outstanding balances of all loans and advances, including balances with other banks;
(b) holdings of debt or equity securities;
(c) unused off-balance-sheet commitments, whether revocable or irrevocable; and
(d) the credit equivalent amounts of all market-related transactions (calculated in accordance with rule 4.4.11, or Division 4.6.E if netting applies).
(4) However, in calculating the gross exposure, do not include:
(a) claims, equity investments and other exposures deducted from the firm's capital;
(b) exposures arising in the course of settlement of market-related contracts; and
(c) exposures to the extent that they have been written off.
(5) For this Part:
(a) an Islamic banking business firm must treat an exposure as reduced (to the extent permitted by Part 4.6) by any applicable CRM technique; and
(b) an Islamic banking business firm that is part of a financial group may offset intragroup amounts due to other deposit-takers within the group.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.3.2 Policies — Large Exposures
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm's large exposure policy must include:

(a) exposure limits, commensurate with the firm's risk tolerance, risk profile and capital, for:
(i) categories of counterparties (for example, sovereigns, other authorised firms and other financial entities, corporate and individual borrowers);
(ii) connected counterparties;
(iii) particular industries or sectors;
(iv) particular countries; and
(v) asset classes (for example, property holdings);
(b) the circumstances in which the exposure limits may be exceeded;
(c) the procedures for approving exceptions to, and deviations from, exposure limits or policies; and
(d) the procedures for identifying, measuring, managing and reporting large exposures.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.3.3 Limits on Exposures
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must not become exposed without limit to a single counterparty. The firm must not give a general guarantee of the obligations of a counterparty.
(2) The total of the firm's net exposures to any 1 counterparty or any 1 group of connected counterparties must not exceed 25% of the firm's regulatory capital.
(3) The total of all of the firm's net large exposures must not exceed 800% of that capital.

Note Subrules (2) and (3) do not apply to a branch. A branch is not required to hold regulatory capital — rule 3.1.2(1).
(4) An Islamic banking business firm may apply to the Regulatory Authority for approval for a proposed exposure in excess of the limits set out in this Chapter. An approval will be granted only in exceptional circumstances and only after the firm satisfies the authority that the proposed exposure does not expose the firm to excessive risk.
(5) The Regulatory Authority may impose a higher capital ratio on the firm to compensate for the additional risk associated with the proposed exposure.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.3.4 Obligation to Measure
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must measure, classify and make provision for each large exposure individually.
(2) The firm must immediately notify the Regulatory Authority if the firm is concerned that risk concentrations or large exposures might significantly affect its capital adequacy. The notice must describe the firm's proposed measures to address its concerns.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 5.4.2 Authority can set Different Limits and Ratios
doc_path: IBANK Chapter 5 Concentration risk and large exposures
IBANK Part 5.4 Powers of Regulatory Authority
IBANK 5.4.2 Authority can set Different Limits and Ratios
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Despite anything in these rules, the Regulatory Authority may, in writing, set specific limits on an Islamic banking business firm's exposures to particular counterparties, groups of counterparties, industries, sectors, regions, countries or asset classes on a case-by-case basis.
(2) If an Islamic banking business firm has 1 or more large exposures (excluding exposures to sovereigns and central banks) or if, in the Regulatory Authority's opinion, the firm is exposed to a significant level of risk concentration, the authority may impose a higher capital ratio on the firm.
(3) In considering whether to increase the firm's capital ratio, the Regulatory Authority will take into account:
(a) whether the increased capital ratio would be consistent with the firm's concentration risk and large exposure policies;
(b) the number of exposures, and the size and nature of each; and
(c) the nature, scale and complexity of the firm's business and the experience of its governing body and senior management.
(4) The Regulatory Authority may also direct the firm to take measures to reduce its level of risk concentration.

Note Under FSR, article 16, the Regulatory Authority may modify or waive the application of a prudential requirement to an authorised firm or firms.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

(1) This Chapter sets out the requirements for an Islamic banking business firm's market risk management policy to identify, measure, evaluate, manage and control or mitigate market risk. This Chapter also sets out how to calculate the firm's market risk capital requirement.
(2) An Islamic banking business firm that operates in a market incurs risks from potential movements in market prices.
(3) In calculating its capital requirement, an Islamic banking business firm must take into account unexpected losses that may arise from market risk.
(4) In determining the value of an asset or liability, the firm must also make appropriate adjustments for uncertainties arising from market risk.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

doc_path: IBANK Division 6.1.A Management of market risk generally
IBANK 6.1.2 Role of Governing Body — Market Risk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm's governing body must ensure that the firm's market risk management policy gives the firm a comprehensive firm-wide view of its market risk and takes into account the risk of a significant deterioration in market liquidity.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

IBANK 6.1.4 Requirements — Capital and Management of Market Risk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:

(2) The firm must also have robust market risk measurement and risk management.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.5 Need for Trading Book
doc_path: IBANK Division 6.1.A Management of market risk generally
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm's trading book consists of the positions held by the firm (whether on-balance-sheet or off-balance-sheet) that must be included in the book in accordance with these rules. Other positions held by the firm must be included in its banking book.

Note A firm is required to have policies to distinguish consistently between trading activities and banking activities — see rule 6.1.8(4).
(2) An Islamic banking business firm must have a trading book if:
(a) it has positions that must be included in the trading book; and
(b) the total value of the positions described in paragraph (a) has exceeded 5% of the total of the firm's on-balance-sheet and off-balance-sheet positions at any time in the previous 12 months.
(3) The firm must include, in the trading book, trading positions and exposures of the following kinds:
(a) a position taken to hedge an exposure in the trading book, using Shari'a-compliant hedging instruments;
(b) a principal broking position in a financial instrument, commodity or commodity Shari'a-compliant hedging instrument;
(c) an exposure from a repurchase agreement, or securities or commodities lending, that is based on a position in a security or commodity included in the trading book;
(d) an exposure from a reverse repurchase agreement, or securities and commodities borrowing, that is based on a position in a security or commodity included in the trading book;
(e) an exposure from an unsettled transaction, a free delivery or an OTC Shari'a-compliant hedging instrument;
(f) an exposure in the form of a fee, commission, interest, dividend or margin on an exchange-traded Shari'a-compliant hedging instrument directly related to a position included in the trading book.

Guidance

Whenever an Islamic banking business firm acts as principal (even in the course of an activity normally described as 'broking' or 'customer business'), the resulting positions should be included in the trading book. This applies even if the nature of the business means that the only risks being incurred by the firm are counterparty risks (that is, no market risk capital requirements apply).
(4) The firm must also include in its trading book:
(a) total-rate-of-return swaps (except those that have been transacted to hedge a banking book credit exposure); and
(b) open short positions in Shari'a-compliant hedging instruments.
(5) The firm must not include in its trading book:
(a) positions held for liquidity management; and
(b) loans (unless they are used to hedge a position or transaction in the trading book).
(6) Trading position, of an Islamic banking business firm, means a position that is held:
(a) for short-term resale;
(b) with the intent of benefiting from actual or expected short-term price movements; or
(c) to lock in arbitrage profits.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.6 No Switching of Instruments Between Books
doc_path: IBANK Division 6.1.A Management of market risk generally
IBANK 6.1.6 No Switching of Instruments Between Books
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must not switch an instrument between its trading book and banking book, unless the Regulatory Authority has, in writing, allowed the firm to do so. The authority may approve a switch subject to 1 or more conditions.
(2) The firm must not benefit from any lower regulatory capital requirement resulting from a switch approved by the authority.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.7 Policies — Market Risk Environment
doc_path: IBANK Division 6.1.A Management of market risk generally
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm's market risk management policy must establish:

(a) effective systems for the accurate and timely identification, measurement, evaluation, management and control or mitigation of market risk, and reporting to the firm's governing body and senior management;
(b) prudent and appropriate market risk limits that are consistent with the firm's risk appetite, risk profile and capital, and with the management's ability to manage;
(c) who is responsible for identifying, measuring and reporting market risk;
(d) procedures for tracking and reporting exceptions to, and deviations from, limits or policies; and
(e) procedures for including positions and exposures in the trading book.
(2) The policy must ensure that all of the firm's transactions are identified and recorded in a timely way and that their valuations are consistent and prudent.

Note For valuation of positions and verification of market prices and model inputs, see Division 6.1.B.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
Amended by QFCRA RM/2024-4 (as from 1st October 2025)

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.8 Policies — Trading Book
doc_path: IBANK Division 6.1.A Management of market risk generally
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm that is required to have a trading book must have clearly defined policies for keeping the book up-to-date and the positions and exposures accurate.
(2) In particular, the firm must have policies on:
(a) what to include, or not include, in the trading book;
(b) managing and reporting trading positions;
(c) valuing positions, including:
(i) clear definitions of the responsibilities of staff involved in the valuation;
(ii) sources of market information, and review of their reliability;
(iii) frequency of independent valuations;
(iv) timing of closing prices;
(v) procedures for adjusting valuations between periods;
(vi) ad-hoc verification procedures; and
(vii) reporting lines for the valuation function that are independent of the function that gave rise to the position.
(3) The policies must be approved by the firm's governing body, and the firm must be able to demonstrate compliance with them if directed by the Regulatory Authority.
(4) The firm must also have adequate policies:
(a) to monitor compliance with the policies and distinguish consistently between trading activities and banking activities;
(b) to deal with legal, regulatory or operational restrictions on immediate liquidation of exposures; and
(c) to monitor the size of its trading book.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.9 Standard Method to be Used
doc_path: IBANK Division 6.1.B Measurement of Risk and Valuation of Positions
IBANK 6.1.9 Standard Method to be Used
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Unless the Regulatory Authority has approved the use of an internal model by an Islamic banking business firm, market risk is, as a general rule, measured using the standard method. The standard method comprises a range of approaches that a firm may use to calculate capital charges from its trading activities.

Note For approval of the use of internal models, see rule 3.1.6.
(2) In the standard method, market risk capital requirement is the sum of the capital charges for:
(a) foreign exchange risk in the trading book and banking book;
(b) options risk in the trading book and banking book;
(c) commodities risk in the trading book and banking book;
(d) inventory risk in the trading book and banking book;
(e) traded equity position risk; and
(f) traded profit rate risk on sukuk and other Shari'a-compliant debt securities and profit-rate-related instruments.

Note The measurements of the risks mentioned in (2) are set out in Part 6.2 to Part 6.6.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.10 Valuing Positions — Mark-to-Market
doc_path: IBANK Division 6.1.B Measurement of Risk and Valuation of Positions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must use the mark-to-market method to value its positions and exposures if there is a market to mark the positions and exposures to. Mark-to-market means a valuation that is based on current market value.

Guidance
1 The Regulatory Authority would expect an Islamic banking business firm to mark-to-market listed securities, because there is a market with observable and reliable prices for such securities.
2 The firm should mark-to-market as much as possible. It should use the prudent side of a bid or offer unless the firm is a significant market maker that can close at mid-market.
3 When estimating fair value, the firm should maximise the use of relevant observable inputs and avoid the use of unobservable inputs.
(2) A position that is marked-to-market must be revalued daily, based on independently sourced current market prices.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

doc_path: IBANK Division 6.1.B Measurement of Risk and Valuation of Positions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
Because of the less liquid nature of many sukuk and equity positions held by an Islamic banking business firm, it is important for the firm to have prudent valuation practices.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.11 Valuing Positions — Mark-to-Model
doc_path: IBANK Division 6.1.B Measurement of Risk and Valuation of Positions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If it is not possible to mark-to-market (for example, in the case of unlisted securities or where the market is inactive), an Islamic banking business firm may use the mark-to-model method to value its positions and exposures. Mark-to-model means a valuation that has to be benchmarked, extrapolated or otherwise calculated from a market input.
(2) The firm must be able to demonstrate that its marking-to-model is prudent.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.11 Guidance
doc_path: IBANK Division 6.1.B Measurement of Risk and Valuation of Positions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm should be extra conservative when marking-to-model. The Regulatory Authority will take into account the following in deciding if the firm's model is prudent:

•   whether senior management is aware of the positions and exposures that are marked to model and whether it understands the uncertainty this might create in reporting the risk or performance of the business
•   the extent to which market inputs are sourced from market prices
•   the appropriateness of the assumptions used by the firm
•   the availability of generally accepted valuation methods for particular products
•   who developed the model
•   whether the firm holds a secure copy of the model
•   the existence of formal control procedures for changing the model
•   how often the model is used to check valuations
•   how aware is the firm's risk management function of the weaknesses of the model and how those weaknesses are reflected in the valuation output
•   the results of comparisons between actual close out values and model outputs
•   the firm's procedures for reviewing the model.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.12 Independent Price Verification
doc_path: IBANK Division 6.1.B Measurement of Risk and Valuation of Positions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An Islamic banking business firm must independently verify market prices and model inputs, to check that those prices and inputs are accurate. The verification must be done at least once a month.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: An Islamic banking business firm must independently verify market prices and model inputs, to check that those prices and inputs are accurate. The verification must be done at least once a month. Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

endnotes: Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.12 Guidance
doc_path: IBANK Division 6.1.B Measurement of Risk and Valuation of Positions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
1 Independent price verification is different from daily mark-to-market. The object of the verification is to regularly check the accuracy of market prices or model inputs and, thereby, eliminate inaccurate daily marks. The verification should be carried out by a unit independent of whoever marked the positions or exposures.
2 The independent marking in the verification process should reveal any error or bias in pricing. It entails a higher standard of accuracy in that the market prices or model inputs are used to determine profit and loss figures, whereas daily marks are used primarily for management reporting in between reporting dates.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.13 Valuation Adjustments
doc_path: IBANK Division 6.1.B Measurement of Risk and Valuation of Positions
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm must consider making adjustments for positions that cannot be prudently valued (such as those that have become concentrated, less liquid or stale). For example, valuation adjustment would be appropriate if pricing sources are more subjective (such as when there is only one available broker quote).
(2) The firm must establish and maintain procedures for considering valuation adjustments. This rule applies whether:
(a) the firm uses the mark-to-market or mark-to-model method; and
(b) whether the valuation is done by the firm itself or a third party.
(3) The firm must consider the following valuation adjustments:
(a) unearned profit;
(b) close-out costs;
(c) operational risks;
(d) early termination;
(e) investing and funding costs;
(f) future administrative costs;
(g) model risk, if relevant;
(h) any other adjustment that the firm considers appropriate.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.14 Meaning of internal risk transfer
doc_path: IBANK 6.1.14 Meaning of internal risk transfer
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An internal risk transfer is an internal written record of a transfer of risk:

(a) within an Islamic banking business firm’s banking book;
(b) between the firm’s banking and trading book; or
(c) between different desks within the trading book.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.15 Capital effect of internal risk transfer from trading book to banking book
doc_path: IBANK 6.1.15 Capital effect of internal risk transfer from trading book to banking book
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
An internal risk transfer from the trading book to the banking book has no effect on the risk-based capital requirement of the Islamic banking business firm concerned. That is, if the firm makes an internal risk transfer from the trading book to the banking book, the transfer is not to be taken into account when the firm calculates its risk-based capital requirement.

Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.16 Capital effect of internal risk transfer of credit and equity risk from banking book to trading book
doc_path: IBANK 6.1.16 Capital effect of internal risk transfer of credit and equity risk from banking book to trading book
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies if an Islamic banking business firm hedges a credit risk or equity risk exposure in the banking book using an SCHI that was purchased through the trading book (that is, using an internal risk transfer).

(2) A credit exposure in the banking book is taken to be hedged for the purpose of calculating the firm’s risk-based capital requirement if and only if:

(a) the trading book enters into an external hedge with an eligible protection provider (see subrule (4)) that exactly matches the internal risk transfer; and
(b) the external hedge is an eligible SCHI (see subrule (4)) in relation to the banking book exposure.

(3) An equity exposure in the banking book is taken to be hedged for that purpose if and only if:

(a) the trading book enters into an external hedge from an eligible protection provider that exactly matches the internal risk transfer; and
(b) the external hedge is recognised as a hedge of a banking book equity exposure.

(4) In subrules (2) and (3):

eligible protection provider means:
(a) a central counterparty;
(b) the State of Qatar or any other sovereign;
(c) an entity that is treated as a sovereign in accordance with the Basel Accords;

(d) a PSE or other entity that has:

(i) a risk weight of 20% or lower; and
(ii) a lower risk weight than the party to whom the protection is provided; or
(e) a parent entity, subsidiary or affiliate of a party to whom the protection is provided that has a lower risk weight than the party.
eligible SCHI has the meaning given by rule 4.6.39.
(5) For the purposes of this rule, an external hedge may be made up of multiple transactions with multiple counterparties as long as the total external hedge exactly matches the internal risk transfer.
(6) If the requirements in subrule (2) are satisfied, the banking book exposure is treated, for capital purposes in the banking book, as being hedged by the banking book leg of the transfer. Both the trading book leg of the transfer and the external hedge must be included in the market risk capital requirements.
(7) If the requirements in subrule (2) are not satisfied, the banking book exposure is not treated, for capital purposes in the banking book, as being hedged by the banking book leg of the transfer. The third-party external hedge must be fully included in, and the trading book leg of the transfer must be fully excluded from, the market risk capital requirements.
(8) A banking book short credit or equity position that was created by an internal risk transfer and is not capitalised under banking book rules must be capitalised under the market risk rules together with the trading book exposure.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.17 Internal risk transfer of general profit rate risk
doc_path: IBANK 6.1.17 Internal risk transfer of general profit rate risk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) This rule applies if an Islamic banking business firm hedges a general profit rate risk (GPRR) exposure in the banking book using an internal risk transfer with its trading book.

(2) The trading book leg of the transfer is treated as a trading book instrument under the market risk framework if (and only if):

(a) the transfer is documented in relation to the profit rate risk that is being hedged and the sources of that risk;
(b) the transfer is done with a dedicated internal risk transfer trading desk that has been specifically approved by the Regulatory Authority for the purpose; and
(c) the transfer is subject to trading book capital requirements under the market risk framework on a stand-alone basis for the dedicated internal risk transfer desk, separate from any other GPRR or other market risks generated by activities in the trading book.
(3) If the requirements in subrule (2) are satisfied, the banking book leg of the transfer must be included in the banking book’s measure of profit rate risk exposures for regulatory capital purposes.
(4) The internal risk transfer desk may include instruments purchased from the market. Such purchases may be executed directly between the desk and the market.
(5) Alternatively, the internal risk transfer desk may obtain the external hedge from the market by a separate non-internal risk transfer trading desk acting as an agent, if and only if the GPRR internal risk transfer entered into with the non-internal desk exactly matches the external hedge from the market. In this case the respective legs of the GPRR internal risk transfer are included in the capital calculations of both the internal risk transfer desk and the non-internal risk transfer desk.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2024-1 (as from 1st July 2024).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.1.18 Internal risk transfers within scope of application of market risk capital requirement
doc_path: IBANK 6.1.18 Internal risk transfers within scope of application of market risk capital requirement
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) Internal risk transfers between an Islamic banking business firm’s internal risk transfer desk and other trading desks receive regulatory capital recognition only if the conditions in rule 6.1.17 (2) are satisfied.
(2) The trading book leg of an internal risk transfer must fulfil the same requirements in rule 6.1.17 (2) as an instrument in the trading book transacted with an external counterparty.

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK Part 6.2 Foreign Exchange Risk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: IBANK Part 6.2 Foreign Exchange Risk

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.2.1 Relation to Market Risk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) In measuring its market risk, an Islamic banking business firm must include the risk of holding or taking positions in foreign currencies, gold and silver (foreign exchange risk). Foreign exchange risk may arise from the firm's trading in the foreign exchange market and other markets; it may also arise from non-trading activities that are denominated in a foreign currency.

Guidance
1 If an Islamic banking business firm is exposed to profit rate risk on positions in foreign currencies, gold and silver, the firm must include the relevant profit rate positions in the calculation of profit rate risk in the trading book-see rule 6.6.2(4).
2 Unlike Basel II, silver and gold are treated under Shari'a as foreign exchange positions (rather than as commodity positions). In Basel II, only gold is treated in that way.
(2) If foreign currency is to be received or delivered under a binding unilateral promise, the firm must report any profit rate exposure from the other leg of the contract in accordance with Part 6.6 (profit rate risk in the trading book).
(3) If gold or silver is to be received or delivered under a binding unilateral promise, the firm must report any foreign currency or profit rate exposure from the other leg of the contract in accordance with this Part or Part 6.6, as the case requires.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.2.2 What to Include in Foreign Exchange Risk
doc_path: IBANK 6.2.2 What to Include in Foreign Exchange Risk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) In calculating the capital charge for foreign exchange risk, an Islamic banking business firm must include in its exposure to each foreign currency:
(a) the net spot position (that is, assets minus liabilities denominated in the currency, including accrued profit and other accrued income and accrued expenses);
(b) the net position of binding unilateral promises by the firm to buy or sell currencies on a specified future date (that are not included in the spot position);

Examples of amounts to be received or paid
•   the principal on currency swaps not included in the spot position
•   profit from swaps and other profit rate transactions.
(c) irrevocable guarantees (and similar instruments) that are certain to be called and likely to be irrecoverable; and
(d) any other items representing an exposure to risk in foreign currencies (for example a specific provision held in the currency in question where the underlying asset is held in a different currency).
(2) The firm may also include in its currency exposure any net future income or expenses that are not yet accrued but already fully hedged. If the firm includes such income or expenses, it must do so consistently and must not select only expected future flows that reduce its position.
(3) If the firm has deliberately taken a position to partly or totally protect itself against the adverse effect of a change in an exchange rate on its capital adequacy ratio, it may exclude the position from its currency exposure insofar as it relates to that hedge, if:
(a) the position is of a structural and non-trading nature;
(b) the structural position does no more than protect the firm's capital adequacy ratio;
(c) the position cannot be traded for speculative or profit-making purposes; and
(d) the exclusion of the position is done consistently, with the treatment of the hedge remaining the same for the life of the assets or other items.
(4) A structural position includes:
(a) a position arising from an instrument that satisfies the criteria for inclusion as capital under Chapter 3;
(b) a position in relation to a net investment in a self-sustaining subsidiary, the accounting consequence of which is to reduce or eliminate what would otherwise be a movement in the foreign currency translation reserve; and
(c) an investment in an overseas subsidiary or other entity in the same corporate group as the firm that, under these rules, is deducted from the firm's capital for capital adequacy purposes.
(5) The firm must also include any currency exposures arising from equity, commodity and profit rate positions.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.2.3 Foreign Exchange Risk on Consolidated Basis
doc_path: IBANK 6.2.3 Foreign Exchange Risk on Consolidated Basis
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) If an Islamic banking business firm is assessing its foreign exchange risk on a consolidated basis, and the inclusion of the currency positions of a marginal operation of the firm is technically impractical, the firm may use, as a proxy for those positions, the internal limit in each currency that the firm applies to the operation. Marginal operation, in relation to a firm, is an operation of the firm that accounts for less than 5% of the firm's total currency positions.
(2) The absolute values of the limits must be added to the net open position in each currency, but only if the actual positions are adequately monitored against those internal limits.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.2.4 Capital Charge — Foreign Exchange Risk
doc_path: IBANK 6.2.4 Capital Charge — Foreign Exchange Risk
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For an Islamic banking business firm that does not write options, net open position in a foreign currency is the sum of:
(a) the firm's currency exposures under rule 6.2.2 for the currency; and
(b) the value of the options and their associated underlying assets measured using the simplified approach in Division 6.3.B.
(2) For an Islamic banking business firm that writes options, net open position in a foreign currency is the sum of:
(a) the firm's currency exposures under rule 6.2.2 for the currency; and
(b) either:
(i) the net delta-based equivalent of the firm's total book of foreign currency options (with separately calculated capital charges for gamma risk and vega risk under Division 6.3.C); or
(ii) the value of the options and their associated underlying assets under the delta-plus method in Division 6.3.C.
(3) The firm must calculate its overall foreign currency net open position by:
(a) calculating the net open position in each foreign currency;
(b) converting the nominal amount (or net present value) of each such net position into Qatari riyals at the current spot market exchange rate;
(c) adding all short net positions and adding all long net positions calculated under paragraphs (a) and (b); and
(d) selecting the greater of the absolute values of the 2 sums in paragraph (c).
(4) The firm must then calculate its net position in gold and silver by:
(a) valuing all gold and silver positions using the US dollar current spot price (regardless of maturity);
(b) offsetting long and short positions; and
(c) converting the absolute value of the resulting net position into Qatari riyals.
(5) To convert the net position in gold and silver into Qatari riyals, the firm must state the position (spot plus forward) in a standard unit of measurement and then convert the net position at the current spot market exchange rate.
(6) The capital charge for foreign exchange risk of an Islamic banking business firm is the sum of:
(a) 8% of the firm's overall foreign currency net open position in each of the foreign currencies it holds; and
(b) 8% of its net position in gold and silver.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm that does not write options must use the simplified approach.
(2) An Islamic banking business firm that writes options must use the delta-plus method.

Note If all the written option positions are hedged by perfectly matched long positions in exactly the same options, no capital charge for options risk is required.

(a) rule 6.3.4 for a position that is a 'long cash and long put' or 'short cash and long call' position; or

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.3.4 Capital Charges — 'Long Cash and Long Put' or 'Short Cash and Long Call'
doc_path: IBANK 6.3.4 Capital Charges — 'Long Cash and Long Put' or 'Short Cash and Long Call'
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For a position that is 'long cash and long put' or 'short cash and long call', the capital charge is calculated by multiplying the market value of the underlying security by the sum of the specific and general risk capital charges for the underlying, and then subtracting the amount by which the option is in-the-money (bounded at zero).

Guidance
1 In cases (such as foreign exchange transactions) where it is unclear which side is the underlying security, the underlying should be taken to be the asset that would be received if the option were exercised. In addition, the nominal value should be used for items if the market value of the underlying instrument could be zero (such as in caps, floors and swaptions).
2 Some options have no specific risk (such as those having a profit rate, currency or commodity as the underlying security); other options on profit-rate-related instruments and options on equities and stock indices, however, would have specific risk.
(2) In the simplified approach, the capital charge is:
(a) 8% for options on currency; and
(b) 15% for options on commodities.
(3) For options with a residual maturity of less than 6 months, an Islamic banking business firm must use the forward price (instead of the spot price) if it is able to do so.
(4) For options with a residual maturity of more than 6 months, the firm must compare the strike price with the forward price (instead of the current price). If the firm is unable to do this, it must take the in-the-money amount to be zero.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.3.5 Capital Charges — 'Long Put' or 'Long Call'
doc_path: IBANK 6.3.5 Capital Charges — 'Long Put' or 'Long Call'
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) For a position that is 'long put' or 'long call', the capital charge is the lesser of:
(a) the market value of the underlying security multiplied by the sum of the specific and general risk capital charges for the underlying; and
(b) the market value of the option.
(2) For subrule (1)(b), the book value of the option may be used instead of the market value if the position is not included in the trading book (for example, options on particular foreign exchange or commodities positions).
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK Division 6.3.C Delta-Plus Method
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.content_text: IBANK Division 6.3.C Delta-Plus Method

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.3.6 Using Delta-Plus Method
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm that writes options must calculate specific risk capital charges separately by multiplying the delta-equivalent value of each option by the risk-weight applicable under Part 6.5 (equity position risk) and Part 6.6 (profit rate risk in the trading book).
(2) In calculating general risk capital charge, the firm must enter delta-weighted positions with a debt security or profit rate as the underlying into the profit rate time bands in table 6.6.8A by using a two-legged approach. Under this approach, there is 1 entry at the time the underlying contract takes effect and a second entry at the time the underlying contract matures.
(3) For an option with a debt security as the underlying, the firm must apply a specific risk capital charge to the delta-weighted position based on the issuer's rating and in accordance with Part 6.6.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.3.7 Relation to Mark-to-Market Method
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm that writes options must include delta-weighted option positions in measuring its market risk.
(2) The firm must report such an option as a position equal to the sum of the market values of the underlying multiplied by the sum of the absolute values of the deltas. Because delta does not cover all risks associated with option positions, the firm must calculate gamma and vega in calculating the regulatory capital charge.

Note Gamma is the rate of change of delta with respect to a change in the price of the underlying. Vega is the sensitivity of the value of an option to a change in the volatility of the underlying.
(3) The firm must calculate delta, gamma and vega using the pricing model used by a recognised exchange, or a proprietary options pricing model approved, in writing, by the Regulatory Authority.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.3.8 Capital Charges — Options
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) The capital charge for an option with equities as the underlying must be based on the delta-weighted positions included in the measurement of specific and general risks in accordance with Part 6.5. (equity position risk).
(2) An Islamic banking business firm that writes options must calculate the capital charge for options on foreign exchange and gold and silver positions in accordance with Part 6.2 (foreign exchange risk). For delta risk, the net delta-based equivalent of the foreign currency, gold and silver options must be included in the measurement of the exposure for the respective currency, gold or silver position.
(3) The capital charge for an option on commodities must be based on the charge calculated using the simplified approach in rule 6.4.6.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.3.9 Gamma Capital Charges
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm that writes options must calculate the capital charge for gamma risk (gamma capital charge) for each option position separately.
(2) To calculate gamma capital charge, calculate the gamma impact of each option in accordance with the following formula:

Gamma impact = 1/2 × gamma × VU2

where:

VU is:x
(a) for a profit rate option:
(i) if the option has a bond as the underlying — the market value of the underlying multiplied by the risk factor applicable under column 3 of table 6.6.8A; or
(ii) if the option has a profit rate as the underlying — the market value of the underlying multiplied by the assumed changes in yield in column 4 of table 6.6.8A;
(b) for options on equities and stock indices — the market value of the underlying multiplied by 8%;
(c) for options on foreign exchange, gold and silver — the market value of the underlying multiplied by 8%; or
(d) for an option on commodities — the market value of the underlying multiplied by 15%.
(3) In calculating the gamma impact for an option mentioned in the definition of VU, the firm must treat as the same underlying:
(a) for profit rates — each time band in column 2 of table 6.6.8A (with each position allocated to separate maturity ladders);
(b) for equities and stock indices — each recognised exchange;
(c) for foreign currencies, gold and silver — each currency pair, gold and silver; and
(d) for commodities — each individual commodity of a kind described in rule 6.4.2(3)(a) or (b).
(4) Each option on the same underlying described in subrules (2) and (3) will have a gamma impact that is positive or negative. The firm must add the individual gamma impacts, resulting in a net gamma impact for each underlying that is either positive or negative.
(5) To calculate the firm's total gamma capital charge, exclude gamma impacts that are positive. The total gamma capital charge is the sum of the absolute values of the net negative gamma impacts.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).

QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.title: IBANK 6.3.10 Vega Capital Charges
QFCRA Rules :: Islamic Banking Business.document_html:
(1) An Islamic banking business firm that writes options must calculate the capital charge for vega risk (vega capital charge) for each option position separately.
(2) To calculate vega capital charge, the firm must multiply the vega for each option mentioned in the definition of VU in rule 6.3.9(2) by a 25% proportional shift in the option's current volatility. The results must then be summed across each underlying.
(3) The total vega capital charge is the sum of the absolute values of the vega capital charges across each underlying.
Derived from QFCRA RM/2015-2 (as from 1st January 2016).
